He keeps bees in the garden.

keep.definition: to stop other people from using something so that it is available for someone
keep.note: typical: keep a seat, a place for someone NOT for: storing
examples: Will you keep a seat for me?
They kept the room for us until six.

keep.definition: to make someone wait before you meet or see them
keep.note: typical: keep someone waiting NOT for: delaying someone
examples: Sorry to keep you waiting.
Don't keep him waiting too long.

keep.definition: to guard a place or to watch around you all the time
keep.note: typical: keep guard, keep watch NOT for: delaying someone
examples: Two soldiers kept guard at the gate.
Someone must keep watch while we sleep.

keep.definition: to provide someone with money, food and other things they need
keep.note: typical: keep a family, keep yourself NOT for: storing things
examples: He did not earn enough to keep a wife and children.
She works two jobs to keep herself.

keep.definition: to guard or protect someone (formal, religious)
keep.note: typical: keep from harm, God keep you NOT for: everyday speech
examples: His only thought was to keep the child from harm.
May the Lord bless you and keep you.

kiss.definition: to touch someone with your lips as a greeting or to show love
kiss.note: typical: kiss someone on the cheek, goodbye NOT for: touching an object
examples: Maggie leaned forward and kissed her cheek.
They kissed goodbye at the station.

kiss.definition: to touch something with your lips as a sign of respect
kiss.note: typical: kiss a ring, a cross, the ground NOT for: kissing a person
examples: She raised the cross to her lips and kissed it.
The pilgrims kissed the ground when they arrived.

kiss.definition: to accept that you will lose something or an opportunity (kiss something goodbye, informal)
kiss.note: typical: kiss your chances goodbye NOT for: greeting someone
examples: If you miss this deadline, you can kiss the contract goodbye.
She knew that she could kiss her career goodbye.

knock.definition: to hit a door or window with your closed hand to get the attention of the people inside
knock.note: typical: knock at/on the door NOT for: hitting people
examples: I knocked and knocked but nobody answered.
Someone knocked on the window.

knock.definition: to hit something with a short, quick action so that it moves or falls
knock.note: typical: knock something over, off, out of NOT for: knocking on a door
examples: Sally knocked over her glass of wine.
He knocked the knife from my hand.

knock.note: typical: knock someone to the ground, unconscious NOT for: bumping into something
examples: He knocked her to the ground.
One punch knocked him unconscious.

knock.definition: to hit something with part of your body by accident
knock.note: typical: knock your head, knee, shin against something NOT for: hitting something on purpose
examples: She knocked her head on a stone.
Morse knocked his shin against a suitcase.

knock.definition: to go to every house in an area to ask people for information or support
knock.note: typical: knock on doors, campaign NOT for: knocking on one door
examples: Volunteers spent the weekend knocking on doors.
Gathering that information means knocking on doors.

knock.definition: to remove a wall or part of a building to make a bigger space
knock.note: typical: knock two rooms into one NOT for: breaking a window
examples: We could knock the two rooms into one.
The wall between the kitchen and dining room has been knocked through.

knock.definition: to make a hole in something, especially a wall
knock.note: typical: knock a hole through a wall NOT for: removing a whole wall
examples: We knocked a hole through the wall into the cupboard.
He knocked a hole in the ceiling.

knock.definition: to criticise someone or their work, especially in an unfair way (informal)
knock.note: typical: knock someone, knock a product NOT for: fair criticism
examples: The British press loves to knock successful people.
Everyone seems to knock the new system.

knock.definition: if an engine or pipes are knocking, they make a noise like something hard being hit
knock.note: typical: engines, pipes NOT for: people knocking on doors
examples: The engine was knocking badly when we started the car.
The pipes knock whenever the heating comes on.

knock.definition: if your heart is knocking, it is beating hard, especially because you are afraid
knock.note: typical: heart knocking, pounding NOT for: knocking on doors
examples: Her heart was knocking as she opened the letter.
His heart knocked against his ribs.

know.note: typical: know the answer, know what/how/where NOT for: being familiar with a person
examples: Who knows the answer?
Do you know what time it is?

know.note: typical: know that, I don't know yet NOT for: having general information
examples: I know I won't get the job.
I don't know if I'll be able to come.

know.definition: to be familiar with a person, a place or a thing
know.note: typical: know someone well, know a place NOT for: knowing facts
examples: I've known her for twenty years.
Do you know the café on the corner?

know.definition: to realise, find out about or understand something
know.note: typical: know the risks, know how difficult NOT for: being familiar with someone
examples: She knew the risks involved.
Suddenly he knew that something was terribly wrong.

know.definition: to have learned a lot about something, or to be skilled and experienced at doing something
know.note: typical: know French, know how to drive NOT for: being sure
examples: I know some French.
Do you know how to use this machine?

know.definition: to be able to recognise someone or something
know.note: typical: know someone by their voice NOT for: being introduced to someone
examples: It had been so long that I hardly knew her.
I knew him by his voice.

know.definition: to understand the difference between two things
know.note: typical: know right from wrong, know sth from sth NOT for: general knowledge
examples: Children must learn to know right from wrong.
He doesn't know a good wine from a bad one.

know.definition: to have experience of a particular feeling or situation
know.note: typical: know happiness, poverty, hunger NOT for: having information
examples: I don't think he ever knew true happiness.
She knows all about being poor.

last.definition: to continue for a particular length of time
last.note: typical: events, periods, hours, weather NOT for: objects remaining useful
examples: Each lesson lasts forty-five minutes.
The hot weather lasted for the whole month of June.

last.definition: to continue to exist, be effective or stay in good condition for a long time
last.note: typical: coats, flowers, relationships NOT for: short events
examples: A good coat will last you ten years.
Cut flowers last longer if you change the water.

last.definition: to manage to stay in the same difficult situation
last.note: typical: can't last long, last out NOT for: objects staying in good condition
examples: They won't be able to last much longer without fresh supplies.
If you go into the job with that attitude, you won't last long.

last.definition: to be enough for someone for a period of time
last.note: typical: money, food, batteries NOT for: events continuing
examples: The batteries should last for twenty hours.
We only had fifty dollars to last us the rest of the month.

laugh.definition: to make sounds with your voice, usually while smiling, because you think something is funny
laugh.note: typical: laugh at a joke, laugh loudly NOT for: speaking
examples: Maria looked at him and laughed.
The kids were laughing so hard they could hardly breathe.

laugh.definition: to say something in a voice that shows you are amused
laugh.note: typical: 'Look at you!' he laughed NOT for: laughing without words
examples: "You look ridiculous!" Nick laughed.
"That was a close one," she laughed.

learn.definition: to gain knowledge of a subject or skill by experience, studying or being taught
learn.note: typical: learn a language, to drive, from someone NOT for: teaching someone
examples: What's the best way to learn a language?
I learnt to drive when I was seventeen.

learn.definition: to find out information or news by hearing it from someone else or by reading it (formal)
learn.note: typical: learn that, learn of, learn about NOT for: studying a subject
examples: She was surprised to learn that he was much older than she had thought.
We have yet to learn who will be the new manager.

learn.definition: to get to know something so well that you can remember it easily
learn.note: typical: learn lines, words, a poem NOT for: studying a subject in general
examples: The actors hardly had time to learn their lines.
I have to learn twenty new words for Friday.

learn.definition: to gradually understand a situation and start behaving in the way you should
learn.note: typical: learn from mistakes, learn to do something NOT for: studying a school subject
examples: You have to learn from your mistakes.
Young hairdressers must learn to treat the client as a person.

leave.definition: to go away from a place or a person
leave.note: typical: leave the room, the station, leave at six NOT for: permanently stopping a job
examples: My baby gets upset when I leave the room.
The plane leaves at half past twelve.

leave.definition: to permanently stop doing a job, living at home or going to school
leave.note: typical: leave home, school, a job, the country NOT for: going out for a short time
examples: How old were you when you left home?
Many missionaries were forced to leave the country.

leave.definition: to stop annoying someone, or to stop touching something, or to avoid getting involved
leave.note: typical: leave someone alone NOT for: going away from a place
examples: Just leave me alone, will you?
Leave that alone; you'll break it.

leave.definition: to put or leave something somewhere, either on purpose or by forgetting it
leave.note: typical: leave a bag, a car, a wallet somewhere NOT for: going away from a place
examples: I think I left my wallet at the office.
Don't leave your bags in the hall.

leave.definition: to let something remain in a particular state or position
leave.note: typical: leave the door open, the engine running NOT for: causing a state
examples: Please leave the window open.
Don't leave the tools lying on the floor.

leave.definition: if an accident, illness or other event leaves you in a particular condition, you are in that condition afterwards
leave.note: typical: leave someone with, leave someone homeless NOT for: placing objects
examples: The infection left him with a weak heart.
The flood left hundreds of families homeless.

leave.definition: if something is left, it remains
leave.note: typical: be left, have something left NOT for: going away
examples: There's only one piece of cake left.
Do we have any milk left?

leave.definition: to deliver a message, note or object for someone to find or take later
leave.note: typical: leave a message, a note NOT for: sending a letter by post
examples: A guy left these flowers for you.
I left a message on his answering machine.

leave.definition: to not do something yet, or to do it later than planned
leave.note: typical: leave something until tomorrow NOT for: doing it at once
examples: Leave the washing-up until the morning.
Don't leave your homework until the last minute.

leave.definition: to let someone else decide or do something
leave.note: typical: leave it to someone, leave the decision to someone NOT for: deciding yourself
examples: I'll leave it up to you to decide.
Is it okay if I leave writing the results to you?

leave.definition: to stop living with or having a relationship with someone
leave.note: typical: leave a husband, a wife, a partner NOT for: going out for a short time
examples: She left her husband after twenty years.
He threatened to leave her.

leave.definition: to arrange for someone to receive something after you die
leave.note: typical: leave money, a house to someone NOT for: giving a gift now
examples: He left all his money to his daughter.
She left her collection of paintings to the museum.

leave.definition: to make a mark that remains afterwards
leave.note: typical: leave a mark, a stain, a scar NOT for: going away
examples: The wine left a permanent stain on the carpet.
The accident left a scar on his face.

leave.definition: to not eat or drink all of something
leave.note: typical: leave food on your plate NOT for: forgetting something
examples: He left most of his dinner.
Don't leave any rice on your plate.

leave.definition: to have a particular amount remaining after something has been taken away (in sums)
leave.note: typical: ten minus four leaves six NOT for: going away
examples: Ten minus four leaves six.
If you take five from nine, that leaves four.

let.definition: to allow someone to do something
let.note: typical: let someone do something, let me have a look NOT for: forcing someone
examples: My dad won't let me go out tonight.
Some parents let their kids do whatever they like.

let.definition: to not stop something from happening, or to make it possible for it to happen
let.note: typical: let something fall, let it cool NOT for: allowing a person to do something
examples: Jenny let the note fall to the ground.
Let the cookies cool down before you eat them.

let.definition: to stop holding something or someone, or to stop worrying about something (let go)
let.note: typical: let go of, let go of the past NOT for: allowing something to happen
examples: Let go! You're hurting me.
Sometimes you just have to learn to let go.

let.definition: to allow someone to leave a place where they have been kept, or to make someone leave their job (let someone go)
let.note: typical: let someone go, release, dismiss NOT for: letting go of an object
examples: The police had to let him go for lack of evidence.
We had to let several members of staff go.

let.definition: used to make a suggestion or to offer help (let's)
let.note: typical: let's go, let me help you NOT for: allowing something
examples: Let's make a start, shall we?
Let me help you with those bags.

let.definition: to allow someone to use a room, flat or building in exchange for rent (British)
let.note: typical: let a flat, a room to someone NOT for: allowing someone to do something
examples: They let the top floor to students.
We're letting our flat while we're abroad.

like.definition: to enjoy something or think that it is nice or good
like.note: typical: like a film, like doing something NOT for: loving a person
examples: I like your jacket.
Paul doesn't like talking in public.

like.definition: to think that someone is nice or enjoy being with them
like.note: typical: like a person, a colleague NOT for: liking things
examples: You'll like my brother.
She's a lovely girl and I like her very much.

like.definition: to approve of something and think that it is good or right
like.note: typical: usually negative: don't like the way NOT for: liking a thing for its taste
examples: I don't like dishonesty.
He doesn't like the way you speak to the children.

like.definition: to try to do something regularly or to want something to happen regularly
like.note: typical: like to do something, like someone to do something NOT for: one-time wishes
examples: I like to get up early and do a bit of work before breakfast.
We like our students to take part in sports.

like.definition: used (as would like) to say that you want something or want to do something
like.note: typical: would like, would you like NOT for: general liking
examples: I'd like a cheeseburger, please.
Would you like a drink?

listen.definition: to pay attention to what someone is saying or to a sound that you can hear
listen.note: typical: listen to music, a speaker, carefully NOT for: hearing a sound by chance
examples: We sat around listening to music.
Listen! There's a strange noise in the engine.

listen.definition: to consider what someone says and accept their advice
listen.note: typical: listen to reason, advice, won't listen NOT for: hearing a sound
examples: I told him not to go, but he wouldn't listen.
She refused to listen to reason.

live.definition: to have your home in a particular place
live.note: typical: live in London, live with parents NOT for: staying for a short time
examples: They lived in Holland for ten years.
Does Paul still live here?

live.definition: if a plant or animal lives in a particular place, it grows or has its home there
live.note: typical: animals, plants, habitats NOT for: people living at home
examples: These birds live on only one island in the Pacific.
Penguins live in cold regions.

live.definition: to be alive at a particular time
live.note: typical: lived in the 1800s NOT for: staying alive
examples: He lived in the eighteenth century.
She lived at a time when women were not expected to work.

live.definition: to be alive, or to stay alive
live.note: typical: live to ninety, not expected to live NOT for: having a home
examples: My grandmother lived to eighty-five.
The baby only lived a few hours.

live.definition: to have a particular type of life or live in a particular way
live.note: typical: live in peace, comfortably, happily NOT for: having a home somewhere
examples: The two communities live peacefully side by side.
Most elderly people prefer to live independently.

live.definition: to have enough money to survive on a particular source of income (live on, live off)
live.note: typical: live on a pension, live off savings NOT for: having a home
examples: She lives on a small pension.
They lived off the money he had saved.

live.note: typical: live a little NOT for: simply being alive
examples: She wanted to get out and live a little.
We're beginning to live at last!

live.definition: to imagine that things are better or different from how they really are
live.note: typical: live in a dream world, in a fantasy NOT for: ordinary living
examples: He lives in a dream world if he thinks it will be easy.
She still lives in the past.

live.definition: if something lives in a particular place, that is where it is kept (informal)
live.note: typical: where do these cups live NOT for: people or animals living in a place
examples: Where do these cups live?
The big dishes live in the cupboard.

live.definition: if an idea lives, it continues to exist and influence people
live.note: typical: memories, ideas, names NOT for: living things
examples: His name will live forever.
That day will always live in my memory.

look.definition: to turn your eyes towards something so that you can see it
look.note: typical: look at, look carefully, look up NOT for: appearing
examples: She looked at her watch.
Dad looked up from his paper and smiled.

look.note: typical: look for, look under, look everywhere NOT for: looking at something
examples: Could you help me look for my contact lens?
I've looked everywhere for my keys.

look.note: typical: look good, look as if NOT for: the colour or shape of something
examples: The future is looking good.
It looks as if it might rain later.

look.note: typical: look tired, look like someone NOT for: appearing to be
examples: You look tired.
My sister doesn't look anything like me.

look.definition: if a building looks in a particular direction, it faces that direction
look.note: typical: look south, over the sea NOT for: people looking
examples: The cabin looks east, so we get the morning sun.
The hotel looks over the harbour.

look.definition: to be planning or expecting to do something (informal)
look.note: typical: be looking to do something NOT for: looking with your eyes
examples: We're looking to buy a new car early next year.
The company is looking to expand abroad.

lose.definition: to stop having a particular attitude, quality or ability, or to have less of something
lose.note: typical: lose interest, weight, confidence, your voice NOT for: misplacing something
examples: Carol lost interest in ballet in her teens.
Have you lost weight?

lose.definition: to not win a game, argument, election or war
lose.note: typical: lose a match, an election, lose by one goal NOT for: misplacing something
examples: They played so badly that they deserved to lose.
The government lost by one vote.

lose.definition: to become unable to find someone or something
lose.note: typical: lose your keys, your way NOT for: not winning
examples: I've lost the tickets for tonight's show.
I followed her but lost her in the crowd.

lose.definition: to no longer have something important or necessary, especially because it is taken from you or destroyed
lose.note: typical: lose a job, a home, a chance, a leg NOT for: misplacing something
examples: David is very upset about losing his job.
Hundreds of people lost their homes in the floods.

lose.definition: to die, or if a relative or friend dies
lose.note: typical: lose your life, lose a husband NOT for: misplacing something
examples: Many people lost their lives in the war.
Sadly, Anna lost the baby.

lose.definition: to waste time, or if a clock or watch loses time, it runs too slowly
lose.note: typical: lose time, a clock loses time NOT for: winning time
examples: Vital minutes were lost because the ambulance came late.
My watch loses about two minutes a day.

lose.definition: to stop knowing where you are, or to become uncertain about what you should do
lose.note: typical: lose your way, your bearings NOT for: misplacing objects
examples: I lost my way in the network of tiny alleys.
The company seems to have lost its way lately.

lose.definition: if two people lose touch, they gradually stop communicating, or if you lose touch with a situation, you are no longer involved in it
lose.note: typical: lose touch with friends, with reality NOT for: losing an object
examples: I've lost touch with all my old school friends.
The minister has lost touch with ordinary voters.

lose.note: typical: lose your temper, your cool NOT for: other emotions
examples: Diana was determined not to lose her temper.
He lost his cool and shouted at the referee.

lose.definition: to become crazy or unable to think clearly
lose.note: typical: lose your mind NOT for: temporary anger
examples: Nicholas looked at her as if she had lost her mind.
I'm going to lose my mind if I stay here any longer.

lose.definition: to pay so much attention to something that you do not notice anything else
lose.note: typical: lose yourself in a book, music NOT for: losing your temper
examples: She lost herself in the beauty of the music.
He lost himself in his work.

lose.definition: if you lose someone who is chasing you, you manage to escape from them
lose.note: typical: lose a pursuer, a tail NOT for: misplacing a person
examples: We'll have a better chance of losing him if we take the back road.
The thief lost the police in the crowd.

lose.definition: to remove a part or feature of something that is not necessary or wanted
lose.note: typical: lose a paragraph, a detail NOT for: misplacing something
examples: You could lose the last paragraph to make it fit on one page.
We decided to lose the extra scene.

lose.definition: to confuse someone when you are explaining something to them (informal)
lose.note: typical: you've lost me NOT for: misplacing someone
examples: Explain it again; you've already lost me.
Sorry, you lost me at the second step.

love.definition: to have strong feelings of affection and romantic attachment for someone
love.note: typical: love your husband, wife, partner NOT for: liking things
examples: I love you, Tracy.
He was the only man she had ever loved.

love.definition: to care very much about someone, especially a family member or close friend
love.note: typical: love your children, parents, friends NOT for: romantic attachment
examples: I love my grandad so much.
She has always loved her younger sister.

love.definition: to like something very much or to enjoy doing something very much
love.note: typical: love food, a place, doing something NOT for: loving people
examples: Jeff loves his work.
We all love to talk about ourselves.

make.definition: to produce something, for example by putting different parts together
make.note: typical: make a box, a dress, a film, furniture NOT for: causing a feeling
examples: She made her own wedding dress.
Paper is made from wood.

make.definition: used with some nouns to say that someone does something
make.note: typical: make a mistake, a decision, a phone call, a suggestion NOT for: producing objects
examples: Anyone can make a mistake.
Could I make a suggestion?

make.definition: to cook or prepare food or drink
make.note: typical: make breakfast, tea, a cake NOT for: producing industrial goods
examples: John was making breakfast in the kitchen.
I'll make you some sandwiches.

make.definition: to cause something to happen, or to cause a particular state or condition
make.note: typical: make someone happy, make something possible NOT for: forcing someone
examples: He makes me laugh.
The use of computers has made it possible for more people to work from home.

make.definition: to force someone to do something
make.note: typical: make someone do something, be made to do something NOT for: causing a feeling
examples: My parents always make me do my homework before I go out.
I was made to wait four hours.

make.definition: to cause a mark, hole or similar sign to appear
make.note: typical: make a hole, a dent, a mark NOT for: producing an object
examples: The cup has made a mark on the table.
Make a hole in the paper with a pencil.

make.definition: to succeed in reaching a place or arriving somewhere in time (make it)
make.note: typical: make it to the station, to the top NOT for: producing something
examples: We just made it to the airport in time.
England looks unlikely to make it to the finals.

make.definition: to succeed in a career or achieve a high position (make it)
make.note: typical: make it as a singer, an actor NOT for: simply arriving
examples: He was told he would never make it as a professional singer.
She worked hard and made it to manager.

make.definition: to be able to go to an event or meeting that has been arranged (make it)
make.note: typical: make it on Sunday, can't make it NOT for: succeeding in a career
examples: I'm sorry, but I won't be able to make it on Sunday.
I'm glad you could make it.

make.definition: to survive after being seriously ill or injured, or to manage to deal with a difficult experience (make it)
make.note: typical: make it through NOT for: attending an event
examples: The doctors didn't think he would make it.
I couldn't have made it through those years without my friends.

make.definition: to succeed in achieving a particular position, rate or level
make.note: typical: make the team, the deadline NOT for: arriving at a place
examples: He was never good enough to make the team.
I don't think we'll make the deadline.

make.note: typical: make money, a profit, a living NOT for: spending money
examples: They made a profit of £140 million.
She hopes to make a living from writing.

make.definition: to have the qualities that are needed for a particular job, use or purpose
make.note: typical: make a good teacher, an ideal venue NOT for: producing objects
examples: I'm sure you will make a very good teacher.
The hall would make an ideal venue for a wedding reception.

make.definition: to be a particular amount when added together
make.note: typical: two and two make four NOT for: producing things
examples: Two and two make four.
There are nine people coming, plus me, which makes ten.

make.definition: to say what you have calculated or estimated something to be
make.note: typical: make that $150, what time do you make it NOT for: earning money
examples: I make that $150 altogether.
What time do you make it?

make.definition: to achieve a particular score in a sports game
make.note: typical: make fifty runs, thirty points NOT for: earning money
examples: Surrey had made 92 by lunchtime.
He made twenty points in the first half.

make.definition: to give someone a new job or position in a group or organisation
make.note: typical: make someone captain, leader, mayor NOT for: choosing a team
examples: She has now been made a full partner.
He was made mayor in 1998.

make.definition: to be interesting or important enough to be printed in a newspaper or reported on television
make.note: typical: make the headlines, the front page NOT for: producing news
examples: News of their divorce made the headlines.
The story made the front page of every paper.

make.definition: to make something complete or successful (informal)
make.note: typical: the hat makes the outfit NOT for: producing something new
examples: The hat really makes the outfit.
Good music makes a party.

match.definition: if one thing matches another, or if two things match, they look good together because of a similar colour, pattern or style
match.note: typical: colours, clothes, furniture NOT for: being the same size
examples: We painted the cabinets green to match the rug.
Do you think this outfit matches?

match.definition: if two things match, they look the same because they are a pair
match.note: typical: socks, gloves, earrings NOT for: colours that go together
examples: Your socks don't match.
The two earrings don't quite match.

match.definition: to have no important difference from something else
match.note: typical: match a description, match the original NOT for: colours going together
examples: The suspect matched the descriptions provided by witnesses.
Their actions do not match their words.

match.definition: to be suitable for a particular person, thing or situation
match.note: typical: match needs, requirements NOT for: looking alike
examples: Teaching materials should match individual students' needs.
We'll help you find a home that matches your requirements.

match.definition: to put two people or things together that are similar or connected
match.note: typical: match something to something NOT for: looking alike
examples: Can you match the animals to the correct countries?
All baggage must be matched with a passenger.

match.definition: to be equal to something in value, size or quality
match.note: typical: few can match, strength matched by intelligence NOT for: looking alike
examples: Few cities in Europe can match the cultural richness of Berlin.
Her skill is matched only by her patience.

match.definition: to give a sum of money that is equal to a sum given by someone else
match.note: typical: match donations, funding NOT for: other kinds of equality
examples: The government has promised to match any private donations.
The company will match whatever you give.

match.definition: if you are matched against someone in a game or competition, you are competing against them
match.note: typical: usually passive: be matched against NOT for: looking alike
examples: Federer was matched against Nadal in the final.
The two teams were evenly matched.

meet.definition: to go to a place where someone will be at a particular time, according to an arrangement
meet.note: typical: meet for lunch, meet at the station NOT for: meeting by chance
examples: I'll meet you by the reception desk.
Why don't we meet for lunch on Friday?

meet.definition: to see someone by chance and talk to them
meet.note: typical: meet someone in town, on the bus NOT for: planned meetings
examples: You'll never guess who I met in town.
I was worried I might meet Henry on the bus.

meet.definition: to see and talk to someone for the first time, or to be introduced to them
meet.note: typical: nice to meet you, we first met NOT for: arranged meetings
examples: We first met in Florence.
Jane, come and meet my brother.

meet.definition: to be waiting for someone at an airport or station when they arrive
meet.note: typical: meet someone at the airport NOT for: general meetings
examples: My dad met us at the station.
I'll come and meet you off the plane.

meet.definition: if a group meets, its members come together in the same place to discuss something
meet.note: typical: committees, councils, clubs NOT for: two friends meeting
examples: The committee meets once a month.
The two groups will meet next week to discuss the project.

meet.definition: to play against another person or team in a competition, or to fight another army in a war
meet.note: typical: teams, armies, opponents NOT for: friendly meetings
examples: Manchester United will meet Blackburn in the sixth round of the Cup.
The two armies finally met on the battlefield.

meet.definition: if two things meet, they touch or join at a particular place
meet.note: typical: roads, rivers, lines, hands NOT for: people arranging to meet
examples: The two roads meet just north of the town.
Their hands met under the table.

meet.definition: to experience a problem, attitude or situation
meet.note: typical: meet resistance, hostility NOT for: welcoming someone
examples: Wherever she went, she met hostility and prejudice.
The plan met strong opposition from local residents.

meet.definition: to deal with a problem or something difficult that you have to do
meet.note: typical: meet a challenge NOT for: meeting a person
examples: The new building will help us meet the challenge of increasing numbers.
They struggled to meet the challenge.

meet.definition: to do or be as good as someone needs, expects or wants
meet.note: typical: meet a need, a demand, requirements, standards NOT for: meeting a person
examples: The company is unable to meet the workers' demands for higher wages.
The service is designed to meet your needs.

meet.definition: to finish something at the time it is meant to be finished
meet.note: typical: meet a deadline NOT for: achieving a goal
examples: We are still hoping to meet the November deadline.
She worked all weekend to meet the deadline.

meet.definition: to achieve something that you are trying to achieve
meet.note: typical: meet a target, a goal NOT for: finishing on time
examples: It's impossible to meet the sales targets.
The scheme did not meet its objectives.

meet.definition: to make a payment that needs to be made
meet.note: typical: meet a cost, a debt, an expense NOT for: meeting needs
examples: The government has promised to meet the cost of clearing up after the floods.
I can't meet my monthly expenses any more.

meet.definition: if two people's eyes meet, they look at each other, or if you meet someone's gaze, you look directly at them
meet.note: typical: eyes meet, meet his gaze NOT for: meeting a person
examples: Our eyes met briefly, then he looked away.
Ruth looked down, unable to meet his eye.

miss.definition: to not go to something or not do something, especially when you want to but cannot
miss.note: typical: miss a meeting, lunch, a game NOT for: being too late
examples: I'm starving; I missed lunch.
He missed twenty games after breaking his wrist.

miss.definition: to fail to hit or catch an object, or to fail to hit something you are aiming at
miss.note: typical: miss the ball, the target NOT for: failing to notice
examples: Every time she missed the ball she became angrier.
The bullet narrowly missed his heart.

miss.definition: to feel sad because someone you love is not with you
miss.note: typical: miss your family, friends NOT for: missing a thing
examples: She missed her family badly.
Will you miss me?

miss.definition: to feel sad because you do not have something or cannot do something that you had or did before
miss.note: typical: miss the sun, miss doing something NOT for: missing a person
examples: I miss my old car, but the bus system is good.
Ben knew he would miss working with Sabrina.

miss.definition: to arrive too late for something such as a train, a bus or a film
miss.note: typical: miss the train, the bus, the start NOT for: not attending on purpose
examples: I overslept and missed the train.
We got there late and missed the beginning of the film.

miss.definition: to fail to use an opportunity
miss.note: typical: miss a chance, an opportunity NOT for: missing a bus
examples: Don't miss the chance to see the mountains.
The opportunity was too good to miss.

miss.definition: to not see, hear or notice something
miss.note: typical: miss a detail, you can't miss it NOT for: feeling sad about something
examples: Perhaps there is something the police have missed.
It's the big hotel on the corner; you can't miss it.

miss.definition: to avoid something bad or unpleasant
miss.note: typical: miss the traffic, miss being hit NOT for: missing something good
examples: If we leave now, we should miss the traffic.
They narrowly missed being killed in the fire.

miss.definition: to notice that something or someone is not in the place you expect them to be
miss.note: typical: miss your wallet, miss someone from a group NOT for: feeling sad
examples: I didn't miss my wallet until it came to paying the bill.
Nobody missed him until after dinner.

mix.definition: if you mix two or more substances, they combine to become a single substance
mix.note: typical: mix ingredients, oil and water NOT for: meeting people
examples: Mix the butter and sugar together, then add the milk.
Oil and water don't mix.

mix.definition: to combine two or more different activities, ideas or groups of things
mix.note: typical: mix business with pleasure NOT for: combining substances
examples: His books mix historical fact with fantasy.
I don't like to mix business with pleasure.

mix.definition: to meet, talk and spend time with other people, especially people you do not know well
mix.note: typical: mix with other people NOT for: combining substances
examples: Charlie doesn't mix well with the other children.
The two groups rarely mix.

mix.definition: if two different ideas or activities do not mix, there are problems when they are combined
mix.note: typical: don't mix NOT for: combining substances
examples: Alcohol and driving don't mix.
Smoking and babies don't mix.

mix.definition: to prepare something, especially food or drink, by mixing things together
mix.note: typical: mix a drink, a cocktail NOT for: combining things in general
examples: Will you mix us some drinks, Bill?
She mixed a cake in a large bowl.

mix.definition: to control the balance of sounds in a recording or film (technical)
mix.note: typical: mix a song, an album NOT for: cooking
examples: The album was mixed in a studio in London.
He mixes the sound for live concerts.

name.definition: to give someone or something a particular name
name.note: typical: name a baby, a street, name someone after NOT for: officially choosing someone
examples: We named our daughter Sarah.
He was named after his father.

name.definition: to say what the name of someone or something is, especially officially
name.note: typical: name a suspect, a victim NOT for: giving a name to a baby
examples: The two victims have not yet been named.
She refused to name the people involved.

name.definition: to officially choose someone or something, especially for an important job or prize
name.note: typical: name someone captain, as manager NOT for: giving a baby a name
examples: Quinn has been named as the new team manager.
The film was named best foreign film.

need.definition: to have to have something or someone because you cannot do something, continue or exist without them
need.note: typical: need money, help, a car NOT for: wanting something
examples: Plants need light in order to survive.
You don't really need a car.

need.definition: to feel that you want something very much
need.note: typical: I need a drink, a break NOT for: objects required to live
examples: I need a drink.
If you need anything, just say.

need.definition: used to say that someone should or has to do something
need.note: typical: need to do something NOT for: needing an object
examples: He needs to see a doctor straight away.
You need to let me know by Monday.

open.definition: to move a door, window or lid so that people, things or air can pass through, or to be moved in this way
open.note: typical: doors, windows, drawers, gates NOT for: unfastening a package
examples: Jack opened the window.
She heard a door open and then close.

open.definition: to unfasten or remove the lid, top or cover of a container or package
open.note: typical: bottles, letters, presents, boxes NOT for: moving doors
examples: Louise opened a bottle of wine.
The children were opening their presents.

open.definition: to raise your eyelids so that you can see
open.note: typical: open your eyes NOT for: opening your mouth
examples: Barry was awake long before he opened his eyes.
Her eyes opened slowly.

open.note: typical: open your mouth NOT for: opening your eyes
examples: He opened his mouth but couldn't think what to say.
The dentist asked me to open wide.

open.definition: if a shop, office or restaurant opens, it starts operating for the first time
open.note: typical: open a shop, an office, a branch NOT for: daily opening hours
examples: Sarah recently opened an office in Genoa.
The new arts centre has been a great success since it opened.

open.definition: if a shop or bank opens at a particular time, it starts business for the day
open.note: typical: banks, shops, opening time NOT for: starting a new business
examples: What time do the banks open?
The bakery opens early.

open.definition: to start an activity, event or set of actions
open.note: typical: open an investigation, a debate, talks NOT for: unfastening things
examples: The attorney's office has opened an investigation.
The committee opened the discussion with a short report.

open.definition: to make a document or computer program ready to use
open.note: typical: open a file, a document, an app NOT for: physical objects
examples: Click on this icon to open the File Manager.
Open the document and read the first page.

open.definition: if a meeting, concert or speech opens in a particular way, it starts in that way
open.note: typical: open with, open the conference NOT for: physical opening
examples: The concert opens with a piece by Beethoven.
Hughes opened the conference with a dramatic speech.

open.definition: to perform a ceremony in which you officially state that a building is ready to be used
open.note: typical: open a hospital, a bridge, a library NOT for: starting a business
examples: The new County Hall was officially opened by the King.
The mayor opened the new library.

open.note: typical: open an account NOT for: opening a physical container
examples: I opened a savings account last week.
You need an ID to open a bank account.

open.definition: to make it possible for cars, goods or people to pass through a place
open.note: typical: open a road, a tunnel, a border NOT for: opening a door
examples: They were clearing away snow to open the tunnel.
The two countries agreed to open their border.

open.definition: if a film or play opens, it starts being shown to the public
open.note: typical: films, plays, shows NOT for: opening a shop
examples: The play opens tonight.
The film opened yesterday to excellent reviews.

pack.definition: to put things into cases or bags ready for a trip
pack.note: typical: pack a bag, a suitcase, your things NOT for: filling a place with people
examples: I forgot to pack my razor.
Have you finished packing yet?

pack.definition: to put something into a box or other container so that it can be moved, sold or stored
pack.note: typical: pack goods, products, in boxes NOT for: packing for a trip
examples: The mushrooms are packed in small boxes.
The company packs the fruit in plastic trays.

pack.definition: to go in large numbers into a space until it is too full, or to make people or animals do this
pack.note: typical: pack into a stadium, a bus, a room NOT for: packing a suitcase
examples: Fifty thousand fans packed into the stadium.
The sheep were packed into a truck.

pack.definition: to cover or fill an object with soft material so that it does not get damaged
pack.note: typical: pack glass, a parcel in paper NOT for: packing for a trip
examples: Glass must be packed in several layers of paper.
He packed the vase in newspaper.

pack.definition: to press snow, soil or sand down so that it becomes hard and firm
pack.note: typical: pack soil, snow NOT for: putting things in boxes

The children packed the snow into a ball.

paint.definition: to put paint on a surface
paint.note: typical: walls, doors, ceilings NOT for: making a picture
examples: The ceiling needs painting.
We painted the door blue.

paint.definition: to make a picture, pattern or design using paint
paint.note: typical: paint a picture, landscapes, portraits NOT for: covering a wall
examples: Turner is famous for painting landscapes.
She paints mainly in acrylics.

paint.definition: to put a coloured substance on part of your face or body to make it different or more attractive
paint.note: typical: paint your nails, faces NOT for: painting walls
examples: The children's faces were painted to look like animals.
She had painted her toenails red.

paint.definition: to describe someone or something in a particular way
paint.note: typical: paint a picture of, paint someone as NOT for: using paint
examples: Dickens painted a grim picture of Victorian life.
The newspapers painted him as a villain.

park.definition: to put a car or other vehicle in a particular place for a period of time
park.note: typical: park a car, a bike NOT for: leaving something behind
examples: You can't park here; it's private property.
She parked the car on the drive.

park.definition: to put something somewhere for a period of time, especially in a way that annoys someone (spoken)
park.note: typical: park something on someone's desk NOT for: vehicles
examples: He parked a load of papers on my desk.
Don't park your bags in the hallway.

park.definition: to sit down in a particular place, usually for a long time (informal)
park.note: typical: park yourself on a sofa, at a table NOT for: vehicles
examples: Connie parked herself on the sofa.
He parked himself in front of the television.

pass.definition: to come up to a particular place, person or object and go past them
pass.note: typical: pass a shop, a person, a car NOT for: giving something to someone
examples: He gave me a smile as he passed.
We passed a group of students outside the theatre.

pass.definition: to go or travel along or through a place
pass.note: typical: pass through, along, over NOT for: going past something
examples: We passed through the gates into a courtyard.
We were just passing through and thought we'd drop in.

pass.definition: to put something around, through or across something else
pass.note: typical: pass a rope, a thread through NOT for: giving something to someone
examples: He passed the rope carefully around the post.
She passed the thread through the eye of the needle.

pass.definition: if a road, river or railway line passes a place, it goes through or near it
pass.note: typical: roads, rivers, railway lines NOT for: people travelling
examples: The road passes right through the town centre.
The railway line passes just north of the city.

pass.definition: to hold something in your hand and give it to someone else
pass.note: typical: pass the salt, pass the ball NOT for: giving a job to someone
examples: Pass the salt, please.
She passed a cup of tea to the headmaster.

pass.definition: to give information or a job to another person so that they can deal with it
pass.note: typical: pass on information, over a job NOT for: handing over an object
examples: I'll pass the information on to our sales department.
They passed the enquiry over to the police.

pass.definition: if time passes, it goes by
pass.note: typical: days, years, minutes passing NOT for: spending time
examples: The days passed slowly.
She became more ambitious as the years passed.

pass.definition: to spend time in a particular way
pass.note: typical: pass the time, pass your life NOT for: time going by
examples: They passed the evening playing cards.
He passed his days reading in the library.

pass.definition: to succeed in an examination or test
pass.note: typical: pass an exam, a test, a driving test NOT for: officially accepting a law
examples: Did you pass all your exams?
She passed her driving test first time.

pass.definition: to officially accept a law or proposal, especially by voting
pass.note: typical: pass a law, a bill, a motion NOT for: passing an exam
examples: The motion was passed by sixteen votes to eleven.
The first Transport Act was passed in 1930.

pass.note: typical: a storm, a feeling, a crisis NOT for: time going by
examples: After a couple of hours the storm passed.
The feeling of sickness soon passed.

pass.definition: to kick, throw or hit a ball to a member of your own team during a game
pass.note: typical: football, rugby, basketball NOT for: handing things to people
examples: He passed to Beckham on the edge of the penalty area.
Are you allowed to pass the ball back to the goalkeeper?

pass.definition: to change from being controlled or owned by one person to being controlled or owned by another (formal)
pass.note: typical: pass to someone, into other hands NOT for: giving an object
examples: The land will pass to my son when I die.
Control of the company has passed to a new owner.

pass.definition: to change from one state or condition into another (formal)
pass.note: typical: pass from one state to another NOT for: changing owners
examples: The substance passes from a liquid to a solid as it cools.
The country passed from a monarchy to a republic.

pass.definition: to officially decide how a criminal will be punished and announce the punishment
pass.note: typical: pass sentence NOT for: giving an opinion
examples: The judge will pass sentence tomorrow.
Judges no longer have the power to pass the death sentence.

pass.definition: to give no answer to a question, because you do not know the answer (spoken)
pass.note: typical: 'Pass.' in quizzes NOT for: refusing an offer
examples: "Who won the World Cup in 1998?" "Pass."
I'm afraid I'll have to pass on that question.

pass.definition: to not accept an invitation or an offer
pass.note: typical: pass on an offer NOT for: failing an exam
examples: I'm afraid I'll have to pass on that offer of coffee.
She passed on the chance to go abroad.

pay.definition: to give someone money for something you buy or for a service
pay.note: typical: pay for lessons, pay cash, pay by card NOT for: receiving money
examples: Mum paid for my driving lessons.
Can I pay by credit card?

pay.definition: to pay money that you owe, such as a bill, rent, tax or debt
pay.note: typical: pay a bill, rent, taxes NOT for: buying goods
examples: I must pay the electricity bill today.
She pays her rent on the first of each month.

pay.definition: to give someone money for the job they do
pay.note: typical: pay a salary, pay workers NOT for: buying goods
examples: The company pays its staff on the last Friday of the month.
He is paid very well for his work.

pay.definition: to watch, listen to or think about someone or something carefully
pay.note: typical: pay attention to NOT for: giving money
examples: I'm sorry, I wasn't paying attention to what you were saying.
They paid no attention to him.

pay.definition: to give money to someone because a court has ordered you to
pay.note: typical: pay a fine, compensation, damages NOT for: ordinary bills
examples: She had to pay a £35 fine for speeding.
The company was forced to pay compensation.

pay.definition: to say something good or polite about someone or to someone
pay.note: typical: pay a compliment, tribute, your respects NOT for: giving money
examples: The minister paid tribute to the emergency services.
I came by to pay my respects to Mrs Owens.

pay.definition: if an action pays, it gives you a good result or advantage
pay.note: typical: it pays to do something, crime doesn't pay NOT for: giving money
examples: It pays to get professional advice before you decide.
Crime doesn't pay.

pay.definition: to suffer because of something you have done
pay.note: typical: pay for a mistake, a crime NOT for: money
examples: You will pay for this mistake.
He paid dearly for his carelessness.

phone.definition: to speak to someone by telephone
phone.note: typical: phone someone, phone up, phone back NOT for: sending a message
examples: I'll phone you this evening.
Stevie phoned to say that he was going to be late.

pick.definition: to choose a person or thing because they are the best or most suitable
pick.note: typical: pick a team, a colour, a course NOT for: picking fruit
examples: Students have to pick three courses from a list of fifteen.
I wasn't picked for the hockey team.

pick.definition: to remove a flower, fruit, nut or vegetable from a plant or tree
pick.note: typical: pick flowers, apples, berries NOT for: choosing
examples: We picked some blackberries to eat on the way.
Amy picked a small bunch of wild flowers.

pick.definition: to remove something small from a place carefully
pick.note: typical: pick something off, from, out of NOT for: picking fruit
examples: She was nervously picking bits of fluff off her sweater.
Ahmed picked the pips from his teeth.

pick.definition: to walk slowly and carefully, choosing exactly where to put your feet
pick.note: typical: pick your way through, across NOT for: choosing people
examples: She picked her way between the puddles.
He picked his way down the narrow staircase.

pick.definition: to use something that is not a key to unlock a lock
pick.note: typical: pick a lock NOT for: choosing something
examples: It is quite easy to pick the lock on a car.
The thief picked the lock in seconds.

plan.definition: to think carefully about something you want to do and decide how and when you will do it
plan.note: typical: plan a trip, a party, ahead NOT for: intending in a general way
examples: He immediately began planning his escape.
We're planning a surprise party for her.

plan.note: typical: plan to do something, plan on doing something NOT for: careful organising
examples: He said he planned to write his essay tonight.
When do you plan on going to Geneva?

plan.definition: to think about something you are going to make and decide what it will be like
plan.note: typical: plan a garden, a building, a system NOT for: organising an event
examples: Planning a small garden is often difficult.
The system needs to be planned carefully.

plant.definition: to put plants or seeds in the ground to grow
plant.note: typical: plant trees, seeds, a garden NOT for: hiding objects
examples: Residents have helped us plant trees.
We've planted tomatoes and carrots in the garden.

plant.definition: to put something firmly in or on something else (informal)
plant.note: typical: plant a kiss, plant your feet NOT for: gardening
examples: She planted her feet firmly and refused to move.
He planted a kiss on her cheek.

plant.definition: to hide stolen or illegal goods in someone's things to make them seem guilty of a crime
plant.note: typical: plant evidence, drugs on someone NOT for: gardening
examples: She claims that the police planted the drugs on her.
The gang planted evidence to blame their rivals.

plant.definition: to put a bomb somewhere (news use)
plant.note: typical: plant a bomb NOT for: gardening
examples: Two men are accused of planting a bomb on the train.
Police arrested a man for planting a bomb outside the embassy.

plant.definition: to put or send someone somewhere, especially secretly, so that they can find out information
plant.note: typical: plant a spy, an agent NOT for: hiding objects
examples: The police had planted undercover detectives at every entrance.
The company planted a spy in its rival's office.

plant.definition: to make someone begin to have an idea or doubt, especially without them realising where it came from
plant.note: typical: plant an idea, a doubt in someone's mind NOT for: gardening
examples: Someone must have planted the idea in his mind.
Her words planted a doubt in my head.

play.definition: if children play, they do things they enjoy, often with other children or with toys
play.note: typical: children, toys, games NOT for: taking part in a sport
examples: The kids were playing in the garden.
Did you like to play with dolls when you were little?

play.definition: to take part in a game or sport
play.note: typical: play football, cards, chess NOT for: children's free play
examples: Karen began playing basketball when she was six.
Men were sitting in the park, playing cards.

play.definition: to use a particular piece, card or player in a game or sport
play.note: typical: play a card, a player NOT for: taking part in a game
examples: Harrison played a ten of spades.
The coach played him at centre forward.

play.definition: to take a particular position on a team
play.note: typical: play goalkeeper, striker, first base NOT for: playing a sport
examples: He plays in goal for the school team.
Garvey played first base for the Dodgers.

play.definition: to hit a ball in a particular way or to a particular place in a game or sport
play.note: typical: play a shot, the ball low NOT for: taking part in a match
examples: She played the ball low, just over the net.
He played the ball to his partner.

play.definition: to perform a piece of music or to use a musical instrument
play.note: typical: play the piano, guitar, a tune NOT for: listening to music
examples: He's learning to play the piano.
She played a Bach prelude.

play.definition: if a radio, CD or other device plays, or you play it, it produces sound, especially music
play.note: typical: play a CD, a record, a song NOT for: performing on an instrument
examples: The bedside radio played softly.
The DJ played the latest tracks.

play.definition: to perform the part of a character in a play or film
play.note: typical: play a role, a character NOT for: being a person in real life
examples: Streep plays a shy, nervous woman.
He played Hamlet at the National Theatre.

play.definition: if a play or film is playing at a theatre or cinema, it is being shown there
play.note: typical: playing at the theatre, cinema NOT for: acting a role
examples: "Macbeth" is playing at the Theatre Royal.
What's playing at the cinema tonight?

play.definition: to have an effect or influence on something
play.note: typical: play a part, a role in something NOT for: acting in a drama
examples: A good diet plays a large part in helping people live longer.
Luck played no role in his success.

play.definition: to behave as if you are a particular kind of person or have a particular quality, even though it is not true
play.note: typical: play dead, play the fool, play dumb NOT for: performing in a drama
examples: Some snakes fool predators by playing dead.
He played the fool at school instead of working.

play.definition: to behave in a particular way in a situation in order to get the result you want
play.note: typical: play it safe, play it cool NOT for: games
examples: How do you want to play this meeting?
Play it safe and cook the eggs thoroughly.

play.definition: to do something to someone as a joke or trick
play.note: typical: play a joke, trick, prank on someone NOT for: ordinary games
examples: The boys played a trick on their teacher.
Someone played a joke on me by hiding my keys.

point.definition: to show something to someone by holding up one of your fingers or a thin object towards it
point.note: typical: point at, point to, point with a finger NOT for: aiming a weapon
examples: "Look!" she said and pointed.
She pointed to a small boat approaching the shore.

point.definition: to hold something so that it is aimed towards a person or thing
point.note: typical: point a gun, a camera at someone NOT for: pointing with a finger
examples: He pointed his gun at the prisoner.
She pointed her camera at me.

point.definition: to face or be aimed in a particular direction
point.note: typical: arrows, signs, clock hands pointing NOT for: people pointing
examples: The arrow always points north.
We found footprints pointing towards the back door.

point.definition: to show someone which direction they should go in
point.note: typical: point someone towards, in the direction of NOT for: pointing at things
examples: She pointed me towards an armchair.
Could you point me in the direction of the bathroom, please?

point.definition: to suggest what someone should do
point.note: typical: point someone towards a career NOT for: showing directions
examples: My teachers were all pointing me towards university.
A good adviser should point you in the right direction.

point.definition: to suggest that something is true
point.note: typical: evidence points to, points towards NOT for: showing a direction
examples: All the evidence pointed towards Blake as the murderer.
Everything points to a quick recovery.

post.definition: to send a letter or package by post (British)
post.note: typical: post a letter, a parcel, a card NOT for: putting something on the internet
examples: She's just gone to post a letter.
I posted the cheque to you last Friday.

post.definition: to push something through someone's letterbox (British)
post.note: typical: post a key, a note through the door NOT for: sending by post
examples: I'll post the key through your letterbox when I leave.
He posted a note through her door.

post.definition: if you are posted somewhere, your employer sends you to work there, usually for several years
post.note: typical: usually passive: be posted to NOT for: sending a letter
examples: He joined the army and was posted to Germany.
She was posted overseas for three years.

post.definition: to put up a public notice on a wall or notice board
post.note: typical: post a notice, results, a sign NOT for: posting online
examples: The exam results were posted on the notice board yesterday.

post.definition: to make someone stand in a particular place in order to watch or guard it
post.note: typical: post a guard, soldiers NOT for: sending someone to work abroad
examples: The general posted guards at every gate.
Police were posted outside the building.

post.definition: to officially record and announce information about a company's finances or an economy
post.note: typical: post profits, losses, figures NOT for: putting up a notice
examples: The company posted record profits for the third quarter.
