post.definition: to put a message or document on the internet so that other people can see it
post.note: typical: post a comment, photos, a video NOT for: sending by post
examples: Could you post those new photos on the website?
She posted a comment under the article.

post.definition: to pay a particular amount of money so that someone can leave prison before their trial
post.note: typical: post bail NOT for: sending a letter
examples: His family posted bail of fifty thousand dollars.
He was released after posting bail.

pull.definition: to use your hands to make something or someone move towards you or in the direction your hands are moving
pull.note: typical: pull a rope, a door, someone's hair NOT for: pushing
examples: Mom! Davey's pulling my hair!
She pulled open the door and hurried inside.

pull.definition: to use force to take something from the place where it is fixed or held
pull.note: typical: pull a tooth, a weed, a nail NOT for: pulling gently
examples: She has to have two teeth pulled.
Vicky had pulled the arm off her doll.

pull.definition: to be attached to something and make it move behind you in the direction you are going
pull.note: typical: tractors, horses, engines pulling NOT for: pulling with your hands
examples: A tractor was pulling a trailer along the lane.
The engine pulled twenty carriages.

pull.definition: to take something out of a bag or pocket with your hand
pull.note: typical: pull out a wallet, a gun NOT for: pulling something towards you
examples: He pulled out his wallet and said, "Let me pay."
Ben pulled a pen from his pocket.

pull.definition: to put on or take off a piece of clothing, usually quickly
pull.note: typical: pull on a sweater, pull off a shirt NOT for: pulling an object
examples: He pulled off his damp shirt.
She pulled on her boots and went out.

pull.definition: to move your body or part of your body away from someone or something
pull.note: typical: pull away, pull free NOT for: pulling something towards you
examples: She tried to pull her hand free.
He pulled away from her and turned to go.

pull.definition: to injure a muscle by stretching it too much
pull.note: typical: pull a muscle NOT for: pulling objects
examples: Paul pulled a muscle trying to lift the freezer.
She pulled a muscle in the second half.

pull.definition: to move a control such as a switch, lever or handle towards you
pull.note: typical: pull a lever, a handle, the trigger NOT for: pulling objects free
examples: He pulled the lever and the door opened.
She pulled the emergency cord.

pull.definition: to open or close curtains or blinds
pull.note: typical: pull the curtains, the blinds NOT for: pulling a rope
examples: It was getting dark, so I pulled the curtains.
Pull the blinds; the sun is too bright.

pull.note: typical: pull a crowd, pull customers NOT for: pulling objects
examples: The festival pulls huge crowds every summer.
The famous chef pulls customers from all over the city.

pull.definition: to succeed in doing something dishonest, or to play a trick on someone (informal)
pull.note: typical: pull a stunt, a trick, a robbery NOT for: ordinary actions
examples: The gang pulled another bank robbery.
Don't you ever pull a stunt like that again!

push.definition: to make someone or something move by pressing them with your hands, arms or body
push.note: typical: push a door, a trolley, a person NOT for: pulling
examples: It didn't move, so she pushed harder.
I slowly pushed the door open.

push.definition: to press a button or switch to make a piece of equipment start or stop working
push.note: typical: push a button, a switch NOT for: pushing a person
examples: I got in and pushed the button for the fourth floor.
Push the green button to start the engine.

push.definition: to use your hands or arms to move people or things out of the way so that you can get past
push.note: typical: push past, push through, push your way NOT for: pressing a button
examples: A fat man pushed past me in his rush to leave.
She pushed her way to the front.

push.definition: to encourage or force someone to do something or to work hard
push.note: typical: push someone to do something, push yourself NOT for: physically pushing
examples: Try not to push your children too hard.
The teachers pushed the students to achieve more.

push.definition: to try to persuade people to accept your ideas or opinions in order to achieve something
push.note: typical: push an agenda, push for reform NOT for: pushing an object
examples: The president is trying to push his agenda in Congress.
He was pushing hard for welfare reform.

push.definition: to change someone's situation, or to make a situation change, especially when some people do not want it to
push.note: typical: push into poverty, push forward NOT for: physically pushing
examples: The law would push even more children into poverty.
Rising rents pushed many families out of the area.

push.definition: to increase or decrease an amount, value or number
push.note: typical: push prices up, push costs down NOT for: moving an object
examples: Slow sales have pushed down orders.
New technology has pushed the cost of health care even higher.

push.definition: if an army pushes somewhere, it moves in that direction
push.note: typical: push north, push forward NOT for: individual people
examples: The army was pushing north.
They pushed deep into enemy territory.

push.definition: to try to sell more of a product or make people notice it (informal)
push.note: typical: push a product, a brand NOT for: pushing physically
examples: The company is pushing its new range of phones.
Shops push expensive items at Christmas.

put.definition: to place something or someone in a particular place or position
put.note: typical: put a cup on the table, put keys in a bag NOT for: writing something
examples: He put the coffee on the table.
Where did you put the keys?

put.definition: to cause someone or something to be in a particular situation or state
put.note: typical: put someone in a good/bad mood, put at risk NOT for: placing physical objects
examples: The long delay put us all in a bad mood.
Don't put yourself in a situation you can't handle.

put.definition: to write or print something somewhere
put.note: typical: put your name, a date, a signature NOT for: placing objects
examples: Put your name at the top of the page.
Did you put a stamp on the envelope?

put.definition: to express something in words in a particular way
put.note: typical: put it simply, politely, put into words NOT for: writing a name
examples: To put it simply, we have no money.
I don't know how to put this politely.

put.definition: to cause someone or something to work, do something or be used
put.note: typical: put to work, to use, to the test NOT for: placing objects
examples: The scheme put unemployed people to work on construction projects.
We put fifteen cars to the test.

put.definition: to consider something as having a particular level of importance or quality
put.note: typical: put family first, put profit before safety NOT for: placing things
examples: Some companies put profit before safety.
He puts his family first.

put.definition: to arrange for someone to go to a place, or to make them go there
put.note: typical: put someone in hospital, to bed NOT for: placing objects
examples: Pneumonia put him in the hospital for a week.
Put the boys to bed around eight o'clock.

put.definition: to take someone to a plane, train or other transport so that they can start a journey
put.note: typical: put someone on a train, a plane NOT for: placing luggage
examples: I put her on the plane for London.
We put the children on the school bus.

put.definition: to add something to something else
put.note: typical: put sugar in tea, put money into an account NOT for: placing an object on a surface
examples: Do you put sugar in your coffee?
She put all her savings into the business.

put.definition: to give or use effort, energy, time or money on something
put.note: typical: put effort, time, money into something NOT for: placing an object
examples: He has put a lot of work into this project.
They put a lot of money into the new school.

put.definition: to ask a question or suggest an idea to someone
put.note: typical: put a question, a proposal to someone NOT for: expressing something simply
examples: I put the question to the minister directly.
She put a proposal to the committee.

put.definition: to throw a heavy metal ball in a sports competition (put the shot)
put.note: typical: put the shot NOT for: throwing other objects
examples: She put the shot over eighteen metres.
He put the shot further than ever before.

read.definition: to look at written words and understand what they mean
read.note: typical: read a book, a letter, instructions NOT for: reading aloud
examples: She picked up the letter and read it.
Read the instructions carefully before you start.

read.definition: to find out information from books, newspapers or other written sources
read.note: typical: read about, read that NOT for: reading a book for pleasure
examples: You can't believe everything you read in the papers.
Did you read about the accident?

read.definition: to say written words aloud so that other people can hear them
read.note: typical: read aloud, read to children NOT for: reading silently
examples: She reads to the children every night.
He read the letter aloud to us.

read.definition: to study a subject at university (British)
read.note: typical: read law, history, English at university NOT for: reading a book
examples: She is reading law at Cambridge.
He read English at Oxford.

read.definition: to understand or interpret something in a particular way
read.note: typical: read a map, a situation, a meter NOT for: reading words
examples: Can you read a map?
I read the situation completely wrongly.

read.definition: if a sign, gauge or instrument reads a particular number or words, that is what it shows or says
read.note: typical: signs, meters, thermometers NOT for: people reading
examples: The sign read "Private Property."
The thermometer reads thirty degrees.

read.definition: if a piece of writing reads in a particular way, it sounds or seems that way when you read it
read.note: typical: reads well, badly, like NOT for: understanding words
examples: The report reads like a novel.
Your essay reads very well.

rest.definition: to stop working or doing an activity for a time and sit or lie down to relax
rest.note: typical: rest for a while, after work NOT for: supporting an object
examples: If you're tired, we'll stop and rest for a while.
The doctor told him to rest for a few days.

rest.definition: to support an object or part of your body by putting it on or against something, or to be supported in this way
rest.note: typical: rest your head, elbows, arms NOT for: relaxing
examples: Rest your head on my shoulder.
Their bikes were resting against the wall.

rest.definition: to stop using a part of your body because it is sore or tired
rest.note: typical: rest your legs, feet, eyes NOT for: relaxing the whole body
examples: I need to sit down and rest my legs.
Rest your eyes for a few minutes after working at the screen.

return.definition: to go or come back to a place where you were before
return.note: typical: return home, to Spain, from a trip NOT for: giving something back
examples: Are you planning to return to Spain?
I have just returned from five months abroad.

return.definition: to give, send or put something back
return.note: typical: return a book, a letter, a product NOT for: coming back to a place
examples: I returned the books to the library.
Please complete the form and return it in the envelope.

return.definition: if a feeling or situation returns, it starts to exist or happen again
return.note: typical: pain, silence, peace, fear NOT for: people going back
examples: If the pain returns, take two of the tablets.
Peace has finally returned to the country.

return.definition: to do something to someone because they have done the same thing to you
return.note: typical: return a smile, a call, a favour NOT for: giving objects back
examples: She smiled at him and he returned her smile.
I'll return the favour some day.

return.note: typical: 'Yes,' he returned NOT for: ordinary conversation
examples: "Yes," he returned. "I'm a lucky man."
"Never," she returned coldly.

return.definition: to hit the ball back to your opponent in a game such as tennis
return.note: typical: return a serve, a shot NOT for: giving objects back
examples: She returned his serve with a powerful shot.
He couldn't return the ball.

return.definition: to elect someone to a political position (British)
return.note: typical: usually passive: be returned to parliament NOT for: sending something back
examples: Yeo was returned to Parliament with an increased majority.
She was returned as MP for Brighton.

return.definition: if a jury returns a verdict, they say whether someone is guilty or not
return.note: typical: return a verdict NOT for: ordinary decisions
examples: The jury returned a verdict of not guilty.
It took the jury three days to return a verdict.

return.note: typical: return a profit, an increase NOT for: giving something back
examples: The group returned increased profits last year.
The fund returned a profit of eight per cent.

ride.definition: to sit on an animal, especially a horse, and make it move along
ride.note: typical: ride a horse, a camel, a donkey NOT for: driving a car
examples: She learned to ride when she was seven.
He rode away across the fields.

ride.definition: to travel on a bicycle or motorbike
ride.note: typical: ride a bike, a motorbike NOT for: travelling in a car
examples: He had never learned to ride a bicycle.
They mounted their bikes and rode off.

ride.definition: to travel in a bus, car or other vehicle that you are not driving (especially American)
ride.note: typical: ride a bus, in the back of a car NOT for: driving a vehicle
examples: We got onto the bus and rode into town.
Ann rides the bus to work.

ride.definition: to travel up or down in a lift (American)
ride.note: typical: ride the elevator up, down NOT for: riding a bus
examples: He rode the elevator down to the first floor.
We rode up to the tenth floor.

ride.definition: to float on water or in the air
ride.note: typical: ships, the moon, riding a wave NOT for: people travelling
examples: The moon was riding high in the sky.
Surfers were riding the waves.

ride.definition: if a child rides on someone's shoulders or back, they are carried in that way
ride.note: typical: ride on shoulders, on someone's back NOT for: riding an animal
examples: The little boy rode on his father's shoulders.
She rode on her uncle's back across the garden.

run.definition: to move very quickly on your legs, faster than walking
run.note: typical: run down the stairs, away, to the door NOT for: travelling by vehicle
examples: I ran down the stairs as fast as I could.
The children came running out of the house.

run.definition: to take part in a race
run.note: typical: run a marathon, in a race NOT for: running to catch a bus
examples: I had never run a marathon before.
He ran in the 3000 metres.

run.definition: to organise or be in charge of an activity, business, organisation or country
run.note: typical: run a restaurant, a shop, a country NOT for: running on foot
examples: For a while she ran a restaurant in Boston.
The hotel is well run and extremely popular.

run.definition: to do something or go somewhere quickly
run.note: typical: run to the shop, run and ask NOT for: long running
examples: Run and ask your mother where she's put the keys.
I need to run to the store for some milk.

run.definition: if a bus, train or other service runs, it takes people from one place to another at fixed times
run.note: typical: buses, trains, ferries NOT for: people running
examples: The buses don't run on Sundays.
The number 67 bus runs to the city centre.

run.definition: if a computer program runs, it operates, or if you run a program, you make it operate
run.note: typical: run software, a program NOT for: physical machines
examples: The software will run on any PC.
I need to run a virus check.

run.definition: if a machine or engine runs, it operates, or if you run it, you make it operate
run.note: typical: run on petrol, electricity, run an engine NOT for: computer programs
examples: She left the engine running.
Most cars run on unleaded fuel.

run.definition: if a tape is running, it is recording, or if you run a tape, you make it move
run.note: typical: tape running, run a tape back NOT for: programs
examples: She didn't realise the tape was running as she spoke.
Run the tape back to the beginning.

run.definition: to print something in a newspaper or magazine, or to broadcast something on television
run.note: typical: run a story, an advert, a series NOT for: organising a business
examples: A local TV station ran her story.
The company is running a series of adverts in national newspapers.

run.definition: to try to be elected to a political position (run for office)
run.note: typical: run for president, for office NOT for: running in a race
examples: She plans to run for mayor.
He ran against Lungren in the last election.

run.definition: if a road, wire or other long thing runs in a particular direction, that is its position, or if you run it somewhere, you put it there
run.note: typical: roads, rivers, cables, mountain ranges NOT for: people running
examples: The road runs along a valley.
Run the cables under the carpet.

run.definition: to move something lightly along a surface
run.note: typical: run your fingers, hand through NOT for: people running
examples: Charles ran his fingers through her hair.
Run the scanner over the bar code.

run.definition: if liquid runs, it flows in a particular direction or place
run.note: typical: water, tears, blood running NOT for: people running
examples: Tears started to run down her cheeks.
Water was running off the roof.

run.definition: if a tap is running, water is coming out of it, or if you run a tap, you make water come out
run.note: typical: run a tap, the cold water NOT for: flowing rivers
examples: Did you leave the tap running?
He ran the tap until the water was hot.

run.definition: to fill a bath with water
run.note: typical: run a bath NOT for: running a tap in general
examples: I could hear her running a bath upstairs.
Could you run me a hot bath?

run.definition: if someone's nose is running, liquid is flowing out of it
run.note: typical: a running nose NOT for: rivers
examples: My nose is running; I think I'm getting a cold.
The child's eyes and nose were running.

run.definition: if something runs for a particular length of time, it can officially be used or lasts for that time
run.note: typical: contracts, insurance, licences NOT for: running on foot
examples: The contract runs for a year.
My car insurance only has another month to run.

run.definition: if a play, show or film runs, it continues to be performed regularly in one place
run.note: typical: a play, a show running NOT for: software
examples: The play ran for two years.
The musical has been running in London since 2018.

run.definition: to happen in a particular way or at a particular time
run.note: typical: run smoothly, run over a period NOT for: moving fast
examples: Andy kept things running smoothly while I was away.
The course runs over a three-year period.

run.definition: to be at a particular level, amount or price
run.note: typical: run at, run to a figure NOT for: moving
examples: Inflation was running at five per cent.
The cost of repairing the damage could run to $5,000.

run.definition: if a story, discussion or text runs in a particular way, it has those particular words or events
run.note: typical: the story runs that, the headline ran NOT for: moving
examples: The story runs that someone offered Lynch a further $500.
"President's marriage really over," ran the headline.

run.definition: if a feeling runs through you, or a thought runs through your mind, you feel or think it quickly
run.note: typical: a shiver ran down my back NOT for: running on foot
examples: A feeling of excitement ran through her body.
The same thought kept running through his mind.

run.definition: if a hole in tights or stockings runs, it gets bigger in a straight line
run.note: typical: tights, stockings NOT for: other clothes tearing
examples: My tights have run.
A ladder ran all the way up her stocking.

run.definition: if a quality, disease or skill runs in a family, many people in that family have it
run.note: typical: run in the family NOT for: personal habits
examples: Diabetes appears to run in families.
Musical talent runs in the family.

run.definition: to have a body temperature higher than normal because you are ill
run.note: typical: run a temperature, a fever NOT for: room temperature
examples: She was running a temperature of 39 degrees.
The child is running a fever.

run.definition: to arrive, go somewhere or do something late, early or at the right time
run.note: typical: run late, run on time NOT for: physical running
examples: I'm running late, so I'll talk to you later.
If the train runs on time, we'll be there by ten.

run.definition: to drive quickly through a red traffic light instead of stopping (informal)
run.note: typical: run a red light NOT for: stopping at a light
examples: He was fined for running a red light.
The car ran the light and hit a cyclist.

save.definition: to make someone or something safe from danger, harm or destruction
save.note: typical: save a life, a marriage, save from drowning NOT for: keeping money
examples: Emergency aid could save millions threatened with starvation.
He saved the child from drowning.

save.definition: to keep money in a bank so that you can use it later, especially by gradually adding to it
save.note: typical: save for a car, a house, save up NOT for: using less money
examples: He managed to save enough to buy a small house.
I'm saving up for a new car.

save.definition: to use less money, time or energy so that you do not waste any
save.note: typical: save time, energy, money NOT for: putting money in a bank
examples: We'll save a lot of time if we go by car.
Everyone is being encouraged to save energy.

save.definition: to keep something so that you can use or enjoy it in the future
save.note: typical: save food, a bottle for a special occasion NOT for: saving money in a bank
examples: We'll save the rest of the food and have it later.
I had a bottle of champagne that I'd been saving for a special occasion.

save.definition: to keep all the objects of a particular kind that you can find, so that you can use them
save.note: typical: save coupons, vouchers, stamps NOT for: saving money
examples: I'm saving vouchers to get a cheap air ticket.
She saves old jars for making jam.

save.definition: to help someone by making it unnecessary for them to do something they do not want to do
save.note: typical: save someone a trip, the trouble NOT for: rescuing someone
examples: If you lent me five pounds, it would save me a trip to the bank.
I'll get a taxi from the station to save you the trouble of coming to collect me.

save.definition: to stop people from using something so that it is available for someone else
save.note: typical: save a seat, a place, some dinner NOT for: keeping something for yourself
examples: Will you save me a seat?
We'll save some dinner for you if you're late.

save.definition: to make a computer keep the work that you have done on it
save.note: typical: save a file, a document, your work NOT for: saving money
examples: Don't forget to save before you close the file.
Did you save the changes you made?

save.definition: to stop the other team from scoring in a game such as football
save.note: typical: goalkeeper saves a shot NOT for: saving money
examples: The goalkeeper just managed to save the shot.
He saved a penalty in the last minute.

say.definition: to express an idea, feeling or thought using words
say.note: typical: say hello, that, what NOT for: pronouncing a single word
examples: "I'm so tired," she said.
A spokesman said that the company would improve its safety standards.

say.definition: if a sign, notice, letter or other written thing says something, that is what is written on it
say.note: typical: signs, notes, letters, instructions NOT for: people speaking
examples: The sign says "No parking."
The letter says that the meeting has been cancelled.

say.definition: if a clock, gauge or other device says something, it shows that information
say.note: typical: clocks, scales, thermometers NOT for: written signs
examples: My watch says half past three.
The gauge says we're almost out of fuel.

say.definition: to pronounce a word or sound
say.note: typical: say a word, someone's name NOT for: expressing ideas
examples: How do you say your last name?
Can you say that word again?

say.definition: used when suggesting or supposing that something might happen or be true
say.note: typical: let's say, say, for example NOT for: reporting speech
examples: If we put out, say, twenty chairs, would that be enough?
Let's say your plan fails; then what?

say.definition: to try to persuade yourself that something is true or not true (say to yourself)
say.note: typical: say to yourself NOT for: talking to other people
examples: I kept saying to myself that this wasn't really happening.
She said to herself, "Stay calm."

say.definition: to report what people generally think or tell others (it is said that, they say)
say.note: typical: they say, it is said that NOT for: a single speaker
examples: They say it will rain all week.
It is said that the old house is haunted.

see.definition: to notice or examine someone or something using your eyes
see.note: typical: see a house, a face, see something happen NOT for: watching a film
examples: The moment we saw the house, we knew we wanted to buy it.
Can you see where the marks are on the wall?

see.definition: to meet or visit someone, or to go to a doctor or other professional
see.note: typical: see a friend, a doctor, a lawyer NOT for: noticing with your eyes
examples: I'm seeing my doctor on Tuesday.
Come and see us next weekend.

see.definition: to find out or check something
see.note: typical: see if, see whether, go and see NOT for: looking at something
examples: Go and see who's at the door.
I'll call and see if they have any tickets left.

see.note: typical: see what you mean, see why NOT for: noticing with your eyes
examples: I can't see why he's so upset.
I see what you mean.

see.definition: to watch a television programme, play, film or other event
see.note: typical: see a film, a play, a match NOT for: noticing something
examples: Did you see that programme on monkeys last night?
We're going to see a play tonight.

see.definition: to think about or consider someone or something in a particular way
see.note: typical: see something as, see things differently NOT for: using your eyes
examples: I see the job as a challenge.
Violence is seen in different ways by different people.

see.definition: used in writing to tell you where you can find information
see.note: typical: see page 58, see below NOT for: looking with your eyes
examples: See p. 58 for more details.
The results are shown in Table 7 (see below).

see.definition: to experience or witness an event or a period of change
see.note: typical: see changes, a decade seeing something NOT for: watching a film
examples: The 1990s saw rapid changes in technology.
She has seen a lot of changes in this town.

see.definition: to make sure that something is done (see that)
see.note: typical: see that something is done NOT for: finding out whether
examples: Please see that the door is locked.
I'll see to it that everyone gets a copy.

sell.definition: to give something to someone in exchange for money
sell.note: typical: sell a car, a house, shares NOT for: offering something in a shop
examples: Toni is selling her car for seven hundred pounds.
The vase was sold to a Dutch buyer.

sell.definition: to offer something for people to buy
sell.note: typical: shops, businesses, goods NOT for: a single sale
examples: Do you sell cigarettes?
Smoke alarms sell for as little as five pounds.

sell.definition: to make people want to buy something
sell.note: typical: scandal sells newspapers NOT for: giving something away
examples: Scandal sells newspapers.
The car's new design will help sell it to consumers.

sell.note: typical: sell well, badly, millions of copies NOT for: people selling
examples: Tickets for the concert just aren't selling.
Her last book sold millions of copies.

sell.definition: to try to make someone accept a new idea or plan
sell.note: typical: sell an idea, a plan to someone NOT for: selling goods
examples: It's hard for any government to sell new taxes to the voters.
He is completely sold on the idea.

sell.definition: to make yourself seem impressive to other people
sell.note: typical: sell yourself at an interview NOT for: selling goods
examples: If you want a promotion, you've got to sell yourself better.
She doesn't know how to sell herself at interviews.

send.definition: to arrange for something to go or be taken to another place, especially by post
send.note: typical: send a letter, a parcel, flowers NOT for: sending a person
examples: Lyn sent some pictures of the wedding.
We sent her a letter of apology.

send.definition: to arrange for someone to go somewhere, or to tell someone to go there
send.note: typical: send a child to school, to bed, to a doctor NOT for: sending things
examples: They sent their daughter to a boarding school.
The company is sending two engineers to Brno.

send.definition: to communicate something to someone electronically, for example a message or an email
send.note: typical: send an email, a text, a message NOT for: sending parcels
examples: I'll send you an email tonight.
She sent me a text to say she'd be late.

send.definition: to make something move quickly in a particular direction
send.note: typical: send something flying, sending a plane into a dive NOT for: posting things
examples: The blast sent glass flying across the room.
The strike sent the ball over the fence.

send.definition: to make someone feel a particular strong feeling
send.note: typical: send shivers up your spine, chills NOT for: posting things
examples: The eerie howl of the siren sent chills up her spine.
The sight of the snake sent a shiver through me.

send.definition: to tell someone something by sending them a message or letter (formal)
send.note: typical: send word NOT for: ordinary messages
examples: They sent word to the king of their arrival.
He sent word that he would be late.

show.note: typical: show a ticket, a photo, a present NOT for: explaining how to do something
examples: The children proudly showed me their presents.
Show your ticket to the woman at the entrance.

show.definition: to provide facts or information that make it clear that something is true or has happened
show.note: typical: figures, studies, evidence show that NOT for: letting someone see an object
examples: Figures showed a nine per cent rise in inflation.
Several studies have shown that aggressive toys lead to bad behaviour.

show.definition: to let your feelings, attitudes or qualities be clearly seen
show.note: typical: show emotion, interest, determination NOT for: hiding something
examples: She had learned not to show her emotions.
He showed great interest in the children.

show.definition: to explain to someone how to do something by doing it yourself or using actions
show.note: typical: show someone how to do something NOT for: providing evidence
examples: Maureen showed Peter how to feed the young animals.
Show me how the machine works.

show.note: typical: stains, bruises, nerves, a scar showing NOT for: letting others see something on purpose
examples: The scar still shows after ten years.
Don't worry; the stain doesn't show.

show.definition: to broadcast or put a film, programme or play on for people to watch
show.note: typical: show a film, a series, be shown on TV NOT for: showing an object
examples: The cinema is showing three new films this week.
The match will be shown live on Saturday.

show.definition: to take someone to a place and guide them
show.note: typical: show someone around, to a seat, to the door NOT for: explaining a process
examples: A waiter showed us to our table.
Let me show you around the building.

show.definition: if a picture, map or diagram shows something, it presents or represents it
show.note: typical: pictures, maps, graphs, charts NOT for: providing evidence in words
examples: The graph shows the rise in prices over ten years.
This map shows the main roads in the region.

show.definition: to put works of art or other things where the public can look at them
show.note: typical: show paintings, a collection, in a gallery NOT for: showing films
examples: The gallery is showing paintings by local artists.
She has shown her work in several cities.

show.definition: to put an animal into a competition with other animals
show.note: typical: show dogs, horses NOT for: showing objects
examples: Do you plan to show your dogs?
She shows horses at county fairs.

touch.note: typical: hardly touch your food, haven't touched the work NOT for: physical contact
examples: You've hardly touched your food.
I haven't touched any of the work yet.

touch.definition: to not hurt someone or not damage something (not touch sb)
touch.note: typical: swear they haven't touched someone NOT for: emotional effects
examples: The older boys swore they hadn't touched the child.
The old building wasn't touched by the fire.

touch.definition: to deal with a particular problem, situation or person
touch.note: typical: the only lawyer who would touch the case NOT for: physical contact
examples: He was the only lawyer who would touch the case.
Nobody would touch the project because it was so risky.

travel.definition: to go from one place to another, especially over a long distance
travel.note: typical: travel abroad, by train, across a country NOT for: moving over short distances
examples: I'd like to travel abroad.
We travelled by train across Eastern Europe.

travel.definition: if light, sound, news or a disease travels, it moves or spreads from one place to another
travel.note: typical: sound, light, news, germs NOT for: people travelling
examples: Light travels faster than sound.
Bad news travels fast.

travel.definition: to move at a particular speed or in a particular direction
travel.note: typical: travel at 100 km/h NOT for: tourism
examples: The car was travelling at ninety miles an hour.
The bullet travelled through the wall.

travel.definition: to visit places and sell goods for a company (British)
travel.note: typical: travel for a company, sales representative NOT for: holiday trips
examples: He travels for a large publishing company.
She travelled all over Europe selling machinery.

travel.definition: if food or drink travels well, it stays in good condition when it is moved
travel.note: typical: wine, fruit that travels well NOT for: people travelling
examples: This wine doesn't travel well.
Apples travel well in a box.

try.definition: to take action in order to do something that you may not be able to do
try.note: typical: try to do something, try hard, try again NOT for: testing something
examples: He tried to control his voice.
Let's have a rest and then we'll try again.

try.definition: to do or use something for a short while to find out if it is suitable, successful or enjoyable
try.note: typical: try a new food, try doing something NOT for: making an effort to succeed
examples: It works really well; you should try it.
They decided to try living in America for a while.

try.definition: to judge a person in a court of law
try.note: typical: try someone for a crime, be tried NOT for: making an effort
examples: He was tried for murder and found guilty.
The case will be tried next month.

try.definition: to make someone feel impatient or annoyed (try someone's patience)
try.note: typical: try someone's patience NOT for: making an effort
examples: The children's constant noise tried her patience.
The long delay tried everyone's temper.

turn.definition: to move your body so that you are looking in a different direction
turn.note: typical: turn around, turn your head, turn away NOT for: a vehicle changing direction
examples: Ricky turned and walked away.
She turned her head in surprise.

turn.definition: to change direction when you are travelling, or to make a vehicle do this
turn.note: typical: turn left, right, a corner, a car NOT for: turning your body
examples: Turn left at the traffic lights.
The road turns sharply to the right.

turn.definition: to start to think about or deal with a particular person, thing or subject instead of what you were thinking about before
turn.note: typical: turn your attention, thoughts to NOT for: physical turning
examples: Many investors have turned their attention to opportunities abroad.
Next the Senator turned to education.

turn.definition: to refuse to help, support or be involved with someone or something (turn your back on someone)
turn.note: typical: turn your back on your family, your faith NOT for: physical turning
examples: How can you turn your back on your own mother?
He turned his back on his old friends.

turn.definition: to move around a central or fixed point, or to make something move in this way
turn.note: typical: wheels, handles, keys, taps NOT for: changing direction while travelling
examples: The wheels turned slowly, then picked up speed.
She gently turned the handle of the door.

turn.definition: to start to have a different quality or colour, or to make something do this (linking verb)
turn.note: typical: turn red, grey, cold, nasty NOT for: physical movement
examples: Rose's hair was already turning grey.
In October the leaves turn orange and yellow.

turn.definition: to become a particular age or to reach a particular time
turn.note: typical: turn 18, it's turned three NOT for: changing quality
examples: My son's just turned eighteen.
It's just turned three.

turn.definition: if the tide turns, the sea starts to come in or go out again
turn.note: typical: the tide turns NOT for: people turning
examples: We waited for the tide to turn.
The tide turns at about six o'clock.

turn.definition: if a war, situation or game turns, or someone turns it, something happens to change the way it is developing
turn.note: typical: turn the game, the tide of the war NOT for: physical turning
examples: Mills turned the game by scoring twice.
The victory turned the tide of the war.

turn.definition: to twist your ankle in a way that injures it
turn.note: typical: turn your ankle NOT for: twisting another body part
examples: Wright turned his ankle in the first minutes of the game.
She turned her ankle on the stairs.

turn.definition: to move a page so that the other side faces up (turn a page, turn over)
turn.note: typical: turn a page NOT for: turning the body
examples: Please turn to page twenty.
He turned the page and kept reading.

understand.definition: to know the meaning of what someone is telling you, or the language that they speak
understand.note: typical: understand English, understand what someone says NOT for: knowing how something works
examples: She doesn't understand English.
I'm sorry, I don't understand. Can you explain that again?

understand.definition: to know or realise how a fact, process or situation works, especially through learning or experience
understand.note: typical: understand how, why, the situation NOT for: understanding words
examples: You don't need to understand how computers work to be able to use them.
I don't really understand the political situation in Northern Ireland.

understand.definition: to realise how someone feels and why they behave the way they do, and to be sympathetic
understand.note: typical: understand someone, understand how you feel NOT for: understanding facts
examples: My parents just don't understand me.
I understand how you feel, but I think you're overreacting.

understand.definition: to believe or think that something is true because you have heard it or read it
understand.note: typical: I understand that, it is understood that NOT for: understanding words
examples: "I understand that he was 62 when he died," McLeish said.
It is understood that the Queen approves of the plan.

use.definition: to do something with a tool, method, service or ability for a particular purpose
use.note: typical: use a phone, a tool, a method NOT for: consuming a supply
examples: Can I use your phone?
Most people now use their cars to go shopping.

use.definition: to take an amount of something from a supply of food, gas, money or other things
use.note: typical: use water, electricity, fuel NOT for: using a tool
examples: We use about £40 worth of electricity a month.
Standard washing machines use about forty gallons of water.

use.definition: to make someone do something for you in order to get something you want, without caring about them
use.note: typical: use someone NOT for: using an object
examples: Can't you see that Howard is just using you?
He used her for his own ends.

use.definition: to take advantage of a situation
use.note: typical: use your position, your skills to do something NOT for: using a tool
examples: She used her position as manager to get jobs for her friends.
He used the delay to prepare his speech.

use.definition: to say or write a particular word or phrase
use.note: typical: use a word, language, a term NOT for: using a physical object
examples: We use the word 'hardware' to describe the actual machine.
Don't use bad language.

use.note: typical: use drugs, he used for years NOT for: using a tool
examples: He started using drugs when he was fifteen.
Do you know anyone who uses?

visit.definition: to go and spend time in a place or with someone, especially for pleasure or interest
visit.note: typical: visit friends, a city, a museum NOT for: officially inspecting something
examples: Eric went to Seattle to visit his cousins.
Which cities did you visit in Spain?

visit.definition: to go to a place as part of your official job, especially to examine it
visit.note: typical: visit a school, a site, troops NOT for: visiting for pleasure
examples: The building inspector is visiting the new housing project.
The Prime Minister visited the flooded area.

visit.definition: to go to see a doctor, lawyer or other professional for treatment or advice (formal)
visit.note: typical: visit a doctor, a dentist NOT for: visiting friends
examples: You should visit your doctor if the pain continues.
She visits a lawyer once a month.

visit.definition: to look at a website on the internet
visit.note: typical: visit a site, a page NOT for: visiting a place
examples: Over 7,000 people visit our site every week.
Please visit our website for more information.

visit.note: typical: visit with someone NOT for: travelling to see them
examples: Why don't you kids play outside while we visit with each other?
The neighbours stopped by to visit for a while.

wait.definition: to stay somewhere or not do something until something happens, someone arrives or something is ready
wait.note: typical: wait for someone, a bus, an answer NOT for: delaying something
examples: Hurry up! Everyone's waiting.
I'm still waiting for my results.

wait.definition: if something can wait, it is not urgent and can be done or dealt with later
wait.note: typical: it can wait, a job can wait NOT for: people standing in a queue
examples: The washing-up can wait until tomorrow.
Is this something that can wait?

walk.definition: to move forward by putting one foot in front of the other
walk.note: typical: walk home, to school, in the hills NOT for: running or driving
examples: We walked all the way to San Rafael.
He loved walking in the hills.

walk.definition: to walk somewhere with someone, especially to make sure that they are safe or to be polite
walk.note: typical: walk someone home, to the gate NOT for: walking alone
examples: It's late; I'll walk you home.
Schools are urging parents to walk their children to school.

walk.definition: to take a dog for a walk for exercise
walk.note: typical: walk the dog NOT for: walking yourself
examples: Grandma's out walking the dog.
I walk my dog twice a day.

walk.definition: if something has walked, it has disappeared and you think someone may have taken it (British, informal)
walk.note: typical: my pen has walked NOT for: someone walking
examples: My pen seems to have walked.
Somebody's walked off with my umbrella again.

walk.definition: to leave a court of law without being punished or sent to prison (walk free)
walk.note: typical: walk free, walk after charges are dropped NOT for: ordinary walking
examples: Ferguson walked free after the charges were dropped.
If more evidence isn't found, Harris will walk.

want.definition: to have a desire for something
want.note: typical: want a drink, want to go, want someone to do something NOT for: needing something urgently
examples: I really want a drink.
She'd always wanted to go to Thailand.

want.definition: to need something, or to ask someone firmly to do something for you
want.note: typical: want something done, want someone to do something NOT for: a simple wish
examples: I want that letter typed today.
I want you to find out what they're planning.

want.definition: to offer or suggest something to someone (do you want …?)
want.note: typical: do you want a drink, me to come NOT for: expressing your own wish
examples: Do you want a drink?
Do you want me to come with you?

want.definition: to say that something is sensible, or that someone should do something (might want to, want to do sth), especially when giving advice
want.note: typical: you might want to, you want to see a doctor NOT for: personal desire
examples: You might want to install anti-virus software.
You want to see a doctor about that cough.

want.definition: to ask for someone to come and talk to you or to come to a particular place (be wanted)
want.note: typical: be wanted on the phone, by the police NOT for: desire
examples: You're wanted on the phone.
The man is wanted by the police.

want.definition: to suffer because you do not have something (formal)
want.note: typical: want for food, shelter NOT for: ordinary desire
examples: In many poorer countries, people still want basic food and shelter.
The children never wanted for anything.

wash.definition: to clean something using water and a type of soap
wash.note: typical: wash dishes, clothes, a car NOT for: washing your own body
examples: This shirt needs washing.
It's your turn to wash the dishes.

wash.definition: to clean your body or part of your body with soap and water
wash.note: typical: wash your hands, hair, face NOT for: washing objects
examples: Amy washed and went to bed.
I'm just going to wash my hands.

wash.definition: if a river, sea or other water washes somewhere, it flows or moves there or carries something there
wash.note: typical: waves washing against, over NOT for: cleaning something
examples: The waves washed over her.
The body was washed ashore by waves.

wash.definition: if an explanation, excuse or argument doesn't wash with someone, they do not believe it or accept it (spoken)
wash.note: typical: that won't wash with me NOT for: cleaning
examples: That excuse won't wash with the boss.
His explanation just doesn't wash.

wash.definition: if cloth washes well, it is easy to clean using soap and water
wash.note: typical: silk doesn't wash well NOT for: washing something yourself
examples: Silk doesn't wash well.
This fabric washes well and dries quickly.

watch.definition: to look at someone or something for a period of time and pay attention to what is happening
watch.note: typical: watch TV, a film, a match, the sunset NOT for: looking after someone
examples: We sat and watched the sunset.
Do you mind if I watch?

watch.definition: to be careful in order to avoid an accident or an unwanted situation
watch.note: typical: watch your head, watch your budget, watch that NOT for: looking at something
examples: Watch he doesn't run into the road.
She's a student and has to watch her budget closely.

watch.definition: to look after someone or something for a short time
watch.note: typical: watch my bag, watch the children NOT for: looking at television
examples: Could you watch my bag while I buy a ticket?
She watched the children while their mother was at work.

watch.definition: to keep someone or something under observation, especially secretly
watch.note: typical: police watching a house, someone NOT for: ordinary viewing
examples: Police have been watching the house for a week.
I felt that someone was watching me.

work.definition: to do a job that you are paid for
work.note: typical: work for a company, as a teacher, full-time NOT for: making an effort without pay
examples: Where do you work?
She works as a consultant for a design company.

work.definition: to do the activities and duties that are part of your job
work.note: typical: work days, nights, late, from home NOT for: having a job in general
examples: Sally isn't working tomorrow.
We're sometimes expected to work twelve-hour days.

work.definition: if you work with a group of people, your job involves trying to help them
work.note: typical: work with children, among the poor NOT for: working with colleagues
examples: She has just retired after thirty-eight years working with children.
He has worked among some of the world's poorest people.

work.definition: to spend time and effort doing something
work.note: typical: work hard, in the garden NOT for: being employed
examples: I've been working in the garden all afternoon.
I'm going to have to work really hard to pass these exams.

work.definition: to try continuously to achieve a particular thing
work.note: typical: work towards, work for, work to do something NOT for: being employed
examples: They are working towards a solution to their problems.
We will work for the release of the hostages.

work.definition: if a machine or piece of equipment works, it does what it is supposed to do
work.note: typical: machines, keys, heaters, software NOT for: people working
examples: You should check that the smoke alarm is working properly.
The delete key doesn't work.

work.definition: to make a machine or piece of equipment do what it is supposed to do
work.note: typical: work a machine, a pump, a camera NOT for: a machine working by itself
examples: My parents can't even work the video.
Do you know how to work this coffee machine?

work.note: typical: a plan, a diet, a drug works NOT for: machines working
examples: Making a marriage work can take a lot of effort.
I've never found a diet that works.

work.definition: if something such as a situation or system works in a particular way, it has a particular effect on someone or something
work.note: typical: work well, in someone's favour NOT for: machines working
examples: The arrangement works well for everyone involved.
Sexism still works against women in many professions.

work.definition: if a painting, design or piece of writing works, it is successful because it has the effect that the artist or writer intended
work.note: typical: a scene, a colour combination works NOT for: machines working
examples: I don't think the scene with the horses really works.
The colour combination just doesn't work for me.

work.definition: to cut, sew or shape a material such as metal, leather or clay to make something
work.note: typical: work metal, clay, leather NOT for: using material in art
examples: The blacksmith worked the metal into a horseshoe.
She worked the clay into a bowl.

work.definition: to use a particular material or substance in order to make something such as a picture, design or jewellery
work.note: typical: work in steel, with silver NOT for: shaping a material
examples: He is a sculptor who works in steel.
She is a jeweller who works with silver.

work.definition: to move somewhere slowly and with difficulty, or to achieve something gradually by working (work your way)
work.note: typical: work your way up, through, across NOT for: ordinary work
examples: We worked our way carefully across the rock.
He worked his way up to head of department.

work.definition: to use and exercise a muscle or part of your body
work.note: typical: work a muscle, your legs NOT for: working in a job
examples: Swimming works every muscle in your body.
This exercise works your lower back.

write.definition: to produce a new book, article, poem or other piece of writing
write.note: typical: write a book, an essay, a poem NOT for: forming letters with a pen
examples: Who wrote 'Harry Potter'?
I can't come with you; I have an essay to write.

write.definition: to earn money by writing books, plays or articles
write.note: typical: write for a newspaper, magazine NOT for: writing a single piece
examples: Maureen Dowd writes for the New York Times.
Sean decided he wanted to write and quit his job.

write.definition: to put words in a letter to someone
write.note: typical: write to someone, write a letter NOT for: forming letters with a pen
examples: I've written to my MP and to the city council.
I wrote her several letters, but she didn't reply.

write.definition: to form letters or numbers with a pen or pencil
write.note: typical: learn to read and write NOT for: writing a piece of text
examples: Kerry could read and write when she was five.
He can't write his name yet.

write.definition: to state something in a book, letter, advertisement or on a label
write.note: typical: be written on, write that NOT for: creating a book
examples: Isabella wrote that she was dying.

write.definition: to write a piece of music or a song
write.note: typical: write a song, a symphony NOT for: writing a book
examples: Mozart wrote the music.

write.definition: to make a program for a computer to use
write.note: typical: write software, code NOT for: writing a document
examples: He writes software programs for financial institutions.
She wrote a program to sort the data.

write.definition: if a computer writes something, it records it on a disk or in its memory
write.note: typical: write data to disk NOT for: people writing
examples: The data was written to disk.
The program writes a copy to the backup drive.

write.definition: to write information on a cheque, form or similar document
write.note: typical: write a cheque, a prescription NOT for: writing a letter
examples: The doctor wrote me a prescription for sleeping pills.
I just wrote a cheque for the lot.

write.definition: if a pen writes, it works properly
write.note: typical: pens, pencils NOT for: people writing
examples: Do any of these pens write?
This pen doesn't write any more.

act.definition: to do something in a particular way or for a particular reason, or to take action
act.note: typical: act quickly, act in self-defence, act to do something NOT for: performing on stage
examples: The company acted correctly in sacking him.

act.definition: to behave in a particular way
act.note: typical: act strangely, act like a baby NOT for: pretending
examples: He's been acting strangely ever since his mother died.
Stop acting like a baby.

act.definition: to pretend to have feelings or qualities that are different from your true ones
act.note: typical: act the fool, act crazy, act a part NOT for: behaving sincerely
examples: That guy is acting crazy.
Stella felt as if she was acting a part.

act.definition: to perform in a play or film
act.note: typical: act a role, in a play NOT for: pretending in real life
examples: I first started acting when I was twelve years old.
She is acting the role of Lady Macbeth six evenings a week.

act.definition: to have an effect or use
act.note: typical: act as a cushion, act on bacteria NOT for: performing a role
examples: The padding acts as a cushion if the player falls.
Disinfectants act on bacteria in two main ways.

afford.definition: to have enough money to buy or pay for something
afford.note: typical: can't afford to buy, can afford a holiday NOT for: being able to take a risk
examples: We can't afford to go on holiday this year.
I couldn't afford the rent.

afford.definition: to be able to do something without risk, trouble or bad results
afford.note: typical: can't afford to lose, to wait NOT for: money
examples: We can't afford to lose any more time.
He can't afford to make another mistake.

afford.definition: to give or provide something such as an opportunity or protection (formal)
afford.note: typical: afford an opportunity, protection, pleasure NOT for: paying money
examples: The window affords a fine view of the harbour.
The course affords students a chance to travel.

agree.definition: to have or express the same opinion about something as someone else
agree.note: typical: agree with someone, agree that, agree on NOT for: saying yes to a plan
examples: Teenagers and their parents rarely agree.
If she felt he was right, she would agree with him.

agree.definition: to say yes to an idea, plan or suggestion
agree.note: typical: agree to do something, agree to a plan NOT for: having the same opinion
examples: I suggested we go somewhere for the weekend, and she agreed at once.
No one really knows why he agreed to do the film.

agree.definition: to make a decision with someone after a discussion with them
agree.note: typical: agree on a date, a price, a plan NOT for: expressing an opinion
examples: We agreed to meet again the following Monday.
They managed to agree on a date for the wedding.

agree.definition: if two pieces of information agree with each other, they match or are the same
agree.note: typical: stories, figures agree NOT for: people agreeing
examples: Your story doesn't agree with what the police have told us.
The two sets of figures don't agree.

allow.definition: to let someone do or have something, or to let something happen
allow.note: typical: allow someone to do something, be allowed NOT for: making something possible
examples: My parents wouldn't allow me to go to the party.
Women are not allowed to enter the mosque.

allow.definition: to make it possible for something to happen or for someone to do something
allow.note: typical: allow for, allow someone to do something NOT for: giving permission
examples: This adjustment of the figures allows a fairer comparison.

allow.definition: to make sure that you have enough time, money or food available for a particular purpose
allow.note: typical: allow time, allow for NOT for: giving permission
examples: Allow yourselves plenty of time to get to the airport.
I've allowed half a bottle of wine for each person.

allow.definition: to accept that something is correct or true, or acceptable according to the rules or law (formal)
allow.note: typical: allow that, the judge allowed the evidence NOT for: giving permission to a person
examples: I allow that there may have been a mistake.
The judge allowed the evidence.

announce.definition: to officially tell people about something, especially a plan or a decision
announce.note: typical: announce a decision, a plan, a result NOT for: saying something loudly
examples: The government has announced plans to create 10,000 new jobs.

announce.definition: to say something, especially something that other people may not like, in a loud and confident way
announce.note: typical: 'I'm leaving,' he announced NOT for: official statements
examples: "I'm not going to their party," Maggie announced.
He stood up and announced that he was ready to go.

announce.definition: to give information to people using a loudspeaker or microphone, especially at an airport or railway station
announce.note: typical: announce a flight, a train NOT for: official plans
examples: They were announcing the arrival of Flight 207 from Minneapolis.
The next train was announced over the loudspeaker.

announce.definition: to officially tell people that someone has arrived at a particular place
announce.note: typical: announce a guest, yourself NOT for: announcing news
examples: The butler announced the guests as they arrived.
He knocked and announced himself at the door.

apologise.definition: to tell someone that you are sorry that you have done something wrong
apologise.note: typical: apologise to someone for something NOT for: expressing a polite regret
examples: I'm so sorry; I do apologise.
He later apologised for his behaviour.

appear.definition: used to say how something seems, especially from what you know about it or can see (linking verb)
appear.note: typical: appear to be, it appears that NOT for: suddenly becoming visible
examples: There appear to be signs of a break-in.
It appears that all the files have been deleted.

appear.definition: used to say that someone or something seems to have a particular quality or feeling (linking verb)
appear.note: typical: appear calm, rude, bigger NOT for: coming into view
examples: He tried hard to appear calm.
The right colours can make a small room appear much bigger.

appear.definition: to start to be seen, to arrive or to exist in a place, especially suddenly
appear.note: typical: appear from nowhere, at the window NOT for: seeming
examples: A man suddenly appeared from behind a tree.
Small cracks appeared in the wall.

appear.definition: to take part in a film, play, concert or television programme
appear.note: typical: appear in a film, on stage, on TV NOT for: suddenly becoming visible
examples: She has already appeared in a number of films.
He appeared on national television to deny the claims.

appear.definition: to be written or shown in a list, book, newspaper or document
appear.note: typical: appear in print, in the paper NOT for: people appearing
examples: The story appeared in all the national newspapers.
Her name appears on the list.

appear.definition: to become widely available or known about
appear.note: typical: new products appearing in shops NOT for: suddenly becoming visible
examples: The new range will be appearing in shops in the autumn.
New courses are appearing every year.

argue.definition: to disagree with someone in words, often in an angry way
argue.note: typical: argue with someone, about something NOT for: giving reasons for an opinion
examples: We could hear the neighbours arguing.
They were arguing about how to spend the money.

argue.definition: to state, giving clear reasons, that something is true or should be done
argue.note: typical: argue that, argue for, against NOT for: an angry quarrel
examples: Croft argued that a date should be set for the withdrawal of troops.
Baker argued against cutting the military budget.

argue.definition: to persuade someone to do or not to do something (British)
argue.note: typical: argue someone into, out of doing something NOT for: quarrelling
examples: Joyce argued me into buying a new jacket.
He argued her out of leaving.

argue.definition: to show that something clearly exists or is true (formal)
argue.note: typical: the statement argues a change NOT for: quarrelling
examples: The statement argues a change of attitude by the management.
Her behaviour argues a lack of confidence.

arrange.definition: to organise or make plans for something such as a meeting, party or trip
arrange.note: typical: arrange a meeting, an appointment, to meet NOT for: putting things in order
examples: Contact your local branch to arrange an appointment.
Have you arranged to meet Mark this weekend?

arrange.definition: to make it possible for someone to have or do something
arrange.note: typical: arrange for a taxi, for someone to do something NOT for: organising an event yourself
examples: The company will arrange for a taxi to meet you at the airport.
Dave arranged for someone to drive him home.

arrange.definition: to put a group of things or people in a particular order or position
arrange.note: typical: arrange flowers, furniture, alphabetically NOT for: planning an event
examples: Ben arranged the flowers in a vase.
The list is arranged alphabetically.

arrange.definition: to write or change a piece of music so that it is suitable for a particular instrument
arrange.note: typical: arrange a song, a symphony for piano NOT for: organising events
examples: The symphony was arranged for the piano.
She arranged the folk songs for a choir.

attack.definition: to deliberately use violence to hurt a person or damage a place
attack.note: typical: be attacked, a gang attacks NOT for: criticising
examples: She was attacked while walking home late at night.
His shop was attacked by a gang of youths.

attack.definition: to start using guns, bombs or other weapons against an enemy in a war
attack.note: typical: troops, tanks, planes attack NOT for: attacks on individuals
examples: Army tanks attacked a village near the capital on Sunday.
The enemy attacked at dawn.

attack.definition: to criticise someone or something very strongly
attack.note: typical: attack a policy, a person NOT for: physical violence
examples: Newspapers attacked the government for failing to cut taxes.
The minister publicly attacked the idea.

attack.definition: if a disease, insect or chemical attacks something, it damages it
attack.note: typical: disease attacks the brain, insects attack crops NOT for: people attacking
examples: The disease attacks the brain and nervous system.
Insects attacked the crops.

attack.definition: to begin to do something in a determined and eager way
attack.note: typical: attack a problem, a meal NOT for: physical violence
examples: She immediately set about attacking the problem.
Martin attacked his meal with great enthusiasm.

attack.definition: to move forward and try to score goals or win points in a sport
attack.note: typical: attack more, attack down the wing NOT for: defending
examples: Brazil began to attack more in the second half.
The team attacked down the left wing.

avoid.definition: to prevent something bad from happening
avoid.note: typical: avoid an accident, a risk, a disaster NOT for: staying away from a person
examples: Road safety is taught to young children to avoid road accidents.
Alan narrowly avoided an accident.

avoid.definition: to stay away from someone or something, or not to use something
avoid.note: typical: avoid someone, a place, certain foods NOT for: preventing an accident
examples: Everyone seemed to be avoiding Nick.
Pregnant women should avoid certain foods such as raw eggs.

avoid.definition: to deliberately not do something, especially something wrong, dangerous or harmful
avoid.note: typical: avoid doing something NOT for: staying away from a person
examples: There are ways of legally avoiding taxes.
You should avoid overspending in the first half of the year.

become.definition: to start to have a feeling or quality (linking verb)
become.note: typical: become warmer, tired, famous NOT for: being suitable for someone
examples: The weather became warmer.
She became more confident as the weeks went by.

become.definition: to start to develop into something, or to start to have a particular job or role
become.note: typical: become a doctor, friends, a problem NOT for: a change of quality
examples: He wants to become a doctor.
The two of them became friends at university.

become.definition: to look good on someone or to be suitable for someone (formal, old-fashioned)
become.note: typical: that dress becomes you NOT for: developing into something
examples: That colour really becomes you.
Such rude behaviour hardly becomes a person of your age.

behave.definition: to act in a particular way
behave.note: typical: behave badly, well, like a child NOT for: how machines or substances react
examples: The children behaved badly all afternoon.
Stop behaving like a baby.

behave.definition: to be polite and obedient, especially when you are a child (behave yourself)
behave.note: typical: behave yourself, behave NOT for: acting in a particular way in general
examples: If you behave yourself, we'll go to the park.
Will you please behave while the guests are here?

behave.definition: if a machine, substance or system behaves in a particular way, it works or reacts in that way
behave.note: typical: metals, machines, materials behaving in a way NOT for: people
examples: Metals behave differently at very low temperatures.
The software behaves strangely when two programs are open.

belong.definition: if something belongs somewhere, that is the right place or situation for it
belong.note: typical: belong in, belong here NOT for: owning something
examples: Put the chair back where it belongs.
That attitude doesn't belong in modern society.

belong.definition: if you feel you belong in a place or situation, you feel happy and comfortable in it because you have the same interests as other people
belong.note: typical: feel you belong, a sense of belonging NOT for: owning something
examples: I worked there for five years but never really felt I belonged.
She finally felt that she belonged in the team.

bend.definition: to move part of your body so that it is not straight or you are not upright
bend.note: typical: bend your knees, bend over, down NOT for: bending an object
examples: Bend your knees, but keep your back straight.
Emma bent over to pick up the coins.

bend.definition: to push or press something so that it is no longer flat or straight
bend.note: typical: bend metal, wire, a pipe NOT for: bending your body
examples: You need a special tool to bend the steel.
He bent the wire into a circle.

bend.definition: to become curved and no longer flat or straight
bend.note: typical: branches, roads, rivers bending NOT for: people bending
examples: Several branches started bending towards the ground.
The road bends sharply to the left.

blow.definition: if the wind or a current of air blows, it moves
blow.note: typical: wind, a breeze blowing NOT for: people blowing air
examples: A cold breeze was blowing hard.
Outside, the weather was blowing a gale.

blow.definition: to move, or to move something, by the force of the wind or a current of air
blow.note: typical: blow away, shut, open NOT for: people blowing out air
examples: Her hair was blowing in the breeze.
A sudden draught blew the door shut.

blow.definition: to send air out from your mouth
blow.note: typical: blow on soup, blow smoke NOT for: the wind
examples: She blew onto her coffee to cool it down.
He blew the smoke right in my face.

blow.definition: to make a sound by passing air through a whistle, horn or similar object
blow.note: typical: blow a whistle, a horn, a trumpet NOT for: making a flow of air
examples: The whistle blew for half time.
A truck went by and blew its horn at her.

blow.definition: to damage or destroy something violently with an explosion or by shooting
blow.note: typical: be blown to pieces, off, up NOT for: a gentle wind
examples: Part of his leg had been blown off.
A bomb like that could blow you to bits.

blow.definition: to lose a good opportunity by making a mistake or by being careless (informal)
blow.note: typical: blow a chance, an opportunity NOT for: the wind
examples: We've blown our chances of getting that contract.
You've got a great future ahead of you; don't blow it.

blow.definition: to spend a lot of money in a careless way, especially on one thing (informal)
blow.note: typical: blow all the money on something NOT for: saving money
examples: I blew all the money I won on a trip to Hawaii.
He blew his savings on a sports car.

blow.definition: to clean your nose by forcing air through it into a cloth or soft paper
blow.note: typical: blow your nose NOT for: blowing smoke
examples: She blew her nose and wiped her eyes.
Blow your nose; it's running.

blow.definition: to kiss your hand and then pretend to blow the kiss towards someone
blow.note: typical: blow someone a kiss NOT for: kissing someone
examples: She leant out of the window and blew him a kiss.
The children blew kisses to their grandma.

blow.definition: if an electrical fuse blows, or a piece of equipment blows a fuse, the electricity suddenly stops working because a thin wire has melted
blow.note: typical: fuses, bulbs blowing NOT for: wind
examples: The floodlights blew a fuse.
The kettle blew a fuse and the lights went out.

blow.definition: if a tyre blows, or a car blows a tyre, it bursts
blow.note: typical: tyres blowing out NOT for: fuses
examples: One of the tyres blew on the motorway.
The car blew a tyre and spun off the road.

blow.definition: to make or shape something by sending air out from your mouth
blow.note: typical: blow bubbles, glass NOT for: blowing your nose
examples: The kids were blowing bubbles in the backyard.
The craftsman blew glass into delicate shapes.

borrow.definition: to use something that belongs to someone else and that you must give back to them later
borrow.note: typical: borrow a pen, a book, money from someone NOT for: lending to someone
examples: Can I borrow your pen for a minute?
You are allowed to borrow six books from the library at a time.

borrow.definition: to take or copy someone's ideas, words or other work and use them in your own work or language
borrow.note: typical: borrow an idea, words from another language NOT for: borrowing an object
examples: English has borrowed words from many languages.
She borrowed the idea from a famous poem.

bother.definition: to make the effort to do something
bother.note: typical: (not) bother to do something, bother with something NOT for: annoying someone
examples: He didn't bother to answer the question.
Many young people didn't bother voting.

bother.definition: to make someone feel slightly worried, upset or concerned
bother.note: typical: it bothers me that, it doesn't bother me NOT for: interrupting someone
examples: Being in a crowd really bothers me.
It really bothered me that he'd forgotten my birthday.

bother.definition: to annoy someone, especially by interrupting them when they are trying to do something
bother.note: typical: bother someone, don't bother me NOT for: causing worry
examples: Danny, don't bother Ellen while she's reading.
It didn't seem worth bothering the doctor about.

bother.definition: if a part of your body bothers you, it is slightly painful or uncomfortable
bother.note: typical: my back is bothering me NOT for: emotional worry
examples: My back's been bothering me.
His knee has been bothering him since the match.

bother.definition: to upset or frighten someone by talking to them when they do not want to talk to you
bother.note: typical: bother someone, a stranger NOT for: slightly annoying someone
examples: Don't worry; my dog won't bother you.
If he starts bothering you, let me know.

bounce.definition: if a ball or other object bounces, or you bounce it, it immediately moves up or away from a surface after hitting it
bounce.note: typical: a ball, bounce off NOT for: people jumping
examples: The ball bounced off the post and into the goal.
The kids were bouncing a ball against the wall.

bounce.definition: to move up and down, especially because you are hitting a surface made of rubber or with springs
bounce.note: typical: bounce on a trampoline, a bed NOT for: a ball bouncing
examples: Lyn was bouncing on the trampoline.
Stop bouncing up and down on the sofa.

bounce.definition: if a cheque bounces, or a bank bounces it, the bank will not pay any money because there is not enough in the account
bounce.note: typical: a cheque bounces NOT for: a ball bouncing
examples: Her cheque bounced because she had no money in the account.
The bank bounced three of my cheques.

bounce.definition: to walk quickly and with a lot of energy
bounce.note: typical: bounce into the room NOT for: objects bouncing
examples: Olivia came bouncing into the room.
He bounced down the stairs with a big smile.

bounce.definition: if something bounces, it moves quickly up and down as you move
bounce.note: typical: hair, curls bouncing NOT for: a ball
examples: Her hair bounced when she walked.
The curls bounced on her shoulders.

bounce.definition: if light or sound bounces, it hits a surface and then moves quickly away from it
bounce.note: typical: bounce off a surface, a wall, a satellite NOT for: a ball
examples: The radio signals are bounced off a satellite.
The light bounced off the water.

bounce.definition: if an email you send bounces, it is returned to you because of a technical problem
bounce.note: typical: an email bounces, bounce back NOT for: a cheque
examples: My email bounced; I think I typed the address wrong.
Several messages bounced back.

bounce.definition: to talk about your ideas with someone in order to get their opinion (bounce ideas off someone)
bounce.note: typical: bounce ideas off colleagues NOT for: physical bouncing
examples: When you work in a team, you can bounce your ideas off each other.
I'd like to bounce a few ideas off you.

celebrate.definition: to show that an event or occasion is important by doing something special or enjoyable
celebrate.note: typical: celebrate a birthday, Christmas, a victory NOT for: praising someone
examples: It's Dad's birthday and we're going out for a meal to celebrate.
How do you usually celebrate New Year?

celebrate.note: typical: poems that celebrate NOT for: a party
examples: The poem celebrates the joys of love.
Her songs celebrate the beauty of the countryside.

celebrate.definition: to perform a religious ceremony, especially the Christian Mass
celebrate.note: typical: celebrate Mass NOT for: a party
examples: The priest celebrated Mass in the village church.
The bishop celebrated the service.

change.definition: to become different, or to make something become different
change.note: typical: change a lot, change into something NOT for: replacing something with a new one
examples: Susan has changed a lot since I last saw her.
The leaves on trees change colour in the autumn.

change.definition: to stop doing or using one thing and start doing or using something else
change.note: typical: change jobs, change course, change the subject NOT for: becoming different
examples: She changed jobs in May.
The ship changed course and headed south.

change.definition: to put or use something new or different in place of something else, especially because it is old, damaged or broken
change.note: typical: change a tyre, the locks, a date NOT for: becoming different
examples: Three boys were changing a tyre by the side of the road.
The time of the meeting has been changed from 11 a.m. to 10:30.

change.definition: to leave one party, group or side and join an opposing one
change.note: typical: change sides NOT for: changing clothes
examples: It's quite rare for politicians to change sides.
Several players changed sides during the match.

change.definition: to take off your clothes and put on different ones
change.note: typical: change your dress, get changed NOT for: changing a baby
examples: You'd better go and get changed.
Sara changed into her swimsuit and ran out for a quick swim.

change.definition: to put a clean nappy on a baby
change.note: typical: change a baby, a nappy NOT for: changing your own clothes
examples: Could you change the baby while I make lunch?
She changed his nappy and put him to bed.

change.definition: to take the dirty sheets off a bed and put on clean ones
change.note: typical: change the sheets, the bed NOT for: changing clothes
examples: I need to change the sheets on the beds.
Have you changed the bed in the guest room?

change.definition: to take something you have bought back to a shop and get something different instead (British)
change.note: typical: change a pair of gloves, a jumper for another NOT for: becoming different
