examples: I bought these gloves for my daughter, but they're too large; can I change them for a smaller size?
You can change the shirt if it doesn't fit.

change.definition: to exchange a larger note or coin for smaller units of money that add up to the same value
change.note: typical: change a £20 note NOT for: exchanging currencies
examples: Can you change a £20 note?
Could you change this into coins for the machine?

change.definition: to exchange money from one country for the same value of money from another country
change.note: typical: change dollars into pesos NOT for: breaking a banknote
examples: I want to change my dollars into pesos.
Where can I change some euros into pounds?

change.definition: to get off one train, bus or aircraft and into another in order to continue your journey
change.note: typical: change trains, buses, planes NOT for: changing clothes
examples: Passengers for Liverpool should change at Crewe.
I had to change planes in Denver.

change.definition: to give someone your place and take theirs, or to take someone else's position in life (change places with someone)
change.note: typical: change places with someone NOT for: changing a plan
examples: Would you mind changing places with me so I can sit next to my friend?
She may be rich, but I wouldn't want to change places with her.

change.definition: to put the engine of a vehicle into a higher or lower gear
change.note: typical: change gear, change up, down NOT for: changing clothes
examples: Change into second gear as you approach the corner.
Change down before you get to the hill.

charge.definition: to ask someone for a particular amount of money for something you are selling
charge.note: typical: charge a fee, a price, rent, interest NOT for: paying money
examples: The hotel charges $125 a night.
The gallery charges an entrance fee.

charge.definition: to record the cost of something on someone's account so that they can pay for it later
charge.note: typical: charge something to an account, a room NOT for: asking for a price
examples: Wilson charged the drinks to his room.
Use a courier and charge it to the department.

charge.definition: to pay for something with a credit card (American)
charge.note: typical: charge something on Visa NOT for: asking for a price
examples: I charged the shoes on Visa.
"How would you like to pay?" "I'll charge it."

charge.definition: to state officially that someone may be guilty of a crime
charge.note: typical: charge someone with murder, theft NOT for: publicly accusing someone
examples: Gibbons has been charged with murder.
Police have charged two men with burglary.

charge.definition: to say publicly that you think someone has done something wrong (formal)
charge.note: typical: charge that NOT for: an official legal charge
examples: Demonstrators have charged that the police used excessive force.
Critics charged that the report ignored key facts.

charge.definition: to deliberately run or walk somewhere quickly
charge.note: typical: charge around, through, out NOT for: attacking
examples: The boys charged around the garden.
She charged out of the room in a rage.

charge.definition: to rush quickly towards someone or something in order to attack them
charge.note: typical: charge the enemy, at someone NOT for: running somewhere
examples: The bear charged towards her at full speed.
The soldiers charged the enemy position.

charge.definition: if a battery charges, or you charge it, it takes in and stores electricity
charge.note: typical: charge a phone, a battery NOT for: running
examples: The shaver can be charged up overnight.
I need to charge my phone.

charge.definition: to order someone to do something or make them responsible for it (formal)
charge.note: typical: charge someone with doing something NOT for: a legal accusation
examples: The commission is charged with investigating war crimes.
He was charged with looking after the funds.

chat.definition: to talk in a friendly and informal way, especially about things that are not important
chat.note: typical: chat to someone, chat away NOT for: a serious discussion
examples: John and I sat up until the early hours chatting.
Mary was there, chatting to her mother.

chat.definition: to communicate with several people in a chat room on the internet
chat.note: typical: chat online, in a chat room NOT for: talking face to face
examples: She spends hours chatting online with friends.
They chatted in a chat room about their favourite band.

check.definition: to do something in order to find out whether something is correct, true or in good condition
check.note: typical: check facts, calculations, check that NOT for: asking permission
examples: Check that all the doors are locked.
Always check your calculations.

check.definition: to ask someone whether something is correct, true or allowed
check.note: typical: check with someone, call to check NOT for: examining something yourself
examples: I'll have to check first before I can give you a refund.
Call the factory to check whether the beds can be delivered today.

check.definition: to suddenly stop yourself from saying or doing something because you realise it would be better not to
check.note: typical: check yourself, check an urge NOT for: examining something
examples: I had to check the urge to laugh out loud.
He grinned, then checked himself.

check.definition: to stop something bad from getting worse, or to slow it down (formal)
check.note: typical: check inflation, the spread of a disease NOT for: examining something
examples: The government is trying to check the growth of unemployment.
New measures were introduced to check the spread of the disease.

check.definition: to mark something with a tick to show that it is correct or has been dealt with (American)
check.note: typical: check a box, check off a list NOT for: examining something
examples: Check the box if you agree to the terms.
She checked the names off on her list.

check.definition: to leave a bag, coat or other item with someone so that they can look after it (American)
check.note: typical: check your coat, your bags NOT for: examining something
examples: Please check your coat at the door.
We checked our bags at the airport.

choose.definition: to decide which one of a number of things or people you want
choose.note: typical: choose a carpet, a winner, choose between NOT for: deciding what you prefer to do
examples: It took us ages to choose a new carpet.
A panel of judges will choose the winner.

choose.definition: to decide to do something because that is what you prefer to do
choose.note: typical: choose to do something NOT for: picking one of several things
examples: He chose to ignore his advice.
You can invest in the stock market, if you choose.

collect.definition: to get things of the same type from different places and bring them together
collect.note: typical: collect information, signatures, data NOT for: collecting as a hobby
examples: The company collects information about consumer trends.
We've been out collecting signatures for our petition.

collect.definition: to get and keep objects of the same type because you think they are attractive or interesting
collect.note: typical: collect stamps, coins, teddy bears NOT for: gathering information
examples: Arlene collects teddy bears.
He has been collecting stamps since he was ten.

collect.definition: to get money that you are owed
collect.note: typical: collect tax, rent, a debt NOT for: asking for donations
examples: The landlady came around once a month to collect the rent.
The agency collects debts for banks.

collect.definition: to ask people to give you money or goods for an organisation that helps people
collect.note: typical: collect for charity NOT for: collecting debts
examples: I'm collecting for Children in Need.
The pupils collected money for the hospital.

collect.definition: if something collects in a place, it gradually increases in amount
collect.note: typical: dust, rainwater collecting NOT for: collecting objects
examples: Rain collected in pools on the road.
Dust had collected on the shelves.

collect.definition: to receive something because you have won a race, game or other contest
collect.note: typical: collect a medal, a prize NOT for: collecting money
examples: Redgrave collected his fifth Olympic gold medal in Sydney.
She collected the trophy at the ceremony.

collect.definition: to make an effort to remain calm and think clearly (collect yourself, your thoughts)
collect.note: typical: collect your thoughts NOT for: gathering objects
examples: I got there early so I had a few minutes to collect my thoughts.
He took a deep breath to collect himself.

collect.definition: to go to a place and take away someone or something that is waiting for you (British)
collect.note: typical: collect a child from school, a parcel NOT for: gathering things over time
examples: Martin's gone to collect the children from school.
I've got to go and collect the book from the library.

comb.definition: to make hair look tidy using a comb
comb.note: typical: comb your hair NOT for: searching a place
examples: She combed her hair in front of the mirror.
He combed the child's wet hair.

comb.definition: to search a place very carefully in order to find something
comb.note: typical: comb a place for something NOT for: tidying hair
examples: Police combed the woods for the missing child.
I combed the shop for a birthday present.

complain.definition: to say that you are not satisfied with something or someone
complain.note: typical: complain about, to someone NOT for: describing a pain
examples: Several customers complained about the service they received.
Neighbours complained to the police about the dogs barking.

complain.definition: to say that you have a pain or illness (complain of)
complain.note: typical: complain of a headache, pain NOT for: criticising something
examples: He complained of a headache and went to bed.
She complained of chest pains.

contact.definition: to write to or telephone someone, or to get in touch with them in another way
contact.note: typical: contact someone by email, phone NOT for: physically touching
examples: You can contact me by email.
Please contact us if you have any problems.

continue.definition: to not stop happening, existing or doing something
continue.note: typical: continue to do something, continue doing NOT for: starting again after a break
examples: Sheila continued to work after she had her baby.
The strike continued for another four weeks.

continue.definition: to start again or start doing something again after an interruption
continue.note: typical: continue the search, fighting continued NOT for: never stopping
examples: After a brief ceasefire, fighting continued.
He picked up his book and continued reading.

continue.definition: to go further in the same direction
continue.note: typical: continue along, down, into NOT for: time passing
examples: We continued along the road for some time.
The road continues northwards to the border.

continue.definition: to stay in the same job or situation
continue.note: typical: continue as director NOT for: moving to another job
examples: Miss Silva will continue as publishing director.
He will continue as captain next season.

continue.definition: to say more after an interruption
continue.note: typical: 'And so,' he continued NOT for: general actions
examples: "And so," he continued, "we will try harder next time."
"There's more," she continued.

correct.definition: to make something right or make it work the way it should
correct.note: typical: correct a mistake, a problem, eyesight NOT for: pointing out someone's error
examples: Some eyesight problems are relatively easy to correct.
You have the right to correct any mistakes in your file.

correct.definition: to show someone that something they said or did is wrong, and make it right
correct.note: typical: correct someone, correct yourself NOT for: fixing a problem
examples: Correct my pronunciation if it's wrong.
"She's in Ireland now." "She was," Farrell corrected him.

correct.definition: if a teacher corrects a student's written work, they write marks on it to show the mistakes in it
correct.note: typical: correct homework, tests, essays NOT for: correcting speech
examples: The teacher spent the whole weekend correcting exam papers.
I still have thirty essays to correct.

cover.definition: to put something over something else in order to hide, close or protect it
cover.note: typical: cover a pot, your face, a table NOT for: forming a layer on a surface
examples: Cover the pot and bake for an hour.
Dan covered his face with his hands.

cover.definition: if something covers a surface, it forms a layer over it
cover.note: typical: snow, dust, mould covering something NOT for: covering something on purpose
examples: Much of the country is covered by snow.
The walls were covered with messages.

cover.definition: to include or deal with a particular subject or group of things
cover.note: typical: a course, a book, a law covering something NOT for: covering a surface
examples: The course covers business law.
The new law covers all kinds of weapons.

cover.note: typical: cover forty miles, a lot of ground NOT for: covering a surface
examples: They were hoping to cover forty miles yesterday.
A leopard can cover a lot of ground very quickly.

cover.note: typical: a city covers 25 square miles NOT for: covering a surface with a layer
examples: The city covers twenty-five square miles.
The forest covers most of the island.

cover.definition: to report the details of an event for a newspaper, television or radio programme
cover.note: typical: cover a war, a trial, an election NOT for: hiding something
examples: I'd just returned from covering the war.
She covers politics for the local paper.

cover.definition: if a sum of money covers the cost of something, it is enough to pay for it
cover.note: typical: cover costs, expenses, fees NOT for: hiding something
examples: The award should be enough to cover her tuition fees.
Airlines are raising fares to cover the rising costs of fuel.

cover.definition: if your insurance covers you or your possessions, it promises to pay you money if you have an accident or something is stolen
cover.note: typical: be covered by insurance NOT for: dealing with a subject
examples: Most policies cover accidental damage to pipes.
Are we covered for theft?

cover.definition: to protect someone by being ready to shoot anyone who attacks them
cover.note: typical: cover me NOT for: hiding with a cloth
examples: I'll make for the door; cover me, will you?
The soldiers covered their comrades as they crossed the bridge.

cover.definition: in sports, to stay close to a member of the opposing team to prevent them from scoring or gaining points
cover.note: typical: cover a player, a striker NOT for: covering a surface
examples: He was told to cover the opposing striker all game.
Two defenders covered the star player.

cover.definition: to perform or record a song that was originally recorded by another artist
cover.note: typical: cover a song, a hit NOT for: reporting news
examples: They've covered several hits from the 1980s.
The band covered an old Beatles song.

cross.definition: to go or stretch from one side of something such as a road, river or room to the other
cross.note: typical: cross the road, a river, a room NOT for: going over a line
examples: It's easy to have an accident just crossing the road.
An old bridge crosses the river.

cross.definition: to go over and beyond a line, track or boundary
cross.note: typical: cross the finish line, a border NOT for: crossing a road
examples: He raised his arms in triumph as he crossed the line.
They crossed the border at night.

cross.definition: if two or more roads or lines cross, or if one crosses another, they go across each other
cross.note: typical: roads, lines, paths crossing NOT for: people crossing a road
examples: The by-pass crosses the main road at a roundabout.
The two lines cross at a right angle.

cross.definition: to mix two different breeds of animal or plant to form a new breed
cross.note: typical: cross cattle, a flower with another NOT for: crossing a road
examples: These cattle were crossed with a breed from the highlands.
A new flower was produced by crossing two varieties.

cross.definition: if an idea or thought crosses your mind, you think about it briefly
cross.note: typical: it crossed my mind that NOT for: physical crossing
examples: It never crossed my mind that she might be lying.
The thought has crossed my mind more than once.

cross.definition: if an expression crosses someone's face, it appears on their face
cross.note: typical: a smile, a look crosses someone's face NOT for: physical crossing
examples: A look of surprise crossed her face.
A faint smile crossed his lips.

cross.definition: to put one leg, arm or finger over another
cross.note: typical: cross your legs, arms, fingers NOT for: crossing a road
examples: She sat down and crossed her legs.
He stood with his arms crossed.

cross.definition: to hope that something will happen in the way you want, by crossing your fingers
cross.note: typical: cross your fingers, keep your fingers crossed NOT for: crossing legs
examples: I'm crossing my fingers that the weather will be fine.
Keep your fingers crossed for me.

cross.definition: if people's paths cross, they meet, usually without expecting it
cross.note: typical: paths cross NOT for: roads crossing
examples: Our paths crossed again twenty years later.
We didn't cross paths again until 2001.

decide.definition: to make a choice or judgment about something, especially after considering all the possibilities or arguments
decide.note: typical: decide to do something, decide whether NOT for: deciding the result of something
examples: Tina has decided to go to Rome for her holidays.
I can't decide whether I like him or not.

decide.definition: to be the thing that determines the result of something
decide.note: typical: decide the outcome, the match NOT for: making a personal choice
examples: A late goal decided the match.
The final vote will decide the matter.

decorate.definition: to paint the inside of a room, put special paper on the walls and so on (British)
decorate.note: typical: decorate a room, a house NOT for: adding pretty things to something
examples: The bathroom is decorated in green and yellow.
We plan to spend the weekend decorating.

decorate.definition: to make something look more attractive by putting something pretty on it
decorate.note: typical: decorate a cake, a tree, the walls NOT for: painting a room
examples: Children's pictures decorated the walls of the classroom.
She decorated the cake with fruit and cream.

decorate.definition: to give someone a medal as an official sign of honour
decorate.note: typical: decorated for bravery NOT for: making something look attractive
examples: The soldiers were decorated for bravery.
He was decorated with the highest award.

depend.definition: used to say that you cannot give a definite answer because the answer will be affected by something else (it depends)
depend.note: typical: it depends, it depends who/what/how NOT for: needing help from someone
examples: "How long are you staying?" "I don't know; it depends."
It depends how much you want to lose.

depend.definition: if something depends on something else, it is directly affected or decided by that thing
depend.note: typical: depend on the weather, on how/what/whether NOT for: needing help from someone
examples: The length of time spent exercising depends on the sport you are training for.
Choosing the right bike depends on what you want to use it for.

depend.definition: to need the support, help or existence of someone or something in order to exist, be healthy or be successful
depend.note: typical: depend on someone for something, depend heavily on NOT for: being affected by something
examples: The country depends heavily on its tourist trade.
We depend entirely on donations from the public.

describe.definition: to say what something or someone is like by giving details about them
describe.note: typical: describe a person, a place, how something happened NOT for: drawing a shape
examples: The police asked her to describe the man.
It's difficult to describe how I feel.

describe.definition: to make a movement that forms the shape of a circle or other figure (formal)
describe.note: typical: describe a circle, an arc NOT for: talking about someone
examples: Her hand described a circle in the air.
The plane described a wide arc over the city.

disagree.definition: to have or express a different opinion from someone else
disagree.note: typical: disagree with someone, about/on something NOT for: two sets of information not matching
examples: He is tolerant of those who disagree with him.
Experts disagree on how much the program will cost.

disagree.definition: if statements, numbers or reports about the same subject disagree, they are different from each other when they should be the same
disagree.note: typical: figures, reports disagree NOT for: people having different opinions
examples: The two reports disagree about the number of casualties.
Their accounts of the accident disagree.

disappear.definition: to become impossible to see any longer
disappear.note: typical: disappear from view, behind a cloud NOT for: being lost
examples: The sun had disappeared behind a cloud.
David watched her car until it disappeared from view.

disappear.definition: to be lost, or to become impossible to find
disappear.note: typical: people, things disappearing NOT for: no longer being visible
examples: The two girls disappeared while walking home from school.
My keys have disappeared again.

disappear.note: typical: species, rainforests, problems disappearing NOT for: being lost temporarily
examples: The rain forest may disappear forever.
Millions of people saw their savings disappear.

discover.definition: to find someone or something, either by accident or by searching
discover.note: typical: discover a body, a cave, the truth NOT for: helping a new talent
examples: Police discovered the body in a field.
She discovered her keys in the bottom of the bag.

discover.definition: to find out a fact or learn something that you did not know before
discover.note: typical: discover that, discover how NOT for: finding a physical object
examples: She discovered that her husband had been lying.
Scientists discovered how the virus spreads.

discover.definition: to find a place or thing that no one has known about before
discover.note: typical: discover a planet, a cure, a new species NOT for: finding something lost
examples: Columbus discovered America.
Astronomers discovered a new planet.

discover.definition: to notice someone who is very good at something and help them become successful and well-known
discover.note: typical: be discovered by an agent NOT for: finding facts
examples: He was discovered by a talent scout when he was sixteen.
The band is still waiting to be discovered.

divide.definition: if something divides, or if you divide it, it separates into two or more parts
divide.note: typical: divide into parts, groups, zones NOT for: sharing between people
examples: Scientists traditionally divide the oceans into zones.
The river divides into three channels.

divide.definition: to keep two areas separate from each other
divide.note: typical: a wall, a river, a curtain dividing something NOT for: separating something into parts
examples: The Wall used to divide East and West Berlin.
Only a thin curtain divided her cabin from his.

divide.definition: to separate something into parts and share them between people
divide.note: typical: divide the money, the work between people NOT for: keeping areas separate
examples: The money will be divided equally among the charities.
They divided the work between the three of them.

divide.definition: to spend part of your time, energy or attention on each of several activities or places
divide.note: typical: divide your time between two things NOT for: sharing money
examples: She divides her time between New York and Paris.
He divides his attention between his job and his family.

divide.definition: to calculate how many times one number contains a smaller number
divide.note: typical: divide by, 21 divided by 3 NOT for: sharing things between people
examples: If you divide 21 by 3, you get 7.
What's six divided by three?

divide.definition: if one number divides into another, it is contained exactly in it one or more times
divide.note: typical: 8 divides into 64 NOT for: calculating a total
examples: Eight divides into sixty-four eight times.
Three divides into nine exactly.

divide.definition: to make people disagree so that they form groups with different opinions
divide.note: typical: divide opinion, voters, a party NOT for: dividing objects
examples: The issue of cloning has sharply divided voters.
The decision divided the party.

doubt.definition: to think that something may not be true or that it is unlikely
doubt.note: typical: doubt that, doubt whether NOT for: not trusting a person
examples: I doubt if it'll make any difference.
"Do you think there'll be any tickets left?" "I doubt it."

doubt.definition: to not trust or have confidence in someone
doubt.note: typical: doubt someone, doubt yourself NOT for: thinking something unlikely
examples: She loved him and had never doubted him.
I have no reason to doubt his word.

dream.definition: to think about something that you would like to happen or have
dream.note: typical: dream of becoming something, dream about NOT for: dreams during sleep
examples: She dreamed of becoming a chef.
He's got the sort of money that you and I can only dream about.

dream.definition: to have a dream while you are asleep
dream.note: typical: dream about someone, that you are falling NOT for: daydreaming
examples: I dreamt about you last night.
It's quite common to dream that you're falling.

dream.definition: to think about something else and not give your attention to what is happening around you
dream.note: typical: dream in class, daydream NOT for: sleeping
examples: She had been dreaming and had not followed the conversation.
Stop dreaming and pay attention!

dream.definition: to imagine that you have done, seen or heard something that you have not
dream.note: typical: you must have dreamt it NOT for: having a dream while asleep
examples: I was sure I posted the letter, but I must have dreamt it.
Did that really happen, or did I dream it?

dream.definition: used to say that you did not think that something would happen (never dreamed)
dream.note: typical: never dreamed that NOT for: sleeping
examples: We never dreamed that we would get through to the next round.
I never dreamed he would say yes.

drive.definition: to control a car, lorry, bus or other vehicle and make it move along
drive.note: typical: drive a car, a bus, learn to drive NOT for: riding a bicycle
examples: So when did you learn to drive?
He drives a BMW estate.

drive.definition: to travel somewhere in a car
drive.note: typical: drive to the airport, drive home NOT for: controlling a vehicle in general
examples: Shall we drive or take the bus?
They drove back to Woodside.

drive.definition: to take someone somewhere in a car, lorry or similar vehicle
drive.note: typical: drive someone home, to the airport NOT for: travelling yourself
examples: She drove Anna to London.
I'll drive you home.

drive.definition: to force a person or animal to go somewhere
drive.note: typical: drive animals, people away, out NOT for: driving a vehicle
examples: Torrential rain drove the players off the course.
They drove the donkeys out of the enclosure.

drive.definition: to strongly influence someone to do something
drive.note: typical: be driven by jealousy, drive someone to do something NOT for: forcing someone to move
examples: The detective wondered what had driven Christine to phone her.
Jealousy drove him to spy on his wife.

drive.definition: to make someone or something get into a bad or extreme state, usually an emotional one
drive.note: typical: drive someone mad, crazy, to despair NOT for: strongly influencing an action
examples: This cough is driving me mad!
The factory had been driven into bankruptcy.

drive.definition: to hit or push something into something else
drive.note: typical: drive a post, a nail into something NOT for: driving a vehicle
examples: We watched Dad drive the posts into the ground.
She drove her heels into the sand.

drive.definition: to make a person or animal work hard
drive.note: typical: drive yourself, drive someone too hard NOT for: driving a vehicle
examples: Don't drive yourself too hard.
The coach drives his players hard.

drive.definition: to move a ball forward in a game by hitting or kicking it hard and fast
drive.note: typical: drive the ball NOT for: driving a vehicle
examples: He drove the ball into the corner of the net.
She drove the ball down the fairway.

drive.definition: to provide the power for a vehicle or machine
drive.note: typical: petrol-driven, battery-driven NOT for: steering a vehicle
examples: A petrol-driven lawnmower is noisy.
The engine drives the wheels through a gearbox.

drive.definition: if rain, snow or wind drives somewhere, it moves very quickly in that direction
drive.note: typical: driving rain NOT for: people driving
examples: The rain drove against the windows.
A cold wind drove the snow across the fields.

drive.definition: to cause something to increase or change quickly
drive.note: typical: drive prices up, drive growth NOT for: steering a vehicle
examples: The oil shortage drove gas prices up by 20 cents a gallon.
Strong demand is driving prices higher.

drop.definition: to stop holding or carrying something so that it falls
drop.note: typical: drop a bag, a glass, a ball NOT for: letting something fall from a plane
examples: He dropped his briefcase on a chair.
She screamed and dropped the torch.

drop.definition: to make something such as a bomb or supplies fall from an aircraft
drop.note: typical: drop bombs, supplies, leaflets NOT for: letting something slip from your hand
examples: Supplies are being dropped for the refugees.
Planes dropped leaflets over the city.

drop.definition: to fall suddenly onto the ground or into something
drop.note: typical: apples dropping, a button dropping off NOT for: deliberately letting something fall
examples: The apples are beginning to drop from the trees.
Your button has dropped off.

drop.definition: to lower yourself or part of your body suddenly
drop.note: typical: drop to your knees, down onto the floor NOT for: objects falling
examples: He dropped down onto the floor and hid under the table.
She dropped her head back against the cushion.

drop.definition: to fall to a lower level or amount, especially a much lower one
drop.note: typical: prices, temperatures, numbers dropping NOT for: objects falling
examples: The number of deaths on the roads has dropped sharply.
Temperatures drop quite dramatically at night.

drop.definition: to reduce the level or amount of something
drop.note: typical: drop the price, your speed NOT for: falling by itself
examples: You might be able to get them to drop the price.
As soon as she saw the police car, she dropped her speed.

drop.definition: to decide not to include someone or something
drop.note: typical: drop a player, a name from a list NOT for: stopping an activity
examples: Taylor was bitterly disappointed to be dropped from the England side.
His name was dropped from the list.

drop.definition: to stop doing something, discussing something or continuing with something
drop.note: typical: drop a case, a plan, a subject at school NOT for: leaving someone out of a team
examples: The case was dropped after new evidence was presented.
Students are allowed to drop history in Year 9.

drop.note: typical: drop the subject, drop it NOT for: stopping a plan or case
examples: To her relief, Julius dropped the subject.
Just drop it, will you? I don't want to talk about it any more.

drop.definition: to take someone somewhere by car and leave them there
drop.note: typical: drop someone at a place, off NOT for: taking something to a place
examples: She dropped Johnny at the school gates at about 8:30.
Just drop me here; I can walk the rest of the way.

drop.definition: to take something to a place and leave it there
drop.note: typical: drop something round, in NOT for: taking a person by car
examples: I'll drop them round to your place later.
Can you drop this package at the post office?

drop.definition: to visit someone you know, usually without arranging a particular time
drop.note: typical: drop by, round, in NOT for: taking someone somewhere
examples: I just dropped by to see how you were getting on.
Why don't you drop in for a drink one evening?

drop.definition: if a path or land drops, it goes down suddenly, forming a steep slope
drop.note: typical: the ground, a cliff dropping away NOT for: falling objects
examples: The cliff dropped down over a hundred feet to the sea below.
On the left the ground drops away.

drop.definition: to suddenly stop having a relationship with someone, especially a romantic one (informal)
drop.note: typical: drop someone NOT for: leaving someone out of a team
examples: She dropped him as soon as she found out he had been seeing another woman.
He was dropped by his girlfriend last month.

dry.definition: to make something dry, or to become dry
dry.note: typical: dry your hair, your hands, clothes drying NOT for: drying dishes
examples: Mrs Brown hung the washing on the line to dry.
Leave the first coat of paint to dry before adding another.

dry.definition: to rub plates, dishes and so on dry with a cloth after they have been washed
dry.note: typical: dry dishes, glasses, plates NOT for: drying yourself
examples: You wash and I'll dry.
Shall I dry these glasses?

earn.definition: to receive an amount of money for the work that you do
earn.note: typical: earn a salary, £20,000, a living NOT for: making a profit from business
examples: He earns nearly £20,000 a year.
She did all sorts of jobs to earn a living.

earn.definition: to make a profit from business or from putting money in a bank
earn.note: typical: earn interest, a profit NOT for: earning wages
examples: The movie earned £7 million on its first day.
You could earn a higher rate of interest elsewhere.

earn.definition: to do something or have qualities that make you deserve something
earn.note: typical: earn a rest, respect, a place NOT for: earning money
examples: I think you've earned a rest.
He soon earned the respect of the players.

encourage.definition: to give someone the courage or confidence to do something
encourage.note: typical: encourage someone to do something, in something NOT for: persuading someone
examples: Cooder was encouraged to begin playing the guitar by his father.
Fleur encouraged Dana in her ambition to become a model.

encourage.definition: to persuade someone to do something
encourage.note: typical: encourage someone to do something NOT for: giving confidence
examples: A 10p rise in cigarette prices is not enough to encourage smokers to stop.
Cantor actively encouraged them to work late.

encourage.definition: to help something to develop or become more likely to happen
encourage.note: typical: encourage growth, competition, discussion NOT for: persuading a person
examples: The government wants to encourage investment.
Warm, wet weather encourages the growth of mould.

enter.definition: to go or come into a place
enter.note: typical: enter a room, a building, a country NOT for: starting a profession
examples: Silence fell as I entered the room.
Few reporters dared to enter the war zone.

enter.definition: if an object enters part of something, it goes inside it
enter.note: typical: a bullet, water entering something NOT for: people entering a room
examples: The bullet had entered his brain.
Water entered through a crack in the wall.

enter.definition: to start working in a particular profession or organisation, or to start studying at a school or university
enter.note: typical: enter the army, politics, university NOT for: entering a room
examples: Both the boys entered the army.
She entered politics in 1996.

enter.definition: to start to take part in an activity, or to become involved in a situation
enter.note: typical: enter an election, negotiations, a war NOT for: entering a competition
examples: He entered the election as the clear favourite.
The rebels were prepared to enter negotiations.

enter.definition: to put information into a computer by pressing the keys
enter.note: typical: enter data, a password NOT for: writing on a form
examples: Press the return key to enter the information.
The names are entered into a database.

enter.definition: if you enter a computer system, you are given permission to use it
enter.note: typical: enter a system, a website, with a password NOT for: typing data
examples: It won't let you enter without a password.
You must log in before you can enter the system.

enter.definition: to write information on a particular part of a form or document
enter.note: typical: enter your name, postcode NOT for: typing into a computer
examples: Don't forget to enter your postcode.
Enter your name in the space provided.

enter.definition: to arrange to take part in a race, competition or examination, or to arrange for someone else to take part
enter.note: typical: enter a competition, a race, an exam NOT for: entering a building
examples: At least thirty schools entered the competition.
She entered her horse in the race.

enter.definition: to begin a period of time when something happens
enter.note: typical: enter a new phase, its third week NOT for: entering a place
examples: The economy has entered a period of recession.
The talks have now entered their third week.

enter.definition: if a new idea, thought or quality enters something, it suddenly starts to exist there
enter.note: typical: a note of panic enters someone's voice NOT for: physical entering
examples: A note of panic entered her voice.
It never entered his head that she might be seeing someone else.

enter.definition: if someone or something enters your life, you start to know them or be affected by them
enter.note: typical: enter someone's life NOT for: entering a building
examples: By the time Angie entered his life, he was almost thirty.
The internet entered our lives only a few years ago.

enter.definition: to make an official statement or record, especially in a court (formal)
enter.note: typical: enter a plea, a protest, a record NOT for: typing data
examples: The defendant entered a plea of not guilty.
The clerk entered the decision in the record.

escape.definition: to get away from a place when someone is trying to catch you or stop you
escape.note: typical: escape from prison, a place NOT for: avoiding danger
examples: He broke down the locked door and escaped.
He escaped from prison in October.

escape.definition: to get away from a dangerous or bad situation
escape.note: typical: escape unhurt, a fire, the heat NOT for: getting out of a place
examples: A boy escaped unhurt when the fire in his room exploded.
They went to the hills to escape the summer heat.

escape.definition: if gas or liquid escapes from somewhere, it comes out
escape.note: typical: gas, steam, water escaping NOT for: people escaping
examples: Vents allow any steam to escape if the system overheats.
Gas was escaping from a broken pipe.

escape.definition: if something escapes you or your notice, you do not notice, remember or understand it
escape.note: typical: escape notice, your attention NOT for: getting away
examples: The name escapes me for the moment.
The mistake escaped everyone's notice.

exchange.definition: to give someone something and receive the same kind of thing from them at the same time
exchange.note: typical: exchange gifts, phone numbers, shirts NOT for: replacing something with another thing
examples: We exchange gifts at Christmas.
We exchanged phone numbers.

exchange.definition: to give someone something and receive something different in return, especially money in a different currency
exchange.note: typical: exchange dollars for pounds NOT for: swapping the same kind of thing
examples: Where can I exchange my dollars for pounds?
She exchanged her old phone for a new model.

exchange.definition: to replace one thing with another (British)
exchange.note: typical: exchange a jacket for another NOT for: giving and receiving gifts
examples: He exchanged the black jacket for a blue one.
I'd like to exchange this book for a different one.

exchange.definition: if two people exchange words, looks or similar things, they say or give them to each other
exchange.note: typical: exchange words, glances, greetings NOT for: exchanging objects
examples: The two women exchanged glances and laughed.
I went over and exchanged greetings with everyone.

exchange.definition: if two people exchange blows, they hit each other
exchange.note: typical: exchange blows NOT for: exchanging words
examples: The two men exchanged blows in the street.
The players exchanged blows after the final whistle.

exchange.definition: to discuss something or share information or ideas
exchange.note: typical: exchange information, ideas, views NOT for: exchanging objects
examples: It's a place where people can chat and exchange ideas.
Delegates exchanged information about their research.

exchange.definition: to complete the final stage of buying a house by signing a contract with the person you are buying it from (especially British)
exchange.note: typical: exchange contracts NOT for: everyday swapping
examples: We hope to exchange contracts on Friday.
They exchanged contracts and got the keys the same day.

excite.definition: to make someone feel happy, interested or eager
excite.note: typical: excite someone, doesn't excite me NOT for: causing a formal reaction
examples: His playing is technically brilliant, but it doesn't excite me.
The idea of travelling alone excites her.

excite.definition: to cause a particular feeling or reaction (formal)
excite.note: typical: excite interest, curiosity, comment, suspicion NOT for: making someone feel happy
examples: The court case has excited a lot of public interest.
He tried not to do anything to excite the suspicion of the police.

expect.definition: to think that something will happen or that someone will do something
expect.note: typical: expect rain, expect to win, expect that NOT for: demanding something
examples: We expect the new road to be finished by spring.
I expected him to say no.

expect.definition: to demand that someone does something because it is a duty or seems reasonable
expect.note: typical: expect obedience, expect someone to do something NOT for: predicting
examples: The officer expects complete obedience from his troops.
The school expects a lot of its students.

expect.definition: to believe that someone or something is going to arrive
expect.note: typical: expect a guest, a parcel, snow NOT for: demanding something
examples: We're expecting Alison home any minute now.
Snow is expected by the weekend.

expect.definition: to think that you will find that someone or something has a particular quality or does a particular thing
expect.note: typical: expect someone to be taller, different NOT for: predicting a future event
examples: I expected her to be taller than me, not shorter.
I'd expected a much bigger house.

expect.definition: if a woman is expecting, she is going to have a baby (be expecting)
expect.note: typical: be expecting a baby NOT for: expecting a guest
examples: She's expecting her second child in June.
They're expecting a baby in the spring.

expect.definition: to suppose that something is probably true (spoken, British)
expect.note: typical: I expect (that) NOT for: demanding something
examples: I expect you're right.
"Do you think they're going to attack?" "I expect so."

explain.definition: to tell someone about something in a way that is clear or easy to understand
explain.note: typical: explain how, why, what to someone NOT for: giving a reason for bad behaviour
examples: The librarian will explain how to use the catalogue system.
He explained the situation to the bank manager.

explain.definition: to give a reason for something or to be a reason for something
explain.note: typical: explain a delay, explain why NOT for: describing how something works
examples: How can you explain that sort of behaviour?
That still doesn't explain how he was able to hide the body.

explain.definition: to tell someone who is angry or upset with you why you did something (explain yourself)
explain.note: typical: explain yourself NOT for: explaining a fact
examples: I'm going to give you five seconds to explain yourself.
The boy was asked to explain himself to the head teacher.

explain.definition: to say clearly what you mean (explain yourself)
explain.note: typical: explain yourself clearly NOT for: justifying actions
examples: Sorry, I'm not explaining myself very well.
Let me explain myself a bit better.

express.definition: to tell or show what you are feeling or thinking by using words, looks or actions
express.note: typical: express an opinion, an interest, sympathy, yourself NOT for: changing a number into another form
examples: Bill's not afraid to express his opinions.
Young children often have difficulty expressing themselves.

express.definition: if someone's face, voice or actions express a feeling, they show it
express.note: typical: a face, a look, a gesture expressing something NOT for: telling someone in words
examples: Her face expressed despair.
His eyes expressed a quiet anger.

express.definition: if something expresses itself, it becomes noticeable (sth expresses itself)
express.note: typical: faith, anger expressing itself in a way NOT for: people speaking
examples: Religious faith expresses itself in a variety of ways.
Her creativity expressed itself in painting.

express.definition: to change an amount or quantity into a different form, especially in mathematics (technical)
express.note: typical: express something as a decimal, in dollars NOT for: saying how you feel
examples: Express three-quarters as a decimal.
The value rises when it is expressed in foreign currency.

fail.definition: to not succeed in achieving something
fail.note: typical: fail in an attempt, fail to do something NOT for: doing badly in a test
examples: It looks likely that the peace talks will fail.
Doctors failed to save the girl's life.

fail.definition: to not do what is expected, needed or wanted (formal)
fail.note: typical: fail to do something, fail in your duty NOT for: not succeeding in an attempt
examples: The letter failed to arrive.
The government are failing in their duty to protect people.

fail.definition: to not pass a test or examination
fail.note: typical: fail an exam, a driving test NOT for: a company failing
examples: I failed my driving test the first time I took it.
He failed maths but passed all his other subjects.

fail.definition: to decide that someone has not passed a test or examination
fail.note: typical: a teacher failing a student NOT for: failing a test yourself
examples: Her work was so bad that I had no choice but to fail her.
The examiner failed two of the candidates.

fail.definition: used to show that you are annoyed by something that you do not accept or understand (fail to see/understand)
fail.note: typical: I fail to see why NOT for: failing a test
examples: I fail to see why you find it so amusing.
I fail to understand why he refused.

fail.definition: if a company or business fails, it is unable to continue because of a lack of money
fail.note: typical: businesses, banks failing NOT for: a machine failing
examples: Thousands of small businesses failed during the recession.
The bank failed in 2009.

fail.definition: if a part of a machine or a body organ fails, it stops working
fail.note: typical: engines, brakes, kidneys failing NOT for: a company failing
examples: The engine failed on take-off.
His kidneys were failing.

fail.definition: if your sight, memory or health is failing, it is gradually getting weaker
fail.note: typical: failing eyesight, health NOT for: a sudden failure
examples: Failing eyesight forced him to retire early.
His memory is failing and he often forgets names.

fail.definition: to do something so regularly that people expect it (never fail to do sth)
fail.note: typical: never fail to do something NOT for: failing a test
examples: My grandson never fails to phone me on my birthday.
She never fails to make me laugh.

fasten.definition: to join the two sides of something such as a coat or bag so that it is closed, or to become joined together with buttons or hooks
fasten.note: typical: fasten a seat belt, a coat NOT for: attaching something to a surface
examples: Fasten your seat belt.
I was so fat that my skirt wouldn't fasten.

fasten.definition: to firmly close a window, gate or similar thing so that it will not open, or to become firmly closed
fasten.note: typical: windows, doors, gates fastened securely NOT for: fastening clothes
examples: Make sure all the windows are securely fastened before you leave.
The gate fastens with a simple latch.

fasten.definition: to attach something firmly to another object or surface
fasten.note: typical: fasten something to a wall, with a pin NOT for: closing clothes
examples: Fasten the poster to the wall with tape.
He fastened the dog's lead to a post.

fear.definition: to feel afraid or worried that something bad may happen
fear.note: typical: fear that, fear for someone's safety NOT for: being afraid of a person
examples: Police fear that there may be further terrorist attacks.
He feared for his children.

fear.definition: to think that the worst possible thing has happened or might happen (fear the worst)
fear.note: typical: fear the worst NOT for: ordinary worrying
examples: When Tom heard about the accident, he immediately feared the worst.
The family feared the worst when he didn't come home.

fear.definition: to be afraid of someone and what they might do
fear.note: typical: be feared, fear someone NOT for: worrying about something bad
examples: As a leader, he was distrusted and even feared.
The villagers feared the local landowner.

fear.definition: used in a polite or formal way to tell someone that you think something bad has happened or is true (I fear)
fear.note: typical: I fear that, I fear so, I fear not NOT for: being afraid
examples: I fear that there is little more we can do.
"Were they satisfied?" "I fear not."

fight.definition: to take part in a war or battle
fight.note: typical: fight in a war, against an enemy NOT for: fighting with fists
examples: The families of those who fought in the war were invited to the ceremony.
Rebel forces were fighting against the army.

fight.definition: to hit and kick another person in order to hurt them, or if two people fight, they hit each other
fight.note: typical: fight someone, two people fighting NOT for: a war
examples: Two guys were fighting with each other in the street.
They were fighting over a girl.

fight.definition: to try hard to do or get something
fight.note: typical: fight for higher wages, for your life NOT for: fighting against something
examples: The men were fighting for higher wages.
Stockley is fighting for his life.

fight.definition: to try very hard to prevent something or to get rid of something unpleasant that already exists
fight.note: typical: fight crime, terrorism, a disease NOT for: fighting to get something
examples: People are fighting against repression and injustice.
We will fight terrorism, wherever it exists.

fight.definition: to take part in an election, or to compete strongly for something such as a job
fight.note: typical: fight an election, a campaign NOT for: a physical fight
examples: The prime minister decided to fight an early general election.
He had to fight several other applicants for the job.

fight.note: typical: fight about, over something NOT for: a physical fight
examples: I heard her fighting with the boss.
They're fighting about who should do the dishes.

fight.definition: to take part in a boxing match
fight.note: typical: fight for a title NOT for: a street fight
examples: Ali fought Foreman for the heavyweight title.
He is fighting for the world title in June.

fight.definition: to try very hard not to have or show a feeling
fight.note: typical: fight your fear, tears, an urge NOT for: fighting a person
examples: She fought her fear.
He fought back tears at the funeral.

fight.definition: to try to get something or to prevent something in a court of law
fight.note: typical: fight a claim, a case NOT for: fighting in a physical sense
examples: The insurance company are fighting the claims in court.
She decided to fight the decision in court.

fight.definition: to move somewhere with difficulty, for example because there are so many people or obstacles (fight your way)
fight.note: typical: fight your way through a crowd NOT for: fighting a person
examples: She fought her way through the crowd.
They fought their way past the guards.

fit.definition: if a piece of clothing fits you, it is the right size for your body
fit.note: typical: clothes, shoes fitting NOT for: looking attractive on someone
examples: His clothes did not fit him very well.
The jacket's fine, but the trousers don't fit.

fit.definition: to try a piece of clothing on someone to see if it is the right size, or to make sure a special piece of equipment is right for someone
fit.note: typical: be fitted for a suit, with a hearing aid NOT for: clothes simply being the right size
examples: I'm being fitted for a new suit tomorrow.
He may need to be fitted with a hearing aid.

fit.definition: if something fits in a place, it is the right size or shape to go there
fit.note: typical: a key fitting a lock, a cover fitting a frame NOT for: having enough space
examples: I couldn't find a key which fitted the lock.
The plastic cover fits neatly over the frame.

fit.definition: if something fits into a place, there is enough space for it
fit.note: typical: fit into a car, a room, a suitcase NOT for: being the right shape
examples: I don't think we'll be able to fit any more people into the car.
We should be able to fit one more in.

fit.definition: to put a piece of equipment or a new part onto a machine so that it is ready to be used
fit.note: typical: fit a lock, a part, a device NOT for: clothes fitting
examples: I need to fit a lock on the door.
The windows are all fitted with security locks.

fit.definition: if something fits another thing, it is similar to it or suitable for it
fit.note: typical: fit a description, a theory, a pattern NOT for: physical size
examples: The punishment should fit the crime.
Police said the car fits the description of the stolen vehicle.

fold.definition: to bend a piece of paper, cloth or similar material by laying or pressing one part over another
fold.note: typical: fold a paper in half, along a line NOT for: making something small and neat
examples: Fold the paper along the dotted line.
It'll fit in if you fold it in half.

fold.definition: to fold something several times so that it makes a small neat shape
fold.note: typical: fold up clothes, a map NOT for: folding once
examples: I wish you kids would fold up your clothes!
He folded the map neatly.

fold.definition: if something such as a table, chair or bed folds, it can be made smaller by bending or closing it
fold.note: typical: fold up, folding chairs, beds NOT for: folding paper
examples: The table folds flat for easy storage.
The buggy folds up in one movement.

fold.definition: if a company or business folds, it closes because it has no money
fold.note: typical: businesses, newspapers, theatres folding NOT for: folding paper
examples: The magazine folded after only six issues.
Many small shops fold in the first year.

fold.definition: to put your arms or hands across each other (fold your arms)
fold.note: typical: fold your arms, hands NOT for: folding paper
examples: She folded her arms and waited.
He sat with his hands folded in his lap.

follow.definition: to move along behind someone or something and go where they go
follow.note: typical: follow someone down the street, a car NOT for: happening afterwards
examples: Are those men following us?
The patrol car followed the BMW for a few miles.

follow.definition: to happen or do something after something else
follow.note: typical: be followed by, there follows NOT for: physically going behind
examples: The agreement followed months of negotiation.
Most EU countries have signed the agreement and the US is expected to follow shortly.

follow.definition: to come directly after something else in a series, list or order
follow.note: typical: the chapters that follow, be followed by NOT for: physically going behind
examples: In English, the letter Q is always followed by U.
We had vegetable casserole with a fruit salad to follow.

follow.definition: to do something in the way that someone has told or advised you to do it
follow.note: typical: follow instructions, advice, a recipe NOT for: going behind someone
examples: He followed the doctor's advice and had no further trouble.
Follow the instructions very carefully when filling in the form.

follow.definition: to go somewhere by a particular way according to road signs or to what someone has told you
follow.note: typical: follow the signs, directions NOT for: following instructions in general
examples: Just follow the signs for the airport.
I followed Brown's directions and found the farm quite easily.

follow.definition: to do the same thing as someone else
follow.note: typical: follow an example, a trend, the latest fashions NOT for: following instructions
examples: Some state schools follow the example of private schools in asking parents to donate money.
She follows the latest fashions.

follow.definition: to believe in and obey a particular set of religious or political ideas
follow.note: typical: follow a religion, a leader NOT for: following the example of someone
examples: Millions of people follow this faith.
He followed the teachings of his master.

follow.definition: to understand an explanation or an argument
follow.note: typical: follow what someone says NOT for: going behind someone
examples: I'm sorry, I don't follow you.
It was hard to follow the plot of the film.

follow.definition: if something follows, it is a logical result of what has been said or done
follow.note: typical: it follows that NOT for: happening later in time
examples: If the first claim is true, it follows that the second one must be true as well.
It doesn't follow that he is guilty just because he ran away.

follow.definition: if a road, path or river follows a particular route, it goes along it
follow.note: typical: a path following the river NOT for: people following someone
examples: The road follows the coast for twenty miles.
The path follows the river through the valley.

follow.definition: to be interested in something and in the way it develops
follow.note: typical: follow a series, a sport, someone's progress NOT for: walking behind someone
examples: Have you been following that crime series on TV?
She follows football very closely.

follow.definition: to continue to happen or develop in a particular way (follow a pattern, course, trend)
follow.note: typical: follow a pattern, a course NOT for: imitating someone
examples: In Australia, the weather follows a fairly predictable pattern.
The disease follows a similar course in most patients.

forget.definition: to not remember facts, information, or people or things from the past
forget.note: typical: forget a name, a date, an appointment NOT for: forgetting to do something
examples: I'm sorry, I've forgotten your name.
What happened that day will never be forgotten.

forget.definition: to not remember to do something that you should do
forget.note: typical: forget to do something NOT for: not remembering facts
examples: Someone has forgotten to turn off their headlights.
Don't forget to post that letter.

forget.definition: to not remember to bring something that you need with you
forget.note: typical: forget your keys, wallet NOT for: forgetting facts
examples: Oh no, I've forgotten my wallet.
He forgot his umbrella and got soaked.

forget.definition: to stop thinking or worrying about someone or something
forget.note: typical: forget him, forget about something NOT for: failing to remember
examples: Forget him; he's not worth it.
After a while you'll forget you're wearing contact lenses.

forget.definition: to not care about or give attention to someone or something any longer
forget.note: typical: forget about your old friends NOT for: failing to remember something
examples: Don't forget about your old friends when you go off to college.
You can't afford to forget your family.

greet.definition: to say hello to someone or welcome them
greet.note: typical: greet someone warmly, with a smile NOT for: reacting to news
examples: Belinda greeted her warmly.
Bill opened the door to Harold and greeted him with cries of welcome.

greet.definition: to react to something in a particular way, especially to news or an event (usually passive)
greet.note: typical: be greeted with applause, anger, silence NOT for: saying hello
examples: The announcement was greeted with loud applause.
The news was greeted with silence.

grow.definition: to increase in amount, size, number or strength
grow.note: typical: support, sales, numbers growing NOT for: people getting older
examples: Support for Mr Thompson is growing.
The number of students at the college has grown from 200 to over 500.

grow.definition: to make a business or part of a business bigger and more successful
grow.note: typical: grow a business, a company NOT for: plants growing
examples: We want to grow the export side of the business.
The firm hopes to grow its customer base.

grow.definition: to become bigger, taller or older over a period of time as part of the process of becoming an adult
grow.note: typical: children, animals growing NOT for: increasing in numbers
examples: You've really grown since I last saw you.
Stan grew two inches in six months.

grow.definition: if plants grow, they exist and develop in a natural way
grow.note: typical: plants, trees, flowers growing NOT for: people cultivating plants
examples: The plants grow wild by the river.
This tree will grow well in most types of soil.

grow.definition: to make plants or crops develop and produce fruit or flowers
grow.note: typical: grow vegetables, food, crops NOT for: plants growing by themselves
examples: Many families own plots of land to grow food.
Britain grows millions of tonnes of potatoes a year.

grow.definition: to not cut your hair, nails or beard so that they get longer
grow.note: typical: grow your hair, a beard, a moustache NOT for: plants growing
examples: I've decided to grow my hair long.
He grew a beard over the summer.

grow.definition: if hair or nails grow, they become longer
grow.note: typical: hair, nails growing NOT for: letting them grow on purpose
examples: Her hair grows very quickly.
His nails grew long and dirty.

grow.definition: to change and become different quite slowly (linking verb)
grow.note: typical: grow louder, older, tired NOT for: becoming physically bigger
examples: The sound was growing louder.
Donna has grown tired of being a model.

grow.definition: to gradually change your opinions and have a feeling that you did not have before (grow to like, hate, respect)
grow.note: typical: grow to like, love, hate NOT for: physical growth
examples: After a while the kids grew to like Mr Cox.
She grew to love the city.

guess.definition: to try to answer a question or form an opinion when you are not sure whether you will be correct
guess.note: typical: guess the answer, guess someone's age NOT for: working something out from clues
examples: I'd say he's around 50, but I'm only guessing.
Can you guess how old she is?

guess.definition: to realise that something is true even though you do not know for certain
guess.note: typical: guess that, guess from something NOT for: random guessing
examples: I guessed that you must be related because you look so similar.
I guessed from his expression that he already knew about the accident.

guess.definition: used to say that you think something is true or likely, although you are not sure (I guess, spoken)
guess.note: typical: I guess so, I guess I'll stay NOT for: guessing an answer
examples: His light's on, so I guess he's still up.
I'm tired, so I guess I'll stay home tonight.

hang.definition: to put something in a position so that the top part is fixed or supported and the bottom part is free to move
hang.note: typical: hang a coat on a hook, washing on a line NOT for: fixing a picture to a wall
examples: Philip hung his coat on a hook behind the door.
She hung the sheets on the washing line.

hang.definition: to be in a position where the top part is fixed or supported and the bottom part is free to move
hang.note: typical: hang from a ceiling, hang down NOT for: putting something somewhere
examples: An old-fashioned gas lamp hung from the ceiling.
Her long hair hung loose about her shoulders.

hang.definition: to fix a picture, photograph or similar object to a wall, or to be fixed there
hang.note: typical: hang a picture, a mirror NOT for: hanging clothes
examples: I wanted to hang the picture in the hall.
A family photograph was hanging on the wall.

hang.definition: to kill someone by dropping them with a rope around their neck as a punishment for a serious crime (past tense and participle: hanged)
hang.note: typical: be hanged for murder NOT for: fixing something to a wall
examples: The man was hanged for murder in 1952.
In some countries, criminals were once hanged in public.

hang.definition: to fasten attractive paper to a wall in order to decorate it
hang.note: typical: hang wallpaper NOT for: hanging pictures
examples: We spent the weekend hanging wallpaper in the hall.
He hung new wallpaper in the bedroom.

hang.definition: to fasten a door in position
hang.note: typical: hang a door NOT for: hanging wallpaper
examples: Hanging a door is quite a tricky job.
The carpenter hung the new front door.

hang.definition: if something such as smoke hangs in the air, it stays in the air for a long time
hang.note: typical: smoke, mist, a smell hanging NOT for: hanging from a hook
examples: The smoke from the bonfires hung in the air.
A thick mist hung over the town.

happen.definition: when something happens, there is an event, especially one that is not planned
happen.note: typical: an accident, something terrible happens NOT for: something happening to a person
examples: When did the accident happen?
This kind of thing happens all the time.

happen.definition: if something happens to someone or something, they are affected by an event
happen.note: typical: something happens to someone NOT for: events happening in general
examples: He should be here by now; something must have happened to him.
What's happened to your coat? It's all ripped.

happen.definition: if you happen to do something, you do it by chance
happen.note: typical: happen to see, to be NOT for: planned actions
examples: I happened to see James in town.
Do you happen to know where she lives?

heat.definition: to make something become warm or hot
heat.note: typical: heat milk, a house, a pan NOT for: cooking food at length
examples: Heat the milk until it boils.
The stove takes a while to heat the room.

hide.definition: to deliberately put or keep something or someone in a place where they cannot easily be seen or found
hide.note: typical: hide a present, evidence, money NOT for: covering something so that it is hard to see
examples: Marcia hid the pictures in her desk drawer.
He was accused of trying to hide evidence from the police.

hide.definition: to cover something so that it cannot be seen clearly
hide.note: typical: trees, hair, a hat hiding something NOT for: deliberately hiding an object
examples: The church roof was half hidden by trees.
Her tangled hair hid her face.

hide.definition: to go or stay in a place where no one will see or find you
hide.note: typical: hide under a bed, from someone NOT for: hiding an object
examples: Quick, he's coming! We'd better hide.
Harry hid under the bed.

hide.definition: to keep someone in a place where other people will not find them
hide.note: typical: hide a person, a refugee NOT for: hiding yourself
examples: The family hid two refugees in their cellar.
He was accused of hiding a criminal.

hide.definition: to keep your feelings or the truth secret so that other people cannot know them
hide.note: typical: hide your disappointment, embarrassment, the fact that NOT for: hiding objects
examples: She laughed to hide her nervousness.
He took off his ring to hide the fact that he was married.

hunt.definition: to chase animals or birds in order to kill or catch them
hunt.note: typical: hunt deer, in packs NOT for: searching for an object
examples: Wolves tend to hunt in packs.
He hunted deer as a kid.

hunt.definition: to look for someone or something very carefully
hunt.note: typical: hunt for shells, clues, a bargain NOT for: chasing animals
examples: The kids were hunting for shells on the beach.
Detectives are busy hunting for clues.

hunt.definition: to search for and try to catch a criminal or an enemy
hunt.note: typical: hunt a killer, a spy NOT for: hunting animals
examples: The police are still hunting the killer.
The FBI were called in to hunt for the spy.

hunt.definition: to hunt foxes as a sport, riding on horses and using dogs (British)
hunt.note: typical: fox hunting NOT for: hunting for food
examples: He hunts twice a week in the winter.
In Britain, people used to hunt foxes with dogs.

hurry.definition: to do something or go somewhere more quickly than usual, especially because there is not much time
hurry.note: typical: hurry to do something, hurry along NOT for: making someone else go faster
examples: If we hurry, we'll get there in time.
They were hurrying to catch their train.

hurry.definition: to make someone do something more quickly
hurry.note: typical: hurry someone, don't hurry me NOT for: going quickly yourself
examples: Don't hurry me; I'm doing this as fast as I can.
She doesn't want to be hurried into making a decision.

hurry.definition: to take someone or something quickly to a place
hurry.note: typical: hurry sth to a place NOT for: hurrying yourself
examples: Emergency supplies have been hurried to the worst-hit areas.
The injured man was hurried to hospital.

hurt.definition: to injure yourself or someone else
hurt.note: typical: hurt yourself, hurt someone's knee NOT for: causing emotional pain
examples: Was anyone hurt in the accident?
Be careful you don't fall and hurt yourself.

hurt.definition: to feel pain in a part of your body
hurt.note: typical: my back hurts, where does it hurt NOT for: injuring someone
examples: My back hurts.
It hurts when I try to move my leg.

hurt.definition: to cause pain in a part of your body
hurt.note: typical: the sun hurts my eyes NOT for: feeling pain
examples: The sun's hurting my eyes.
These shoes hurt my feet.

hurt.definition: to make someone feel very upset or unhappy
hurt.note: typical: hurt someone's feelings NOT for: physical pain
examples: I didn't mean to hurt your feelings.
It hurt me to think that you hated me.

hurt.definition: to have a bad effect on someone or something, especially by making them less successful or powerful
hurt.note: typical: hurt a company, someone's chances NOT for: physical pain
examples: Foreign competition has hurt the company's position in the market.
The scandal hurt his chances of being elected.

hurt.definition: to feel very upset or unhappy about something, or to lack something important (be hurting, American)
hurt.note: typical: be hurting, hurting for something NOT for: physical pain
examples: Martha's going through a divorce and really hurting right now.
The team is hurting for quarterbacks.

ignore.definition: to deliberately pay no attention to something that you have been told or that you know about
ignore.note: typical: ignore advice, a warning, a rule NOT for: refusing to speak to a person
examples: He ignored all the warning signs.
Everybody completely ignored the question.

ignore.definition: to deliberately not speak to someone or not look at them, although they are there
ignore.note: typical: ignore someone NOT for: ignoring advice
examples: I said hello, but she just ignored me.
They ignored each other for the whole evening.

imagine.definition: to form a picture or idea in your mind about what something could be like
imagine.note: typical: imagine life without something, imagine what it's like NOT for: wrongly thinking something is true
examples: Imagine that you have just won a million pounds.
Can you imagine what it's like when it's really hot out here?

imagine.definition: to have a false or wrong idea about something
imagine.note: typical: you're just imagining things NOT for: forming a picture in your mind
examples: Perhaps she'd just imagined it.
I had imagined it would be much bigger.

imagine.definition: to think that something is true or may happen, without being sure or having proof (not in progressive)
imagine.note: typical: I imagine that NOT for: forming a picture
examples: "A very complicated subject, I imagine," said Edwin.
I imagine that you are tired after the long journey.

improve.definition: to make something better, or to become better
improve.note: typical: improve your English, a situation, improve with age NOT for: becoming worse
examples: A course for students wishing to improve their English.
Many wines improve with age.

include.definition: if one thing includes another, the second thing is part of the first (not in progressive)
include.note: typical: the price includes, the course includes NOT for: making someone part of a group
examples: Does the price include postage?
The curriculum includes courses in computing.

include.definition: to make someone or something part of a larger group or set
include.note: typical: include someone, include in a list NOT for: being a part of something
examples: The team is stronger now that they've included Roscoe.
Service is included in the bill.

increase.definition: to become bigger in amount, number or degree, or to make something bigger
increase.note: typical: increase by 10%, increase in price NOT for: becoming smaller
examples: The population increased dramatically in the first half of the century.
Food prices increased by 10% in less than a year.

interest.definition: to make someone want to pay attention to something and find out more about it
interest.note: typical: it might interest you NOT for: persuading someone to buy
examples: Here's an article which might interest you.
What interests me is the history of these places.

interest.definition: to give something a lot of attention because you want to find out more about it (interest yourself in something, formal)
interest.note: typical: interest yourself in NOT for: making someone curious
examples: He had always interested himself in foreign affairs.
She interested herself in local politics.

interest.definition: to try to persuade someone to buy, do or eat something
interest.note: typical: interest someone in a product, a drink NOT for: making someone curious
examples: The salesman tried to interest me in the higher-priced model.
Could I interest you in a drink?

introduce.definition: to tell people who someone is when they first meet, or to bring two people together for the first time
introduce.note: typical: introduce someone to someone, introduce yourself NOT for: presenting a programme
examples: Let me introduce my sister to you.
She introduced herself to the guests.

introduce.definition: to start using a new system, law, idea or product
introduce.note: typical: introduce a system, a law, a rule NOT for: bringing an animal to a new place
examples: The government wants to introduce a system of identity cards.
The school introduced new rules on homework.

introduce.definition: to bring a type of thing to a place for the first time
introduce.note: typical: introduce an animal, plant, species NOT for: presenting a new idea
examples: The grey squirrel was introduced into Britain from North America.
Rabbits were introduced into Australia in the 19th century.

introduce.definition: to show someone something or tell them about it for the first time
introduce.note: typical: introduce someone to something NOT for: presenting two people to each other
examples: Malcolm introduced me to the joys of wine tasting.
The teacher introduced the children to poetry.

introduce.definition: to speak at the beginning of a television or radio programme or a public event, to say what it is about
introduce.note: typical: introduce a programme, a speaker NOT for: introducing two people
examples: Jim Adams will introduce tonight's programme.
She introduced the guest speaker.

introduce.definition: to make something new start to happen or exist in a situation
introduce.note: typical: introduce a feeling, an atmosphere NOT for: passing a law
examples: The peace agreement has introduced a feeling of optimism here.
The new manager introduced a more relaxed atmosphere.

introduce.definition: to formally present a possible new law to be discussed
introduce.note: typical: introduce a bill, legislation NOT for: introducing a person
examples: Several senators introduced legislation aimed at stopping sexual harassment.
The bill was introduced in the House last week.

invite.definition: to ask someone to come to a party, wedding, meal or other event
invite.note: typical: invite someone to a party, for a drink NOT for: politely asking someone to do something
examples: Who should we invite to the party?
Why don't you invite her for a drink one evening?

invite.definition: to politely ask someone to do something
invite.note: typical: be invited to do something NOT for: asking someone to an event
examples: Anyone interested in contributing articles is invited to contact the editor.
Members are invited to submit their ideas.

invite.definition: to encourage something bad to happen, especially without intending to
invite.note: typical: invite trouble, criticism, attack NOT for: asking people to events
examples: Any government that sells arms to dictators is inviting trouble.
His careless remarks invited criticism.

join.definition: to become a member of an organisation, society or group
join.note: typical: join a club, the army, a party NOT for: meeting someone
examples: When did you join the Labour Party?
I decided to join the army.

join.definition: to begin to take part in an activity that other people are involved in
join.note: typical: join a campaign, a search, a scheme NOT for: becoming a member
examples: Church leaders have joined the campaign to end foxhunting.
Many people sacrificed their weekend to join the search.

join.definition: to go somewhere in order to be with someone or do something with them
join.note: typical: join someone for lunch, at a table NOT for: taking part in an organisation
examples: She joined her aunt in the sitting room.
I'll join you later.

join.definition: to do something together with someone else, or as a group
join.note: typical: join together, join someone in doing something NOT for: connecting objects
examples: Three police forces have joined together to buy a helicopter.
I'm sure you'll all join me in thanking today's speaker.

join.definition: to connect or fasten things together
