join.note: typical: join two pieces, join something to something NOT for: roads meeting
examples: Join the two pieces of wood with strong glue.
The island is joined to the mainland by a causeway.

join.definition: if two roads, rivers or similar things join, they come together at a particular point
join.note: typical: a river joining the sea, roads joining NOT for: fastening objects
examples: The River Dart joins the sea at Dartmouth.
The two roads join at the village.

join.definition: to go and stand at the end of a line of people (join a queue)
join.note: typical: join the queue, a line NOT for: becoming a member
examples: He went in and joined the queue for the toilets.
We joined the line for tickets.

join.definition: if people join hands, they hold each other's hands
join.note: typical: join hands NOT for: connecting things
examples: They joined hands and danced round and round.
The children joined hands in a circle.

juggle.definition: to keep three or more objects moving through the air by throwing and catching them very quickly
juggle.note: typical: juggle balls, with five balls NOT for: managing several jobs
examples: One guy was juggling with five balls.
He can juggle three oranges.

juggle.definition: to try to fit two or more jobs, activities and so on into your life, especially with difficulty
juggle.note: typical: juggle a job with children NOT for: throwing objects
examples: It's hard trying to juggle a job with kids and the housework.
She juggles work and study.

juggle.definition: to change things or arrange them in a different way in order to get a result that you want
juggle.note: typical: juggle figures, the budget NOT for: throwing objects
examples: The company juggled the figures to hide its losses.
He juggled the schedule to fit in the meeting.

kick.definition: to hit something with your foot
kick.note: typical: kick a ball, a door, someone NOT for: moving your legs without hitting something
examples: Billy was kicking a ball around the yard.
The police kicked the door down.

kick.definition: to move your legs as if you were kicking something
kick.note: typical: kick your legs, kick off your shoes NOT for: hitting something
examples: He kicked off his shoes and lay back on the bed.
The baby was kicking her legs in the air.

kick.definition: to feel annoyed with yourself because you have done something silly or made a mistake (kick yourself, spoken)
kick.note: typical: you'll kick yourself NOT for: physically kicking
examples: You'll kick yourself when I tell you the answer.
He kicked himself for forgetting her birthday.

kick.definition: to stop doing something that is a harmful habit (kick the habit)
kick.note: typical: kick the habit NOT for: hitting something
examples: The scheme helps smokers to kick the habit.
It took him years to kick his drinking habit.

kill.definition: to make a person, animal or plant die
kill.note: typical: kill a person, an animal, germs NOT for: stopping a machine
examples: The driver and his passenger were killed in the crash.
Bleach kills household germs.

kill.definition: to make something stop operating or to make something fail
kill.note: typical: kill the engine, a plan, local trade NOT for: causing death
examples: Joe pulled in and killed the engine.
The out-of-town shopping centre will kill local trade.

kill.definition: to be very angry with someone (informal)
kill.note: typical: Mum will kill me NOT for: causing a death
examples: Mom will kill me if I'm late.
My dad will kill me when he sees the dent.

kill.definition: to make someone feel annoyed, sad or concerned
kill.note: typical: it kills me to see NOT for: causing a death
examples: It kills me to see him wasting his talent.
It kills her that nobody noticed.

kill.definition: to spend time doing something while you are waiting for something else (kill time)
kill.note: typical: kill time NOT for: causing death
examples: We had an hour to kill before the train.
He killed time by reading magazines.

kill.definition: if a part of your body is killing you, it hurts very much (informal)
kill.note: typical: my feet are killing me NOT for: causing death
examples: My feet are killing me after that long walk.
His back was killing him all week.

knit.definition: to make clothing out of wool or similar thread using two long needles or a machine
knit.note: typical: knit a sweater, scarf, socks NOT for: sewing
examples: My grandmother taught me how to knit.
Emily knitted him some socks.

knit.definition: to use a basic stitch in knitting (the plain stitch, as opposed to purl)
knit.note: typical: knit one, purl one NOT for: making a whole garment
examples: Knit one row, then purl one row.
Knit the next two stitches together.

knit.definition: to join people, things or ideas more closely together, or to be joined closely together
knit.note: typical: closely knit, tightly knit, knit together NOT for: making clothes
examples: It's a closely knit community.
Harold is part of a tightly knit team.

knit.definition: to bring your eyebrows together in a frown (knit your brows)
knit.note: typical: knit your brows NOT for: making clothes
examples: He knitted his brows and looked at the page.
She knitted her brows in concentration.

land.definition: if an aircraft, boat or space vehicle lands, or if someone lands it, it arrives on the ground, water or another surface after travelling
land.note: typical: planes, boats, spacecraft landing NOT for: objects dropping from a height
examples: The plane landed safely at 8:15.
Astronauts first landed on the Moon in 1969.

land.definition: to come down through the air onto something
land.note: typical: land on the roof, in a bush NOT for: aircraft arriving at an airport
examples: A large branch landed on the hood of my car.
Louis fell out of the tree and landed in a holly bush.

land.definition: if a boat or aircraft lands people or goods, it brings them to a place and the people get out or the goods are carried out
land.note: typical: land troops, passengers, cargo NOT for: the vehicle itself arriving
examples: The troops were landed by helicopter.
The boat landed its catch at dawn.

land.definition: to succeed in getting a job, contract or similar thing that was difficult to get (informal)
land.note: typical: land a job, a contract, a part NOT for: physically arriving
examples: He landed a job with a law firm.
Bill has just landed himself a part in a Broadway show.

land.definition: to cause someone to have serious problems or to be in a difficult situation
land.note: typical: land someone in trouble, hospital, court NOT for: physically landing
examples: Connie's going to land herself in big trouble if she keeps arriving late.
The illness landed her in hospital.

land.definition: to arrive unexpectedly and cause problems
land.note: typical: land on someone's desk NOT for: planned arrivals
examples: Just when I thought my problems were over, this letter landed on my desk.
A new crisis landed on the manager's desk.

land.definition: to succeed in hitting someone (land a punch, blow)
land.note: typical: land a punch, a blow NOT for: aircraft landing
examples: He landed a heavy punch on his opponent's jaw.
She landed a blow to the head.

land.note: typical: land a fish, a salmon NOT for: catching anything else
examples: He landed a huge trout after a ten-minute fight.
She finally landed the salmon.

lead.definition: to take someone somewhere by going in front of them while they follow, or by pulling them gently
lead.note: typical: lead someone to a chair, lead the way NOT for: being in charge
examples: A nurse took her arm and led her to a chair.
The horses were led to safety.

lead.definition: to go in front of a line of people or vehicles
lead.note: typical: lead a parade, a march NOT for: taking one person somewhere
examples: A firetruck was leading the parade.
The band led the procession through the town.

lead.definition: to be in charge of an organisation, country, team or group of people who are trying to do something
lead.note: typical: lead a party, an investigation, a campaign NOT for: going in front
examples: He has led the party for over twenty years.
The investigation will be led by Inspector Scarfe.

lead.definition: to cause something to happen or to cause someone to do something
lead.note: typical: lead to a war, a career, lead someone to do something NOT for: being in charge
examples: A degree in English could lead to a career in journalism.
What led him to quit his job?

lead.definition: to make someone believe something, especially something that is not true
lead.note: typical: lead someone to believe, expect NOT for: going in front
examples: He had led everyone to believe that his family was very wealthy.
The hotel was not at all what we had been led to expect.

lead.definition: to influence someone to make them do something that is wrong
lead.note: typical: lead someone into crime, be easily led NOT for: being in charge
examples: His brother led him into a life of crime.
He's not a bad boy; he's just easily led.

lead.definition: to be more successful than other people, companies or countries in a particular activity
lead.note: typical: lead the world, the market, the field NOT for: winning a game
examples: US companies lead the world in biotechnology.
The company leads the market in solar panels.

lead.definition: to be winning a game or competition
lead.note: typical: lead 1-0, lead the race NOT for: being in charge
examples: At half-time, Brazil led 1-0.
With fifteen laps to go, Schumacher led the race.

lead.definition: if a road, path or door leads somewhere, it goes to that place
lead.note: typical: a road, path, door leading to a place NOT for: taking a person somewhere
examples: This road leads to the airport.
A narrow path leads down to the beach.

lead.definition: to live a particular kind of life
lead.note: typical: lead a normal life, a quiet life NOT for: being in charge
examples: If the operation succeeds, Carly will be able to lead a normal life.
They lead a nomadic existence.

lead.definition: to control the way a discussion or conversation develops
lead.note: typical: lead the conversation back to something NOT for: taking someone somewhere
examples: I tried to lead the conversation back to the subject of money.
The interviewer led the discussion towards politics.

lend.definition: to let someone borrow money or something that belongs to you for a short time
lend.note: typical: lend someone money, a book, a car NOT for: a bank giving a loan
examples: Can you lend me £10 until tomorrow?
I lent my CD player to Dave and haven't got it back yet.

lend.definition: if a bank or financial institution lends money, it lets someone have it on condition that they pay it back later with interest
lend.note: typical: banks lending money, a mortgage NOT for: lending a book to a friend
examples: A lot of banks are unwilling to lend money to new businesses.
The building society agreed to lend us £60,000.

lend.definition: to give a situation or event a particular quality (formal)
lend.note: typical: lend dignity, interest, charm to something NOT for: lending objects
examples: The presence of members of the royal family lent a certain dignity to the ceremony.
The candles lent the room a warm glow.

lie.definition: to be in a flat position on the floor, a bed or another surface
lie.note: typical: lie on the bed, in the sun, awake NOT for: telling an untruth
examples: He was lying on the bed smoking a cigarette.
The dog was lying on the floor.

lie.definition: to put yourself into a flat position on the floor or a bed
lie.note: typical: lie down, lie back NOT for: being already flat
examples: Lie flat on the floor.
She lay back against the pillows.

lie.definition: to be in a flat position on a surface (of things)
lie.note: typical: papers lying on a desk NOT for: people lying down
examples: The papers were lying neatly on his desk.
A thin layer of snow lay on the ground.

lie.definition: if a problem, answer, blame or cause lies somewhere, it exists or can be found there
lie.note: typical: the problem lies in, the fault lies with NOT for: physical position
examples: Part of the blame must lie with social services.
The difficulty lies in providing sufficient evidence.

lie.definition: if a town, village or other place lies in a particular place, it is in that place
lie.note: typical: a town lying in a valley NOT for: people lying down
examples: The town lies in a small wooded valley.
The Tasman Sea lies between Tasmania and Australia.

lie.definition: if something lies ahead of you or in the future, it is going to happen to you
lie.note: typical: what lies ahead NOT for: physical position
examples: How will we cope with the difficulties that lie ahead?
A long journey lay before us.

lie.definition: to be in a particular state or condition (linking verb)
lie.note: typical: lie empty, open, hidden, in ruins NOT for: lying flat
examples: The book lay open on the table.
The town now lay in ruins.

lie.definition: to be in a particular position in a competition (British)
lie.note: typical: lie second, third NOT for: physical position
examples: Liverpool are lying third in the championship.
He lay fourth after the first lap.

lie.definition: to deliberately tell someone something that is not true
lie.note: typical: lie to someone, lie about something NOT for: lying flat
examples: I could tell from her face that she was lying.
She lied about her age.

lie.definition: if a picture, account or statistic lies, it does not show the true facts or situation
lie.note: typical: statistics can lie, the camera never lies NOT for: people telling lies
examples: Statistics can often lie.
The camera never lies.

lift.definition: to move something or someone upwards into the air
lift.note: typical: lift a box, a lid, a child NOT for: moving only a part of your body
examples: He lifted the lid on the pot of soup.
They lifted Andrew onto the bed.

lift.definition: to move a part of your body up to a higher position
lift.note: typical: lift your hand, arm, head, eyes NOT for: lifting objects
examples: She lifted her hand to knock on the door once again.
He lifted his head to look at her.

lift.definition: to remove a rule or law that says something is not allowed
lift.note: typical: lift a ban, a restriction, sanctions NOT for: raising a physical object
examples: The government plans to lift its ban on cigar imports.
The council lifted the restrictions on water use.

lift.definition: to take people or things to or from a place by aircraft
lift.note: typical: troops, supplies lifted by helicopter NOT for: lifting by hand
examples: More troops are being lifted into the area as the fighting spreads.
The injured climbers were lifted to hospital by helicopter.

lift.definition: if cloud or mist lifts, it disappears
lift.note: typical: the fog, mist, cloud lifts NOT for: lifting something by hand
examples: By ten o'clock the fog had lifted.
We waited for the mist to lift.

lift.definition: if feelings of sadness lift, they disappear
lift.note: typical: depression, gloom, mood lifts NOT for: physical lifting
examples: Jan's depression seemed to be lifting at last.
Her mood lifted as soon as the sun came out.

lift.definition: to take words or ideas from someone else's work and use them as your own
lift.note: typical: lift a passage, an idea from a book NOT for: stealing objects
examples: The words were lifted from an article in a medical journal.
He lifted whole paragraphs from his friend's essay.

lift.note: typical: lift a wallet, CDs from a shop NOT for: borrowing something
examples: They had lifted dozens of CDs from the store.
Someone lifted my purse on the train.

lift.definition: to make prices, profits or an economy increase
lift.note: typical: lift the economy, profits, sales NOT for: lifting objects
examples: The U.S. may use tax cuts to lift the economy.
The good news lifted share prices.

lift.definition: to dig up vegetables that grow under the ground
lift.note: typical: lift potatoes, carrots, bulbs NOT for: picking fruit
examples: She was lifting potatoes in the garden.
We lift the onions in late summer.

light.definition: to start to burn, or to make something start to burn
light.note: typical: light a fire, a candle, a cigarette NOT for: giving light to a room
examples: He stopped to light a cigarette.
I couldn't get the candles to light.

light.definition: to provide light for a place
light.note: typical: a room lit by a lamp, well lit, poorly lit NOT for: setting fire to something
examples: The room was lit by one large, central light.
The kitchen was warm and brightly lit.

list.definition: to write a list of things, or mention things one after the other
list.note: typical: list names, prices, hotels NOT for: putting a person on an official list
examples: The guidebook lists 1,000 hotels and restaurants.
Please list your main duties in the form.

list.definition: to put someone or something on an official list
list.note: typical: listed in critical condition, listed for trial NOT for: writing any ordinary list
examples: Several passengers were listed in critical condition.
The case was listed for trial in the Crown Court.

list.definition: if a ship lists, it leans to one side
list.note: typical: a ship, a boat lists NOT for: writing a list
examples: The ship began to list badly after hitting the rock.
The boat was listing to one side.

lock.definition: to fasten something, usually with a key, so that other people cannot open it
lock.note: typical: lock a door, a car, a drawer NOT for: becoming stuck
examples: Did you lock the car?
I can't get this drawer to lock.

lock.definition: to put something in a place and fasten the door or lid with a key
lock.note: typical: lock sb or sth in a room, a safe NOT for: only locking a door
examples: Lock the cat in the kitchen.
She locked the documents in the safe.

lock.definition: to become fixed in one position and impossible to move, or to make something fixed
lock.note: typical: wheels, joints lock; locked in an embrace NOT for: using a key
examples: The wheels suddenly locked.
Their eyes locked together for an instant.

lock.definition: if you are locked in a situation, you cannot get out of it
lock.note: typical: locked in a contract, in a cycle NOT for: physical locking
examples: The company is locked into a five-year contract.
The two groups are locked in a vicious cycle of killing.

mark.definition: to write or draw on something so that someone will notice it
mark.note: typical: mark a page, a box, a document 'urgent' NOT for: marking schoolwork
examples: I've marked the pages you need to look at.
A document marked 'confidential' was on his desk.

mark.definition: to make a mark on something in a way that spoils its appearance
mark.note: typical: mark the floor, a table, a wall NOT for: writing on purpose
examples: Take off your shoes so you don't mark the floor.
The table marks easily, so please be careful.

mark.note: typical: mark an occasion, an anniversary NOT for: spoiling a surface
examples: Celebrations were held to mark Australia Day.
Mrs Lawson was given a gold watch to mark the occasion.

mark.note: typical: mark a grave, a route, a place on a map NOT for: celebrating
examples: A simple wooden cross marked her grave.
He had marked the route on the map in red.

mark.definition: if a date marks an event, the event happened on that date in an earlier year
mark.note: typical: this week marks the anniversary of NOT for: celebrating the event
examples: This week marks the 250th anniversary of the birth of Joseph Priestley.
Today marks ten years since the school opened.

mark.definition: to be a sign of an important change or stage in development
mark.note: typical: mark a turning point, the end of an era NOT for: writing on something
examples: Her latest novel marks a turning point in her development as a writer.
These elections mark the end of an era.

mark.definition: if something is marked by a quality, it is a typical or important part of it (passive)
mark.note: typical: marked by beauty, violence, conflict NOT for: physical marks
examples: The villages of East Anglia are marked by beautiful churches.
His rule was marked by cruelty.

mark.definition: to read written work and give it a number or letter to show how good it is (especially BrE)
mark.note: typical: mark exams, essays, homework NOT for: writing on a page to show something
examples: I've got a pile of exam papers to mark.
The teacher marked our essays over the weekend.

mark.definition: to stay close to a player of the opposite team during a game (especially BrE)
mark.note: typical: mark a striker, a player NOT for: grading work
examples: He was told to mark the opposing team's best player.
The defender marked him closely all game.

marry.definition: to become someone's husband or wife
marry.note: typical: marry someone, marry young, marry late NOT for: performing the ceremony
examples: He married Bea in 1925.
I'm going to ask her to marry me.

marry.definition: to perform the ceremony at which two people get married
marry.note: typical: the priest, the judge who married us NOT for: becoming husband or wife
examples: The priest who married us was really nice.
A judge married them in the town hall.

marry.definition: to find a husband or wife for one of your children
marry.note: typical: marry your daughters to rich men NOT for: marrying yourself
examples: She was determined to marry all of her daughters to rich men.
They married their son to a girl from a good family.

marry.definition: to combine two different ideas, designs or styles (formal)
marry.note: typical: marry tradition with modern style NOT for: weddings
examples: The building's design marries a traditional style with modern materials.
He writes fiction that marries realism and the supernatural.

mean.definition: to have or represent a particular meaning
mean.note: typical: a word, a sign, a light means something NOT for: a person intending something
examples: What does 'patronizing' mean?
The red light means 'Stop'.

mean.definition: to intend a particular meaning when you say something
mean.note: typical: what do you mean, what she means NOT for: signs or words having meaning
examples: It's pretty obvious what she means.
What I mean is, I don't feel alone anymore.

mean.definition: to intend to do something, or to intend that someone else should do something
mean.note: typical: mean to do sth, mean no harm NOT for: results
examples: I've been meaning to ask you if you want to come for a meal.
I didn't mean to upset you.

mean.definition: to have a particular result or involve something
mean.note: typical: will mean trouble, mean doing sth NOT for: intending
examples: The merger will mean the closure of the company's Sydney office.
My new job will mean travelling all over the world.

mean.definition: if a name or word means something to you, you are familiar with it
mean.note: typical: mean nothing, mean anything to you NOT for: a word's definition
examples: He said his name was 'Randall' but it meant nothing to me.
Does the name Bryce mean anything to you?

mean.definition: to be serious about what you are saying or writing
mean.note: typical: mean it, mean what you say NOT for: intending to do something
examples: With children, if you say 'no', you have to mean it.
You don't really mean that, do you?

mean.note: typical: mean a lot, mean the world to sb NOT for: meaning of words
examples: The medal meant a lot to him.
He meant the world to her.

mean.definition: to be a sign that something is true or will happen
mean.note: typical: does not mean that, clear skies mean NOT for: intending
examples: Finding a lump does not necessarily mean you have cancer.
Clear skies mean that it will be a cold night.

mend.definition: to repair something that is torn or broken
mend.note: typical: mend clothes, shoes, a toy NOT for: bones healing
examples: My father used to mend our shoes.
When are you going to mend that light in the hall?

mend.definition: if a broken bone mends, it becomes whole again (informal)
mend.note: typical: a leg, a bone mends NOT for: repairing objects
examples: His leg isn't mending as quickly as he'd expected.
The bone should mend in about six weeks.

mend.definition: to end a quarrel or difficult situation by dealing with the problem
mend.note: typical: mend matters, relations NOT for: repairing objects
examples: I've tried to mend matters between us, but she's still very angry.
He tried to mend relations with his brother.

mention.definition: to talk or write about something or someone, usually quickly and without much detail
mention.note: typical: mention a name, a problem, an idea NOT for: describing in detail
examples: Was my name mentioned at all?
He mentioned that he was having problems, but he didn't explain.

move.definition: to change from one place or position to another, or to make something do this
move.note: typical: move closer, move a car, no one moved NOT for: changing home
examples: Could you move your car, please? It's blocking the road.
He moved closer to her.

move.definition: to go to live or work in a different place
move.note: typical: move house, move to a new city, move offices NOT for: shifting position
examples: We've moved seven or eight times in the last five years.
They've moved into bigger offices in London.

move.definition: to change from one opinion or way of thinking to another, or to persuade someone to do so
move.note: typical: move on an issue; she won't be moved NOT for: physical movement
examples: Neither side is willing to move on the issue of territory.
She won't be moved; it doesn't matter what you say.

move.definition: to make progress in a particular way or at a particular rate
move.note: typical: things move quickly, move in the right direction NOT for: physical movement
examples: Things moved quickly once the contract was signed.
The negotiations seem to be moving in the right direction.

move.definition: to start taking action, especially to deal with a problem
move.note: typical: move on, move against, move fast NOT for: changing place
examples: The governor has yet to move on any of the recommendations.
You'll have to move fast if you want to get a place on the course.

move.definition: to change to a different job or class, or to make someone do so
move.note: typical: move sb to another class, department NOT for: moving house
examples: Several students were moved from the beginners' class into the intermediate one.
He spent five years there before moving to Madrid as a manager.

move.definition: to make someone feel strong emotions, especially sadness or sympathy
move.note: typical: deeply moved, move to tears NOT for: physical movement
examples: Russell was deeply moved by what he heard.
His speech moved the audience to tears.

move.definition: to cause someone to do something
move.note: typical: be moved to do sth, feel moved to NOT for: emotional effect
examples: Seeing her there had moved him to think about the time they had together.
I have never before felt moved to write, but I must protest.

move.definition: to change the time or order of something
move.note: typical: move a meeting, a date NOT for: moving objects
examples: Could we move the meeting to Thursday?
They moved the exam to next week.

move.definition: to start talking or writing about a different subject
move.note: typical: move on to, move away from NOT for: moving house
examples: We seem to be moving away from the main point of the discussion.
Let's move on to the next question.

move.definition: to change the position of a piece in a game such as chess
move.note: typical: move a piece, a pawn NOT for: moving furniture
examples: It's your turn to move.
She moved her queen across the board.

move.definition: to officially make a proposal at a meeting (formal)
move.note: typical: move that, move an amendment NOT for: everyday proposals
examples: I move to approve the minutes as read.
They want to move an amendment to the bill.

move.note: typical: this car can really move NOT for: ordinary movement
examples: This car can really move!
The runner was really moving down the track.

move.definition: if goods are moving, they are being bought, especially at a particular rate
move.note: typical: homes, products moving slowly NOT for: people moving
examples: The highest-priced homes are still moving slowly.
Winter coats are moving fast this year.

note.definition: to notice or pay careful attention to something
note.note: typical: note the time, note that, note how NOT for: writing something down
examples: He carefully noted the time when they left the building.
Please note that the bill must be paid within ten days.

note.definition: to mention something because it is important or interesting
note.note: typical: the judge noted that, it should be noted NOT for: writing notes
examples: The judge noted that Miller had no previous criminal record.
The report notes a sharp rise in prices.

notice.definition: to realize that someone or something exists, especially because you can see, hear or feel them
notice.note: typical: notice a change, notice that, notice sb doing sth NOT for: giving a formal warning
examples: He noticed a woman in a black dress sitting across from him.
Did you notice him leaving the party early?

notice.definition: to get attention, or to make someone get attention (be noticed, get noticed)
notice.note: typical: get yourself noticed, go unnoticed NOT for: seeing small details
examples: These clothes will get you noticed and enhance your image.
She wanted to be noticed by the director.

offer.definition: to ask someone if they would like to have something, or to hold it out to them
offer.note: typical: offer sb a drink, a job, a seat NOT for: offering money for something
examples: Can I offer you something to drink?
They offered him a very good job, but he turned it down.

offer.definition: to say that you are willing to do something
offer.note: typical: offer to help, offer to pay NOT for: giving something
examples: My dad has offered to pick us up.
It was nice of you to offer.

offer.definition: to provide something that people need or want
offer.note: typical: offer advice, support, an opportunity NOT for: handing someone a thing
examples: Your doctor should be able to offer advice on diet.
The Centre offers a wide range of sports facilities.

offer.definition: to say that you are willing to pay a particular amount of money for something
offer.note: typical: offer $5,000 for a house, offer a reward NOT for: offering help
examples: They've offered us £75,000 for the house.
The police are offering a reward for any information.

order.definition: to ask for food or a drink in a restaurant, bar etc
order.note: typical: order a meal, a coffee, are you ready to order NOT for: ordering goods online
examples: Anne ordered another glass of wine.
Are you ready to order?

order.definition: to ask for goods or services to be supplied
order.note: typical: order a computer, a taxi, a book NOT for: ordering food in a restaurant
examples: I've ordered a new computer from the supplier.
I'll order you a taxi.

order.definition: to tell someone that they must do something, using official power or authority
order.note: typical: order sb to do sth, the court ordered NOT for: asking politely
examples: Tom was ordered to pay £300 as compensation.
Her doctor had ordered her to rest for a week.

order.definition: to arrange things in a particular order
order.note: typical: ordered alphabetically, by size NOT for: giving commands
examples: The list is ordered alphabetically.
The files are ordered by date.

organise.definition: to make the necessary arrangements so that an activity can happen effectively
organise.note: typical: organise an event, a trip, a meeting NOT for: tidying things
examples: The course was organised by a training company.
Students need to learn how to organise their work.

organise.definition: to manage a group of people who are doing something
organise.note: typical: organise a group, a campaign, yourselves NOT for: planning an event alone
examples: The lawyer helped to organise a group of parents who took action for their children.
The scientists need to organise themselves and work as a team.

organise.definition: to arrange something so that it is more ordered or sensible
organise.note: typical: organise your life, your time NOT for: planning an event
examples: He doesn't need you to organise his life for him.
Organise yourself to arrive at places on time.

organise.definition: to arrange things in a particular order or pattern
organise.note: typical: organise files, ideas, books NOT for: managing people
examples: We are learning about how genes are organised.
She organised her notes by topic.

organise.definition: to form a trade union or persuade people to join one
organise.note: typical: workers organise NOT for: planning events
examples: The law gives workers the right to organise and bargain collectively.
They tried to organise the factory workers.

own.definition: to have something that belongs to you and is legally yours
own.note: typical: own a house, a car, a business NOT for: borrowing or using something
examples: The building is owned by the local council.
Many more people now own their own homes.

paddle.definition: to move a small light boat through water using a paddle
paddle.note: typical: paddle a canoe, a kayak NOT for: walking in water
examples: She and her husband paddled a canoe down the Mississippi.
I desperately tried to paddle for the shore.

paddle.definition: to walk for pleasure without shoes or socks in shallow water (BrE)
paddle.note: typical: children paddling in the sea NOT for: swimming or boating
examples: Children were paddling in the sea.
We took off our shoes and paddled in the stream.

paddle.definition: to swim with short quick movements
paddle.note: typical: a dog paddling NOT for: boating
examples: The dog was paddling furiously after the ducks.
He paddled to the edge of the pool.

peel.definition: to remove the skin from fruit or vegetables
peel.note: typical: peel an apple, potatoes, an orange NOT for: paint coming off
examples: Peel and dice the potatoes.
She peeled an orange and shared it.

peel.definition: if skin, paper or paint peels, it comes off in small pieces
peel.note: typical: paint peels, wallpaper peeling, skin peels NOT for: removing skin yourself
examples: The paper was peeling from the wall.
After the holiday my sunburnt skin started to peel.

peel.definition: to lose an outer layer or surface
peel.note: typical: walls peeling, a peeling nose NOT for: removing fruit skin
examples: The walls were peeling from the damp.
His nose was peeling after a day on the beach.

peel.definition: to remove the outer layer from something
peel.note: typical: peel away, off, back NOT for: peeling fruit
examples: Peel away the waxed paper from the bottom of the cake.
She peeled back the plastic cover.

please.definition: to make someone happy or satisfied
please.note: typical: please a customer, hard to please NOT for: saying 'please' politely
examples: She did everything she could to please him.
Most children are eager to please.

please.definition: to want or like to do something (used in some phrases)
please.note: typical: do what you please, as you please NOT for: making someone happy
examples: She does what she pleases.
You can spend the money however you please.

plug.definition: to fill a hole or block something
plug.note: typical: plug a hole, a leak, a gap NOT for: connecting electrical equipment
examples: We used mud to plug up the holes in the roof.
The workers plugged the leak with cement.

plug.definition: to advertise a book, film or product by mentioning it publicly
plug.note: typical: plug a new book, a film on TV NOT for: blocking a hole
examples: Arnie was on the show to plug his new movie.
She used every interview to plug her album.

plug.definition: to provide something that is needed because there is not enough
plug.note: typical: plug the gap, a shortage NOT for: blocking a hole
examples: With so few trained doctors, paramedics were brought in to plug the gap.
Temporary staff were hired to plug the shortage.

polish.definition: to rub a surface until it becomes smooth and shiny
polish.note: typical: polish shoes, silver, a floor, furniture NOT for: making a text better
examples: He polished his boots before the interview.
I spent the afternoon polishing the car.

polish.definition: to improve a piece of writing, a speech or a performance by making small changes
polish.note: typical: polish an essay, a speech, a presentation NOT for: rubbing a surface
examples: She polished her speech the night before the conference.
The band polished the song until it sounded perfect.

pour.definition: to make a liquid or other substance flow out of or into a container by tilting it
pour.note: typical: pour coffee, milk, water, sand NOT for: rain or crowds
examples: Can you pour me a glass of water?
He poured the sauce over the pasta.

pour.definition: if a lot of liquid or smoke comes out of somewhere, to flow out in large amounts
pour.note: typical: smoke, blood or water pouring out NOT for: pouring from a container
examples: Water was pouring through the hole in the roof.
Black smoke poured from the engine.

pour.definition: to rain very heavily without stopping
pour.note: typical: it's pouring, it poured all day NOT for: a person pouring a drink
examples: It poured all night, so the match was cancelled.
We got soaked because it was pouring with rain.

pour.definition: if many people or things arrive or leave a place at the same time, to move in large numbers
pour.note: typical: crowds, letters, messages pouring in or out NOT for: liquids
examples: Fans poured out of the stadium after the game.
Complaints poured in after the broadcast.

pour.definition: if light comes into or out of a place in large amounts, to shine strongly
pour.note: typical: sunlight pouring through a window NOT for: pouring a drink
examples: Sunlight poured into the kitchen in the morning.
Bright light poured out of the open door.

practise.definition: to do an activity many times in order to get better at it
practise.note: typical: practise the piano, a speech, a skill, doing sth NOT for: working as a doctor or lawyer
examples: She practises the violin for an hour every day.
We practised parking the car in the empty car park.

practise.definition: to use a particular method, custom or technique as part of your usual behaviour
practise.note: typical: practise a technique, a custom, a method NOT for: training for a skill
examples: The farmers still practise an old method of growing rice.
Many people there practise traditional crafts.

practise.definition: to work as a doctor, lawyer or similar professional
practise.note: typical: practise medicine, law, as a dentist NOT for: rehearsing a skill
examples: She practised as a lawyer for twenty years.
He is not allowed to practise medicine in this country.

practise.definition: to follow the rules of a religion in your daily life
practise.note: typical: practise a religion, your faith NOT for: improving a skill
examples: They are free to practise their religion openly.
He no longer practises, although he was raised as a Catholic.

prefer.definition: to like someone or something more than another, so that you would choose it if you could
prefer.note: typical: prefer tea to coffee, prefer to do sth, prefer doing sth NOT for: simply liking something
examples: I prefer walking to taking the bus.
Most of my friends prefer to stay at home on Sundays.

prepare.definition: to make a meal or a substance ready, especially by following steps
prepare.note: typical: prepare a meal, dinner, a sauce, a mixture NOT for: getting yourself ready
examples: He prepared a simple salad for lunch.
The chemist prepared the solution carefully.

prepare.definition: to write or make a document, plan or other piece of work that will be used later
prepare.note: typical: prepare a report, a speech, a plan, a map NOT for: cooking
examples: The team prepared a report for the board.
She is preparing a presentation for tomorrow.

prepare.definition: to make plans or arrangements for something that will happen in the future
prepare.note: typical: prepare for an exam, a trip, a meeting, to do sth NOT for: cooking food
examples: We are preparing for our holiday in Spain.
The students are preparing for their final exams.

prepare.definition: to make yourself mentally or physically ready for something you expect to happen
prepare.note: typical: prepare yourself for bad news, a shock, a fight NOT for: preparing food
examples: She took a deep breath and prepared herself for the news.
The runners prepared themselves for the long race.

prepare.definition: to give someone the training or skills they need for a job or situation
prepare.note: typical: prepare students, children, a team for sth NOT for: preparing yourself
examples: The course prepares students for university life.
Good coaches prepare their players for tough matches.

press.definition: to push something firmly against a surface
press.note: typical: press your hand against the wall, press a pedal NOT for: pushing a button
examples: He pressed his face against the cold window.
She pressed her hand against the door and listened.

press.definition: to push a button or switch so that a machine starts or something happens
press.note: typical: press a button, a key, a switch, a bell NOT for: pushing something against a surface
examples: Press the red button to stop the machine.
He pressed the doorbell and waited.

press.definition: to make clothes smooth using a hot iron
press.note: typical: press a shirt, a suit, trousers NOT for: crushing fruit
examples: She pressed her shirt before the interview.
I need to press these trousers tonight.

press.definition: to move in a particular direction by pushing, usually in a crowd
press.note: typical: the crowd pressed forward, against sth NOT for: pushing a button
examples: The crowd pressed forward to see the singer.
People pressed against the barriers at the front.

press.definition: to try hard to persuade someone to do or say something, often by asking many times
press.note: typical: press sb to do sth, press sb for an answer NOT for: physical pushing
examples: Reporters pressed the minister for an answer.
They pressed him to reveal the name of the winner.

press.definition: to put weight or force on something to make it flat or to squeeze liquid out of it
press.note: typical: press flowers, grapes, olives NOT for: ironing clothes
examples: She pressed the flowers between the pages of a heavy book.
The olives are pressed to make oil.

press.definition: to hold someone or something close to your body
press.note: typical: press sb/sth to you, to your chest NOT for: pushing a surface
examples: She pressed the baby to her chest.
He pressed the letter to his heart.

press.definition: to offer something to someone and try to make them accept it
press.note: typical: press sth on sb NOT for: asking someone to do something
examples: Our host pressed a second helping on every guest.
She pressed some money on him, but he refused it.

press.definition: to lift a heavy weight above your chest or head using only your arms
press.note: typical: press a weight, a barbell NOT for: pushing buttons
examples: He can press more than a hundred kilos.
She pressed the bar slowly above her head.

press.definition: to make a copy of a record or CD by shaping plastic or metal
press.note: typical: press records, vinyl, CDs NOT for: pressing clothes
examples: The label pressed only a thousand copies of the album.
The factory presses vinyl records every day.

pretend.definition: to behave as if something is true when you know it is not, either for fun or to trick people
pretend.note: typical: pretend to be asleep, pretend (that) NOT for: telling lies about facts only
examples: The children pretended to be pirates.
He pretended not to see me in the street.

pretend.definition: to claim that something is true, especially about yourself, when it is not
pretend.note: typical: I can't pretend to understand, pretend to be sth NOT for: playing games
examples: I don't pretend to know much about art.
The book doesn't pretend to be a complete history.

promise.definition: to tell someone that you will definitely do something or that something will happen
promise.note: typical: promise to do sth, promise sb (that), promise sth to sb NOT for: showing signs of something
examples: She promised to call me on Friday.
He promised us that the work would be finished by Monday.

promise.definition: to show signs that something good or interesting is likely to happen
promise.note: typical: promise to be sth, promise rain, a good result NOT for: making a vow to someone
examples: The meeting promises to be very interesting.
The grey sky promised rain later in the day.

protect.definition: to keep someone or something safe from harm, damage or illness
protect.note: typical: protect children, the environment, from/against sth NOT for: insurance cover
examples: Sunscreen protects your skin from the sun.
The law is meant to protect workers.

protect.definition: if an insurance company protects you or your property, it will pay money if something is lost, stolen or damaged
protect.note: typical: be protected by insurance NOT for: keeping someone safe from danger
examples: Your home is protected against fire and theft.
Are you fully protected if the trip is cancelled?

protect.definition: to help the industries of your own country by taxing or limiting foreign goods
protect.note: typical: protect local industry, jobs, farmers NOT for: protecting people
examples: The government protected its steel industry with high taxes on imports.
Some countries protect their farmers from cheap foreign food.

pump.definition: to make a liquid or gas move in a particular direction using a pump
pump.note: typical: pump water, air, oil into/out of sth NOT for: the heart's beating
examples: They pumped water out of the flooded cellar.
He pumped air into the bicycle tyre.

pump.definition: to bring water, oil or another supply up from under the ground
pump.note: typical: pump water from a well, pump gas AmE NOT for: moving air into a tyre
examples: The village pumps clean water from a deep well.
He works at the station pumping petrol for customers.

pump.definition: if your heart pumps, it moves blood or beats quickly and strongly
pump.note: typical: your heart is pumping NOT for: using a machine
examples: My heart was pumping as I ran up the stairs.
Blood pumps around the body with every heartbeat.

pump.definition: to work a pump by moving a handle or lever up and down
pump.note: typical: pump (away) at sth NOT for: a heart beating
examples: She pumped at the handle until water came out.
He pumped away at the old bellows.

pump.definition: if a liquid pumps out of something, it comes out suddenly in small amounts
pump.note: typical: blood pumping from a wound NOT for: using a machine
examples: Blood pumped from the cut on his arm.
Oil pumped out of the broken pipe.

pump.definition: to ask someone a lot of questions to get information from them
pump.note: typical: pump sb for information NOT for: moving a liquid
examples: The reporter tried to pump her for details about the plan.
They pumped him for information about the company.

punch.definition: to hit someone or something hard with your closed hand
punch.note: typical: punch sb in the face, on the nose NOT for: making holes
examples: He punched the man in the stomach.
She punched the wall in frustration.

punch.definition: to make a hole in something using a tool or a sharp object
punch.note: typical: punch a hole, a ticket, holes in paper NOT for: hitting people
examples: The guard punched my ticket as I got on the train.
He punched two holes in the paper to put it in the folder.

punch.definition: to push a button or key on a machine
punch.note: typical: punch a button, a key, a number NOT for: hitting someone
examples: She punched the button for the top floor.
He punched in the code and the door opened.

punish.definition: to make someone suffer because they have done something wrong or broken a rule
punish.note: typical: punish a child, a criminal, sb for (doing) sth NOT for: rewarding behaviour
examples: Parents should not punish children for telling the truth.
The company was punished for ignoring safety rules.

punish.definition: to give a particular penalty for a crime, so that anyone guilty of it suffers in that way
punish.note: typical: be punished by a fine, death, prison NOT for: personal feelings
examples: In some countries, theft is punished by prison.
The offence is punished with a heavy fine.

punish.definition: to make yourself feel guilty or unhappy because of something you have done
punish.note: typical: punish yourself for sth NOT for: punishing other people
examples: Don't punish yourself over one small mistake.
She keeps punishing herself for missing the call.

question.definition: to ask someone questions in order to get information, especially officially
question.note: typical: question a suspect, a witness, sb about sth NOT for: doubting something
examples: The police questioned him for several hours.
The teacher questioned the pupils about the missing book.

question.definition: to express doubt about whether something is true, right or sensible
question.note: typical: question a decision, a claim, whether sth is true NOT for: asking someone questions
examples: Nobody dared to question the manager's decision.
I question whether this plan will really work.

quit.definition: to leave a job, school or similar place, especially before finishing
quit.note: typical: quit a job, school, a team NOT for: stopping a habit
examples: He quit his job after an argument with his boss.
She quit school at sixteen.

quit.definition: to stop doing something, especially a bad or annoying habit
quit.note: typical: quit smoking, quit doing sth, quit it NOT for: leaving a job
examples: He quit smoking last year.
Quit complaining and help me!

quit.definition: to leave a house or flat that you have been renting (BrE, legal)
quit.note: typical: quit the premises, a rented flat NOT for: leaving a job
examples: The tenants were told to quit the premises within a week.
The landlord asked them to quit the property by Friday.

quit.note: typical: quit a building, a country, a room NOT for: informal use in speech
examples: The soldiers quit the town at dawn.
The president quit the hall without a word.

race.definition: to compete against someone or something in a race
race.note: typical: race against sb, race a car, a horse NOT for: hurrying
examples: She will race against the best runners in the world.
They raced their boats across the bay.

race.definition: to move or take someone somewhere very quickly
race.note: typical: race home, race into a room, race sb to hospital NOT for: competing
examples: He raced into the house to answer the phone.
The injured man was raced to hospital.

race.definition: to try to do something very quickly because you want to be first or there is little time
race.note: typical: race to do sth, race against time NOT for: sports contests
examples: Rescuers raced to reach the trapped miners.
Companies are racing to launch the new product.

race.definition: if your heart or mind races, it works faster than usual because you are afraid or excited
race.note: typical: my heart was racing, my mind was racing NOT for: physical competitions
examples: My heart raced as I opened the letter.
Her mind raced as she tried to think of an answer.

race.definition: if an engine races, it runs too fast
race.note: typical: the engine races NOT for: people running
examples: The engine raced when the car lost grip on the ice.
He heard the motor race and then stop.

reach.definition: to get to a particular point, stage or level in a process or development
reach.note: typical: reach the final, a stage, an age, a conclusion NOT for: stretching your arm
examples: Our team reached the final for the first time.
The children have reached an age where they can look after themselves.

reach.definition: if something reaches a particular amount or rate, it increases until it gets to that point
reach.note: typical: temperatures, prices, numbers reaching a level NOT for: arriving somewhere
examples: Temperatures are expected to reach 40 degrees tomorrow.
The cost of the project reached a million pounds.

reach.definition: to agree on or decide something after a lot of discussion
reach.note: typical: reach an agreement, a decision, a verdict NOT for: moving your arm
examples: The two sides finally reached an agreement.
It took the jury two days to reach a verdict.

reach.definition: to stretch out your arm in order to touch, pick up or get something
reach.note: typical: reach for sth, reach into a bag, reach out a hand NOT for: arriving at a place
examples: She reached into her bag for her keys.
I can't reach the top shelf without a chair.

reach.definition: to be big enough or long enough to get to a particular point
reach.note: typical: a cable, skirt or branches reaching a point NOT for: arriving somewhere
examples: The cable isn't long enough to reach the socket.
Her hair reaches down to her waist.

reach.definition: to arrive at a place after a journey
reach.note: typical: reach London, the village, the top NOT for: stretching your arm
examples: We reached the hotel just before midnight.
The letter took a week to reach me.

reach.definition: to get in touch with someone, especially by telephone
reach.note: typical: reach sb by phone, at an address NOT for: arriving at a place
examples: You can reach me on my mobile after six.
I tried to reach her all day, but her phone was off.

record.definition: to write down or store information so that it can be looked at in the future
record.note: typical: record data, details, a verdict, expenses NOT for: sound or video
examples: The nurse recorded the patient's temperature every hour.
She recorded every penny she spent in a notebook.

record.definition: to store sound, music or television programmes on tape, disc or a device so that people can hear or watch them later
record.note: typical: record an album, a song, a film, a programme NOT for: writing notes
examples: The band recorded their new album in London.
I'll record the match and we can watch it tonight.

record.definition: if an instrument records something such as speed or temperature, it measures it and keeps the information
record.note: typical: record a temperature, wind speed, an earthquake NOT for: music
examples: The machine recorded wind speeds of over 100 mph.
The thermometer recorded a low of minus ten degrees.

refuse.definition: to say firmly that you will not do something that someone has asked you to do
refuse.note: typical: refuse to do sth, flatly refuse NOT for: saying no to a gift
examples: She asked him to leave, but he refused.
The workers refused to go back to work.

refuse.definition: to say no to something that you have been offered
refuse.note: typical: refuse an offer, a job, food, a drink NOT for: refusing to do something
examples: He refused a second piece of cake.
She refused the job because the pay was too low.

refuse.definition: to not give or allow someone something that they want, especially officially
refuse.note: typical: refuse sb sth, be refused a visa, entry NOT for: saying no to an offer
examples: She was refused a work permit.
The bank refused them a loan.

relax.definition: to rest or do something enjoyable, especially after working
relax.note: typical: relax at home, relax with a book, a bath helps you relax NOT for: loosening rules
examples: I just want to sit down and relax.
A hot bath should help to relax you.

relax.definition: to become calm after being nervous or upset, or to make someone feel this way
relax.note: typical: relax! start to relax, relax sb NOT for: loosening muscles
examples: He relaxed when he saw the dog was friendly.
Relax, everything is going to be fine.

relax.definition: if a part of your body relaxes, or you relax it, it becomes less stiff or tight
relax.note: typical: relax your shoulders, muscles, grip NOT for: feeling calm
examples: Gentle exercise can relax stiff shoulder muscles.
She let her hands relax in her lap.

relax.definition: to make rules, laws or controls less strict
relax.note: typical: relax a rule, a law, restrictions NOT for: resting
examples: The government decided to relax the travel rules.
The school relaxed its dress code for the summer.

remain.definition: to continue to be in the same state or condition
remain.note: typical: remain calm, silent, seated, unchanged NOT for: staying in a place
examples: Please remain seated until the plane stops.
The boy remained silent during the meeting.

remain.definition: to stay in the same place without moving away (formal)
remain.note: typical: remain at home, in the UK, in a room NOT for: informal speech
examples: She was too ill to remain at home.
The refugees were allowed to remain in the country.

remain.definition: to continue to exist or be left after other things have gone, been used or destroyed
remain.note: typical: little remains, what remains of sth NOT for: staying in a place
examples: Little of the old castle remains today.
Only a few cookies remained on the plate.

remain.definition: to be left still to be dealt with or done
remain.note: typical: remain to be done, settled, discussed NOT for: staying in a state
examples: Several points remain to be settled.
A few jobs still remain to be finished.

remember.definition: to have a picture or idea in your mind of people, events or places from the past
remember.note: typical: remember a name, a face, doing sth NOT for: not forgetting a task
examples: I remember my first day at school.
She clearly remembers meeting him at a party.

remember.definition: to bring information or facts that you know back into your mind
remember.note: typical: remember a number, a password, what/how/why NOT for: remembering the past
examples: I can't remember her phone number.
He suddenly remembered that he had left the oven on.

remember.definition: to not forget something that you must do, get or bring
remember.note: typical: remember to do sth, remember your keys NOT for: recalling a past experience
examples: Remember to lock the door when you leave.
I hope he remembers the tickets.

remember.definition: to keep a particular fact in mind, especially as a warning or advice
remember.note: typical: remember that..., it should be remembered that NOT for: recalling a memory
examples: Remember that not everyone has as much money as you.
It should be remembered that the work took years.

remember.definition: to think with respect about someone who has died, often in a ceremony
remember.note: typical: remember the dead, the fallen, a victim NOT for: remembering facts
examples: On this day we remember those who died in the war.
The town remembers the victims every year.

remember.definition: to be known and talked about for something important you did in the past (usually passive)
remember.note: typical: be remembered for/as sth NOT for: recalling something yourself
examples: He is best remembered for his travel books.
She wanted to be remembered as a kind teacher.

remind.definition: to make someone remember something that they must do
remind.note: typical: remind sb to do sth, about sth NOT for: bringing back memories of a person
examples: Please remind me to buy milk tonight.
She reminded her son that he had a dentist appointment.

remind.definition: to make someone remember a person or something that happened in the past, often because of similarity
remind.note: typical: remind sb of sth/sb NOT for: telling someone to do a task
examples: That song always reminds me of our first holiday.
You remind me of my brother.

remove.definition: to take something away from the place where it is
remove.note: typical: remove a stain, a lid, sth from sth NOT for: dismissing a person
examples: Please remove your shoes at the door.
Books may not be removed from the library.

remove.definition: to get rid of something so that it no longer exists
remove.note: typical: remove a stain, an obstacle, a rule NOT for: taking something off a place
examples: This cleaner will remove wine stains.
The college removed the rules that kept women out.

remove.definition: to force someone out of an important position or job
remove.note: typical: remove sb from office, a post NOT for: taking things away
examples: Congress can remove the president from office.
The headteacher was removed from his post.

remove.definition: to take off a piece of clothing (formal)
remove.note: typical: remove a hat, a coat, gloves NOT for: everyday speech
examples: He removed his hat and gloves.
She removed her coat and sat down.

rent.definition: to pay money regularly to live in a house or room, or to use something that belongs to someone else
rent.note: typical: rent a flat, a room, land from sb NOT for: letting your property to others
examples: Most students rent rooms in their second year.
Some farmers rent land from the council.

rent.definition: to let someone live in a house or room that you own, or use your land, in return for money
rent.note: typical: rent out a room, a flat to sb NOT for: paying to live somewhere
examples: She rents out two rooms to students.
He rents the cottage to tourists in summer.

rent.definition: to pay money to use something for a short period of time, especially in American English
rent.note: typical: rent a car, a bike, equipment NOT for: paying monthly for housing
examples: Will you rent a car while you are in Spain?
We rented skis for the weekend.

repair.definition: to fix something that is damaged, broken or not working properly
repair.note: typical: repair a roof, a car, shoes, a machine NOT for: making up for a mistake
examples: He repaired the broken window himself.
Where can I get my watch repaired?

repair.definition: to put right harm or damage you have caused, especially to a relationship or reputation (formal)
repair.note: typical: repair the damage, a relationship, trust NOT for: fixing objects
examples: The company tried to repair the damage to its reputation.
They worked hard to repair their friendship after the argument.

repeat.definition: to say or write something again
repeat.note: typical: repeat a question, a word, yourself NOT for: doing an action again
examples: Could you repeat your name, please?
He repeated that he had never seen the letter.

repeat.note: typical: repeat an experiment, a mistake, a year at school NOT for: saying words again
examples: Repeat the exercise three times a day.
The team hopes to repeat last year's success.

repeat.definition: to say something that someone else has just said, especially in order to learn it
repeat.note: typical: repeat after me, repeat a sentence NOT for: telling a secret
examples: Listen to the teacher and repeat each word.
Repeat after me: I will not be late.

repeat.definition: to tell someone something that you have heard, especially something secret
repeat.note: typical: repeat a secret, a rumour, gossip NOT for: saying your own words again
examples: Please don't repeat what I told you.
I shouldn't repeat this, but she is leaving the company.

repeat.definition: to broadcast a television or radio programme again
repeat.note: typical: a series, a show repeated on TV NOT for: doing an activity again
examples: The series will be repeated next summer.
The programme was repeated on Sunday afternoon.

reply.definition: to answer someone by saying or writing something
reply.note: typical: reply to a letter, an email, a question NOT for: reacting with an action
examples: She has not replied to my message yet.
"I don't know," he replied.

reply.definition: to react to an action by doing something else
reply.note: typical: reply with force, reply by doing sth NOT for: answering a question
examples: The army replied to the attack with heavy gunfire.
The company replied by lowering its prices.

report.definition: to give people information about recent events, especially in the news
report.note: typical: report the news, a story, on an event NOT for: telling the police
examples: Journalists reported that three people had been injured.
She reports on politics for a national newspaper.

report.definition: to tell someone about what has been happening or what you have been doing as part of your job
report.note: typical: report on progress, on sth to sb NOT for: news stories
examples: I want you to report on your progress next week.
The team will report to the committee in May.

report.definition: to officially give information to the public
report.note: typical: report an increase, a result, figures NOT for: reporting a crime
examples: Doctors have reported a rise in cases of flu.
The company reported a profit of ten million pounds.

report.definition: to tell the police or someone in authority that an accident or crime has happened
report.note: typical: report a theft, an accident, sb missing NOT for: news stories
examples: I'd like to report a stolen bicycle.
The plane was reported missing last night.

report.definition: to complain about someone to someone in authority
report.note: typical: report sb to sb, report sb for sth NOT for: news reporting
examples: He reported his neighbour to the police for making noise.
The referee reported two players for fighting.

report.definition: to go to a place and officially say that you have arrived
report.note: typical: report to reception, for duty NOT for: giving news
examples: All visitors must report to the main office.
The soldiers reported for duty at six.

ring.definition: to make a bell produce a sound, or if a bell makes a sound
ring.note: typical: ring a bell, the doorbell, the bell rings NOT for: telephoning
examples: She rang the doorbell twice.
The school bell rang at four o'clock.

ring.definition: to telephone someone (BrE), or if a telephone makes a sound
ring.note: typical: ring sb, the phone rings NOT for: bells in a church
examples: I'll ring you tomorrow morning.
The phone rang just as we sat down.

ring.definition: if your ears ring, or a place rings with a sound, it is filled with a continuous sound
ring.note: typical: ears ringing, a room ringing with laughter NOT for: telephoning
examples: My ears were ringing after the concert.
The hall rang with cheers.

ring.note: typical: ring a building, a town; be ringed with sth NOT for: drawing a circle
examples: Police ringed the building.
The lake is ringed with tall trees.

ring.definition: to draw a circle around something (BrE)
ring.note: typical: ring the correct answer, the mistakes NOT for: surrounding a place
examples: Ring the correct answer in pencil.
The teacher ringed every spelling mistake in red.

rip.definition: to tear something quickly and violently, or to be torn like this
rip.note: typical: rip a shirt, paper, a letter open NOT for: copying music
examples: He ripped his jacket on a nail.
She ripped the envelope open.

rip.definition: to remove something quickly and violently with your hands
rip.note: typical: rip sth out, off, away, down NOT for: gently taking something
examples: He ripped the poster off the wall.
She ripped a page out of the notebook.

rip.definition: to copy music from a CD to a computer or player
rip.note: typical: rip a CD, songs, an album NOT for: tearing
examples: I ripped all my old CDs onto my laptop.
He ripped the album so he could listen on his phone.

roll.definition: to move along a surface by turning over and over, or to make something do this
roll.note: typical: a ball rolls, roll a barrel, a coin NOT for: moving on wheels
examples: The ball rolled under the car.
He rolled the barrel across the yard.

roll.definition: to turn your body over one or more times while lying down
roll.note: typical: roll over, roll onto your side NOT for: objects turning
examples: The children rolled down the grassy hill.
She rolled over and went back to sleep.

roll.definition: to make something into the shape of a tube or ball
roll.note: typical: roll sth into a ball, a tube; roll up a map NOT for: flattening
examples: Roll the dough into small balls.
He rolled the poster and put it in a tube.

roll.definition: to make something flat by pressing something heavy over it
roll.note: typical: roll dough, pastry, a lawn NOT for: forming a ball
examples: Roll the pastry thinly on a floured table.
The workers rolled the road surface flat.

roll.definition: to fold the sleeves or legs of clothes upwards so they are shorter
roll.note: typical: roll up your sleeves, trousers NOT for: making clothes flat
examples: He rolled up his sleeves and started washing the dishes.
She rolled her jeans up to her knees.

roll.definition: to move on wheels, or to make something with wheels move
roll.note: typical: a car rolls, roll a trolley, a pram NOT for: round objects turning
examples: The car rolled slowly down the hill.
The waiter rolled the trolley to our table.

roll.definition: to move over a surface smoothly without stopping
roll.note: typical: tears, drops rolling down a face NOT for: wheels
examples: Tears rolled down her cheeks.
A drop of rain rolled off the leaf.

roll.definition: to move continuously in a particular direction, as mist or waves do
roll.note: typical: mist, clouds, waves rolling in NOT for: single objects
examples: Thick fog rolled in from the sea.
We watched the waves roll onto the beach.

roll.definition: to throw dice as part of a game
roll.note: typical: roll the dice, a six NOT for: rolling a ball
examples: He rolled the dice and got a six.
It's your turn to roll.

roll.definition: if drums or thunder roll, they make a long low sound
roll.note: typical: thunder, drums rolling NOT for: moving objects
examples: Thunder rolled across the valley.
The drums rolled before the king appeared.

roll.definition: if a machine such as a camera or printing press rolls, it operates
roll.note: typical: the cameras roll, the presses roll NOT for: round objects turning
examples: The cameras began to roll.
The presses are rolling all night to print the paper.

roll.definition: if a ship or plane rolls, it leans from side to side with the movement of water or air
roll.note: typical: a ship rolling in a storm NOT for: a person turning over
examples: The ship rolled heavily in the storm.
The little plane rolled in the wind.

roll.definition: to make a cigarette by hand using tobacco and paper
roll.note: typical: roll a cigarette, roll your own NOT for: folding paper
examples: He sat down and rolled a cigarette.
It's cheaper to roll your own.

roll.definition: to move your shoulders forwards, up and back down
roll.note: typical: roll your shoulders NOT for: moving your eyes
examples: She rolled her shoulders to loosen them up.
He rolled his shoulders after a long day at the desk.

roll.definition: to move your eyes around and up, especially to show that you are annoyed or think something is silly
roll.note: typical: roll your eyes NOT for: moving shoulders
examples: She rolled her eyes when he told the joke again.
My sister rolled her eyes at the idea.

row.definition: to make a boat move across water using oars
row.note: typical: row a boat, row across a lake NOT for: arguing
examples: They rowed across the lake at sunrise.
He used to row for his university.

row.note: typical: row about money, with a neighbour NOT for: moving a boat
examples: They rowed about money all the time.
I heard the neighbours rowing last night.

sail.definition: to travel on or across water in a boat or ship
sail.note: typical: sail across the sea, around the world NOT for: flying
examples: They sailed across the Atlantic in a small yacht.
Three ships sailed past the lighthouse.

sail.definition: to begin a journey by boat or ship
sail.note: typical: the ship sails at noon, sail for a place NOT for: arriving
examples: The ferry sails at nine o'clock.
They sail for Greece next week.

sail.definition: to control or direct a boat with sails
sail.note: typical: sail a boat, a yacht; learn to sail NOT for: travelling as a passenger
examples: My uncle taught me to sail.
She sailed the small boat safely into the harbour.

sail.definition: to move quickly and smoothly through the air
sail.note: typical: a ball sailing over a fence NOT for: boats
examples: The ball sailed over the wall.
A paper plane sailed across the classroom.

sail.definition: to move forwards in a graceful, confident way
sail.note: typical: sail into a room, past sb NOT for: boats
examples: She sailed into the room as if she owned it.
He sailed past the guards without a glance.

search.definition: to try to find someone or something by looking very carefully
search.note: typical: search for sth, search a house, a room NOT for: computer queries
examples: Police searched the woods for the missing child.
I searched through my bag for my keys.

search.definition: to use a computer to find information
search.note: typical: search the Web, a database for sth NOT for: looking in a room
examples: She searched the Internet for cheap flights.
You can search the database by name.

search.definition: to examine someone or their belongings to see if they are hiding something
search.note: typical: search sb for weapons, drugs, a bag NOT for: looking for a lost thing
examples: The guards searched him for weapons.
Customs officers searched our bags at the airport.

search.definition: to try hard to find an explanation, solution or answer
search.note: typical: search for a cure, an answer, a solution NOT for: looking in a place
examples: Scientists are searching for a cure.
He searched for the right words to say.

search.definition: to look at something very carefully to find out or decide something
search.note: typical: search sb's face, eyes NOT for: searching a place
examples: She searched his face for any sign of the truth.
He searched her eyes for an answer.

seem.definition: to give the impression of being or doing something, or to appear to be true
seem.note: typical: seem happy, tired, seem to do sth, it seems that NOT for: real physical action
examples: She seems very friendly.
It seems that nobody remembers the name.

seem.definition: used with can't or couldn't to say you have tried to do something but are unable to
seem.note: typical: can't seem to do sth NOT for: describing how things look
examples: I can't seem to relax tonight.
He couldn't seem to find the right words.

seem.definition: used to make a statement less strong, more polite or less certain
seem.note: typical: I seem to have lost, it would seem that NOT for: strong factual claims
examples: I seem to have left my keys at home.
It would seem that someone forgot to lock the door.

serve.definition: to give someone food or drink, especially at a meal or in a restaurant
serve.note: typical: serve dinner, coffee, food hot NOT for: helping a shop customer
examples: Breakfast is served until ten o'clock.
The waiter served the soup with fresh bread.

serve.definition: if food serves a number of people, there is enough of it for that number
serve.note: typical: serves four, six NOT for: giving food to a guest
examples: This recipe serves four people.
The pie is big enough to serve six.

serve.definition: to help customers in a shop, bank or similar place
serve.note: typical: serve customers, clients NOT for: serving food
examples: Only one assistant was serving customers.
Are you being served?

serve.definition: to be useful or helpful for a particular purpose
serve.note: typical: serve as sth, serve a purpose, serve sb well NOT for: working for an organisation
examples: The old sofa served as a bed.
The box will serve the purpose.

serve.definition: to spend time doing duties or work for an organisation, country or person
serve.note: typical: serve as sth, serve in the army, on a committee NOT for: serving food
examples: He served as ambassador to France.
She served in the navy for ten years.

serve.definition: to have a particular effect or result (formal)
serve.note: typical: serve as a warning, serve to do sth NOT for: giving food
examples: The accident should serve as a warning to others.
One example serves to illustrate the problem.

serve.definition: to provide an area or group of people with something necessary
serve.note: typical: be served by an airport, bus service NOT for: serving a person
examples: The town is served by two railway lines.
The clinic serves thousands of local families.

serve.definition: to spend a period of time in prison
serve.note: typical: serve a sentence, time, ten years NOT for: working for a company
examples: He served a three-year sentence for fraud.
She is serving time for theft.

serve.definition: to start a point in tennis or similar games by hitting the ball over the net
serve.note: typical: serve an ace, serve first NOT for: serving food
examples: It's your turn to serve.
She served three aces in a row.

serve.definition: to officially send or give someone a written order to appear in court
serve.note: typical: serve a summons, a writ, papers on sb NOT for: serving a prison sentence
examples: He was served a summons for speeding.
The court served the papers on the company.

sew.definition: to use a needle and thread to make or repair clothes or to fasten something to them
sew.note: typical: sew a button, a patch, a hem NOT for: tying things with rope
examples: She sewed a button on my coat.
I learned to sew at school.

shake.definition: to move quickly and with force from side to side or up and down, or to make something do this
shake.note: typical: shake a bottle, a tree, the ground shakes NOT for: shivering from fear
examples: Shake the bottle before you open it.
The whole house shook when the lorry passed.

shake.definition: if someone or part of their body shakes, it makes small quick movements because of fear, cold, illness or strong feeling
shake.note: typical: shake with fear, cold, laughter NOT for: moving an object
examples: His hands were shaking with nerves.
She shook with laughter.

shake.definition: to shock or upset someone badly
shake.note: typical: be shaken by news, an accident NOT for: moving objects
examples: The news of the accident shook her badly.
He was shaken by the sudden noise.

shake.definition: to make someone's confidence or belief weaker
shake.note: typical: shake sb's confidence, faith, belief NOT for: physical movement
examples: The defeat shook the team's confidence.
Nothing could shake his belief in her.

share.definition: to have or use something together with other people
share.note: typical: share a room, a taxi, a bill with sb NOT for: dividing into parts
examples: The three of us shared a taxi.
I share an office with two other teachers.

share.definition: to let someone have or use something that belongs to you
share.note: typical: share your toys, food with sb NOT for: renting a place together
examples: He never wanted to share his toys.
Will you share your chips with me?

share.definition: to divide something between two or more people
share.note: typical: share sth between, among sb NOT for: sharing information
examples: They shared the cake between the children.
The money was shared out among the winners.

share.definition: to have an equal part of a responsibility, cost or work
share.note: typical: share the cost, the blame, the housework NOT for: owning an object together
examples: We share the responsibility for the children.
They share the bills equally.

share.definition: to have the same opinion, quality or experience as someone else
share.note: typical: share sb's view, concern, interest NOT for: using objects together
examples: I share your concern about the plan.
He shares his mother's sense of humour.
