share.definition: to tell other people about an idea, secret, problem or experience
share.note: typical: share your ideas, a story, a photo NOT for: dividing goods
examples: Students were asked to share their ideas with the class.
She shared the good news on social media.

shave.definition: to cut hair very close to the skin, usually with a razor
shave.note: typical: shave your face, legs, head NOT for: cutting thin slices
examples: He shaves every morning.
She shaved her legs before the holiday.

shave.definition: to remove very thin pieces from the surface of something
shave.note: typical: shave cheese, chocolate, wood NOT for: cutting hair
examples: Shave some chocolate over the cake.
The carpenter shaved a thin layer from the door.

shine.note: typical: the sun shines, a light shines NOT for: rubbing something
examples: The sun was shining all day.
The moon shone brightly over the lake.

shine.definition: to point a light in a particular direction
shine.note: typical: shine a torch, a light on/at sth NOT for: giving out light by itself
examples: Shine your torch over here, please.
He shone a light into the dark cellar.

shine.note: typical: shoes, hair or a table shining NOT for: the sun shining
examples: The floor shone after she had polished it.
Her hair shone in the sunlight.

shine.definition: to make something bright by rubbing it (the past form is shined)
shine.note: typical: shine shoes, silver NOT for: giving out light
examples: He shined his shoes before the interview.
She shined the silver for the dinner party.

shine.definition: if your eyes or face shine, you look very happy
shine.note: typical: eyes shining with excitement, joy NOT for: reflecting light
examples: Her eyes shone with excitement.
His face shone with pride.

shine.definition: to be very good at something, especially so that people notice you
shine.note: typical: shine at school, at sport, in a role NOT for: giving out light
examples: The concert gave young players a chance to shine.
She really shines at maths.

shoot.definition: to deliberately kill or injure someone with a gun
shoot.note: typical: shoot a man, shoot sb dead, in the leg NOT for: taking photographs
examples: The police shot the suspect when he pulled a gun.
He was shot in the arm during the robbery.

shoot.definition: to make a bullet or arrow come out of a weapon
shoot.note: typical: shoot a gun, a rifle, arrows, at sb NOT for: hurting a person
examples: Don't shoot! I'm coming out.
He taught me to shoot a rifle.

shoot.definition: to hunt and kill animals or birds as a sport
shoot.note: typical: shoot birds, deer, pheasants NOT for: shooting people
examples: They spent the weekend shooting grouse.
He likes to shoot in Scotland.

shoot.definition: to move quickly in a particular direction, or to make something do this
shoot.note: typical: shoot past, across, up NOT for: using a gun
examples: A cat shot across the garden.
The fountain shoots water into the air.

shoot.definition: to kick or throw a ball towards a goal or basket to try to score
shoot.note: typical: shoot from outside the area, at goal NOT for: using a weapon
examples: He shot from the halfway line.
She shot and the ball hit the post.

shoot.definition: to give someone a quick look or glance, often to show a feeling
shoot.note: typical: shoot sb a look, a glance NOT for: using a gun
examples: She shot him an angry look.
He shot a worried glance at his mother.

shoot.definition: to take photographs or make a film of something
shoot.note: typical: shoot a film, a scene, photos NOT for: using a gun
examples: The movie was shot in New Zealand.
They shot the last scene at dawn.

shoot.definition: if pain shoots through your body, you feel it move quickly and sharply
shoot.note: typical: pain shoots through, along sth NOT for: using a gun
examples: A sharp pain shot along his arm.
Pain shot through her leg when she stood up.

shoot.definition: if a plant shoots, a new stem or leaves start to grow
shoot.note: typical: plants shoot in spring NOT for: using a gun
examples: The bulbs began to shoot in March.
The old tree shot new branches this year.

shop.definition: to go to shops to buy things
shop.note: typical: shop for food, go shopping, shop online NOT for: informing the police
examples: She shops at the market every Saturday.
We went shopping for new shoes.

shop.definition: to tell the police about someone who has done something illegal (BrE, informal)
shop.note: typical: be shopped by sb NOT for: buying things
examples: He was shopped by his ex-wife.
Someone shopped them to the police.

shout.note: typical: shout at sb, shout for help, shout a warning NOT for: writing in capitals
examples: He shouted for help.
She shouted at the children to come inside.

shout.definition: to write in capital letters in an email or message so that you seem angry
shout.note: typical: don't shout in emails NOT for: speaking loudly
examples: Please don't shout at me in your messages.
Writing everything in capitals looks as if you are shouting.

shut.definition: to close something, or to become closed
shut.note: typical: shut a door, window, drawer, your eyes NOT for: shops closing for business
examples: Please shut the window; it's cold.
She shut her eyes and tried to sleep.

shut.definition: to stop being open to the public, for a short time or permanently (BrE)
shut.note: typical: a shop, bank, factory shuts NOT for: closing a door
examples: The post office shuts at five o'clock.
They shut the factory last year.

sign.definition: to write your name on something to show that you wrote it, agree with it or were there
sign.note: typical: sign a letter, a cheque, a form, a petition NOT for: using hand gestures
examples: Please sign here at the bottom.
Over a hundred people have signed the petition.

sign.definition: to make an agreement or official document legal by writing your name on it
sign.note: typical: sign a contract, a treaty, a deal NOT for: signing a letter
examples: The two countries signed a trade agreement.
I signed the contract yesterday.

sign.definition: to make someone join a team or company by agreeing a contract, or to join one this way
sign.note: typical: sign a player, a singer, sign for a club NOT for: signing a document alone
examples: The club signed a young striker last week.
She signed with a major record label.

sign.definition: to try to tell someone something by using signs or movements
sign.note: typical: sign to sb to do sth NOT for: signing a document
examples: He signed to the waiter to bring the bill.
She signed for us to come inside.

sign.definition: to use sign language, or to translate something into it
sign.note: typical: sign to a deaf person, sign a speech NOT for: signing a form
examples: She signs fluently because her parents are deaf.
The interpreter signed the whole speech.

sip.definition: to drink something slowly, taking very small mouthfuls
sip.note: typical: sip coffee, tea, wine, a drink NOT for: drinking quickly
examples: She sipped her tea and looked out of the window.
He sipped at the hot soup carefully.

sketch.definition: to draw a quick, rough picture of something
sketch.note: typical: sketch a face, a building, a plan NOT for: a detailed finished painting
examples: She sketched the old bridge in her notebook.
He sketched a map on the back of an envelope.

sketch.definition: to describe something in a general way, giving only the main ideas
sketch.note: typical: sketch out a plan, an idea, a programme NOT for: drawing pictures
examples: The manager sketched a plan for the new project.
He sketched the main points of his proposal.

skip.definition: to not do something that you usually do or should do
skip.note: typical: skip lunch, class, a meeting NOT for: jumping
examples: She skipped breakfast and ran for the bus.
He skipped the class three times this month.

skip.definition: to not read, mention or deal with something that would normally come next
skip.note: typical: skip a chapter, the details, skip to sth NOT for: missing an event
examples: I decided to skip the first chapter.
Let's skip to the last point on the list.

skip.definition: to go from one subject to another with no fixed order
skip.note: typical: skip from one topic to another NOT for: physical movement
examples: She skips from one topic to another when she talks.
The speaker kept skipping around the subject.

skip.definition: to move forwards with quick steps and little jumps
skip.note: typical: skip along, away, across NOT for: avoiding a task
examples: The little girl skipped down the path.
He skipped away, singing happily.

skip.definition: to jump over a rope that you swing over your head and under your feet (BrE)
skip.note: typical: skip for exercise, in the playground NOT for: skipping a meal
examples: The girls were skipping in the playground.
Boxers often skip to keep fit.

skip.definition: if a ball or similar object skips off a surface, it quickly bounces away after hitting it
skip.note: typical: a ball skipping off a surface NOT for: people jumping
examples: The ball skipped off the wet grass.
A stone skipped across the road.

smell.definition: to notice or recognise a particular smell
smell.note: typical: smell smoke, gas, burning NOT for: giving off a smell
examples: Can you smell something burning?
I smelled coffee as soon as I came in.

smell.note: typical: smell good, delicious, of smoke, like sth NOT for: noticing a smell
examples: The soup smells delicious.
His coat smelled of smoke.

smell.note: typical: your feet smell, a room smells NOT for: a pleasant smell
examples: Your socks smell!
The fridge smelled terrible after the power cut.

smell.definition: to put your nose near something to find out what its smell is like
smell.note: typical: smell a flower, food, a bottle NOT for: noticing a smell by accident
examples: She bent down to smell the roses.
Smell the milk to see if it is still fresh.

smell.definition: to have the ability to notice and recognise smells
smell.note: typical: can't smell with a cold NOT for: a bad smell
examples: I have a cold and can't smell anything.
Dogs smell much better than humans.

smoke.definition: to breathe in smoke from a cigarette, pipe or similar, or to do this as a habit
smoke.note: typical: smoke a cigarette, a pipe, cigars NOT for: producing smoke
examples: He doesn't smoke or drink much.
Do you mind if I smoke?

smoke.definition: if something smokes, it gives off smoke
smoke.note: typical: a chimney, engine, fire smokes NOT for: breathing in smoke
examples: The engine was smoking after the crash.
The chimney smoked all evening.

smoke.definition: to give fish or meat a special taste by hanging it in smoke
smoke.note: typical: smoke salmon, ham, cheese NOT for: smoking cigarettes
examples: They smoke the fish over wood chips.
We bought some smoked sausage at the market.

sneak.definition: to go somewhere secretly and quietly so that nobody sees or hears you
sneak.note: typical: sneak in, out, away, past sb NOT for: walking openly
examples: They sneaked off without paying.
She sneaked out of the house after her parents fell asleep.

sneak.definition: to take or give something to someone secretly
sneak.note: typical: sneak sth into/past sb, sneak sb a note NOT for: openly handing things over
examples: He sneaked his camera into the concert.
She sneaked me a note during the lesson.

sneak.definition: to quickly and secretly take something unimportant from someone (informal)
sneak.note: typical: sneak sweets, a biscuit, cigarettes from sb NOT for: serious theft
examples: We used to sneak cigarettes from Dad.
He sneaked a biscuit from the tin.

sneak.definition: to look at something quickly and secretly, especially something you should not see
sneak.note: typical: sneak a look, a glance, a peek NOT for: staring openly
examples: She sneaked a look at his phone.
He sneaked a glance at the answers.

sneeze.definition: to suddenly push air out through your nose with a noise, for example when you have a cold
sneeze.note: typical: sneeze because of dust, a cold, pollen NOT for: coughing
examples: The dust made him sneeze.
She started coughing and sneezing.

sniff.definition: to breathe air in through your nose noisily, for example when you are crying or have a cold
sniff.note: typical: sniff when crying, with a cold NOT for: smelling something on purpose
examples: He sniffed and wiped his nose.
Stop sniffing and blow your nose.

sniff.definition: to breathe in through your nose in order to smell something
sniff.note: typical: sniff a flower, food, sniff at sth NOT for: crying or having a cold
examples: The dog sniffed at the carpet.
He opened the milk and sniffed it.

sniff.definition: to say something in a way that shows you think it is not good enough
sniff.note: typical: 'Is that all?' she sniffed NOT for: breathing in
examples: "Is that all?" she sniffed.
"We usually stay somewhere better," he sniffed.

sniff.definition: to breathe in a harmful drug or chemical through the nose
sniff.note: typical: sniff glue NOT for: smelling food
examples: The teacher warned them about the dangers of sniffing glue.
He was ill after sniffing the chemical.

solve.definition: to find or provide a way of dealing with a problem
solve.note: typical: solve a problem, a dilemma, a crisis NOT for: answering a puzzle
examples: Money alone will not solve all our problems.
They have found a way to solve the traffic problem.

solve.definition: to find the correct answer to a problem or the explanation for something difficult
solve.note: typical: solve a crime, a mystery, a puzzle, an equation NOT for: reducing difficulties
examples: The police solved the case within a week.
She solved the maths problem in two minutes.

sound.definition: to seem a particular way when someone hears or reads about it
sound.note: typical: sound tired, happy, strange, like sth NOT for: producing noise
examples: You sound tired. Are you okay?
That sounds like a great idea.

sound.definition: if something such as a horn or bell sounds, or you sound it, it makes a noise
sound.note: typical: a bell, horn, alarm sounds NOT for: seeming a certain way
examples: The alarm sounded at midnight.
The driver sounded his horn.

sound.definition: to publicly give a warning or tell people about a danger
sound.note: typical: sound a warning, the alarm, a note of caution NOT for: making a noise with an instrument
examples: The minister sounded a warning about rising prices.
Scientists have sounded the alarm over climate change.

sound.definition: to pronounce a letter or letters in a word (technical)
sound.note: typical: a sounded or silent letter NOT for: seeming a certain way
examples: The 'k' in 'knee' is not sounded.
In French, the final 's' is often not sounded.

spend.definition: to use money to pay for goods or services
spend.note: typical: spend money on sth, spend £10 NOT for: using time
examples: I can't afford to spend any more money this week.
They spend a lot on food.

spend.definition: to use time doing something or to pass time in a place
spend.note: typical: spend time with sb, a week in/at sth, doing sth NOT for: using money
examples: She spends all her free time painting.
We spent the summer in Italy.

spend.definition: to stay somewhere for a night
spend.note: typical: spend the night at sb's house, in a hotel NOT for: using money
examples: She spent the night at a friend's house.
We had to spend the night in a hotel.

spend.definition: to use effort or energy to do something
spend.note: typical: spend energy, effort on sth NOT for: money
examples: I love to cook, but I don't have the energy to spend every evening.
He spent a lot of effort on the project.

sprint.definition: to run very fast for a short distance
sprint.note: typical: sprint to the bus, the finish, the line NOT for: running a long distance
examples: She sprinted down the road to catch the bus.
He sprinted the last hundred metres to win.

squeeze.definition: to press something firmly with your fingers or hand
squeeze.note: typical: squeeze sb's hand, a trigger, a ball NOT for: getting liquid out
examples: She smiled and squeezed his hand.
He squeezed the trigger, but nothing happened.

squeeze.definition: to get liquid out of something by pressing it
squeeze.note: typical: squeeze oranges, lemons, a cloth NOT for: pressing a hand
examples: Squeeze a little lemon juice onto the fish.
She squeezed the water out of the sponge.

squeeze.definition: to get into or through a very small space, or to push something into one
squeeze.note: typical: squeeze into, through, past sth NOT for: pressing liquid out
examples: Five of us squeezed into the back seat.
He squeezed through a gap in the fence.

squeeze.definition: to succeed, win or pass by only a very small amount
squeeze.note: typical: squeeze through to the next round NOT for: pressing something
examples: Greece just squeezed through to the next round.
He squeezed through the exam with a bare pass.

squeeze.definition: to strictly limit the amount of money available to a company or organisation
squeeze.note: typical: squeeze a budget, profits, funding NOT for: pressing objects
examples: The government is squeezing the railways' budget.
Rising costs are squeezing small businesses.

steal.definition: to take something that belongs to someone else without permission and without paying
steal.note: typical: steal money, a car, a wallet from sb NOT for: borrowing
examples: Someone stole my bicycle last night.
He was caught stealing from the shop.

steal.definition: to use someone else's ideas or work as if they were your own
steal.note: typical: steal an idea, a design, a song NOT for: taking physical things
examples: She accused him of stealing her ideas.
The company stole the design from a rival.

steal.definition: to move quietly so that nobody notices you
steal.note: typical: steal in, out, away, across NOT for: running openly
examples: He dressed quietly and stole out of the house.
She stole across the room without a sound.

steal.definition: in sports such as baseball or basketball, to take control of the ball or reach the next base before the other team expects
steal.note: typical: steal the ball, a base NOT for: crime
examples: He stole the ball four times in the first half.
The runner stole second base.

stir.definition: to move a liquid or soft mixture round and round with a spoon or similar tool in order to mix it
stir.note: typical: stir the soup, tea, sauce, paint, often with a spoon NOT for: shaking a closed container or mixing with a machine
examples: She stirred the sauce slowly so that it wouldn't burn.
Stir a spoonful of honey into your tea.

stir.definition: to move slightly, or to make something move slightly
stir.note: typical: a sleeping person, leaves or curtains stirring in a breeze NOT for: big, deliberate movements
examples: The baby stirred in her sleep but did not wake up.
A light wind stirred the leaves of the old oak.

stir.definition: to leave or move from a particular place, mostly used in negative sentences
stir.note: typical: not stir from your seat, bed or house NOT for: ordinary walking or travelling
examples: He refused to stir from the sofa all afternoon.
Nobody stirred when the fire alarm went off.

stir.definition: to make someone feel a strong emotion or remember something, or (of a feeling) to start to be felt
stir.note: typical: stir emotions, memories, the imagination; anger stirs in you NOT for: physical mixing
examples: The old song stirred memories of her childhood.
Anger began to stir inside him as he read the letter.

stir.definition: to make someone start doing something, especially to take action
stir.note: typical: stir sb to action, protest or anger NOT for: ordinary requests or orders
examples: The speech stirred thousands of people to join the march.
Her story stirred him to do something about the problem.

suck.definition: to pull liquid, air or smoke into your mouth using your lips and the muscles of your mouth
suck.note: typical: suck juice through a straw, suck in air or smoke NOT for: drinking from a cup by tipping it
examples: The little boy sucked up his milkshake through a straw.
She sucked in a deep breath before diving.

suck.definition: to hold something in your mouth and pull on it or rub it with your tongue and lips
suck.note: typical: suck a sweet, a lemon, your thumb NOT for: chewing or biting something
examples: The baby was sucking her thumb in her sleep.
He sat sucking a mint during the whole film.

suck.definition: to pull someone or something with great force into or out of a place
suck.note: typical: sucked into an engine, a whirlpool or a vacuum; sucked under water NOT for: gentle pulling
examples: A small bird was sucked into the plane's engine.
The strong current sucked the swimmer under.

suggest.definition: to tell someone an idea or plan for them to think about
suggest.note: typical: suggest doing sth; suggest (that) sb (should) do sth NOT for: suggest sb to do sth (incorrect); giving orders
examples: I suggest taking a taxi because the buses are slow tonight.
She suggested that we should meet an hour earlier.

suggest.definition: to make something seem likely to be true; to show it indirectly
suggest.note: typical: evidence, research, figures suggest (that)... NOT for: proving something completely
examples: Recent studies suggest that sleep affects memory.
The footprints suggest that someone walked here recently.

suggest.definition: to name someone or something as suitable for a job or purpose
suggest.note: typical: suggest sb for a post, a prize or a role NOT for: officially choosing someone
examples: Can you suggest anyone for the new design job?
The teacher suggested Marek for the maths competition.

suggest.definition: to say something in an indirect way; to imply
suggest.note: typical: Are you suggesting (that)...? NOT for: stating something openly
examples: Are you suggesting that I made a mistake?
His silence seemed to suggest he disagreed.

suggest.definition: to make someone think of something or imagine it
suggest.note: typical: a colour, shape, sound or smell suggests sth NOT for: describing something in detail
examples: The soft music suggested a calm summer evening.
The painting's dark colours suggest sadness.

support.definition: to agree with a person, group or idea and want them to succeed, often by helping them
support.note: typical: support a plan, a party, a campaign, a decision NOT for: just listening to an idea without taking a side
examples: Most of the villagers support the plan to build a new school.
We support our teachers in their work.

support.definition: to help someone by being kind and sympathetic during a difficult time
support.note: typical: support a friend, a family member through an illness or loss NOT for: financial help
examples: Her friends supported her through the divorce.
He supported his mother when she was ill.

support.definition: to provide enough money for someone to pay for the things they need to live
support.note: typical: support a family, support yourself NOT for: giving a small gift of money
examples: She works two jobs to support her three children.
He cannot support himself on such a low salary.

support.definition: to give money to a group, organisation or event so that it can continue
support.note: typical: support a charity, a school, an artist NOT for: paying for goods or services
examples: Local companies support the hospital with regular donations.
I support several animal charities.

support.definition: to hold the weight of something and keep it from falling
support.note: typical: pillars, beams, a bridge, your own weight supporting sth NOT for: holding something in your hand for a short time
examples: Four strong columns support the roof.
The old chair could not support his weight.

support.definition: to show or prove that an idea or statement is correct
support.note: typical: evidence, facts, results support a theory NOT for: proving something completely
examples: The new data support our earlier findings.
There is little evidence to support his claim.

support.definition: to be a fan of a sports team and want it to win, especially in British English
support.note: typical: support a football team NOT for: taking part in the sport yourself
examples: My brother has supported Liverpool since he was six.
Which team do you support?

surprise.note: typical: surprise sb; it surprises me that... NOT for: shocking someone in a very serious or frightening way
examples: His sudden question surprised her.
It doesn't surprise me that they lost.

surprise.definition: to find or attack someone when they are not expecting it, especially when they are doing something wrong
surprise.note: typical: surprise a burglar, an enemy, a thief NOT for: arranging a pleasant surprise party for someone
examples: The guard surprised two thieves in the warehouse.
The soldiers surprised the enemy camp at dawn.

survive.definition: to continue to live after an accident, war, illness or attack
survive.note: typical: survive a crash, an operation, a disease; only two survived NOT for: continuing to exist (things, ideas)
examples: Only three of the climbers survived the storm.
She survived the illness and returned to work.

survive.definition: to continue to live normally in spite of many problems
survive.note: typical: survive a crisis, a difficult period NOT for: physical danger to life
examples: The family survived the difficult years after the factory closed.
I'm tired, but I'll survive.

survive.definition: to manage to live when you have very little money
survive.note: typical: survive on a small salary or little food NOT for: living comfortably
examples: Many students survive on very little money.
How can anyone survive on such a low wage?

survive.definition: to continue to exist after a long time
survive.note: typical: buildings, customs, documents survive from the past NOT for: people who stay alive
examples: A few paintings from the old church still survive.
The tradition has survived for over a thousand years.

survive.note: typical: a business, company or industry survives a recession NOT for: personal survival after an accident
examples: Many small shops did not survive the economic crisis.
The team survived the cuts and kept playing.

survive.definition: to live longer than someone else, usually someone close to you
survive.note: typical: be survived by your wife, husband, children NOT for: surviving an accident
examples: He is survived by his wife and two daughters.
She survived her husband by ten years.

swing.definition: to move smoothly backwards and forwards, or from side to side, while hanging from a fixed point
swing.note: typical: arms, a door, a rope or a lamp swinging NOT for: moving in a straight line without hanging
examples: The old sign swung in the wind outside the shop.
She walked down the street with her bag swinging at her side.

swing.definition: to move in a smooth curve, or to make something move this way
swing.note: typical: swing your arm, a bat, a door NOT for: slow, straight movements
examples: He swung the heavy bag onto his shoulder.
The car swung left into the narrow lane.

swing.definition: to change from one opinion, mood or situation to another
swing.note: typical: voters swing to a party; moods swing NOT for: small, gradual changes
examples: Public opinion has swung against the new law.
Her mood swung from joy to anger within minutes.

swing.definition: to try to hit someone or something with a sweeping movement of your arm or an object
swing.note: typical: swing at sb/sth with a fist, bat or club NOT for: gentle touching
examples: He swung at the ball but missed it completely.
The boxer swung a heavy punch at his opponent.

swing.definition: to sit on a swing and make it move backwards and forwards
swing.note: typical: children swinging in the park NOT for: sitting on a bench or chair
examples: The twins spent the afternoon swinging in the garden.
She loved swinging as high as she could.

switch.definition: to change from one thing, method or subject to another
switch.note: typical: switch jobs, schools, topics, to a different system NOT for: small adjustments
examples: She switched to a vegetarian diet last year.
The company switched from paper to digital invoices.

switch.definition: to exchange one thing or person for another
switch.note: typical: switch places, seats or plates with sb NOT for: permanently replacing something
examples: Could we switch seats so I can see the screen?
He switched the labels to confuse everyone.

switch.definition: to change the way a machine works by using a switch or control
switch.note: typical: switch the heating, oven or setting to sth NOT for: turning something completely on or off
examples: Switch the oven to a lower setting after ten minutes.
He switched the radio to another channel.

taste.definition: to have a particular flavour (a linking verb)
taste.note: typical: taste good, sweet, awful; taste of/like sth NOT for: describing how something smells or looks
examples: This soup tastes of garlic and lemon.
The coffee tasted bitter.

taste.definition: to notice or recognise the flavour of food or drink
taste.note: typical: can taste, could taste the salt, difference NOT for: smelling or touching things
examples: I can taste a little ginger in this cake.
Can you taste the difference between these two waters?

taste.definition: to eat or drink a small amount of something to find out what it is like
taste.note: typical: taste the sauce, wine, soup while cooking NOT for: eating a full meal
examples: She tasted the soup and added some salt.
He tasted every cheese before buying one.

taste.definition: to experience something for the first time, often something pleasant or new
taste.note: typical: taste freedom, success, power NOT for: food or drink
examples: After years in prison, he finally tasted freedom.
The team tasted victory for the first time this season.

test.definition: to examine someone's body, blood or health to find out if they have an illness or a substance in them
test.note: typical: test sb for a disease, drugs; test positive or negative NOT for: giving a school exam
examples: The doctor tested her blood for iron.
All the athletes are tested for banned drugs.

test.definition: to examine a substance or thing to find out its qualities or what it contains
test.note: typical: test water, soil, a sample for sth NOT for: judging a person's abilities
examples: Scientists tested the river water for chemicals.
The lab tests every batch of milk.

test.definition: to ask someone questions or give them tasks to find out what they know or can do
test.note: typical: test sb on sth; test students' skills NOT for: informal chatting
examples: The teacher will test us on irregular verbs tomorrow.
The exam tests your reading and writing skills.

test.definition: to use something to see if it works well
test.note: typical: test a new product, method or program; test sth out NOT for: using something normally every day
examples: Engineers are testing the new bridge design.
I tested the app on three different phones.

test.definition: to put pressure on something so that you can see how strong or patient it is
test.note: typical: test sb's patience, strength, loyalty NOT for: checking facts
examples: The long delay tested everyone's patience.
The rough sea tested the strength of the small boat.

tie.definition: to fasten something using string, rope or a similar thing
tie.note: typical: tie sth to/around sth; tie a parcel, a boat, a horse NOT for: joining things with glue or nails
examples: He tied the boat to the post.
She tied the parcel with a red ribbon.

tie.definition: to make a knot in something such as a lace, ribbon or scarf
tie.note: typical: tie your shoelaces, a tie, a scarf, a bow NOT for: untying things
examples: The little boy is learning to tie his shoelaces.
She tied her hair back with a scarf.

tie.definition: to finish a game or competition with the same score as another player or team
tie.note: typical: tie with sb; tie for first place NOT for: losing by a small margin
examples: The two teams tied three all.
Anna and Peter tied for second place.

tie.definition: to be closely connected with something, or dependent on it (be tied to sth)
tie.note: typical: be tied to sth in the passive NOT for: physically fastening something
examples: Her pay is tied to how well the company does.
The flat is tied to his job, so he must leave if he quits.

tie.definition: to be limited by a situation or job so that you cannot do what you want (be tied to/by sth)
tie.note: typical: be tied to the house, to a desk, by school holidays NOT for: being physically fastened
examples: Young parents are often tied to the house.
I don't want to be tied to one place.

tip.definition: to lean or tilt something so that it is no longer level, or to fall over like this
tip.note: typical: tip a chair, a cup, a boat NOT for: pushing something in a straight line
examples: Don't tip your chair back like that.
The boat tipped suddenly and everyone shouted.

tip.definition: to pour or empty something out of a container by tilting it
tip.note: typical: tip sth into/out of/onto sth NOT for: pouring carefully from a jug
examples: She tipped the rice into the pan.
He tipped the rubbish out of the bag.

tip.definition: to give someone such as a waiter or taxi driver a small extra amount of money for their service
tip.note: typical: tip a waiter, a driver, a hairdresser NOT for: paying the main price of something
examples: We tipped the waiter ten per cent.
He tipped the driver two pounds.

tip.definition: to be thought likely to succeed or win (usually passive)
tip.note: typical: be tipped to win, for the top, as a future champion NOT for: actually winning
examples: The young player is tipped to win the tournament.
She is widely tipped as the next director.

tour.definition: to visit several places in a country or area, often for pleasure or for performances
tour.note: typical: tour a country, a region, the islands; a band touring NOT for: a short visit to one place
examples: They toured Italy for three weeks in the summer.
The band is touring Europe next spring.

tour.definition: to go round a place or be shown round it
tour.note: typical: tour a factory, a museum, a school NOT for: travelling to another town
examples: The mayor toured the new hospital this morning.
We toured the old castle with a guide.

train.definition: to teach someone the skills they need for a particular job or activity
train.note: typical: train sb to do sth; train as a nurse, a pilot NOT for: giving a one-time piece of advice
examples: The company trains new staff in the first two weeks.
She was trained as a nurse in Brno.

train.definition: to practise or exercise regularly, especially for a sport or competition
train.note: typical: train for a race, a match, the Olympics NOT for: exercising once in a while for fun
examples: He trains every morning before school.
The team is training for the final match.

train.definition: to teach an animal to do something or behave in a particular way
train.note: typical: train a dog, a horse NOT for: teaching a person a job
examples: We trained our puppy to sit on command.
The horses were trained to pull heavy carts.

train.definition: to point or aim something such as a camera or gun at a target
train.note: typical: train a camera, a gun, a telescope on sth NOT for: throwing something at a target
examples: The police trained their guns on the car.
He trained his camera on the nest.

translate.definition: to change written or spoken words into another language
translate.note: typical: translate sth from X into Y; translate a book, a text NOT for: explaining difficult words in the same language
examples: She translated the novel from Czech into English.
This poem doesn't translate well.

translate.definition: to produce or result in a particular effect (if one thing translates into another, it causes it)
translate.note: typical: translate into sth, as higher prices, more jobs NOT for: language translation
examples: Higher sales will translate into more jobs.
The extra training translated into better results.

translate.definition: to mean the same as something else when expressed in a different way
translate.note: typical: translate into/to sth (figures, amounts) NOT for: changing languages
examples: These figures translate into a profit of ten per cent.
A small difference in price translates to a big saving.

translate.definition: to change an idea, plan or feeling into another form, especially into action or reality
translate.note: typical: translate ideas, plans into action NOT for: translating words
examples: The government must translate its promises into action.
It is hard to translate a good idea into a useful product.

treat.definition: to behave towards someone or something in a particular way
treat.note: typical: treat sb well/badly, like/as sth NOT for: treating an illness
examples: The teacher treats all the children fairly.
They treated the guests like members of the family.

treat.definition: to deal with or regard something in a particular way
treat.note: typical: treat sth as/seriously/carefully NOT for: medical care
examples: Please treat this information as confidential.
The police treated the matter very seriously.

treat.definition: to try to cure an illness or injury using medicine, operations or other care
treat.note: typical: treat a patient, a wound, a disease (with sth) NOT for: preventing an illness
examples: Doctors treated him for a broken leg.
The infection was treated with antibiotics.

treat.definition: to buy or do something special for someone because you know they will enjoy it
treat.note: typical: treat sb to sth; treat yourself NOT for: paying a normal bill
examples: I'll treat you to lunch today.
She treated herself to a new pair of shoes.

treat.definition: to put a special substance on something, or use a process on it, to protect, clean or preserve it
treat.note: typical: treat wood, water, fabric (with sth) NOT for: giving medicine to a patient
examples: The wood was treated to protect it from rain.
The water is treated before it reaches our homes.

trim.definition: to cut a small amount off something to make it neat or shorter
trim.note: typical: trim hair, a hedge, a beard, nails NOT for: cutting something completely down
examples: The hairdresser trimmed my fringe.
He trimmed the hedge before the weekend.

trim.definition: to reduce the size or amount of something
trim.note: typical: trim costs, a budget, a workforce NOT for: removing something completely
examples: The company trimmed its costs by ten per cent.
The government trimmed the budget again.

trim.definition: to decorate the edge of something with another material
trim.note: typical: be trimmed with lace, fur, ribbon NOT for: covering something completely
examples: The coat was trimmed with white fur.
She trimmed the curtains with blue ribbon.

tune.definition: to make a musical instrument produce the correct sound by adjusting it
tune.note: typical: tune a piano, a guitar, a violin NOT for: playing an instrument
examples: He tuned his guitar before the concert.
A man comes once a year to tune the piano.

tune.definition: to make small changes to an engine so that it works as well as possible
tune.note: typical: tune an engine, a car NOT for: major repairs
examples: He spent the weekend tuning his motorbike.
The mechanic tuned the engine in an hour.

tune.definition: to adjust a radio or television so that it receives a particular station or channel
tune.note: typical: be tuned to sth; tune a radio to a station NOT for: simply switching a radio on
examples: The radio was tuned to a classical music station.
She tuned the TV to the news channel.

tune.definition: to be adjusted or developed precisely so that something reacts quickly and effectively (finely or highly tuned)
tune.note: typical: finely tuned senses, systems, engines NOT for: loosely organised things
examples: Bats have finely tuned hearing.
The team is a highly tuned machine.

twist.definition: to bend something or wind it round by turning or curling it
twist.note: typical: twist wire, rope, hair around/together NOT for: breaking something in half
examples: She twisted the wire into a small circle.
He twisted the towel around his hand.

twist.definition: to turn a part of your body or yourself to face another way
twist.note: typical: twist your head, body, neck NOT for: turning your whole body to walk away
examples: He twisted round to look at the noise behind him.
She twisted in her seat to talk to her friend.

twist.definition: to turn something with your hand in order to open, close, remove or attach it
twist.note: typical: twist a lid, a cap, a knob off/on NOT for: pulling something straight out
examples: Jack twisted the cap off the bottle.
Twist the knob to the left to turn it on.

twist.definition: to curve in a series of bends (of a road, river or path)
twist.note: typical: a road or river twisting through hills NOT for: a straight road
examples: The road twisted between the mountains.
The river twists through the valley.

twist.definition: to change the true or intended meaning of what someone said, usually to gain an advantage
twist.note: typical: twist sb's words, the facts NOT for: honestly explaining a statement
examples: The newspaper twisted her words to make her look foolish.
Don't twist the facts to suit your argument.

twist.definition: to hurt a joint such as your ankle or wrist by turning it too suddenly
twist.note: typical: twist your ankle, wrist, knee NOT for: breaking a bone
examples: He slipped on the ice and twisted his ankle.
She twisted her wrist while playing tennis.

type.definition: to write something using a computer keyboard or typewriter
type.note: typical: type a letter, an email, a password, a word NOT for: writing by hand
examples: She typed her name into the box.
I need to type this report before the meeting.

vote.definition: to show your choice in an election or decision by marking a ballot, raising a hand or a similar action
vote.note: typical: voting for a person, party or proposal. NOT for: choosing something informally, such as a restaurant.
examples: Citizens over eighteen are allowed to vote in the national election.
The members voted to postpone the meeting until spring.

vote.definition: to put someone in or remove them from a position of power by means of votes
vote.note: typical: voted into or out of office or parliament. NOT for: hiring or firing someone by a manager's decision.
examples: The mayor was voted out of office after only one term.
Voters have voted a new government into power.

wake.definition: to stop sleeping, or to make someone else stop sleeping
wake.note: typical: waking naturally or being woken by a sound or person. NOT for: becoming more alert while already awake.
examples: I woke at six because of the noise in the street.
Please don't wake the baby when you come in.

warn.definition: to tell someone that something bad or dangerous may happen so that they can avoid it
warn.note: typical: warning about danger, risk or a threat. NOT for: giving ordinary friendly advice.
examples: The sign warns visitors about the strong currents.
Doctors have warned people not to go out in the heat.

warn.definition: to tell someone about something in advance so that it does not surprise or upset them
warn.note: typical: warning someone about a coming change or visit. NOT for: serious danger.
examples: Warn your parents that we will arrive late tonight.
She warned me that the house would be a mess.

waste.definition: to use more money, time or energy than is useful or sensible
waste.note: typical: wasting resources on something pointless. NOT for: spending money carefully.
examples: Leaving the lights on all night wastes electricity.
I wasted two hours waiting for a bus that never came.

waste.definition: to fail to make full use of someone's ability or of an opportunity
waste.note: typical: passive, about talent or chances. NOT for: physical loss of an object.
examples: She is wasted in a job that asks so little of her.
You would be wasting a great chance if you said no.

waste.definition: to be wasted on someone: to be something good that the person cannot appreciate
waste.note: typical: be wasted on, about gifts, advice or beauty. NOT for: ordinary waste of money.
examples: Fine music is wasted on a child that age.
My advice was wasted on him because he never listened.

wave.definition: to move your hand to greet someone, say goodbye or attract attention
wave.note: typical: waving at or to a person. NOT for: moving a flag or object back and forth.
examples: The children waved at the train as it passed.
He waved goodbye and walked to his car.

wave.definition: to move from side to side, or to make something do this
wave.note: typical: flags, arms and branches moving in the air. NOT for: greeting someone.
examples: Flags were waving in the wind above the stadium.
The fans waved their scarves during the song.

wave.definition: to show someone which way to go by moving your hand
wave.note: typical: waving someone through, on or away. NOT for: giving spoken directions.
examples: The officer waved the cars through the gate.
A guard waved us away from the entrance.

wave.definition: if hair waves, it forms loose curls
wave.note: typical: describing naturally or artificially curly hair. NOT for: tight curls or straight hair.
examples: Her hair waves naturally when it is damp.
He had his hair waved for the wedding.

wear.definition: to have clothes, shoes, glasses or jewellery on your body
wear.note: typical: clothing and accessories on the body. NOT for: carrying something in a bag.
examples: She was wearing a blue coat and a red scarf.
Do you have to wear a uniform at your school?

wear.definition: to have your hair or beard in a particular style
wear.note: typical: wearing hair long, short, loose or tied. NOT for: cutting hair.
examples: He wears his hair in a ponytail.
She wore her hair short all through her twenties.

wear.definition: to become thinner or weaker through long use, or to make something do this
wear.note: typical: cloth, shoes, tyres and stone becoming damaged by use. NOT for: damage caused by one sudden event.
examples: The soles of these boots have worn very thin.
Years of walking have worn a path across the field.

wear.definition: to have a particular expression on your face
wear.note: typical: wear a smile, frown or look of surprise. NOT for: feeling an emotion without showing it.
examples: He wore a proud smile as his daughter received the prize.
The teacher wore a worried frown all morning.

whistle.definition: to make a high or musical sound by blowing air through your lips
whistle.note: typical: whistling a tune, or at or to a person. NOT for: singing with words.
examples: He whistled happily as he walked down the road.
She whistled to her dog to make it come back.

whistle.definition: to make a high sound by blowing a whistle
whistle.note: typical: referees, police and coaches using a whistle. NOT for: shouting an order.
examples: The referee whistled and the players stopped.
The coach whistled twice to call everyone in.

whistle.definition: to move quickly through the air with a high sound
whistle.note: typical: wind, bullets or arrows passing by. NOT for: slow, quiet movement.
examples: The wind whistled through the gaps in the old windows.
An arrow whistled past his head.

whistle.definition: if a kettle or train whistles, it makes a high sound as steam is forced out
whistle.note: typical: kettles and steam trains. NOT for: electric alarms or sirens.
examples: The kettle whistled and she poured the tea.
The old steam train whistled as it entered the station.

whistle.definition: if a bird whistles, it makes a high musical sound
whistle.note: typical: birds singing in a clear tone. NOT for: animals that bark or growl.
examples: A blackbird was whistling in the garden at dawn.
The birds whistled in the trees outside my window.

win.definition: to be the best or most successful in a competition, game, election or fight
win.note: typical: contests with a winner and a loser. NOT for: getting something just by luck without competing.
examples: Our team won the match by two goals.
Who do you think will win the election next year?

win.definition: to get something as a prize for success in a contest
win.note: typical: winning a medal, trophy or sum of money. NOT for: earning a salary.
examples: She won a gold medal at the Games.
He won a thousand pounds in the lottery.

win.definition: to get something you want through your efforts or abilities
win.note: typical: win support, respect, trust or a contract. NOT for: buying something with money.
examples: The new manager quickly won the respect of the staff.
Their bid won the firm a contract to build the bridge.

win.definition: if something wins you something, it causes you to gain it
win.note: typical: an action or performance winning someone a reward or friends. NOT for: a person choosing to take something.
examples: That speech won her a lot of new supporters.
Being rude will not win you any friends.

wipe.definition: to rub a surface with something in order to remove dirt or liquid
wipe.note: typical: wiping a table, face or hands with a cloth. NOT for: washing with plenty of water.
examples: Please wipe the table with a clean cloth.
He wiped his hands on a towel.

wipe.definition: to remove dirt, liquid or marks by rubbing
wipe.note: typical: wiping something off or away from a surface. NOT for: cutting or scraping something off.
examples: She wiped the tears from her face.
Wipe the dust off the shelves before you paint.

wipe.definition: to remove information stored on a tape, video or computer
wipe.note: typical: wiping a disk, drive or recording. NOT for: deleting a single file.
examples: Someone wiped all the data from the laptop.
The old recording was wiped and used again.

wipe.definition: to dry dishes after they have been washed
wipe.note: typical: wiping plates and cups with a cloth, especially in British English. NOT for: drying hair or the body.
examples: I'll wash the plates and you can wipe them.
He wiped the cups and put them away.

wish.definition: formal: to want to do something or to want it done
wish.note: typical: formal speech and writing, as in wish to speak to someone. NOT for: everyday conversation, where want is used.
examples: If you wish to cancel your order, please contact us.
You may leave now if you wish.

wish.definition: to want something to be true although it is impossible or unlikely
wish.note: typical: wish with the past tense or past perfect. NOT for: plans that you can really carry out.
examples: I wish I lived closer to the sea.
She wishes she had studied harder at school.

wish.definition: to say that you hope someone will have good luck or happiness
wish.note: typical: wishing someone luck, a good holiday or every happiness. NOT for: ordering someone to do something.
examples: We wish you a very happy birthday.
They shook hands and wished him luck.

wish.definition: to want something very much, especially when it seems unlikely, or to ask for it silently as if by magic
wish.note: typical: wish for something hard to get, often in stories. NOT for: asking for something directly.
examples: He often wished for a quieter life.
The girl closed her eyes and wished for a pony.

wonder.definition: to think about something you are not sure of and try to guess the answer
wonder.note: typical: wonder who, what, why, how or whether. NOT for: asking someone a direct question.
examples: I wonder how the meeting is going.
She wondered whether she had locked the door.

wonder.definition: to feel surprised at something and find it hard to believe
wonder.note: typical: I don't wonder, or no wonder, in British English. NOT for: casual curiosity.
examples: Sometimes I wonder at his behaviour.
I don't wonder you're tired after that long journey.

wonder.definition: to doubt or question whether something is true
wonder.note: typical: wonder if or whether with a sceptical feeling. NOT for: making plans.
examples: I wonder if he has any idea what he is doing.
Sometimes I wonder whether the effort is worth it.

worry.definition: to feel anxious or unhappy about someone or something so that you think about it a lot
worry.note: typical: worry about, over or that, about problems and people. NOT for: short surprise or fear.
examples: I worry about my son when he drives at night.
There is no need to worry about the exam.

worry.note: typical: something or someone worries a person. NOT for: making someone angry.
examples: The strange noise from the engine worries me.
I didn't tell her because I didn't want to worry her.

worry.note: typical: a small irritation that bothers someone. NOT for: serious fear or anxiety.
examples: The heat didn't seem to worry them.
Does it worry you if I leave the window open?

achieve.definition: to successfully complete something or get a good result, usually through hard work
achieve.note: typical: achieve a goal, success, result or aim. NOT for: receiving something without effort.
examples: She achieved excellent results in her final exams.
They finally achieved their aim of opening a school.

achieve.definition: to be successful in a particular kind of job or activity
achieve.note: typical: achieve in a field or at school. NOT for: a single task.
examples: We want every pupil to achieve in the subjects they choose.
He is an ambitious man who has achieved a great deal in business.

admit.definition: to agree, often unwillingly, that something is true
admit.note: typical: admit that, admit to, I must admit. NOT for: confessing a crime.
examples: I admit that I was a little afraid of the dark.
He admitted to me that he was jealous of his brother.

admit.definition: to say that you have done something wrong, especially a crime
admit.note: typical: admit doing something, or admit to a crime. NOT for: simply agreeing with a fact.
examples: The driver admitted causing the accident.
After questioning, she admitted to stealing the money.

admit.definition: to allow someone to enter a place such as a theatre, stadium or hospital
admit.note: typical: admit someone to a place, often passive. NOT for: letting a friend into your home.
examples: Only ticket holders will be admitted to the stadium.
The patient was admitted to hospital last night.

advise.definition: to tell someone what you think they should do
advise.note: typical: advise someone to do something, or advise that. NOT for: giving a firm order.
examples: My lawyer advised me to say nothing.
Experts advise that you drink plenty of water in hot weather.

advise.definition: to give advice as a job on a subject you know well
advise.note: typical: advise on a subject, or advise someone on something. NOT for: casual suggestions from a friend.
examples: She advises the government on environmental policy.
A consultant advises us on tax matters.

advise.definition: formal: to tell someone about something
advise.note: typical: advise someone of or that, in formal letters. NOT for: everyday conversation.
examples: We will advise you of any change to the schedule.
The company advised customers that prices would rise.

affect.definition: to do something that produces a change or effect in someone or something
affect.note: typical: influence of weather, illness, decisions or events. NOT for: causing something new to exist.
examples: The new law will affect millions of workers.
Heavy rain affected the harvest this year.

affect.definition: to make someone feel strong emotions
affect.note: typical: usually passive, about sadness, shock or sympathy. NOT for: mild interest.
examples: We were all deeply affected by the news.
She was too affected by the film to speak.

affect.definition: formal: to pretend to have a feeling, manner or way of speaking
affect.note: typical: affect an accent, indifference or boredom. NOT for: real feelings.
examples: He affected an air of complete boredom.
She used to affect a French accent.

aim.definition: to try or intend to achieve something
aim.note: typical: aim to do something or aim for a result. NOT for: a plan you have not decided on.
examples: We aim to finish the work by Friday.
The team is aiming for a place in the final.

aim.definition: to direct something at a particular person or group
aim.note: typical: aimed at teenagers, a criticism aimed at someone. NOT for: pointing a physical object.
examples: The programme is aimed at young children.
Her comments were aimed at the manager.

aim.definition: to point a weapon or object towards something you want to hit or reach
aim.note: typical: aim a gun, arrow or ball at a target. NOT for: only wanting to achieve a goal.
examples: The archer aimed carefully at the target.
He aimed the ball at the corner of the goal.

apply.definition: to make a formal request for something such as a job, a place at a university or permission
apply.note: typical: apply for or to. NOT for: asking a friend informally.
examples: She applied for a job at the hospital.
He applied to three universities.

apply.definition: to have an effect on or be relevant to a particular person, group or situation
apply.note: typical: rules, laws and offers applying to someone. NOT for: using a method yourself.
examples: These rules apply to all students.
The discount only applies to online orders.

apply.definition: to use a method, idea or rule in a particular situation
apply.note: typical: apply something to something, or apply in practice. NOT for: spreading a substance.
examples: Teachers apply the same method to every class.
It is hard to apply these ideas in real life.

apply.definition: to work hard at something with full attention
apply.note: typical: apply yourself to a task. NOT for: putting something on a surface.
examples: He would do well if only he applied himself.
She applied herself to learning the language.

apply.definition: to make a piece of equipment operate by pressing or pushing
apply.note: typical: apply the brakes. NOT for: switching a device on with a button.
examples: The driver applied the brakes and the car stopped.
He applied the handbrake before getting out.

apply.definition: to put or spread something such as paint, cream or medicine onto a surface
apply.note: typical: apply cream, paint or make-up. NOT for: mixing ingredients.
examples: Apply the cream evenly over your skin.
She applied a second coat of paint to the door.

apply.definition: to use force or pressure on something
apply.note: typical: apply force or pressure. NOT for: pressing a button once.
examples: The mechanic applied pressure to the bolt until it turned.
You must apply enough force to open the lid.

apply.definition: to use a word or name to describe someone or something
apply.note: typical: apply a label or term to a person or thing. NOT for: choosing a name for a baby.
examples: The term genius is rarely applied to scientists today.
It is unfair to apply that label to him.

appreciate.definition: to understand how serious or important a situation is, or how someone feels
appreciate.note: typical: appreciate the importance, difficulty or that. NOT for: being thankful.
examples: He didn't fully appreciate the risks of the plan.
I appreciate that this is a difficult time for you.

appreciate.definition: to be grateful for something someone has done
appreciate.note: typical: I really appreciate your help, I'd appreciate it if. NOT for: understanding a problem.
examples: Thank you, I really appreciate your help.
We would appreciate it if you replied soon.

appreciate.definition: to enjoy and value the good qualities of someone or something
appreciate.note: typical: appreciate art, music, food or a person's talent. NOT for: simply liking something.
examples: She can really appreciate good music.
Few people appreciate how hard he works.

appreciate.definition: to increase in value over time
appreciate.note: typical: houses, property and investments gaining value. NOT for: things that lose value.
examples: Property in this area has appreciated sharply.
Antique furniture usually appreciates over the years.

approve.definition: to officially accept a plan, proposal or decision
approve.note: typical: a committee or council approving a plan. NOT for: simply liking something.
examples: The council approved the plan for a new library.
The board approved the budget yesterday.

approve.definition: to think that someone or something is good, right or suitable
approve.note: typical: approve of someone or something, usually with of. NOT for: giving official permission.
examples: Her parents don't approve of her choice of friends.
I don't approve of children eating so many sweets.

assist.definition: to help someone do a task or job, often in a formal or professional way
assist.note: typical: assist (sb) with/in sth; formal work contexts NOT for: casual help between friends (use help)
examples: Two nurses will assist the surgeon during the operation.
A volunteer assisted me with filling in the forms.

assist.definition: to make something easier for someone to do or achieve
assist.note: typical: assist sb (in doing sth); equipment, tools, advice as subject NOT for: to give someone money or a gift
examples: A good map will assist you in finding the hotel.
Special software assists students who have difficulty reading.

assume.definition: to believe something is true without having proof
assume.note: typical: assume (that) ...; reasonable/safe to assume NOT for: to be certain because you have checked
examples: I assumed you had already eaten, so I didn't cook anything.
It is safe to assume that prices will rise next year.

assume.definition: to take on power, control or a duty, or start a job or position
assume.note: typical: assume control/responsibility/power/the role of NOT for: to take a physical object into your hands
examples: The new manager will assume responsibility for the budget in May.
The general assumed command of the army after the coup.

assume.definition: to pretend to have a feeling or way of behaving that you do not really have
assume.note: typical: assume an air/expression/manner of NOT for: to feel something honestly
examples: She assumed a look of surprise when we gave her the gift.
He assumed an air of calm although he was terrified.

assume.definition: to begin to have a particular quality, size or appearance
assume.note: typical: assume importance/proportions/a new meaning NOT for: to become a person or animal
examples: The dispute began to assume serious proportions.
The old custom has assumed a new meaning for young people.

assume.definition: to be built on the idea that something else is correct
assume.note: typical: a theory/forecast/plan assumes (that) ... NOT for: people believing something (use sense 1)
examples: The budget assumes that sales will grow by five percent.
This model assumes that all customers behave in the same way.

attach.definition: to fasten or join one thing to another
attach.note: typical: attach sth to sth; labels, wires, documents NOT for: to join two people together
examples: Please attach a photograph to the application form.
He attached a rope to the back of the boat.

attach.definition: to feel affection for someone or something (usually be attached to)
attach.note: typical: be/become attached to sb/sth (people, places, pets) NOT for: physical fastening
examples: Children quickly become attached to the animals on the farm.
She was deeply attached to the house she grew up in.

attach.definition: to consider something to be important or valuable
attach.note: typical: attach importance/value/significance to sth NOT for: giving a physical object to someone
examples: Employers attach great importance to good communication skills.
I don't attach much value to what he says.

attach.definition: if blame or responsibility attaches to someone, they are held responsible
attach.note: typical: blame/responsibility/guilt attaches (to sb) NOT for: people as the subject doing the attaching
examples: No blame attaches to the driver for the accident.
A certain shame attached to anyone who left the village.

attach.definition: if a quality, feeling or idea attaches to something, it is connected with it
attach.note: typical: stigma/meaning/risk attaches to sth NOT for: physical connection
examples: A lot of risk attaches to investing in new companies.
Strong feelings attach to this old song for many people.

attach.definition: to be a part of or work for a larger organisation, often for a limited time
attach.note: typical: be attached to a unit/department/ministry NOT for: permanent employment in a company
examples: The officer was attached to the embassy in Paris for a year.
The small clinic is attached to the city hospital.

attach.definition: to add a file or document to an email or message
attach.note: typical: attach a file/document/CV to an email NOT for: fastening paper with a clip (use sense 1 context)
examples: I've attached the report to this email.
Remember to attach your CV when you apply online.

attach.definition: to join yourself to someone and stay with them, often when they do not want you
attach.note: typical: attach yourself to sb NOT for: friendly, welcome company
examples: A stray dog attached itself to us on the hike.
He attached himself to our group at the party.

attach.definition: to make an agreement or permission depend on a condition
attach.note: typical: attach a condition/conditions/strings to sth NOT for: physically fixing a thing
examples: The bank attached several conditions to the loan.
They attached no strings to their offer of help.

attach.definition: to describe or judge someone or something with a simple label
attach.note: typical: attach a label/tag to sb/sth NOT for: sticking a real label on an object
examples: It is unfair to attach a label to every young person.
Critics tried to attach a label to her style of music.

attempt.definition: to try to do something, especially something difficult
attempt.note: typical: attempt to do sth; attempt a task/climb/jump NOT for: easy everyday actions (use try)
examples: The climbers will attempt to reach the summit at dawn.
She attempted a difficult dive and scored full marks.

attend.definition: to be present at an event such as a meeting, class or ceremony
attend.note: typical: attend a meeting/lecture/wedding/conference NOT for: casual spoken English (use go to)
examples: Over two hundred people attended the opening ceremony.
He could not attend the meeting because of illness.

attend.definition: to go regularly to a school, church, clinic or similar place
attend.note: typical: attend school/college/church/classes NOT for: a single visit
examples: Both my children attend the local primary school.
She attends a weekly yoga class.

attend.definition: to happen or exist together with something else (formal)
attend.note: typical: danger/uncertainty/difficulty attends sth; formal writing NOT for: people going to events
examples: Great uncertainty attended the start of the project.
The excitement that attends a big launch was missing.

base.definition: to have your main place of work or business in a particular place (usually passive or reflexive)
base.note: typical: be based in/at/near (a city, a building); base yourself in NOT for: using an idea as a starting point
examples: Our company is based in Prague.
She based herself in Lisbon while she looked for work.

breathe.definition: to take air into your lungs and let it out again
breathe.note: typical: breathe deeply/normally/through your nose; breathe air NOT for: speaking
examples: The patient was breathing normally after the operation.
It was hard to breathe in the smoky room.

breathe.definition: to blow air, smoke or a smell out of your mouth
breathe.note: typical: breathe on sth; breathe smoke/garlic over sb NOT for: normal quiet breathing
examples: He breathed on the window and drew a face in the mist.
The dog breathed hot air over my hand.

breathe.definition: if skin or a surface breathes, air can reach it
breathe.note: typical: skin/wounds/plants breathe; let your skin breathe NOT for: people taking in air
examples: Take the bandage off so the wound can breathe.
Wood floors need to breathe, so don't seal them completely.

breathe.definition: if cloth breathes, air can pass through it so you stay cool and dry
breathe.note: typical: fabric/shoes/clothing breathes NOT for: waterproof or plastic materials
examples: Cotton breathes better than nylon in hot weather.
These walking boots breathe, so your feet stay dry.

breathe.definition: to let wine stand open so air can improve its taste
breathe.note: typical: let the wine breathe; leave red wine to breathe NOT for: people or animals
examples: Open the bottle an hour early and let the wine breathe.
Red wine tastes smoother if it has had time to breathe.

breathe.definition: to say something very quietly, almost in a whisper (written)
breathe.note: typical: 'quote,' she breathed; literary writing NOT for: normal speech or shouting
examples: 'Don't move,' she breathed.
'It's beautiful,' he breathed, staring at the view.

bury.definition: to put a dead person in the ground, in a grave
bury.note: typical: bury sb in/at a place; be buried in a churchyard NOT for: burning a body
examples: They buried their grandfather in the village cemetery.
She asked to be buried next to her husband.

bury.definition: to put something under the ground, often to hide or store it
bury.note: typical: bury treasure/cables/waste; be buried beneath sth NOT for: covering something with a cloth
examples: Pirates are said to have buried gold on the island.
The pipes are buried a metre below the road.

bury.definition: to cover someone or something completely so they cannot get out (usually passive)
bury.note: typical: be buried under snow/rubble/mud NOT for: gentle covering with a blanket
examples: Several cars were buried under the landslide.
The village was buried in two metres of snow.

bury.definition: to push your face or head into something, often to hide it or show strong feeling
bury.note: typical: bury your face/head in your hands/a pillow NOT for: putting an object underground
examples: She buried her face in her hands and cried.
The child buried his head in his mother's coat.

bury.definition: to give all your attention to something so that you forget everything else
bury.note: typical: bury yourself in work/a book NOT for: hiding a body or object
examples: After the divorce he buried himself in his work.
She buried herself in a novel to forget the noise.

calculate.definition: to find a number, amount or price by using mathematics
calculate.note: typical: calculate the cost/distance/speed/total NOT for: guessing without working it out
examples: Use this tool to calculate how much paint you need.
The software calculates your tax automatically.

calculate.definition: to think carefully about what is likely to happen as a result of something
calculate.note: typical: calculate the risk/effect/chances NOT for: exact number work
examples: The company calculated the risks before entering the new market.
He had not calculated how angry his boss would be.

calculate.definition: be calculated to: to be planned or intended to have a particular effect (passive)
calculate.note: typical: be calculated to shock/impress/upset sb NOT for: being accidentally effective
examples: The advert was calculated to attract young buyers.
His speech was calculated to offend no one.

capture.definition: to catch a person and hold them as a prisoner
capture.note: typical: capture a suspect/soldier/rebel leader NOT for: catching a ball or an idea
examples: Police captured the escaped prisoner near the border.
Several soldiers were captured during the battle.

capture.definition: to take control of a place or thing from an enemy in a war
capture.note: typical: capture a town/fort/ship/city NOT for: buying a company
examples: The army captured the bridge at dawn.
Rebels captured the airport last night.

capture.definition: to catch an animal that has been chased or hunted
capture.note: typical: capture a tiger/wolf/escaped animal NOT for: fishing or hunting for food
examples: Rangers finally captured the bear that had entered the town.
The zoo staff captured the monkey with a net.

capture.definition: to record or show a feeling, scene or situation successfully in pictures or words
capture.note: typical: capture the mood/atmosphere/moment/essence NOT for: taking a prisoner
examples: The photo captures the joy of the winning team.
Her poem captures what it feels like to leave home.

capture.definition: to make someone very interested in something
capture.note: typical: capture sb's imagination/attention/interest NOT for: physical arrest
examples: The story of the lost explorer captured the public's imagination.
The magician captured the children's attention at once.

capture.definition: to win something such as a share of a market or a political seat from competitors
capture.note: typical: capture a market/seat/share/title NOT for: military conquest
examples: The new phone captured ten percent of the market in a year.
The party captured three seats from its rivals.

cause.definition: to make something happen, especially something bad
cause.note: typical: cause damage/problems/delays/trouble; cause sb to do sth NOT for: deliberately creating something good (use create/produce)
examples: Heavy rain caused flooding across the region.
His rude comment caused her to leave the room.

challenge.definition: to say that something is wrong, unfair or not legal, or to question the authority of someone
challenge.note: typical: challenge a decision/idea/view/authority NOT for: friendly invitation to a game
examples: The lawyers plan to challenge the court's decision.
Few students dared to challenge the teacher's authority.

challenge.definition: to invite someone to compete or fight against you
challenge.note: typical: challenge sb to a game/race/duel; challenge for a title NOT for: questioning an opinion
examples: He challenged his brother to a chess match.
Two teams are challenging for the league title.

challenge.definition: to test someone's skills and make them work hard in a good way
challenge.note: typical: a job/task/problem challenges you NOT for: bullying or threatening
examples: I need a job that really challenges me.
The puzzle challenged even the best students in class.

claim.definition: to say that something is true, although it has not been proved
claim.note: typical: claim (that) ...; claim to be/have sth; claim responsibility/victory NOT for: simply telling a known fact
examples: He claims that he never saw the letter.
A small group claimed responsibility for the attack.

claim.definition: to officially ask for money you have a right to
claim.note: typical: claim benefit/compensation/expenses/damages; claim sth back NOT for: borrowing money from a friend
examples: You can claim back the cost of your travel.
She claimed compensation after the accident.

claim.definition: to say you have a right to own or take something
claim.note: typical: claim asylum/ownership/land/lost property NOT for: taking something unfairly
examples: He arrived at the airport to claim his lost suitcase.
Several families claimed the land as their own.

claim.definition: if a war, accident or disease claims lives, people die because of it
claim.note: typical: disaster/disease/storm claims lives (news style) NOT for: a person making a statement
examples: The earthquake claimed more than a hundred lives.
The fire claimed three lives last night.

claim.definition: if something claims your attention, it needs and gets your notice
claim.note: typical: claim attention/notice (formal) NOT for: asking for a prize
examples: Several urgent matters claimed the committee's attention.
The loud music claimed everyone's attention.

clarify.definition: to make something easier to understand by explaining it more clearly
clarify.note: typical: clarify a point/position/issue/statement NOT for: making something physically clean
examples: Could you clarify what you mean by 'soon'?
The minister clarified the government's position on tax.

clarify.definition: to make a fat such as butter clear and pure by heating it
clarify.note: typical: clarify butter (cooking) NOT for: explaining an idea
examples: Chefs often clarify butter before frying fish.
Clarified butter keeps longer than ordinary butter.

combine.definition: to join, mix or work together with something else
combine.note: typical: combine sth with/and sth; factors combine to do sth NOT for: separating things
examples: Combine the flour and the eggs in a large bowl.
Several factors combined to cause the crisis.

combine.definition: to have two or more different features or qualities at the same time
combine.note: typical: combine A with B/A and B (qualities, roles) NOT for: physically mixing things
examples: The hotel combines modern comfort with traditional style.
She combines her studies with a part-time job.

comment.definition: to give your opinion or say something about someone or something
comment.note: typical: comment on sth; comment that ...; declined to comment NOT for: asking a question
examples: Nobody wanted to comment on the rumours.
She commented that the soup needed more salt.

commit.definition: to do something wrong or illegal
commit.note: typical: commit a crime/murder/fraud/suicide/an offence NOT for: good or neutral actions
examples: He was arrested for committing several burglaries.
Police are trying to find who committed the fraud.

commit.definition: to promise to do something or to take a definite position
commit.note: typical: commit yourself to (doing) sth; refuse to commit NOT for: being forced
examples: I can't commit myself to a date yet.
The company committed itself to reducing waste.

commit.definition: to stay loyal to a serious, long-term relationship or person
commit.note: typical: commit (to sb); afraid to commit NOT for: using money or time
examples: He was afraid to commit after his last relationship.
They decided to commit and moved in together.

commit.definition: to decide to use money, time or people for a particular purpose
commit.note: typical: commit money/time/resources/troops to sth NOT for: crimes
examples: The government committed millions to the new railway.
She committed three evenings a week to the project.

commit.definition: to send someone to a court of law to be tried (British English)
commit.note: typical: commit sb for trial; magistrates/court NOT for: American courts
examples: The two men were committed for trial at the Crown Court.
The magistrate committed the accused for trial.

commit.definition: to order someone to be kept in a hospital or prison
commit.note: typical: commit sb to prison/hospital/an institution NOT for: voluntary admission
examples: The judge committed him to a secure hospital.
She was committed to prison for six months.

commit.definition: to learn something so well that you remember it exactly (formal)
commit.note: typical: commit sth to memory NOT for: forgetting
examples: Actors must commit their lines to memory.
He committed the whole poem to memory in a day.

commit.definition: to write something down so that it is recorded (formal)
commit.note: typical: commit sth to paper/writing NOT for: saying aloud
examples: She never committed her ideas to paper.
He committed his thoughts to paper before the meeting.

compete.definition: to try to win customers or sales against other companies or countries
compete.note: typical: compete with/against sb for sth; compete in a market NOT for: friendly sports
examples: Small shops cannot compete with the big supermarkets.
Several firms are competing to win the contract.

compete.definition: to try to get something and stop others from having it
