compete.note: typical: compete for attention/jobs/resources/affection NOT for: working together
examples: Three candidates are competing for the same job.
The brothers always competed for their father's attention.

compete.definition: to take part in a race, game or contest
compete.note: typical: compete in/at an event; compete against sb NOT for: just watching
examples: She will compete in the 400 metres next week.
Over fifty athletes are competing at the games.

compete.definition: if something cannot compete, it is not as good or interesting as something else
compete.note: typical: sth can't compete with sth; negative sentences NOT for: positive comparisons
examples: Books can't compete with video games for some children.
The old cinema couldn't compete with streaming.

concentrate.definition: to think very hard about what you are doing and give it all your attention
concentrate.note: typical: concentrate (on sth); can't concentrate NOT for: gathering things in one place
examples: I can't concentrate when the television is on.
Please concentrate on the road while you drive.

concentrate.definition: to be present in large numbers in one place, or to put people or things together in one place
concentrate.note: typical: be concentrated in/at/around a place (often passive) NOT for: paying attention
examples: Most of the factories are concentrated in the north.
The government concentrated its troops near the border.

concentrate.definition: to make a liquid stronger by removing some of the water from it
concentrate.note: typical: concentrate juice/a solution; concentrated NOT for: mixing with extra water
examples: The factory concentrates orange juice before freezing it.
Boiling the sauce for ten minutes will concentrate its flavour.

concern.definition: if a story, book or report concerns something, it is about it (not passive)
concern.note: typical: the book/study/report concerns sb/sth; formal NOT for: spoken English (use be about)
examples: The report concerns the safety of old bridges.
This chapter concerns the early years of the war.

concern.definition: to make someone feel worried or upset
concern.note: typical: concern sb; it concerns me that ... NOT for: being interested
examples: His long silence concerned her.
It concerns me that so few people voted.

concern.definition: if a rule, activity or situation concerns someone, it affects or involves them (not passive)
concern.note: typical: this concerns you/everyone; matters that concern sb NOT for: a person feeling worried
examples: The new law concerns all drivers over seventy.
This meeting concerns the whole department.

concern.definition: to be interested in or involved with something, often when you should not or need not be (formal)
concern.note: typical: concern yourself with/about sth NOT for: worry for someone else's safety
examples: You needn't concern yourself with the details.
She never concerned herself with other people's opinions.

confirm.definition: to show that something is definitely true, usually by giving more proof
confirm.note: typical: confirm a theory/suspicion/result; test results confirm sth NOT for: giving an opinion with no evidence
examples: The lab tests confirmed that the water was safe to drink.
Her notes confirm what the witness said.

confirm.definition: to say that something is definitely true, especially when people were unsure
confirm.note: typical: confirm a rumour/report/story; refuse to confirm NOT for: proving something with evidence (use sense 1 sentences with proof)
examples: The company would not confirm that the factory will close.
The spokesman confirmed the news this morning.

confirm.definition: to tell someone that an arrangement, date or decision is now definite or official
confirm.note: typical: confirm a booking/appointment/date; be confirmed as sth NOT for: making a first suggestion or plan
examples: Please confirm your reservation by Friday.
He was confirmed as team captain after the vote.

confirm.definition: to make someone believe even more strongly that an idea or feeling is right
confirm.note: typical: confirm your fears/doubts/suspicions NOT for: facts that nobody doubted
examples: His strange silence only confirmed my doubts.
The first results confirmed our worst fears.

confirm.definition: to be accepted as a full member of the Christian church in a special ceremony (passive)
confirm.note: typical: be confirmed (in a church) NOT for: joining a club or a group that is not religious
examples: She was confirmed at the age of thirteen.
Both boys will be confirmed in the spring.

confuse.definition: to make someone unable to think clearly or understand something
confuse.note: typical: confuse sb; confusing instructions NOT for: making someone surprised in a good way
examples: The long list of rules confused the new students.
Don't confuse me with so many questions.

confuse.definition: to think wrongly that one person or thing is another
confuse.note: typical: confuse sb/sth with sb/sth NOT for: mixing things together on purpose
examples: Many people confuse butter with margarine.
I always confuse the twins because they look so alike.

confuse.definition: to make a problem or situation even harder to understand
confuse.note: typical: confuse the issue/matter NOT for: explaining a problem clearly
examples: Adding more figures will only confuse the issue.
His comments confused the argument instead of helping it.

connect.definition: to join two or more things together
connect.note: typical: connect sth to/with sth; a bridge connects two places NOT for: sticking things with glue (use stick)
examples: A short tunnel connects the two buildings.
Connect the printer to the computer with this cable.

connect.definition: to see or show that a fact, event or person is related to something else
connect.note: typical: connect sb/sth with sth; be connected to a crime NOT for: physically joining objects
examples: Nothing connects the missing money with the manager.
I never connected her name with the famous author.

connect.definition: to join something to the main supply of electricity, gas or water, or to a phone or computer network
connect.note: typical: connect to the internet/wifi; get connected NOT for: joining two people in a conversation (see sense 5)
examples: Has your new flat been connected to the internet yet?
The electrician will connect the cooker tomorrow.

connect.definition: (of a train, flight, etc.) to arrive in time for passengers to change to another one
connect.note: typical: a connecting flight/train; connect with sth NOT for: two vehicles that are physically joined
examples: My flight from Prague connects with a plane to Rome.
The bus connects with the evening train.

connect.definition: to join two telephone lines so that people can speak to each other
connect.note: typical: I'll connect you; hold on while I connect you NOT for: joining computers or devices
examples: Please wait while I connect you to the manager.
The operator connected her to her brother.

consider.definition: to think about something carefully before making a decision
consider.note: typical: consider doing sth; consider an offer/option NOT for: having an opinion about someone (see sense 2)
examples: We are considering moving to a bigger house.
You should consider all the options before you decide.

consider.definition: to think of someone or something in a particular way, or have a particular opinion
consider.note: typical: consider sb/sth (to be) sth; be considered likely/unlikely NOT for: thinking about a decision in progress
examples: Most people consider him a very honest man.
The test is considered too difficult for beginners.

consist.definition: to be made up of two or more things or people
consist.note: typical: consist of sth; consist mainly/largely of sth NOT for: passive forms (not 'is consisted of')
examples: The team consists of six players and a coach.
The meal consisted of soup, bread and cheese.

contain.definition: to have something inside, as a box, bag or place does
contain.note: typical: a box/bag/room contains sth NOT for: a document or substance containing something (see senses 2 and 3)
examples: The suitcase contained only old clothes.
This room contains a large collection of maps.

contain.definition: (of a document, book or speech) to include something
contain.note: typical: the letter/report contains information; be contained in sth NOT for: physical objects inside a container
examples: The report contains several serious mistakes.
The answer is contained in the last paragraph.

contain.definition: (of a substance) to have something as one of its parts
contain.note: typical: contain sugar/nuts/vitamins NOT for: a container holding things
examples: Does this bread contain milk?
Orange juice contains a lot of vitamin C.

contain.definition: to control strong feelings such as anger or excitement
contain.note: typical: contain your anger/excitement; contain yourself NOT for: stopping a disease from spreading (see sense 5)
examples: She could barely contain her excitement.
He was so angry he could hardly contain himself.

contain.definition: to stop something harmful from spreading or getting worse
contain.note: typical: contain a fire/an epidemic/a threat NOT for: feelings (see sense 4)
examples: Firefighters worked all night to contain the fire.
The government tried to contain the spread of the virus.

contain.definition: to surround an area or an angle (technical, used in geometry)
contain.note: typical: the angle contained by two lines NOT for: everyday talk about boxes or ingredients
examples: The two sides contain an angle of ninety degrees.
Find the area contained by the four lines.

control.definition: to have power over a country, place or organisation and decide what happens there
control.note: typical: control a country/company/city NOT for: checking quality (see sense 6)
examples: One family controls most of the local land.
Rebel soldiers now control the northern part of the country.

control.definition: to limit the amount or spread of something so that it does not become a problem
control.note: typical: control prices/disease/the spread of sth NOT for: managing your own feelings (see sense 4)
examples: The government is trying to control rising prices.
Vaccines help control the spread of many diseases.

control.definition: to make someone or something do what you want
control.note: typical: control a crowd/an animal/a child NOT for: running a company
examples: The teacher could not control the noisy class.
He struggled to control the frightened horse.

control.definition: to stay calm and not show strong feelings such as anger
control.note: typical: control your temper/anger/emotions; control yourself NOT for: machines
examples: She counted to ten to control her temper.
He controlled himself and answered politely.

control.definition: to make a machine, process or system work in a particular way
control.note: typical: control the temperature/speed; remote-controlled NOT for: people or crowds
examples: This switch controls the heating in the house.
The pilot controls the plane with two pedals and a stick.

control.definition: to make sure that something is done correctly
control.note: typical: control the quality of sth NOT for: having political power over a place
examples: The factory strictly controls the quality of its food.
Inspectors control the safety of the equipment every month.

convince.definition: to make someone feel certain that something is true
convince.note: typical: convince sb (that)/of sth NOT for: making someone do something (see sense 2)
examples: Her evidence convinced the jury that he was innocent.
I couldn't convince him of the danger.

convince.definition: to persuade someone to do something
convince.note: typical: convince sb to do sth NOT for: making someone believe a fact without any action
examples: She convinced her parents to let her go abroad.
They tried to convince him to stay.

cope.definition: to deal successfully with a difficult problem or situation
cope.note: typical: cope with sth; find it hard to cope NOT for: treating an illness with medicine
examples: She copes well with the stress of her job.
I don't know how they cope with three small children.

cope.definition: (of a system or machine) to be able to handle a certain amount or type of work
cope.note: typical: cope with sth; can't cope with the demand NOT for: people dealing with personal problems
examples: The old server cannot cope with so many users.
The bridge was built to cope with heavy traffic.

crash.definition: (of a vehicle or its driver) to have an accident by hitting something violently
crash.note: typical: a car/plane crashes; crash into sth NOT for: a computer failing (see sense 4)
examples: The small plane crashed into a field.
He crashed his father's car on the first day.

crash.definition: to hit something extremely hard while moving, causing damage or a loud noise
crash.note: typical: crash into/through/against sth NOT for: a gentle touch
examples: A rock crashed through the roof of the shed.
Huge waves crashed against the harbour wall.

crash.definition: to make a sudden loud noise
crash.note: typical: thunder crashed; cymbals crashed NOT for: a quiet or soft sound
examples: Thunder crashed above the hills.
The drums crashed and the crowd cheered.

crash.definition: (of a computer or a program) to suddenly stop working
crash.note: typical: the system/computer crashed NOT for: a machine that wears out slowly
examples: My laptop crashed while I was writing the report.
The website crashes whenever too many people log in.

crash.definition: (of a stock market or shares) to suddenly lose a lot of value
crash.note: typical: the market/shares crashed NOT for: prices falling slowly
examples: Share prices crashed after the bank's announcement.
The market crashed and many people lost their savings.

crash.definition: (British English) to lose very badly in a sports match
crash.note: typical: crash to defeat; crash out of a cup NOT for: a vehicle accident
examples: The home team crashed to a 5-0 defeat.
They crashed out of the competition in the first round.

crash.definition: (spoken) to stay at someone's home for the night, or to fall asleep quickly because you are very tired
crash.note: typical: crash at sb's place; crash out on the sofa NOT for: formal writing
examples: Can I crash at your flat tonight?
He came home and crashed out on the bed.

crash.definition: (informal) to go to a party without being invited
crash.note: typical: crash a party/wedding NOT for: arriving as a guest
examples: Some students tried to crash the wedding.
We crashed the party and nobody noticed.

criticise.definition: to say that you do not approve of someone or something, or talk about their faults
criticise.note: typical: criticise sb for (doing) sth; be heavily criticised NOT for: giving praise
examples: Teachers criticised the new rules for being unfair.
He was criticised for arriving late to the meeting.

criticise.definition: (formal) to give judgements about the good and bad points of something
criticise.note: typical: criticise each other's work NOT for: only attacking someone's faults
examples: The students criticise each other's essays in class.
Critics were invited to criticise the new design.

damage.definition: to cause physical harm to something or to a part of someone's body
damage.note: typical: damage crops/a building/your health NOT for: ruining someone's reputation (see sense 2)
examples: The storm damaged several houses along the coast.
Loud music can damage your hearing.

damage.definition: to have a bad effect on something so that it becomes weaker or less successful
damage.note: typical: damage a reputation/career/relationship NOT for: harming a physical object only
examples: The scandal damaged the company's reputation.
Lies can damage a friendship.

deal.definition: to give playing cards to each player in a game
deal.note: typical: deal the cards; whose turn is it to deal? NOT for: selling things
examples: It's your turn to deal the cards.
She dealt five cards to each player.

deal.definition: (informal) to buy and sell illegal drugs
deal.note: typical: deal drugs; deal in drugs NOT for: legal business
examples: He was arrested for dealing drugs.
Some of the gang members dealt on the street.

deal.definition: to cause harm to something or someone, usually in news reports
deal.note: typical: deal a blow to sb/sth NOT for: everyday small problems
examples: The floods dealt a severe blow to local farmers.
The news dealt a heavy blow to the team's hopes.

decline.definition: to become smaller, weaker or less important
decline.note: typical: sales/numbers/standards decline NOT for: refusing an offer (see sense 2)
examples: The number of visitors has declined this year.
Her health began to decline after the age of eighty.

decline.definition: to say politely that you will not accept or do something
decline.note: typical: decline an invitation/offer NOT for: saying no rudely or angrily
examples: He declined the invitation to the party.
She politely declined the offer of a lift.

defend.definition: to protect someone or something from attack
defend.note: typical: defend sb/sth against/from sth; defend yourself NOT for: arguing in words (see sense 2)
examples: Soldiers were sent to defend the border.
She learned judo to defend herself.

defend.definition: to use arguments to support someone or something that is being criticised
defend.note: typical: defend sb/sth against criticism; defend your views NOT for: protecting in a physical fight
examples: He defended his friend when others laughed at him.
She defended her decision in front of the whole class.

defend.definition: to speak for someone in a court of law
defend.note: typical: defend a client/suspect NOT for: accusing someone
examples: The lawyer defended the young man in court.
Who will defend the accused woman?

defend.definition: (in sport) to try to stop the other team from scoring
defend.note: typical: defend well; defend a lead NOT for: attacking play
examples: The team defended well for the whole match.
They defended the goal with all ten players.

define.definition: to describe something exactly and say what makes it different from other things
define.note: typical: define sth as sth; clearly defined NOT for: giving only a rough idea
examples: The contract clearly defines the duties of each worker.
It is hard to define exactly what makes a good teacher.

define.definition: to explain the exact meaning of a word or idea
define.note: typical: define a term/word NOT for: only translating a word
examples: Can you define the word 'democracy'?
The book defines each key term in a short box.

define.definition: to show the edge or shape of something clearly
define.note: typical: sharply/clearly defined NOT for: explaining ideas
examples: A dark line defines the edge of the field.
The bright light defined the shape of the mountains.

delay.definition: to wait until a later time before doing something
delay.note: typical: delay a decision; delay doing sth NOT for: making someone else late (see sense 2)
examples: The council delayed its decision until next month.
Don't delay; call the doctor today.

delay.definition: to make someone or something late
delay.note: typical: a delayed flight/train; be delayed by sth NOT for: choosing to postpone something
examples: Heavy snow delayed all the morning trains.
I was delayed at work and missed the bus.

deliver.definition: to take goods, letters or parcels to a person or place
deliver.note: typical: deliver sth to sb; deliver the post/pizza NOT for: giving a speech (see sense 2)
examples: The shop will deliver the sofa on Monday.
A man delivered a parcel to our door.

deliver.definition: to give a speech, talk or lecture to an audience
deliver.note: typical: deliver a speech/lecture/address NOT for: everyday talk (people usually say give a talk)
examples: The president delivered a speech to the nation.
She delivered the opening lecture of the conference.

deliver.definition: to do what you promised or are expected to do
deliver.note: typical: deliver on a promise; deliver the goods NOT for: carrying objects
examples: The new manager must deliver results quickly.
The company failed to deliver on its promises.

deliver.definition: to help a woman give birth, or to give birth to a baby
deliver.note: typical: deliver a baby NOT for: sending letters or parcels
examples: The midwife delivered the baby at home.
The doctor delivered twins last night.

deliver.definition: to give a blow, shock or warning to someone or something
deliver.note: typical: deliver a blow/warning/message NOT for: taking goods to people
examples: The champion delivered a hard punch to his rival.
The leader delivered a clear warning to the rebels.

deliver.definition: to officially announce a decision or judgement
deliver.note: typical: deliver a verdict/judgment NOT for: casual opinions
examples: The jury delivered its verdict after two days.
The court will deliver its judgment on Friday.

deliver.definition: (formal) to put someone into someone else's control
deliver.note: typical: deliver sb to sb NOT for: taking goods to a place
examples: The guard delivered the prisoner to the police.
He was betrayed and delivered to the enemy.

deliver.definition: (mainly American English) to get the votes or support of a group of people in an election
deliver.note: typical: deliver the vote/the state NOT for: delivering goods
examples: The senator hopes to deliver the farm vote.
The mayor could not deliver his city for the party.

demand.definition: to ask for something firmly because you think you have a right to it
demand.note: typical: demand an answer/that sb do sth; demand to know NOT for: asking politely
examples: The workers demanded higher pay.
She demanded to speak to the manager.

demand.definition: to need something in order to succeed or be done well
demand.note: typical: demand attention/skill/care NOT for: asking someone firmly for something
examples: This job demands a lot of patience.
The problem demands a quick answer.

destroy.definition: to damage something so badly that it no longer exists or cannot be repaired
destroy.note: typical: destroy a building/the environment/hope NOT for: small damage
examples: The fire destroyed the old library.
Pollution is destroying the forest.

destroy.definition: to ruin someone's life, career or reputation completely
destroy.note: typical: destroy sb/sb's career NOT for: damaging a thing
examples: The scandal destroyed his career.
The news almost destroyed her.

destroy.definition: (informal) to defeat an opponent very easily
destroy.note: typical: destroy a team/rival NOT for: a close game
examples: Our team destroyed the visitors 6-0.
She destroyed her opponent in the final.

destroy.definition: to kill an animal, especially because it is ill or dangerous
destroy.note: typical: an animal had to be destroyed NOT for: killing people
examples: The injured horse had to be destroyed.
The dog was destroyed after the attack.

determine.definition: to find out the facts about something
determine.note: typical: determine the cause/how/whether sth happened NOT for: making a choice (see sense 3)
examples: Experts are trying to determine the cause of the crash.
The tests will determine whether the water is safe.

determine.definition: to directly influence or decide what something will be
determine.note: typical: determine the outcome/result/size of sth NOT for: investigating facts
examples: The weather will determine how many people come.
Your exam results determine which class you go into.

determine.note: typical: determine a date/price/policy NOT for: a personal wish to do something (see sense 4)
examples: The court has not yet determined the date of the trial.
The committee will determine the rules next week.

determine.definition: (formal) to decide firmly to do something
determine.note: typical: determine to do sth NOT for: describing a stubborn person (use determined as an adjective)
examples: She determined to finish the course whatever happened.
They determined to leave before dawn.

develop.definition: to grow or change into something bigger, stronger or more advanced
develop.note: typical: develop into/from sth; develop rapidly NOT for: starting to be ill (see sense 5)
examples: The small village developed into a busy town.
The economy has developed quickly in the last ten years.

develop.definition: to design or make a new idea, product or system over a period of time
develop.note: typical: develop a drug/product/system NOT for: growing naturally
examples: Engineers are developing a faster electric car.
The company developed its own software.

develop.definition: to start to have a feeling or quality that then becomes stronger
develop.note: typical: develop a taste/interest/sense of sth NOT for: skills you practise (see sense 4)
examples: She developed a strong interest in music.
He slowly developed a sense of humour.

develop.definition: (of a skill or ability) to become stronger, or to make it stronger
develop.note: typical: develop skills/abilities/muscles NOT for: new products
examples: The course helps students develop their writing skills.
Regular exercise will develop your muscles.

develop.definition: to start to have a disease or illness
develop.note: typical: develop cancer/a cough/symptoms NOT for: a skill or interest
examples: He developed a bad cold after the trip.
Some patients develop an allergy to the medicine.

develop.definition: to begin to have a physical fault
develop.note: typical: develop a crack/fault/problem NOT for: people becoming ill
examples: The pipe developed a small leak.
The car developed engine trouble on the motorway.

develop.definition: (of a problem or difficult situation) to begin to happen or become worse
develop.note: typical: trouble/a crisis develops; develop into sth NOT for: pleasant changes
examples: A crisis is developing in the region.
The small quarrel developed into a serious fight.

develop.definition: to make an argument or idea clearer by giving more detail
develop.note: typical: develop a point/an idea/an argument NOT for: inventing a physical product
examples: The author develops this idea in the next chapter.
You need to develop your argument more clearly.

develop.definition: to use land for building or for other useful purposes
develop.note: typical: develop land/a site/an area NOT for: personal growth
examples: The council plans to develop the empty land by the river.
The area was developed for new housing.

develop.definition: to make a photograph from a film using chemicals
develop.note: typical: develop a film/photos NOT for: digital pictures
examples: I took the film to a shop to be developed.
She developed the pictures in her darkroom.

differ.definition: to be different from something in some way
differ.note: typical: differ from sth; differ in sth; differ widely NOT for: disagreeing in opinion (see sense 2)
examples: The two towns differ greatly in size.
My opinion differs from yours in one important way.

differ.definition: (of people) to have opposite opinions about something
differ.note: typical: differ about/on/over sth NOT for: things that are simply not the same
examples: The two leaders differed on how to deal with the crisis.
Doctors differ about the best treatment.

disappoint.definition: to make someone feel unhappy because something they hoped for did not happen or was not as good as expected
disappoint.note: typical: disappoint sb; sorry to disappoint you NOT for: surprising someone in a good way
examples: I hate to disappoint the children, but we can't go.
The film really disappointed me.

disappoint.definition: to stop something from happening that someone hoped for
disappoint.note: typical: disappoint sb's hopes/expectations/plans NOT for: making a person sad directly
examples: The poor harvest disappointed the farmers' hopes.
The result disappointed all our expectations.

discourage.definition: to persuade someone not to do something, especially by making it seem difficult or bad
discourage.note: typical: discourage sb from doing sth NOT for: 'discourage someone to do'
examples: His parents discouraged him from becoming a singer.
High prices discourage people from buying new cars.

discourage.definition: to make someone less confident or less willing to do something
discourage.note: typical: don't let sth discourage you; feel discouraged NOT for: persuading someone with reasons
examples: One bad mark should not discourage you.
Constant criticism discouraged the young writer.

discourage.definition: to make something less likely to happen
discourage.note: typical: discourage growth/crime/waste NOT for: talking to people
examples: Strong locks discourage burglars.
Cold weather discourages the growth of mould.

display.definition: to show something to people or put it where people can see it easily
display.note: typical: display goods/results/photos NOT for: showing feelings (see sense 2)
examples: The shop displays its newest bags in the window.
The results will be displayed on the school notice board.

display.definition: to clearly show a feeling, attitude or quality by what you do or say
display.note: typical: display courage/emotion/skill NOT for: placing objects in a shop or museum
examples: She displayed great courage during the rescue.
He never displays his anger in public.

display.definition: (of a computer or screen) to show information
display.note: typical: the screen/computer displays sth NOT for: printing on paper
examples: The screen displays the time and the date.
An error message was displayed on the monitor.

display.definition: (of a male bird or animal) to behave in a special way to attract a mate
display.note: typical: peacocks display; birds display NOT for: people showing off
examples: The male bird displays its bright feathers in spring.
Several males were displaying at the edge of the lake.

distribute.definition: to share things among a group of people, especially in a planned way
distribute.note: typical: distribute food/leaflets/money to/among sb NOT for: selling goods to shops (see sense 2)
examples: Volunteers distributed blankets to the flood victims.
Someone was distributing leaflets outside the station.

distribute.definition: to supply goods to shops and companies so that they can sell them
distribute.note: typical: distribute products/goods/newspapers NOT for: giving free things to people
examples: The firm distributes bread to local supermarkets.
This magazine is distributed in forty countries.

distribute.definition: to spread something over a large area
distribute.note: typical: distribute weight/heat evenly NOT for: sharing things between people
examples: Distribute the weight of the bag evenly across your back.
Spread the sauce so that it is distributed over the whole pizza.

distribute.definition: (of animals, plants, etc.) to exist in different parts of an area or group (passive)
distribute.note: typical: be widely/evenly distributed NOT for: someone giving things out
examples: This bird is widely distributed across Europe.
The wealth is not evenly distributed in the country.

donate.definition: to give something, especially money, to a person or an organisation to help them
donate.note: typical: donate money/food/clothes to sb NOT for: giving a present to a friend
examples: She donated fifty pounds to the animal shelter.
Local shops donated food for the party.

donate.definition: to allow a doctor to take blood or a part of your body for use in treating someone else
donate.note: typical: donate blood/a kidney/organs NOT for: giving money
examples: He donates blood twice a year.
She donated a kidney to her brother.

edit.definition: to prepare a text, film or similar material for printing or broadcasting by removing mistakes or unsuitable parts
edit.note: typical: edit a letter/report/video NOT for: writing new text
examples: The newspaper edits readers' letters before printing them.
She edited the video to remove the noisy parts.

edit.definition: to prepare a book or article for printing by deciding what to include and in what order
edit.note: typical: edit a book/collection/essays NOT for: correcting spelling only
examples: He edited a collection of short stories.
The professor edited the volume of essays.

edit.definition: to prepare a film by deciding which parts to use and in what order
edit.note: typical: edit a film/a scene NOT for: written texts
examples: They spent a month editing the film.
The director edited the final scene again.

edit.definition: to be in charge of what is included in a newspaper or magazine
edit.note: typical: edit a newspaper/magazine NOT for: working on a single article
examples: She edited a fashion magazine for ten years.
He edits the school newspaper.

educate.definition: to teach a child at a school, college or university (usually passive)
educate.note: typical: be educated at/in sth NOT for: training in a short skill
examples: He was educated at a small village school.
The school educates children from the age of five.

educate.definition: to give people information about a subject or show them a better way to do something
educate.note: typical: educate sb about/in/on sth NOT for: formal schooling
examples: The campaign aims to educate people about healthy food.
We must educate drivers about the dangers of speed.

elect.definition: to choose someone for an official position by voting (usually passive)
elect.note: typical: elect sb to/as sth; democratically elected NOT for: appointing someone without a vote
examples: The people elected her mayor.
He was elected to parliament in 2019.

elect.note: typical: elect to do sth NOT for: choosing a leader by voting
examples: You may elect to pay in monthly parts.
She elected to stay at home.

employ.definition: to pay someone to work for you
employ.note: typical: employ sb as sth; the factory employs 500 people NOT for: using a tool or method (see sense 2)
examples: The hotel employs about eighty people.
She was employed as a nurse.

employ.definition: to use a method, object or skill in order to achieve something
employ.note: typical: employ a method/technique/tactic NOT for: paying a worker
examples: The police employed new methods to catch the thieves.
Teachers employ different techniques in class.

employ.definition: (formal, usually passive) to spend your time doing a particular thing
employ.note: typical: be employed in (doing) sth NOT for: having a job at a company
examples: Her evenings are employed in writing letters.
He is employed in repairing old boats.

enclose.definition: to surround something completely, often with a wall or fence
enclose.note: typical: enclose a garden/yard/area NOT for: putting something in an envelope (see sense 2)
examples: A high wall encloses the garden.
They enclosed the field with a fence.

enclose.definition: to put something in an envelope or package together with a letter
enclose.note: typical: please find enclosed sth; enclose a cheque NOT for: fencing an area
examples: I enclose a copy of my certificate.
Please enclose a stamped envelope with your letter.

ensure.definition: to make certain that something will happen or be true
ensure.note: typical: ensure (that) sth is done; ensure the safety of sb NOT for: buying insurance (American insure)
examples: Please ensure that all the doors are locked.
The new rules ensure the safety of the workers.

entertain.definition: to amuse or interest people in a way that gives them pleasure
entertain.note: typical: entertain sb with sth; entertain the children NOT for: inviting guests (see sense 2)
examples: The comedian entertained the crowd for an hour.
She entertained the children with funny stories.

entertain.definition: to invite people to your home for a meal or party, or to take customers out for a meal
entertain.note: typical: entertain guests/clients NOT for: amusing people with a show
examples: They love to entertain friends at weekends.
The company pays for me to entertain clients.

entertain.definition: (formal) to consider an idea or let yourself think that something might be true
entertain.note: typical: entertain an idea/hope/doubt NOT for: amusing people
examples: She would never entertain the idea of moving abroad.
I entertained some doubts about the plan.

equip.definition: to provide a person or place with the things needed for an activity or job
equip.note: typical: equip sb/sth with sth; be well equipped NOT for: giving only knowledge (see sense 2)
examples: The school was equipped with new computers.
The team was well equipped for the long climb.

equip.definition: to give someone the information and skills they need to do something
equip.note: typical: equip sb with/for/to do sth NOT for: giving tools or machines
examples: The course equips students with useful skills.
Good training equips nurses to deal with emergencies.

establish.definition: to start a company, organisation or system that is meant to last for a long time
establish.note: typical: establish a company/school/system NOT for: finding out facts (see sense 3)
examples: The school was established in 1890.
They plan to establish a new research centre.

establish.definition: to begin a relationship or situation that will continue
establish.note: typical: establish contact/links/relations NOT for: a one-time meeting
examples: The two countries established diplomatic relations.
I tried to establish contact with the author.

establish.definition: to find out facts that prove something is true
establish.note: typical: establish the facts/that/whether sth is true NOT for: starting a company
examples: The police must establish what really happened.
Tests established that the man was ill.

establish.definition: to make people accept that you can do something or have a particular quality
establish.note: typical: establish yourself as sth; establish a reputation NOT for: starting an institution
examples: She quickly established herself as a good lawyer.
The young player established a reputation for speed.

examine.definition: to look at something carefully and thoroughly to find out more about it
examine.note: typical: examine sth for sth; examine how/whether NOT for: testing students (see sense 3)
examples: The police examined the car for fingerprints.
The report examines the causes of the problem.

examine.definition: (of a doctor) to look at your body to check that you are healthy
examine.note: typical: examine a patient; be examined by a doctor NOT for: looking at objects
examples: The doctor examined the child's throat.
I need to be examined before I start the job.

examine.definition: (formal) to ask someone questions to test their knowledge of a subject
examine.note: typical: be examined in/on sth NOT for: a doctor's check
examples: Students will be examined on world history.
She was examined in French and Spanish.

examine.definition: (in law) to ask someone questions officially in a court
examine.note: typical: examine a witness NOT for: school tests
examples: The lawyer examined the witness for an hour.
The expert was examined in court.

exclude.note: typical: exclude sth from sth; a diet that excludes sth NOT for: keeping people out (see sense 2)
examples: The price excludes tax.
Some figures were excluded from the report.

exclude.definition: to not allow someone to take part in something or to enter a place, especially in an unfair way
exclude.note: typical: exclude sb from sth; feel excluded NOT for: leaving out items from a list
examples: The club excluded women for many years.
She felt excluded when the others whispered.

exclude.definition: (British English) to officially make a child leave school because of bad behaviour
exclude.note: typical: be excluded from school NOT for: adults or workplaces
examples: The boy was excluded from school for fighting.
Two pupils were excluded last term.

exclude.definition: to decide that something is not a possibility
exclude.note: typical: exclude the possibility of sth; exclude sth as a cause NOT for: leaving people out
examples: Doctors have excluded a serious illness.
We cannot exclude the possibility of rain.

exist.definition: to be present or to happen in a particular place or situation
exist.note: typical: sth still exists; cease to exist; opportunities exist NOT for: living a hard life (use survive)
examples: Old customs still exist in many villages.
The problem does not exist in our school.

exist.note: typical: Do ghosts exist?; as if sb didn't exist NOT for: describing where something is
examples: Dinosaurs existed millions of years ago.
Some people believe that aliens really exist.

expand.definition: to become larger in size, number or amount, or to make something larger
expand.note: typical: expand rapidly; expand the economy/the range NOT for: opening new shops or factories (see sense 2)
examples: The city has expanded quickly over the last twenty years.
Metal expands when it is heated.

expand.definition: (of a company or business) to open new shops, factories, etc. and grow bigger
expand.note: typical: expand a business; expand into a new market NOT for: things getting physically bigger
examples: The bakery plans to expand into two more towns.
The company is expanding its business abroad.

expand.definition: (literary) to become more confident and start to talk more
expand.note: typical: he began to expand after a drink NOT for: businesses growing
examples: After a cup of tea, she started to expand and tell us her stories.
He expanded a little once he felt safe among friends.

experience.definition: to have a problem, event or situation happen to you or affect you
experience.note: typical: experience problems/difficulties/delays NOT for: feeling an emotion (see sense 2)
examples: Many travellers experienced long delays at the airport.
Children need to experience things for themselves.

experience.definition: to feel a particular emotion, pain, etc.
experience.note: typical: experience pain/fear/joy/nausea NOT for: events that happen to you
examples: She experienced a sudden feeling of fear.
Many people experience pain in cold weather.

experiment.definition: to try using various ideas or methods to find out how good or effective they are
experiment.note: typical: experiment with sth NOT for: a formal science test (see sense 2)
examples: She likes to experiment with new recipes.
The teacher left the children to experiment with paint.

experiment.definition: to do a scientific test to find out if an idea is true or to get more information
experiment.note: typical: experiment on animals/with a substance NOT for: trying out ideas for fun
examples: Scientists experiment on mice in the laboratory.
They experimented with a new kind of plastic.

experiment.definition: to try doing something to find out what it feels like, for example using drugs
experiment.note: typical: experiment with drugs/alcohol NOT for: scientific tests
examples: Many teenagers experiment with cigarettes.
He admitted he had experimented with drugs at university.

explore.definition: to discuss or think about something carefully
explore.note: typical: explore ways/the possibility/an idea NOT for: travelling around a place (see sense 2)
examples: The council will explore ways of reducing traffic.
I am going to explore the idea of studying abroad.

explore.definition: to travel around an area in order to find out about it
explore.note: typical: explore a city/island/cave NOT for: discussing ideas
examples: We spent the weekend exploring the old town.
The divers explored the wreck of the ship.

explore.definition: to look for something such as oil, minerals or gold
explore.note: typical: explore for oil/gas/gold NOT for: tourism or sightseeing
examples: The company is exploring for oil in the North Sea.
They explored the hills for gold.

extend.definition: to continue for a longer period of time, or to make something last longer
extend.note: typical: extend a deadline/visa/contract/stay NOT for: making a building bigger (see sense 3)
examples: The school extended the deadline by a week.
I'd like to extend my visit by two days.

extend.definition: to continue for a particular distance or over a particular area
extend.note: typical: extend across/over/to/from sth NOT for: making something last longer
examples: The forest extends for many miles.
The garden extends down to the river.

extend.definition: to make a room, building, road, etc. bigger or longer
extend.note: typical: extend the kitchen/the house/the road NOT for: lasting longer in time
examples: They want to extend the kitchen by two metres.
The city plans to extend the motorway.

extend.definition: to affect or include more people, things or places
extend.note: typical: extend to/beyond sth; extend a rule/service to sb NOT for: physical size
examples: The new law extends to all workers.
The bank extended its services to small businesses.

extend.definition: (formal) to offer someone help, sympathy, thanks, an invitation, etc.
extend.note: typical: extend a welcome/an invitation/thanks to sb NOT for: stretching your body
examples: We would like to extend a warm welcome to our guests.
The mayor extended an invitation to the team.

extend.definition: to stretch out a hand, arm or leg
extend.note: typical: extend your hand/arm NOT for: offering formal help
examples: He extended his hand and smiled.
She extended her arm to reach the book.

extend.definition: (in sport) to increase the number of points or goals by which you are ahead
extend.note: typical: extend a lead NOT for: making something longer in time
examples: The team extended its lead to ten points.
She extended her lead in the second half of the race.

face.definition: to be in a difficult situation that will affect you and that you must deal with
face.note: typical: face problems/a challenge/charges; be faced with sth NOT for: looking in a direction (see sense 5)
examples: The company faces serious financial problems.
He faces up to ten years in prison.

face.definition: to accept that a difficult situation exists even though you would prefer to ignore it (also face up to sth)
face.note: typical: face the fact/the truth; face up to sth NOT for: a danger that threatens you
examples: You must face the truth about your health.
She finally faced up to her mistakes.

face.definition: (can't face) to feel unable to do something because it seems too unpleasant or difficult
face.note: typical: can't face sth/doing sth NOT for: looking at someone
examples: I can't face another long meeting today.
He couldn't face telling her the bad news.

face.definition: to talk to or deal with someone when this is unpleasant or difficult
face.note: typical: face sb; face the world NOT for: sitting opposite a person
examples: I don't know how I can face him after what I said.
She was too upset to face her friends.

face.definition: to be opposite someone or something, or to look or point in a particular direction
face.note: typical: face north/the sea/each other NOT for: dealing with a problem
examples: The two men stood facing each other.
My room faces the garden.

face.definition: to play against an opponent or team in a game or competition
face.note: typical: face an opponent in the final NOT for: dealing with a danger
examples: Spain will face Italy in the final.
The champion faces a tough opponent tonight.

face.definition: (of a building) to be covered on the outside with a layer of stone, concrete, etc. (passive)
face.note: typical: be faced with stone/brick NOT for: looking in a direction
examples: The house is faced with local stone.
The wall was faced with white tiles.

fascinate.definition: to attract someone and be extremely interesting to them
fascinate.note: typical: fascinate sb; be fascinated by sth NOT for: frightening someone
examples: The idea of time travel fascinates me.
Snakes have always fascinated the boy.

feature.definition: to include something as a special or important part, or to be included as an important part
feature.note: typical: feature in sth; feature prominently; feature sb as sth NOT for: showing a film (see sense 2)
examples: The exhibition features paintings by local artists.
Fear features strongly in his books.

feature.definition: to show a film, play, etc.
feature.note: typical: the cinema features sth; be featured in sth NOT for: including a special part
examples: The theatre is featuring films by Charlie Chaplin this week.
The festival features three new plays.

fetch.definition: (especially British English) to go and get something or someone and bring them back
fetch.note: typical: fetch sb sth; fetch sth from sth NOT for: selling at a price (see sense 2)
examples: Please fetch a chair from the kitchen.
I'm going to fetch the children from school.

fetch.definition: to be sold for a particular amount of money, especially at an auction
fetch.note: typical: fetch a high price/$20 million NOT for: bringing something back
examples: The painting is expected to fetch two million pounds.
Old coins can fetch a lot of money.

fetch.definition: (British English) to make people react in a particular way
fetch.note: typical: fetch a cheer/a laugh NOT for: going to get an object
examples: His joke fetched a big laugh from the audience.
The goal fetched a loud cheer from the crowd.

flow.definition: (of a liquid, gas or electricity) to move in a steady continuous stream
flow.note: typical: flow into/through/over sth; flow freely NOT for: people or goods moving in large numbers (see sense 3)
examples: The river flows into the sea.
Air flowed freely through the open windows.

flow.definition: to move or hang smoothly and loosely
flow.note: typical: hair/a dress flows NOT for: liquids moving in a pipe
examples: Her long hair flowed down over her shoulders.
The curtains flowed gently in the breeze.

flow.definition: (of goods, people or information) to move from one place to another in large numbers or amounts
flow.note: typical: money/people/information flows into/out of sth NOT for: water or electricity
examples: Money has been flowing into the country.
Refugees were flowing across the border.

focus.definition: to give special attention to one particular person or thing
focus.note: typical: focus on sth; focus your attention/mind NOT for: using a camera (see sense 2)
examples: She tried to focus her mind on her work.
The report focuses on the problem of waste.

focus.definition: to point a camera or telescope at something and adjust it so you can see clearly
focus.note: typical: focus on sth; focus the camera NOT for: general attention
examples: He focused the camera on the bird.
She focused her binoculars on the tree.

focus.definition: (of your eyes) to look at something and see it clearly
focus.note: typical: your eyes focus on sth NOT for: cameras and telescopes
examples: It took a moment for my eyes to focus in the dark.
Her eyes focused on the face in the crowd.

focus.definition: to aim beams of light onto a particular place
focus.note: typical: focus a light/beam on sth NOT for: paying attention
examples: The lens focuses the sun's rays on a single spot.
They focused the spotlight on the singer.

forbid.definition: to tell someone that they are not allowed to do something, or that something is not allowed
forbid.note: typical: forbid sb to do sth; forbid sb from doing sth; strictly forbid NOT for: God forbid
examples: My parents forbid me to stay out late.
The law strictly forbids smoking in schools.

forbid.definition: (formal) to make it impossible for someone to do something
forbid.note: typical: lack of time/space forbids sth NOT for: giving an order
examples: Lack of space forbids a full list of names.
Shortage of time forbids a longer talk.

force.definition: to make someone do something they do not want to do
force.note: typical: force sb to do sth; force yourself to do sth; be forced into sth NOT for: opening something by strength (see sense 5)
examples: The heavy rain forced us to cancel the match.
I had to force myself to get up early.

force.definition: to make someone or something move in a particular direction using great strength
force.note: typical: force sth open/back/off course NOT for: making someone obey
examples: The wind forced the ship off course.
He forced the window open with a knife.

force.definition: to push very hard in order to get somewhere
force.note: typical: force your way through/into/past sth NOT for: opening a lock
examples: She forced her way through the crowd.
The fans forced their way into the stadium.

force.definition: to make something happen or change, especially faster than planned
force.note: typical: force a decision/resignation/the pace; force prices down NOT for: making a person move
examples: The scandal forced his resignation.
High costs forced prices up.

force.definition: to open a door, lock or window using physical strength, often causing damage
force.note: typical: force a door/lock/window NOT for: making someone do something
examples: The thief forced the lock on the back door.
Police forced the door to get inside.

force.definition: (force the issue) to make it necessary for people to take action instead of waiting
force.note: typical: force the issue NOT for: using physical strength
examples: She forced the issue by asking for a decision.
He wanted to force the issue before the meeting ended.

force.definition: (force sb's hand) to make someone do something unwillingly or earlier than planned
force.note: typical: force sb's hand NOT for: opening a door
examples: The bad news forced the manager's hand.
The newspaper story forced their hand.

force.definition: (force a smile/laugh) to make yourself smile or laugh although you feel upset
force.note: typical: force a smile/laugh NOT for: making others act
examples: He forced a smile and said thank you.
She forced a laugh to hide her disappointment.

found.definition: to start an organisation, company, school or city, often by providing the money
found.note: typical: found a company/school/city; be founded in 1990 NOT for: past tense of find
examples: The school was founded in 1850.
She founded a charity for homeless animals.

found.definition: (passive) to have as the main idea, belief or base
found.note: typical: be founded on/upon sth NOT for: starting a company
examples: The system is founded on trust.
Their friendship was founded on shared interests.

found.definition: (technical) to melt metal and pour it into a mould to make tools or parts
found.note: typical: found metal/iron NOT for: starting an organisation
examples: The workers found the iron into large bells.
The factory founds parts for engines.

gather.definition: to come together and form a group, or to make people do this
gather.note: typical: gather round/around/together; a crowd gathered NOT for: collecting objects (see sense 3)
examples: A crowd gathered outside the shop.
Please gather round so that everyone can see.

gather.definition: to believe that something is true because of what you have seen or heard
gather.note: typical: I gather (that); as far as I can gather NOT for: collecting things
examples: I gather you have had some problems.
She is his niece, from what I can gather.

gather.definition: to collect things or information together from different places
gather.note: typical: gather information/signatures/up/together NOT for: people meeting
examples: The police gathered evidence at the scene.
She gathered up the clothes and put them in a bag.

gather.definition: (gather speed/force/momentum) to move faster or become stronger
gather.note: typical: gather speed/strength/momentum NOT for: collecting objects
examples: The train gathered speed on the hill.
The protest movement is gathering momentum.

gather.definition: (gather dust) to stay unused for a long time
gather.note: typical: gather dust NOT for: collecting things on purpose
examples: The old books just gather dust on the shelf.
His guitar has been gathering dust for years.

gather.definition: to pull material into small folds, or to pull clothing closer to you
gather.note: typical: be gathered at the waist; gather your skirt NOT for: collecting people or things
examples: The skirt is gathered at the waist.
She gathered her coat around her.

gather.definition: (gather yourself/your strength/your thoughts) to prepare yourself for something difficult
gather.note: typical: gather your thoughts/courage NOT for: collecting objects
examples: He took a moment to gather his thoughts.
She gathered her courage and spoke.

gather.definition: (literary) to become gradually more cloudy or darker
gather.note: typical: storm clouds/darkness gather NOT for: people meeting
examples: Dark clouds were gathering over the hills.
The shadows gathered as evening came.

gather.definition: (literary) to take someone in your arms or draw them close to you
gather.note: typical: gather sb to you/gather sb up NOT for: collecting objects
examples: She gathered the child to her and held him tight.
He gathered her up in his arms.

guarantee.definition: to promise that something will happen, or that a product will be repaired or replaced if it breaks
guarantee.note: typical: guarantee (that); guarantee sb sth; be guaranteed for a year NOT for: promising to repay a loan (see sense 2)
examples: I can guarantee you an interview.
The watch is guaranteed for two years.

guarantee.definition: to promise to pay back money that someone else has borrowed if they do not pay it themselves
guarantee.note: typical: guarantee a loan NOT for: promising results
examples: My parents guaranteed the loan for the flat.
The bank wants someone to guarantee the loan.

guarantee.definition: to make it certain that something will happen
guarantee.note: typical: guarantee success/safety; be guaranteed to do sth NOT for: making a promise to a person
examples: Talent does not guarantee success.
This news is guaranteed to make her angry.

guide.definition: to take someone to a place
guide.note: typical: guide sb through/along/to sth NOT for: giving advice or influence
examples: He guided us through the narrow streets.
A waiter guided them to their table.

guide.definition: to help someone or something to move in a particular direction
guide.note: typical: guide sb/sth into/towards sth NOT for: showing a way of doing something
examples: She guided the old man towards a chair.
Lights guide the ships into the harbour.

guide.definition: to influence someone's behaviour or ideas
guide.note: typical: guide sb; be guided by sth NOT for: leading people on a walk
examples: Teenagers need adults to guide them.
She was guided by her love of music.

guide.definition: to show someone the right way to do something, especially something difficult
guide.note: typical: guide sb through sth NOT for: physical movement
examples: The teacher guided the class through the exercise.
This book guides you through the process step by step.

handle.definition: to do the things that are necessary to complete a job
handle.note: typical: handle the paperwork/accounts/a case NOT for: touching an object (see sense 5)
examples: She handles all the accounts for the company.
The case is being handled by a good lawyer.

handle.definition: to deal with a situation or problem by behaving in a particular way
handle.note: typical: handle a situation/crisis/complaint well NOT for: dealing with people (see sense 3)
examples: The manager handled the problem very well.
I can handle it myself.

handle.definition: to deal with a person or behave towards them in a particular way, especially to keep them happy
handle.note: typical: handle a customer/child; be difficult to handle NOT for: dealing with tasks
examples: Some customers are hard to handle.
She knows how to handle difficult children.

handle.definition: to not become upset in a difficult situation
handle.note: typical: can't handle stress/it NOT for: doing a job
examples: He doesn't handle stress very well.
She can't handle it when people shout.

handle.definition: to touch something or pick it up and hold it in your hands
handle.note: typical: handle a weapon/the goods/animals NOT for: dealing with a problem
examples: Please handle the glasses carefully.
He had never handled a gun before.

handle.definition: to control the movement of a vehicle or animal; (of a vehicle) to be easy or hard to control
handle.note: typical: handle a car/horse; handles well/badly NOT for: dealing with paperwork
examples: I'm not sure I can handle such a big truck.
The car handles well on wet roads.

handle.definition: to move goods from one place to another
handle.note: typical: the port/post office handles goods/parcels NOT for: touching things
examples: The airport handles millions of passengers a year.
The Post Office handles billions of letters.

hesitate.definition: to pause before saying or doing something because you are nervous or not sure
hesitate.note: typical: hesitate about/over sth; hesitate to do sth NOT for: politely encouraging someone (see sense 2)
examples: She hesitated for a moment before answering.
He hesitated over whether to accept the job.

hesitate.definition: (don't hesitate to do sth) used to tell someone it is fine to do something without worrying
hesitate.note: typical: don't hesitate to contact/call/ask NOT for: being unsure
examples: Don't hesitate to call me if you need help.
Please don't hesitate to ask any questions.

highlight.definition: to make a problem or subject easy to notice so that people pay attention to it
highlight.note: typical: highlight a problem/an issue/the need for sth NOT for: marking text with a pen (see sense 2)
examples: The report highlights the need for better schools.
Your CV should highlight your best skills.

highlight.definition: to mark words with a special coloured pen or in a different colour on a computer
highlight.note: typical: highlight a word/a line/a name NOT for: making people notice a problem
examples: She highlighted the important words in yellow.
Highlight the text and then press Copy.

highlight.definition: to make some parts of your hair a lighter colour than the rest
highlight.note: typical: have your hair highlighted NOT for: marking text
examples: She had her hair highlighted at the salon.
He highlighted his hair with blond streaks.

hire.definition: to pay money to use something for a short period of time
hire.note: typical: hire a car, a bike, a hall, equipment for a day or a week NOT for: buying something permanently; using it for free
examples: We hired a van for the weekend to move the furniture.
You can hire skis and boots at the bottom of the slope.

hire.definition: to give someone a job or pay them to do a particular piece of work
hire.note: typical: hire staff, a lawyer, a consultant, a builder NOT for: dismissing someone; asking a friend for a free favour
examples: The restaurant hired three new waiters for the summer season.
She hired an accountant to sort out her tax return.

host.definition: to provide the place and organisation for an event so that people can take part
host.note: typical: host a conference, a tournament, the Olympics, a party NOT for: simply attending an event; paying for a ticket
examples: Brazil agreed to host the next international football tournament.
Our school will host a science fair in March.

host.definition: to present a radio or television programme and introduce its guests
host.note: typical: host a show, a quiz, a talk programme, an awards ceremony NOT for: appearing as a guest; writing the script
examples: He hosts a late-night comedy show on Fridays.
The awards ceremony will be hosted by a well-known actress.

identify.definition: to recognise someone or something and be able to say who or what they are
identify.note: typical: identify a suspect, a body, a bird, a voice, a symptom NOT for: meeting someone for the first time; guessing without evidence
examples: Witnesses were unable to identify the driver of the car.
Can you identify this plant from its leaves?

identify.definition: to find out or discover exactly what something is, especially a cause, problem or source
identify.note: typical: identify a cause, a problem, a need, a risk, a gene NOT for: solving the problem; ignoring it
examples: Engineers have identified the fault that caused the power cut.
The survey identified several areas where the service could improve.

identify.definition: to be a feature that makes someone or something easy to recognise
identify.note: typical: a badge, accent, uniform or mark that identifies someone as something NOT for: hiding who someone is; naming a person in a list
examples: The red scarf identified him as a supporter of the home team.
Her strong northern accent identified her immediately.

impress.definition: to make someone feel admiration or respect because of what you do or show
impress.note: typical: impress an employer, a teacher, a judge, a date, an audience NOT for: annoying someone; pressing something into a surface
examples: She impressed the interviewers with her clear answers.
He bought a new suit to impress his future in-laws.

impress.definition: to make someone understand how important or serious something is
impress.note: typical: impress on someone the importance, value or need of something NOT for: physically pushing something; simply mentioning a fact once
examples: Our teacher impressed on us the importance of arriving on time.
The doctor tried to impress the seriousness of the situation on him.

impress.definition: to press something into a soft surface so that it leaves a mark or pattern
impress.note: typical: a pattern, footprint or design impressed in clay, wax or snow NOT for: making an emotional impression; printing on paper with ink
examples: The potter impressed a small leaf design into the wet clay.
A deep footprint was impressed in the soft mud beside the river.

indicate.definition: to show that something is true or likely to be true
indicate.note: typical: research, results, signs or evidence indicate that something is so NOT for: proving something beyond doubt; hiding information
examples: Recent figures indicate that sales are falling.
The dark clouds indicate that rain is on the way.

indicate.definition: to make your wishes, plans or opinions clear by saying or doing something
indicate.note: typical: indicate a willingness, an intention, a preference NOT for: refusing to answer; making a final decision
examples: The minister has indicated that he may resign.
Please indicate your choice of meal on the form.

indicate.definition: to direct attention to something or someone, for example by pointing
indicate.note: typical: indicate a person, a place, a direction with a hand or finger NOT for: describing in long detail; touching something
examples: She indicated the empty chair with a nod of her head.
The guide indicated a path leading up the hill.

indicate.definition: to represent or mark something on a map, chart or diagram
indicate.note: typical: a line, symbol, colour or arrow indicates something on a graph or map NOT for: explaining a theory in words; writing a long report
examples: The red dots on the map indicate the locations of the schools.
A dotted line indicates the border between the two regions.

indicate.definition: to show with lights or a hand signal which way you are about to turn a vehicle
indicate.note: typical: indicate left or right before turning or changing lane (British English) NOT for: sounding the horn; stopping the car
examples: Always indicate before you overtake another car.
The cyclist forgot to indicate and nearly caused an accident.

influence.definition: to have an effect on how someone thinks, acts or develops, or on how something turns out, without forcing it
influence.note: typical: influence a decision, an outcome, a vote, a child, public opinion NOT for: ordering someone directly; physically moving something
examples: Advertising can strongly influence what young people choose to buy.
Several factors influenced the committee's final decision.

inform.definition: to officially or formally tell someone about something
inform.note: typical: inform the police, a customer, staff, someone of a change NOT for: casual chatting; asking a question
examples: Please inform the office if you cannot attend the meeting.
We regret to inform you that the flight has been cancelled.

inform.definition: to influence or shape someone's attitude, opinion or the content of something
inform.note: typical: experience, research or beliefs informing a decision, a view or a piece of work NOT for: telling someone a fact; reporting a crime
examples: Her years as a nurse inform everything she writes about healthcare.
The new policy was informed by detailed scientific research.

inherit.definition: to receive money, property or a title from someone after they have died
inherit.note: typical: inherit a house, a fortune, a farm, a title from a relative NOT for: buying something; being given a gift while the giver is alive
examples: She inherited her grandmother's cottage in the countryside.
He will inherit the family business when his father retires.

inherit.definition: to take over a situation, problem or responsibility from someone who had it before you
inherit.note: typical: a new leader, manager or government inheriting a problem, a debt, a mess NOT for: creating a problem yourself; receiving money from a death
examples: The new manager inherited a team with very low morale.
The government inherited a huge debt from its predecessor.

inherit.definition: to have the same physical or personal qualities as your parents or ancestors
inherit.note: typical: inherit eye colour, a talent, a temper, a disease from a parent NOT for: learning a skill at school; copying someone's behaviour on purpose
examples: She inherited her father's dark curly hair.
Many people inherit a tendency to certain illnesses from their families.

inherit.definition: to get something that another person no longer wants or needs
inherit.note: typical: inherit old furniture, clothes, a car, a desk from someone NOT for: receiving money after a death; buying second-hand goods
examples: The younger brother inherited his sister's old bicycle.
We inherited a sofa from the people who lived here before us.

insert.definition: to put something into something else
insert.note: typical: insert a key, a coin, a card, a needle into a slot or hole NOT for: removing something; throwing something away
examples: Insert your card into the machine and enter your PIN.
She carefully inserted the key into the lock.

insert.definition: to add something to the middle of a piece of writing or a document
insert.note: typical: insert a word, a paragraph, a clause, a comment into a text NOT for: deleting a sentence; writing a document from the beginning
examples: The editor inserted a short note at the end of the paragraph.
Please insert your name in the space provided.

insist.definition: to say very firmly that something is true, even when others doubt it
insist.note: typical: insist that you are right, innocent, telling the truth; insist on your innocence NOT for: politely suggesting something; demanding an action
examples: He insisted that he had never seen the letter before.
She kept insisting on her innocence.

insist.definition: to demand firmly that something must happen or be done
insist.note: typical: insist on payment, on a rule, that someone does something NOT for: gently asking for a favour; stating a fact
examples: I insist that you stay for dinner.
The teacher insisted on complete silence during the exam.

insist.definition: to keep doing something in a stubborn way, especially something annoying or inconvenient
insist.note: typical: insist on doing something, such as talking, wearing or arguing, in spite of problems NOT for: doing something once by accident; giving up easily
examples: He always insists on wearing sandals, even in the snow.
She will insist on telling the same joke at every party.

inspire.definition: to make someone feel confident, enthusiastic and eager to do something
inspire.note: typical: inspire a team, students, young people, someone to do something NOT for: frightening someone; ordering someone to work
examples: The coach's speech inspired the players to play harder.
Her courage inspired many people to join the campaign.

inspire.definition: to cause someone to have a particular feeling or reaction
inspire.note: typical: inspire confidence, respect, trust, fear, loyalty NOT for: feeling an emotion yourself; breathing in
examples: The new leader does not inspire much confidence.
His honesty inspired great trust in his colleagues.

inspire.definition: to give someone the idea for a book, painting, song or other creative work
inspire.note: typical: a place, event or person inspiring a story, a poem, a design NOT for: copying another work exactly; finishing a project
examples: The novel was inspired by a trip to Morocco.
A walk along the beach inspired her to write a poem.

install.definition: to put a piece of equipment in place and connect it so that it is ready to use
install.note: typical: install a boiler, cameras, a heating system, a new kitchen NOT for: repairing broken equipment; simply buying a machine
examples: The company installed solar panels on the roof.
A new fire alarm will be installed next week.

install.definition: to put software onto a computer so that it is ready to use
install.note: typical: install a program, an app, an update, antivirus software NOT for: deleting a program; writing the software
examples: I installed the new version of the app on my phone.
You need to install the driver before you use the printer.

install.definition: to formally put someone into an important job or position, often with a ceremony
install.note: typical: install a president, a bishop, a chancellor, a new leader NOT for: hiring someone for an ordinary job; electing someone by vote
examples: The new bishop will be installed at a ceremony in the cathedral.
He was installed as head of the university last year.

install.definition: to settle yourself comfortably in a place as if you plan to stay for a long time
install.note: typical: install yourself in an armchair, a flat, a corner, a seat NOT for: leaving a place quickly; fitting equipment
examples: She installed herself in the best armchair and refused to move.
The guests installed themselves in the garden for the whole afternoon.

intend.definition: to have something in your mind as a plan or purpose
intend.note: typical: intend to do something; intend someone to understand; intend no harm NOT for: doing something by accident; hoping without any plan
examples: I intend to finish this report before the weekend.
I never intended you to feel left out.

intend.definition: to provide or design something for a particular person or purpose
intend.note: typical: be intended for children, for beginners, for use in schools NOT for: planning a future action; describing something that happened by chance
examples: This guide is intended for people who have never used a computer.
The gift was intended for my sister, not for me.

interrupt.definition: to stop someone from continuing to speak or do something by suddenly speaking or making a noise
interrupt.note: typical: interrupt a speaker, a meeting, a conversation, someone's work NOT for: waiting politely for someone to finish; ending a job permanently
examples: Please don't interrupt me while I'm speaking.
Sorry to interrupt, but there is a phone call for you.

interrupt.definition: to make a process or activity stop for a time
interrupt.note: typical: interrupt a journey, a broadcast, supply, studies, sleep NOT for: finishing something successfully; stopping something for ever
examples: The football match was interrupted by heavy rain.
A power cut interrupted the television broadcast.

interrupt.definition: to break the continuous line, surface or view of something
interrupt.note: typical: a building, wall or tree interrupting a view, a line, a landscape NOT for: stopping a conversation; moving an object
examples: A single tall chimney interrupts the view of the hills.
The smooth surface of the lake was interrupted by a few small rocks.

invade.definition: to enter a country or area with an army in order to take control of it
invade.note: typical: invade a country, a territory, an island; troops invading NOT for: visiting as a tourist; defending a country
examples: The army invaded the neighbouring country at dawn.
Troops invaded the island and took control of the port.

invade.definition: to go into a place in large numbers, especially when you are not wanted
invade.note: typical: tourists, fans, insects or protesters invading a town, a pitch, a house NOT for: a single person entering quietly; welcoming guests
examples: Thousands of fans invaded the pitch after the final whistle.
Ants have invaded our kitchen again.

invade.definition: to get involved in something in an unwanted and annoying way
invade.note: typical: invade someone's privacy, space, life, territory NOT for: respecting someone's privacy; helping someone politely
examples: The newspaper was accused of invading the family's privacy.
I don't want anyone invading my personal space on the train.

involve.definition: to have something as a necessary part or result
involve.note: typical: a job, plan or activity involving work, risk, cost, travel NOT for: describing a person who takes part; simply owning something
examples: The new job involves a lot of travelling.
Learning a language involves practising every day.

involve.definition: to include or affect someone or something
involve.note: typical: an accident, crime, change or dispute involving people or things NOT for: leaving someone out; describing what a job requires
examples: The police are investigating a robbery involving three men.
The changes will involve everyone in the department.

involve.definition: to ask or allow someone to take part in something
involve.note: typical: involve children, staff, the public, the community in a decision or activity NOT for: forcing someone to do work alone; excluding someone
examples: The teacher tried to involve every child in the discussion.
The council wants to involve local people in planning the new park.

involve.definition: to take part actively in something yourself
involve.note: typical: involve yourself in a cause, a project, someone's business NOT for: staying away from something; making someone else do it
examples: She involved herself in every aspect of the school's fundraising.
He refused to involve himself in his neighbours' argument.

irritate.definition: to make someone feel annoyed or impatient, especially by doing something repeatedly
irritate.note: typical: a noise, habit, remark or behaviour irritating someone NOT for: making someone really furious; entertaining someone
examples: His constant humming really irritates me.
It irritates her when people arrive late.

irritate.definition: to make a part of the body feel sore, red or uncomfortable
irritate.note: typical: irritate the skin, eyes, throat, lungs NOT for: curing an illness; hurting someone's feelings
examples: The strong soap irritated her skin.
Smoke from the fire irritated my eyes.

judge.definition: to form an opinion about someone or something after thinking carefully about the facts
judge.note: typical: judge a person, a situation, a distance, whether something is right NOT for: guessing wildly; deciding a sports result
examples: You shouldn't judge a person by their clothes.
It is hard to judge whether the plan will work.

judge.definition: to make a guess or estimate based on what you have seen, heard or learned
judge.note: typical: judging by or judging from the evidence, the look, the sound NOT for: knowing something for certain; announcing an official verdict
examples: Judging by the clouds, it will rain this afternoon.
