Judging from his smile, the exam went well.

judge.definition: to decide who wins a competition or which entry is best
judge.note: typical: judge a contest, a race, a show, a baking competition NOT for: taking part in a competition; deciding a court case
examples: She was asked to judge the school poetry competition.
The dogs will be judged on their appearance and behaviour.

judge.definition: to form a critical opinion of someone, often in an unfair way
judge.note: typical: judge people for their choices, appearance or mistakes; don't judge NOT for: giving a fair assessment; praising someone
examples: Please don't judge me for forgetting your birthday.
People are too quick to judge those who are different.

judge.definition: to decide in a court of law whether someone is guilty of a crime
judge.note: typical: a court, jury or magistrate judging a case, a crime or an accused person NOT for: casual personal opinions; reporting a crime to the police
examples: The court will judge the case next month.
He was judged guilty of fraud by the jury.

justify.definition: to give an acceptable reason or explanation for something that others think is wrong or unreasonable
justify.note: typical: justify a decision, an action, a cost, yourself NOT for: apologising; hiding the truth
examples: How can the company justify raising prices again?
He tried to justify his late arrival with a story about traffic.

justify.definition: to be a good enough reason for something
justify.note: typical: the result, danger or need justifies an action, a cost, a response NOT for: excusing a crime for no reason; explaining a past event
examples: Nothing can justify such cruel behaviour.
The long queues did not justify the high ticket price.

justify.definition: to arrange text so that the lines are straight at the left and right edges
justify.note: typical: justify text, a paragraph, a column in a document NOT for: making text bigger; correcting spelling errors
examples: Select the paragraph and click the button to justify the text.
Newspapers often justify their columns so that both edges are straight.

lack.definition: to not have something, or not have enough of something that you need
lack.note: typical: lack confidence, skill, money, experience, evidence NOT for: using 'in' or 'of' after it (use 'be lacking in' instead); losing something you had
examples: The young team lacked experience in big matches.
Many villages lack clean drinking water.

lack.definition: to have plenty of something, used mainly in negative phrases
lack.note: typical: not lack for critics, friends, money, work NOT for: describing a shortage; use in affirmative statements
examples: She never lacked for friends at university.
The artist does not lack for admirers.

launch.definition: to start something big or important, such as a campaign, an investigation or an attack
launch.note: typical: launch a campaign, investigation, attack, career, appeal NOT for: starting small everyday actions (use 'start' or 'begin')
examples: The charity launched an appeal to help flood victims.
Police have launched an investigation into the fire.

launch.definition: to make a new product, book or service available to the public for the first time
launch.note: typical: launch a product, brand, app, book, service NOT for: ordinary selling of an existing product
examples: The company will launch its new phone in September.
The airline launched a cheap route to Prague this spring.

launch.definition: to put a boat or ship into the water for the first time or after it has been built or repaired
launch.note: typical: launch a ship, boat, lifeboat, yacht NOT for: putting something in water by accident
examples: Workers launched the new ferry after months of construction.
The crew launched the lifeboat in rough seas.

launch.definition: to send a rocket, missile or spacecraft into the air or into space
launch.note: typical: launch a rocket, missile, satellite, probe NOT for: throwing small objects (use 'throw')
examples: The agency launched a weather satellite last night.
The ship launched two missiles at the target.

launch.definition: to make a computer program start running
launch.note: typical: launch an app, program, browser, game NOT for: installing or downloading software
examples: Click the icon to launch the program.
The app takes a few seconds to launch on older phones.

launch.definition: to jump forward or upward into the air with great energy
launch.note: typical: launch yourself forwards, up, off, from, at sb NOT for: gentle or slow movements
examples: The cat launched itself off the wall and landed on the table.
He launched himself at the ball and caught it.

lay.definition: to put someone or something down carefully in a flat position
lay.note: typical: lay a hand on sb, lay a wreath, lay sth flat, lay a baby down NOT for: the past of 'lie' (lay, lain) meaning to be flat
examples: She laid the baby gently in the cot.
He laid the map flat on the table.

lay.definition: to put bricks, carpet, cables, pipes or similar materials in the correct place
lay.note: typical: lay bricks, carpet, cables, pipes, foundations NOT for: placing small loose objects
examples: Workmen are laying a new cable under the road.
They laid the carpet in a single afternoon.

lay.definition: if a bird, insect or reptile lays eggs, it produces them
lay.note: typical: lay eggs (hens, turtles, insects) NOT for: mammals giving birth
examples: Turtles come to this beach to lay their eggs.
Our hens lay about ten eggs a day.

lay.definition: to arrange knives, forks, plates and so on on a table ready for a meal (BrE)
lay.note: typical: lay the table, lay a place NOT for: serving the food itself
examples: Can you lay the table while I finish the soup?
She laid places for six guests.

lay.definition: to risk an amount of money on the result of a race or game
lay.note: typical: lay money, lay a bet, lay £50 on sth NOT for: investing in business or shares
examples: He laid ten pounds on the favourite to win.
She laid a small bet on the final.

lean.definition: to move or bend your body in a particular direction
lean.note: typical: lean forward, back, over, towards sb NOT for: standing straight or walking
examples: She leaned forward to hear what he was saying.
Lean back and relax for a moment.

lean.definition: to support yourself in a sloping position against a wall or another surface
lean.note: typical: lean against, on a wall, rail, desk, counter NOT for: depending on a person emotionally (use 'lean on' only in that phrasal sense)
examples: He leaned against the doorframe and watched us.
A few tourists were leaning on the bridge railing.

lean.definition: to put something in a sloping position where it is supported, or to be in that position
lean.note: typical: lean sth against, on sth; ladder, bike, mirror leaning against a wall NOT for: hanging something from a hook
examples: She leaned her bike against the fence.
A ladder was leaning against the side of the house.

lean.definition: to slope or bend away from an upright position
lean.note: typical: trees, towers, walls leaning NOT for: a person moving their body on purpose
examples: The old shed leans badly to one side.
The trees were leaning in the strong wind.

limit.definition: to stop an amount or number from increasing beyond a particular point
limit.note: typical: limit imports, numbers, spending, speed, access NOT for: forbidding something completely (use 'ban')
examples: The school limits each class to twenty pupils.
Seating is limited to five hundred people.

limit.definition: to stop someone from doing what they want or from developing beyond a particular point
limit.note: typical: limit opportunities, choices, growth, yourself to sth NOT for: physical restraint such as tying someone up
examples: A lack of money limited her choices.
I limit myself to one cup of coffee a day.

limit.definition: to exist or happen only in a particular place, group or area of activity (usually be limited to)
limit.note: typical: be limited to an area, group, region, roof NOT for: active use with a person as the subject
examples: The damage was limited to the kitchen.
The disease is limited to a few villages.

link.definition: to be related to something in some way (usually be linked)
link.note: typical: be linked to, with sth; closely, directly, strongly linked NOT for: describing a physical connection between objects (use sense 3)
examples: Police believe the two robberies are linked.
Some illnesses are linked to a poor diet.

link.definition: to make a connection between two or more things or people
link.note: typical: link people, ideas, events, together; link A to B NOT for: joining physical objects
examples: A shared love of music linked the two friends.
Researchers try to link early habits to later health.

link.definition: to join things, people or places together in a physical way
link.note: typical: link a bridge, road, pipe, rope to/with sth; link arms NOT for: relating ideas only
examples: A long bridge links the island and the mainland.
The climbers were linked together by a rope.

link.definition: to show or say that there is a connection between people, situations or things
link.note: typical: link sb to a crime, scandal, club, group NOT for: proving that a link really exists
examples: Reports linked the minister to the scandal.
Nothing linked the suspect to the stolen car.

link.definition: to make one thing depend on another
link.note: typical: link pay, rises, aid, funding to performance, results NOT for: simply mentioning two things together
examples: The firm links bonuses to sales targets.
Aid will be linked to progress on reform.

link.definition: to connect computers or other electronic systems so that signals or messages can pass between them
link.note: typical: link computers, devices, networks, up, to a server NOT for: connecting people socially
examples: All the offices are linked to a central computer.
You can link your phone to the speaker by Bluetooth.

load.definition: to put a large quantity of something into a vehicle or container
load.note: typical: load a van, truck, dishwasher, washing machine, boat; load up NOT for: unloading or emptying (opposite is 'unload')
examples: It took an hour to load the van.
Will you help me load the dishwasher?

load.definition: to put a necessary part into something so that it can work
load.note: typical: load a gun, camera, printer, film, paper, bullets NOT for: filling something with a liquid
examples: He loaded the camera with a new roll of film.
She loaded paper into the printer.

load.definition: to put a program or data into a computer, or to be put into a computer
load.note: typical: load a program, file, page, game; a website loads slowly NOT for: saving a file
examples: The page takes ages to load on my phone.
Press the button to load the saved game.

load.definition: if a ship, aircraft or other vehicle loads, goods or people are put onto it
load.note: typical: ship, plane, lorry loads at a port or airport NOT for: a person putting things in a house
examples: The first ship to load at the new port arrived on Monday.
The plane loaded quickly and took off on time.

locate.definition: to discover exactly where something is
locate.note: typical: locate the source, position, leak, fault, missing person NOT for: finding something by chance (use 'come across')
examples: Engineers could not locate the source of the leak.
Rescuers finally located the missing hikers.

locate.definition: to be in a particular position or place (usually be located)
locate.note: typical: be located in, near, on, at, in the centre of NOT for: the action of finding something
examples: The hotel is located near the station.
Our office is located on the third floor.

locate.definition: to put or build something in a particular place
locate.note: typical: locate a shop, factory, school, office, store in an area NOT for: discovering where something already is
examples: The company decided to locate its factory near the port.
Large supermarkets are usually located on the edge of towns.

locate.definition: to come to a place and start a business or company there (American English)
locate.note: typical: locate in a city, region, area, state NOT for: moving house; applies to businesses
examples: Many software firms have located in this city.
We want to attract companies to locate in our region.

maintain.definition: to keep something going in the same way or at the same level as it has been
maintain.note: typical: maintain contact, standards, a relationship, control, order, your position NOT for: repairing something that has broken
examples: The hotel prides itself on maintaining high standards.
It is hard to maintain contact when you live abroad.

maintain.definition: to make a level or rate of activity or movement stay the same
maintain.note: typical: maintain a temperature, speed, level, balance, pace, fitness NOT for: increasing a level
examples: The heating system maintains a steady temperature in the room.
The runner maintained a fast pace for the whole race.

maintain.definition: to say firmly that something is true, even if others doubt it
maintain.note: typical: maintain that..., maintain your innocence, critics maintain NOT for: giving a neutral opinion or a guess
examples: He has always maintained his innocence.
Critics maintain that the plan will cost too much.

maintain.definition: to keep a machine, road, building or equipment in good condition by checking and repairing it regularly
maintain.note: typical: maintain a road, engine, building, equipment, website NOT for: building or creating something new
examples: The council maintains the roads in this area.
The engine must be properly maintained.

maintain.definition: to provide money or food so that someone can live
maintain.note: typical: maintain a family, child, wife, student NOT for: lending or giving a one-time gift of money
examples: He had to maintain two children on a small salary.
She worked nights to maintain her elderly mother.

manage.definition: to direct or control a business, department, team and the people, money or equipment involved
manage.note: typical: manage a company, shop, team, department, project, hotel NOT for: simply owning a business
examples: She manages a small hotel in the mountains.
The football club was badly managed for years.

manage.definition: to succeed in doing something difficult, especially after trying hard
manage.note: typical: manage to do sth, somehow manage, barely manage NOT for: easy tasks done without effort; 'manage' + ing form
examples: I finally managed to open the stuck window.
How did you manage to finish so early?

manage.definition: to succeed in dealing with problems or living in a difficult situation
manage.note: typical: manage without, manage with, manage somehow NOT for: running an organisation
examples: We didn't have proper tools, but we managed somehow.
How do you manage without a car?

manage.definition: to use time, money or other resources sensibly and without waste
manage.note: typical: manage your time, money, resources, stress, budget NOT for: spending carelessly
examples: You need to learn to manage your time better.
A budget helps families manage their money.

manage.definition: to have just enough money to pay for the things you need to live
manage.note: typical: manage on a small income, just about manage, manage on $75 a week NOT for: living comfortably or saving money
examples: It will be tight, but I think we'll manage on one salary.
Many students manage on very little money.

manage.definition: to be able to do something or carry something without help (spoken)
manage.note: typical: can you manage?, manage a suitcase, manage on your own NOT for: tasks that clearly need more than one person
examples: Can you manage that heavy bag?
Thank you, but I can manage on my own.

manage.definition: to succeed in keeping something neat, organised or under control
manage.note: typical: manage a garden, house, large property alone NOT for: running a business
examples: He'll never manage such a big garden alone.
She finds it hard to manage a house this size.

manage.definition: to control the behaviour of a person or animal
manage.note: typical: manage a child, class, patient, horse, difficult person NOT for: controlling a machine or a company
examples: The teacher found it hard to manage such a noisy class.
Some dogs are difficult to manage on a lead.

matter.definition: to count as important to someone, or to make a difference to what happens
matter.note: typical: it doesn't matter, matter to sb, matter a great deal, what matters is NOT for: the noun meaning a subject or problem; progressive forms
examples: It does not matter what you wear as long as you look neat.
Money was the only thing that mattered to him.

measure.definition: to find the size, length, amount or speed of something using standard units
measure.note: typical: measure length, rainfall, temperature, a room, sb for clothes NOT for: guessing a size without checking
examples: The tailor measured him for a new suit.
Scientists measured the rainfall over three months.

measure.definition: to judge the importance, value or true nature of something
measure.note: typical: measure success, effectiveness, progress, performance, by sth NOT for: calculating exact numbers
examples: It is too early to measure the effect of the new law.
Success should not be measured only by exam results.

measure.definition: to be a particular size, length or amount (linking verb)
measure.note: typical: measure 6 x 6 metres, measure 6.5 on the Richter scale NOT for: passive use or use with a continuous tense
examples: The room measures four metres by five.
The earthquake measured 6.5 on the Richter scale.

monitor.definition: to keep watching and checking something over time in order to follow how it develops
monitor.note: typical: monitor progress, a patient, the situation, temperature, levels NOT for: watching something once or briefly
examples: Doctors will monitor your blood pressure for a week.
The government is monitoring the situation closely.

monitor.definition: to listen in secretly to private calls or foreign broadcasts
monitor.note: typical: monitor calls, emails, broadcasts, communications NOT for: openly listening to a conversation
examples: He suspected that his phone calls were being monitored.
Officials monitored foreign radio broadcasts every day.

motivate.definition: to be what causes a person to act in a certain way
motivate.note: typical: be motivated by money, greed, fear, a desire for sth NOT for: forcing someone to act against their will
examples: Was he motivated only by a desire for power?
Nobody knows what motivated her to leave her job.

motivate.definition: to make someone want to achieve something and be willing to work hard to do it
motivate.note: typical: motivate students, staff, employees, a team, sb to do sth NOT for: ordering or forcing people to work
examples: A good teacher knows how to motivate her students.
The bonus scheme is designed to motivate staff to work harder.

mount.definition: to plan, organise and begin an event or a course of action
mount.note: typical: mount a campaign, challenge, exhibition, attack, search, rescue NOT for: small personal plans
examples: The museum is mounting an exhibition of Danish painting.
Rebels mounted an attack on the city at dawn.

mount.definition: to increase gradually in amount or degree, usually in the progressive
mount.note: typical: tension, pressure, costs, evidence, losses are mounting NOT for: sudden or one-time increases
examples: Tension is mounting as we wait for the final result.
Debts continued to mount through the winter.

mount.definition: to get on a horse or bicycle (formal)
mount.note: typical: mount a horse, bike, bicycle, platform NOT for: getting into a car or onto a bus
examples: She mounted her horse and rode away.
The rider mounted slowly and took the reins.

mount.definition: to go up steps, stairs or a similar raised surface (formal)
mount.note: typical: mount the stairs, steps, pavement, platform NOT for: climbing a mountain or a wall
examples: He mounted the steps and knocked on the door.
The car suddenly mounted the pavement.

mount.definition: to fix a picture, photograph or object onto a backing or support so that it looks better or can be used
mount.note: typical: mount a picture, photo, display, gem, camera on/onto sth NOT for: hanging a picture on a nail
examples: Please mount your photographs on white card.
The camera is mounted on a tripod.

narrow.definition: to make something narrower, or to become narrower
narrow.note: typical: narrow your eyes, a road, river, path, gap narrows NOT for: making something shorter in length
examples: He narrowed his eyes and looked at the sign.
The path narrows near the top of the hill.

narrow.definition: if a range, difference or gap narrows, or if something narrows it, it becomes smaller
narrow.note: typical: narrow a gap, lead, choice, range, field, margin NOT for: physical width
examples: The gap between rich and poor has started to narrow.
Choices narrowed once the deadline passed.

negotiate.definition: to discuss something with other people in order to reach an agreement, especially in business or politics
negotiate.note: typical: negotiate a deal, contract, peace, price, salary, with sb NOT for: arguing without trying to agree
examples: Union leaders negotiated a shorter working week.
The government refused to negotiate with the group.

negotiate.definition: to succeed in getting past or over a difficult place on a road, path or similar route
negotiate.note: typical: negotiate a bend, corner, obstacle, slope, rapids NOT for: agreeing something in talks
examples: The driver carefully negotiated the narrow bend.
The climbers negotiated a steep icy slope.

object.definition: to say or feel that you are against something or do not accept it
object.note: typical: object to sth, object to doing sth, if nobody objects NOT for: the noun 'object'; mild disliking without saying anything
examples: Several residents objected to the new road.
I don't object to working late once in a while.

object.definition: to state a fact or opinion as a reason for opposing something
object.note: typical: object that..., the lawyer objected, 'No,' she objected NOT for: simple agreement or neutral comment
examples: The group objected that the policy would harm patients.
'That is not fair,' the child objected.

observe.note: typical: observe a change, drop, difference, pattern, behaviour NOT for: using it in the progressive tense
examples: Scientists have observed a drop in ozone levels.
Visitors may observe the animals from a safe distance.

observe.definition: to watch someone or something carefully, especially in order to learn something
observe.note: typical: observe a patient, class, experiment, wildlife, behaviour NOT for: glancing at something quickly
examples: The students observed a lesson taught by an experienced teacher.
Researchers observed the birds for several weeks.

observe.definition: to say or write what you have noticed about a situation (formal)
observe.note: typical: observe that..., as sb observed, 'Sid looks ill,' he observed NOT for: ordering or instructing someone
examples: 'He looks tired,' she observed.
The writer observed that humans fall into two groups.

observe.definition: to do what you are supposed to do according to a law or agreement
observe.note: typical: observe a law, rule, ceasefire, regulation, speed limit NOT for: breaking or ignoring rules
examples: Both sides have observed the ceasefire so far.
All drivers must observe the speed limit.

observe.definition: to do things and obey rules that are part of a religion, custom or special day
observe.note: typical: observe a holiday, custom, tradition, fast, silence, Sabbath NOT for: simply attending a ceremony as a guest
examples: Many families observe the tradition of lighting candles.
Muslims observe a fast during Ramadan.

obtain.definition: to get something that you want, especially through your own effort, skill or work (formal)
obtain.note: typical: obtain permission, information, a visa, a licence, results, evidence NOT for: everyday situations where 'get' sounds more natural
examples: You must obtain permission from the principal.
Further information can be obtained from head office.

obtain.definition: if a situation, system or rule obtains, it continues to exist (formal)
obtain.note: typical: conditions, rules, practices no longer obtain NOT for: the sense of getting something; progressive forms
examples: These conditions no longer obtain in most countries.
The same rules still obtain in the old system.

occupy.definition: to have a place as your home or base and use it
occupy.note: typical: occupy a house, flat, room, building, property NOT for: briefly visiting a place
examples: The family has occupied the house for ten years.
The building was bought and occupied by new owners.

occupy.definition: to keep a person busy or take up their time
occupy.note: typical: occupy your time, yourself, sb with (doing) sth NOT for: describing a short or simple task
examples: Football occupies most of his free time.
She kept the children occupied with puzzles.

occupy.definition: to fill a particular amount of space
occupy.note: typical: occupy space, a wall, an area, the whole room NOT for: more casual speech where 'take up' is normal
examples: The new desk occupies almost the whole room.
Family photos occupied an entire wall.

occupy.definition: to enter a place with a large group and take control of it, especially by force
occupy.note: typical: occupy a country, city, building, university, an occupying army NOT for: people visiting a place peacefully
examples: Soldiers occupied the capital within a week.
Students occupied the university building overnight.

occupy.definition: if something occupies your mind, thoughts or attention, you think about it more than anything else
occupy.note: typical: occupy sb's mind, thoughts, attention NOT for: physical space
examples: Work will occupy your mind and help you forget him.
The problem occupied her thoughts for days.

occupy.definition: to use something such as a room, seat or bed
occupy.note: typical: occupy a seat, bed, room, hospital bed, table NOT for: temporarily passing through
examples: Many patients occupying hospital beds could go home.
The seat was already occupied.

occupy.definition: to have an official position or job
occupy.note: typical: occupy a post, position, office, role NOT for: simply doing a job without a formal title
examples: He occupied several important government posts.
She has occupied the position of director since 2019.

occur.definition: to take place or come about, especially in a formal or written style
occur.note: typical: occur suddenly, accidentally, at night, an accident, explosion, event occurs NOT for: everyday speech where 'happen' is more natural; plans or arranged events
examples: The explosion occurred shortly after midnight.
Most accidents occur in the home.

occur.definition: to be found or to exist in a particular place or among a particular group
occur.note: typical: occur in, among, naturally, mainly, frequently, rates occur NOT for: single events happening once
examples: The disease occurs mainly in young children.
This rare plant occurs only on a few islands.

offend.definition: to make someone feel angry, hurt or insulted by what you say or do
offend.note: typical: offend sb, deeply offend, be offended by, not to offend NOT for: causing physical harm
examples: His careless joke offended several guests.
I hope my question didn't offend you.

offend.definition: to seem wrong, ugly or unacceptable to someone
offend.note: typical: offend the eye, offend sb's sense of, offend taste NOT for: describing something merely boring or ordinary
examples: The new tower block offends the eye.
Some scenes in the film may offend viewers.

offend.definition: to commit a crime or crimes (formal)
offend.note: typical: offend again, likely to offend, young people offend NOT for: single breaking of a minor rule at school
examples: Many of the prisoners are likely to offend again.
He first offended at the age of fifteen.

offend.definition: to go against people's ideas of what is morally acceptable (formal)
offend.note: typical: offend against decency, good taste, morality NOT for: upsetting one particular person
examples: The advert offends against basic standards of decency.
Broadcasters must not offend against good taste.

operate.definition: to use and control a machine or equipment, or (of a machine) to work in a particular way
operate.note: typical: operate a machine, crane, computer, vehicle; equipment operates safely NOT for: repairing or building a machine
examples: Only trained staff may operate the crane.
The system operates at very low temperatures.

operate.definition: to work in a particular place or way (of a business or organisation), or to run a business or organisation
operate.note: typical: a company operates in, from, a country; operate a hospital, business, service NOT for: starting a business for the first time
examples: The firm operates from a small office in Brno.
The charity operates a free medical clinic.

operate.definition: to work properly (of a system, service or process), or to run such a system or service
operate.note: typical: a system, service, scheme operates; operate a bus service, rule NOT for: switching a machine on
examples: The tax system now operates more efficiently.
The company operates a night bus service.

operate.definition: to cut into a person's body in order to repair or remove a damaged part
operate.note: typical: operate on sb/sth, surgeons operate, operate on a knee NOT for: operating a body part directly; use 'operate on' not 'operate' + object
examples: Surgeons will operate on her knee tomorrow.
Doctors had to operate immediately to remove the bullet.

operate.definition: to do your job or try to achieve things in a particular way or under particular conditions
operate.note: typical: operate independently, effectively, in difficult conditions, alone NOT for: working a machine
examples: Some people cannot operate in noisy offices.
The team prefers to operate independently.

operate.definition: to be active or working in a particular area (of soldiers, police or similar groups)
operate.note: typical: troops, patrols, submarines, gangs operate in an area NOT for: ordinary shops or companies
examples: Security patrols operate in the most dangerous districts.
Enemy submarines were operating in the area.

operate.definition: to have a particular purpose or function
operate.note: typical: operate as a filter, guide, barrier, warning NOT for: being a person's job title
examples: The foam operates as an effective filter.
The manual is designed to operate as a guide for owners.

operate.definition: to have an effect on something
operate.note: typical: forces, laws, factors operating on, in sth NOT for: people doing an action on purpose
examples: Different pressures operate on each species.
Several social factors operate in this situation.

oppose.definition: to disagree with a plan or idea and try to stop it from happening or succeeding
oppose.note: typical: oppose a plan, proposal, law, change, war, strongly oppose NOT for: simple dislike without taking action
examples: Local people strongly oppose the new motorway.
Several senators opposed the bill.

oppose.definition: to compete or fight against a person or group in a battle, contest or election
oppose.note: typical: be opposed by a candidate, rival, army, team NOT for: agreeing with a plan
examples: She is opposed by two other candidates in the election.
The army opposed the invaders at the border.

outline.definition: to describe something in a general way, giving the main points but not the details
outline.note: typical: outline a plan, proposal, idea, policy, case NOT for: giving a full detailed explanation
examples: The manager outlined her plans for next year.
He briefly outlined the main arguments.

outline.definition: to show or draw the edge of something so that its shape is clear (usually passive)
outline.note: typical: outlined in red, outlined against the sky NOT for: filling in an area with colour
examples: The mountains were outlined against the evening sky.
Our land is outlined in red on the map.

overtake.definition: to pass a moving vehicle or person because you are going faster and want to get in front
overtake.note: typical: overtake a car, lorry, runner, on a bend, overtake on the left NOT for: arriving somewhere earlier by a different route
examples: He pulled out to overtake the lorry.
Never try to overtake on a bend.

overtake.definition: to become more successful, advanced or important than someone or something else
overtake.note: typical: overtake a rival, competitor, country, in sales, rankings NOT for: simply being faster in a race
examples: Television soon overtook cinema as the main form of entertainment.
China may overtake the US as the largest economy.

overtake.definition: if something bad, especially a strong feeling, overtakes you, it happens suddenly and affects you strongly
overtake.note: typical: be overtaken by emotion, panic, sleep, fear NOT for: pleasant or gradual feelings
examples: She was overtaken by a wave of emotion and began to cry.
A sudden feeling of panic overtook him.

owe.definition: to have to pay money back to someone, or to be in debt to them
owe.note: typical: owe money, rent, tax, sb £50, owe a bank NOT for: giving someone a gift or paying immediately
examples: I owe my brother twenty pounds.
The company owes millions to its suppliers.

owe.definition: to be in a position where someone has done you a favour so that you should help them in return
owe.note: typical: owe sb a favour, owe sb one, he owes me NOT for: owing money
examples: Joe owes me a favour after I helped him move.
I owe you one for taking my shift.

owe.definition: to feel that you should give someone an explanation or say sorry
owe.note: typical: owe sb an explanation, an apology, an answer NOT for: money or physical objects
examples: You owe her an apology for what you said.
The minister owes the public an explanation.

owe.definition: to have something or achieve something because of what someone else has done, or to know that their help was important to you
owe.note: typical: owe sth to sb, owe sb a lot, owe your life to sb, owe a debt of gratitude NOT for: debts of money
examples: He probably owes his life to her quick action.
I owe my parents a great deal.

owe.definition: to be successful or exist because of the influence or effect of something or someone
owe.note: typical: success owes much, more to sth than to sth else NOT for: causing something harmful
examples: Their success owes more to luck than to planning.
The design owes much to older buildings in the region.

owe.definition: to feel you should do something for someone because they have helped or supported you
owe.note: typical: owe it to sb to do sth, owe it to your team, supporters NOT for: paying a debt
examples: You owe it to your supporters not to give up.
We owe it to our parents to work hard.

owe.definition: to have a duty of loyalty or obedience to someone
owe.note: typical: owe loyalty, allegiance, duty, obedience to sb NOT for: friendly feelings or ordinary thanks
examples: The provinces owed allegiance to the Emperor.
Soldiers owe loyalty to their commander.

participate.definition: to take part in an activity together with other people (formal)
participate.note: typical: participate in a discussion, competition, activity, programme, fully, actively NOT for: only watching an event; everyday speech where 'take part' sounds more natural
examples: Everyone in the class is expected to participate in the discussion.
Over fifty schools participated in the competition.

perform.definition: to entertain an audience by acting, singing, playing music or dancing
perform.note: typical: perform a play, concert, song, dance, on stage NOT for: saying what part an actor pretends to be (use 'play')
examples: The band will perform at the festival on Saturday.
The children perform two plays every year.

perform.definition: to do a piece of work, task or duty, especially something difficult or useful
perform.note: typical: perform a task, duty, operation, experiment, function, ceremony NOT for: everyday small actions like washing or walking
examples: Surgeons performed an emergency operation last night.
The software performs several useful functions.

perform.definition: to work or achieve results in a particular way (of a person, machine, team or economy)
perform.note: typical: perform well, badly, poorly, under pressure, the economy performs NOT for: entertaining an audience
examples: The new car performs well on wet roads.
Students perform better when they feel relaxed.

permit.definition: to allow something to happen, especially by an official decision, rule or law (formal)
permit.note: typical: permit sb to do sth, be permitted, not permitted, smoking permitted NOT for: everyday permission where 'let' or 'allow' sounds more natural
examples: Smoking is permitted only in the lounge.
Pupils are not permitted to use phones in class.

permit.definition: to make it possible for something to happen
permit.note: typical: permit a view, access, growth; weather permitting; if time permits NOT for: giving formal permission
examples: The large windows permit a clear view of the lake.
We will have a picnic, weather permitting.

persuade.definition: to make someone decide to do something, especially by giving reasons or asking many times
persuade.note: typical: persuade sb to do sth, persuade sb into doing sth, easily persuaded NOT for: forcing someone to act
examples: I finally persuaded her to come to the party.
Don't let them persuade you into buying it.

persuade.definition: to make someone believe something or feel sure about it
persuade.note: typical: persuade sb that..., persuade sb of sth, not persuaded NOT for: ordering someone to do something
examples: She could not persuade the jury of his innocence.
I am not persuaded by these arguments.

pose.definition: to be or create something that may cause a problem, danger or difficulty
pose.note: typical: pose a threat, danger, risk, problem, challenge, question NOT for: asking someone politely for something
examples: The chemical poses no real danger to people.
Rising prices pose a serious problem for families.

pose.definition: to sit or stand in a particular position in order to be photographed or painted
pose.note: typical: pose for a photograph, picture, portrait, camera NOT for: moving naturally while being filmed
examples: The whole family posed for a photograph.
She posed for the painter for months.

pose.definition: to ask a question, especially one that needs careful thought
pose.note: typical: pose a question, problem, dilemma NOT for: asking simple everyday questions
examples: In her book she poses the question of how much we really need.
The report poses several difficult questions.

pose.definition: to pretend to be someone else in order to deceive people
pose.note: typical: pose as a doctor, police officer, journalist, customer NOT for: acting in a play or film
examples: He was caught posing as a lawyer.
Two thieves posed as electricians to get inside.

pose.definition: to dress or behave in a way that is meant to impress people with your wealth or style
pose.note: typical: pose in expensive clothes, in front of people, showing off NOT for: being photographed
examples: He liked to pose in front of his friends with his new car.
Some of the visitors were just posing in designer clothes.

position.definition: to carefully put something in a particular place or position
position.note: typical: position yourself, position the cursor, microphone, camera, troops NOT for: throwing or dropping things carelessly
examples: Position the microphone close to your mouth.
I positioned myself near the door.

position.definition: to be in a situation where you can do something successfully (usually be well positioned)
position.note: typical: be well, ideally, perfectly positioned to do sth NOT for: describing physical location only
examples: We are ideally positioned to benefit from growing demand.
The company is well positioned to compete abroad.

possess.definition: to have a particular quality or ability (formal)
possess.note: typical: possess skill, talent, power, courage, qualities NOT for: everyday speech where 'have' is normal; progressive forms
examples: Different workers possess different skills.
He no longer possessed the strength to argue.

possess.definition: to have or own something (formal or legal)
possess.note: typical: possess a weapon, drugs, licence, property, illegally NOT for: borrowing or renting something; progressive forms
examples: Neither of them possessed a credit card.
He was found guilty of possessing illegal drugs.

possess.definition: if a strong feeling possesses you, it suddenly takes hold of you and affects how you behave (literary)
possess.note: typical: a rage, fear, madness, passion possessed her NOT for: ordinary feelings in everyday speech
examples: A mad rage possessed him and he threw the chair.
Fear suddenly possessed the crowd.

predict.definition: to say that something will happen in the future, before it happens
predict.note: typical: predict the weather, result, future, outcome, that..., be predicted to do sth NOT for: stating something that has already happened
examples: Newspapers predicted that the champion would win again.
Nobody can predict what the effects will be.

present.definition: to give something to someone, especially at a formal or official occasion
present.note: typical: present sb with sth, present an award, prize, cheque, gift NOT for: giving a casual gift to a friend
examples: The mayor presented the winners with their medals.
She was presented with a bunch of flowers.

present.definition: to cause something to happen or exist, especially a problem or an opportunity
present.note: typical: present a problem, difficulty, challenge, opportunity, risk NOT for: showing or describing something
examples: The new rules present difficulties for small firms.
Large classes present many problems for teachers.

present.definition: to behave and speak in a particular way when you meet people
present.note: typical: present yourself well, badly, confidently NOT for: giving a speech
examples: He presents himself well at interviews.
She presents herself as a calm professional.

present.definition: to show or describe someone or something in a particular way
present.note: typical: present a picture, argument, case, evidence, sb as sth NOT for: giving a gift
examples: The film presents the hero as a brave but flawed man.
We will present the figures in a chart.

present.definition: to give a talk or offer an idea or plan so that people can consider it
present.note: typical: present a report, plan, proposal, findings, paper NOT for: sending a document in the post
examples: The manager will present the report on Friday.
The team presented its plans to the bank.

present.definition: to show an official document or ticket to someone in authority
present.note: typical: present a passport, ticket, card, identification NOT for: giving a gift
examples: You must present your passport at the border.
Passengers should present their tickets at the gate.

present.definition: to introduce and host a television or radio programme (British English)
present.note: typical: present a show, programme, news, radio, documentary NOT for: acting in a drama
examples: She presents the evening news on television.
He has presented a radio show for ten years.

present.definition: to show an illness by having particular symptoms (medical)
present.note: typical: present with fever, symptoms, pain, a rash NOT for: describing a symptom in everyday talk
examples: Three patients presented with fever and headaches.
The child presented with a high temperature.

present.definition: if an opportunity or situation presents itself, it suddenly happens or becomes available
present.note: typical: opportunity, chance, problem presents itself NOT for: people introducing themselves
examples: I'll tell her when the opportunity presents itself.
A chance to travel presented itself unexpectedly.

preserve.definition: to protect something or someone from being harmed or destroyed
preserve.note: typical: preserve woodland, buildings, wildlife, the environment, a monument NOT for: causing damage
examples: We must preserve our old woodlands.
The society works to preserve historic buildings.

preserve.definition: to make something continue without changing
preserve.note: typical: preserve peace, order, freedom, the status quo, a way of life NOT for: starting something new
examples: Her main task was to preserve peace in the region.
They tried to preserve a normal family life.

preserve.definition: to treat food so that it can be stored for a long time without going bad
preserve.note: typical: preserve fruit, fish, meat, vegetables, in brine, in oil NOT for: simply storing food in a fridge
examples: Olives are often preserved in salt water.
She preserved the plums as jam.

prevent.definition: to stop something from happening, or to stop someone from doing something
prevent.note: typical: prevent accidents, disease, crime; prevent sb from doing sth NOT for: delaying something only for a short time
examples: Regular exercise helps prevent heart disease.
A back injury prevented him from playing.

proceed.definition: to continue with something that has been planned or already started (formal)
proceed.note: typical: proceed with a plan, election, project, work, further NOT for: everyday speech where 'go ahead' is more natural
examples: The council decided to proceed with the building work.
Before proceeding further, let us define our terms.

proceed.note: typical: work, talks, matters, proceedings proceed according to plan NOT for: people travelling somewhere
examples: Work is proceeding according to plan.
The talks proceeded without problems.

proceed.definition: to do something next, after having done something else, sometimes showing surprise or annoyance
proceed.note: typical: proceed to do sth, proceed to explain, take, ruin NOT for: starting something for the first time
examples: He took off his coat and proceeded to clean the table.
She then proceeded to tell everyone my secret.

proceed.definition: to move or travel in a particular direction (formal)
proceed.note: typical: proceed to the gate, towards, along, north NOT for: continuing with a plan
examples: Passengers should proceed to gate twenty-five.
The convoy proceeded along the coast road.

produce.definition: to cause a particular result or effect
produce.note: typical: produce a result, effect, change, reaction, improvement NOT for: making a physical object
examples: The new drug produced remarkable results.
Her speech produced a strong reaction.

produce.definition: to make something to be sold, used or enjoyed by people
produce.note: typical: produce goods, cars, a meal, a report, food, a record NOT for: causing a natural effect
examples: The factory produces a hundred cars an hour.
How did you produce a meal so quickly?

produce.definition: to grow something or make it naturally
produce.note: typical: produce fruit, milk, oxygen, wine, crops, plants produce NOT for: factory manufacturing
examples: This region produces the grapes used for champagne.
Plants produce oxygen in sunlight.

produce.definition: to bring out an object or show something so that people can see or consider it
produce.note: typical: produce a gun, ticket, passport, evidence, proof, document NOT for: making something new
examples: He produced a gun and demanded the money.
They could not produce any evidence.

produce.definition: to organise the money and control the making of a film, play or similar show
produce.note: typical: produce a film, play, programme, album, show NOT for: directing the actors
examples: She produced three successful films.
The BBC will produce the new series.

produce.definition: to give birth to a baby or to young animals
produce.note: typical: produce kittens, young, offspring, a litter, a child NOT for: laying eggs or growing plants
examples: An adult cat may produce kittens three times a year.
The mare produced a healthy foal.

progress.definition: to improve or develop so that you reach a more advanced stage
progress.note: typical: progress well, steadily, to a higher level, through the stages, beyond NOT for: moving a vehicle forward
examples: Her English is progressing well.
He progressed from trainee to manager in five years.

progress.definition: to continue (of work or a project), or to make a project continue
progress.note: typical: work, talks, investigation progress; progress the plan NOT for: finishing something completely
examples: Work on the bridge is progressing quickly.
We hope to progress the project next week.

progress.definition: to pass (of time) or to develop as an event continues
progress.note: typical: as the evening, meeting, game, year progresses NOT for: improving in quality
examples: As the evening progressed, the room got noisier.
The film becomes darker as it progresses.

progress.note: typical: progress slowly, along the road, towards the exit, traffic progresses NOT for: improving or developing
examples: The queue progressed very slowly.
The convoy progressed along the valley.

promote.definition: to help something to develop or increase
promote.note: typical: promote trade, growth, health, peace, understanding, equality NOT for: advertising a product
examples: The government wants to promote economic growth.
Regular exercise promotes good health.

promote.definition: to give someone a better and more responsible job (usually passive)
promote.note: typical: be promoted to manager, director, captain, sergeant NOT for: moving someone to a different office at the same level
examples: She was promoted to head of department.
He was promoted after only a year.

promote.definition: to advertise or publicly support a product, film, event or similar thing in order to sell it
promote.note: typical: promote a book, film, album, product, brand, tour NOT for: making a product
examples: The actor is visiting Paris to promote her new film.
The company promotes its products on social media.

promote.definition: to move a sports team up to a higher group or league (British English, usually passive)
promote.note: typical: be promoted to the Premier League, First Division, next season NOT for: giving a player a new job
examples: The club was promoted to the top division.
They hope to be promoted next season.

promote.definition: to try to persuade people to support or use something
promote.note: typical: promote an idea, policy, cause, use of, healthy eating NOT for: selling goods
examples: The campaign promotes the use of public transport.
He promoted the idea of a four-day working week.

promote.definition: to organise and be responsible for a large public event such as a concert or a match
promote.note: typical: promote a concert, boxing match, festival, fight NOT for: advertising an everyday product
examples: He promoted several big concerts in the city.
The company promotes boxing events across Europe.

propose.definition: to suggest something as a plan or course of action (formal)
propose.note: typical: propose a plan, change, solution, that..., propose doing sth NOT for: giving someone a present; do not say 'propose someone something'
examples: She proposed a compromise to end the dispute.
The report proposes building a new bridge.

propose.definition: to intend or plan to do something (formal)
propose.note: typical: propose to do sth, what do you propose to do NOT for: suggesting something to other people
examples: I propose to leave early tomorrow.
What do you propose to do about the noise?

propose.definition: to ask someone to marry you
propose.note: typical: propose to sb, propose marriage, on one knee NOT for: suggesting a business plan
examples: He proposed to her on the beach.
She was surprised when he proposed.

protest.definition: to take part in a public event or action to show disapproval of or opposition to something
protest.note: typical: protest against, about, at a decision, law, plan, outside a building NOT for: complaining quietly to one person
examples: Thousands of students protested against the new law.
Workers protested outside the factory gates.

protest.definition: to say strongly that you disagree with something or are angry about it because it seems wrong or unfair
protest.note: typical: protest that..., 'No!' she protested, protest loudly, strongly NOT for: marching in the street
examples: 'That's not fair!' he protested.
She protested that she had not been given enough time.

protest.definition: to state very firmly that something is true when other people do not believe you
protest.note: typical: protest your innocence, protest that she was not, still protesting NOT for: simply stating a fact in a calm way
examples: He still protests his innocence.
Maria protested that she had never met the man.

prove.definition: to show that something is true by giving facts or evidence
prove.note: typical: prove a point, theory, guilt, innocence, prove sb wrong, prove that... NOT for: testing something to see if it works
examples: The tests proved that the method works.
She wanted to prove them all wrong.

prove.definition: to turn out to be difficult, useful, a problem or similar (linking verb)
prove.note: typical: prove difficult, useful, popular, costly, prove to be a mistake NOT for: showing a fact with evidence
examples: The task proved harder than we expected.
The new system proved to be a great success.

prove.definition: to show how good or capable you are at doing something
prove.note: typical: prove yourself, prove yourself in a new job, to your boss NOT for: showing that a fact is true
examples: The young player is eager to prove himself.
When I started the job, I felt I had to prove myself.

prove.definition: to show other people that you are a particular type of person
prove.note: typical: prove yourself (to be) a leader, reliable, brave, a good teacher NOT for: showing a fact is true
examples: She proved herself to be a reliable colleague.
He has proved himself a talented writer.

provide.definition: to give something to someone or make it available because they need or want it
provide.note: typical: provide food, help, a service, information, provide sb with sth, provide sth for sb NOT for: do not say 'provide someone something'
examples: The hotel provides free breakfast for guests.
The school provides pupils with books.

provide.definition: to produce or supply something useful as a result
provide.note: typical: provide an answer, explanation, evidence, clue, opportunity NOT for: giving food or equipment
examples: The search provided the police with several clues.
The report provides an explanation for the delay.

provide.definition: to state in a law, rule or agreement that something must happen (formal)
provide.note: typical: the law, contract, rule, treaty provides that... NOT for: giving help to a person
examples: The contract provides that payment must be made in thirty days.
The law provides that all workers must have a break.

publish.definition: to arrange for a book, magazine or similar work to be written, printed and sold
publish.note: typical: publish a book, novel, dictionary, magazine, first published in NOT for: only printing copies for yourself
examples: The novel was first published in 1998.
The company publishes school textbooks.

publish.definition: to print a letter, article or similar piece in a newspaper or magazine
publish.note: typical: publish a letter, article, photograph, story, poem NOT for: writing a private letter
examples: The newspaper published her letter on Monday.
They published a photo of the winners.

publish.definition: to make official information such as a report available for everyone to read
publish.note: typical: publish a report, figures, results, findings, list, guidelines NOT for: keeping information secret
examples: The government will publish the figures tomorrow.
The committee published its findings online.

publish.definition: to have your own written or musical work printed and sold
publish.note: typical: publish a paper, a novel, an article, publish regularly NOT for: reading someone else's work
examples: University staff are expected to publish regularly.
She published her first poems at nineteen.

purchase.note: typical: purchase a ticket, house, car, goods, online, in advance NOT for: everyday speech where 'buy' sounds more natural
examples: You can purchase tickets online in advance.
The company purchased the land for development.

pursue.definition: to continue doing an activity or trying to achieve something over a long period
pursue.note: typical: pursue a career, goal, aim, interest, policy, studies, dream NOT for: physically chasing someone
examples: She plans to pursue a career in medicine.
The company pursues a policy of low prices.

pursue.definition: to continue trying to find out about or discuss a subject
pursue.note: typical: pursue the matter, question, argument, claim, enquiry further NOT for: starting a new subject
examples: The reporter did not dare to pursue the matter further.
The police will pursue the enquiry.

pursue.definition: to chase or follow someone or something in order to catch or attack them
pursue.note: typical: pursue a suspect, criminal, car, enemy, prey NOT for: long-term personal goals
examples: Two officers pursued the thief across the field.
The lion pursued the zebra.

pursue.definition: to keep trying to persuade someone to have a romantic relationship with you
pursue.note: typical: pursue sb, aggressively, for months NOT for: chasing a criminal
examples: He pursued her for months before she agreed to a date.
She felt uncomfortable when a colleague began to pursue her.

qualify.definition: to have the right to have or do something, or to give someone that right
qualify.note: typical: qualify for benefit, a loan, a discount, a place; qualify sb for sth NOT for: passing an exam
examples: Children from low-income families qualify for free meals.
Membership qualifies you for a discount.

qualify.definition: to pass an examination or finish a course of study so that you can do a particular job
qualify.note: typical: qualify as a doctor, teacher, lawyer, pilot, after qualifying NOT for: reaching a sports final
examples: She qualified as a nurse last year.
After qualifying, he worked abroad for two years.

qualify.definition: to have the necessary qualities to be considered a particular thing
qualify.note: typical: qualify as an expert, a date, a success, an emergency NOT for: passing a test
examples: That mess doesn't qualify as a tidy kitchen.
Two hours' delay hardly qualifies as a disaster.

qualify.definition: to give someone the skills or knowledge needed to do something
qualify.note: typical: qualify sb for sth, qualify sb to do sth, a certificate qualifies you to NOT for: simply having the right to a benefit
examples: This course qualifies you to work as a translator.
Her experience qualifies her for the job.

qualify.definition: to reach the necessary standard to enter or continue in a competition
qualify.note: typical: qualify for the final, World Cup, next round, team qualifies NOT for: passing an exam
examples: Our team has qualified for the final.
She qualified for the Olympics at seventeen.

qualify.definition: to add a comment or condition to a statement to make it less strong or general (formal)
qualify.note: typical: qualify a statement, claim, remark, criticism, with a few words NOT for: gaining a qualification
examples: He qualified his praise with a few criticisms.
I should qualify that statement slightly.

quote.definition: to repeat exactly what someone else has said or written
quote.note: typical: quote from a book, quote a passage, poem, be quoted as saying, quote sb on sth NOT for: summarising in your own words
examples: She quoted a line from the poem.
The minister was quoted as saying that taxes would rise.

quote.definition: to give a piece of information that is written down, usually so it can be identified
quote.note: typical: quote a number, figure, reference, code, price list NOT for: repeating someone's words
examples: Please quote your reference number in all letters.
He quoted a figure of 200 accidents a year.

quote.definition: to give something as an example to support what you are saying
quote.note: typical: quote an example, a case, a study, statistics, quote sth as sth NOT for: repeating a sentence word for word
examples: She quoted the case of a man who had lost his job.
The article quotes Sweden as a good example.

quote.definition: to tell a customer the price you will charge for a service or product
quote.note: typical: quote a price, quote sb for a job, quote £500, quote for the work NOT for: asking the price of something
examples: The builder quoted us £8,000 for the new roof.
They quoted a very low price for the repairs.

quote.definition: to give the price of a share or currency (usually passive)
quote.note: typical: be quoted at, on the stock exchange, shares, the pound is quoted NOT for: giving a price to a customer
examples: The pound was quoted at just under $1.30.
The company is quoted on the London stock exchange.

raise.definition: to move or lift something to a higher position
raise.note: typical: raise your hand, a flag, your glass, the lamp, your eyebrows NOT for: increasing a number or price
examples: Raise your hand if you know the answer.
He raised his glass and thanked everyone.

raise.definition: to increase an amount, number or level
raise.note: typical: raise prices, taxes, standards, awareness, the minimum wage NOT for: lifting an object
examples: Many shops have raised their prices.
The campaign aims to raise awareness of the disease.

raise.definition: to collect money that can be used for a particular purpose
raise.note: typical: raise money, funds, £1 million, for charity NOT for: earning a salary
examples: The students raised £2,000 for charity.
The club is trying to raise money for a new roof.

raise.definition: to improve the quality or standard of something
raise.note: typical: raise standards, the level, your game, quality NOT for: increasing a price
examples: Better training will raise standards in schools.
The team needs to raise its game.

raise.definition: to begin to talk about a subject so that it can be considered
raise.note: typical: raise a question, an issue, a point, an objection, a subject NOT for: asking a child to look after
examples: She raised the issue at the meeting.
He raised an important question about safety.

raise.definition: to cause a particular feeling or reaction
raise.note: typical: raise doubts, fears, hopes, concerns, a laugh, suspicion NOT for: lifting a physical object
examples: The results raise doubts about the study.
The story raised a few smiles.

raise.definition: to move your eyes, head or face so that you are looking up
raise.note: typical: raise your eyes, head, face, eyebrows NOT for: lifting a heavy object
examples: She raised her eyes and looked at him.
He did not raise his head from the book.

raise.definition: to move yourself into an upright position
raise.note: typical: raise yourself on one elbow, raise yourself up from the bed NOT for: lifting another person
examples: He raised himself on one elbow to watch.
She raised herself from the pillows.

raise.definition: to look after a child or young animal until it is grown up (especially American English)
raise.note: typical: raise a child, children, a family, sons, daughters, animals NOT for: building a house
examples: She raised three sons on her own.
They raised their children in a small village.

rate.definition: to think that someone or something has a particular quality, value or standard, or to be considered as having it
rate.note: typical: be rated as, rate highly, rate sb the best, rate as one of the best NOT for: measuring speed or speed limits
examples: The critics rate her as the best player in the league.
The film rates as one of his finest.

rate.definition: to think that someone or something is very good (British English, informal)
rate.note: typical: rate sb, rate sth, never rated him NOT for: giving a score in a test
examples: I never rated him as a manager.
Most of the staff really rate their new boss.

rate.definition: to deserve something (informal, especially American English)
rate.note: typical: rate a mention, a thank-you, an apology, a place NOT for: judging quality
examples: The small town did not rate a mention in the news.
They rate a big thank-you for their effort.

rate.definition: to officially judge a film as suitable for people of a particular age (usually passive)
rate.note: typical: be rated PG, 15, G, R, X, by the board NOT for: judging how good a film is
examples: The film is rated 15 in Britain.
The cartoon was rated G.

react.definition: to behave in a particular way or show a particular emotion because of something that has happened or been said
react.note: typical: react to, angrily, calmly, badly, quickly, react by doing sth NOT for: starting an action without a cause
examples: How did he react to the news?
The government reacted by banning all marches.

react.definition: to change when mixed with another chemical substance (technical)
react.note: typical: react with, chemicals, a metal, acid, oxygen NOT for: people's behaviour
examples: Sodium reacts violently with water.
Iron reacts with oxygen to form rust.

react.definition: to increase or decrease in value because of something that happens (of prices or financial markets)
react.note: typical: markets, prices, shares, the pound react to news, sharply, favourably NOT for: people showing feelings
examples: Share prices reacted sharply to the news.
The market reacted favourably to the plan.

react.definition: to become ill because a chemical, drug or food enters your body
react.note: typical: react badly to antibiotics, a drug, a food, a bite NOT for: showing feelings
examples: Some people react badly to nuts.
She reacted to the medicine and felt dizzy.

realise.definition: to know and understand something, or to begin suddenly to understand it
realise.note: typical: realise that, realise the truth, a mistake, too late, suddenly NOT for: do not say 'realise about something'
examples: I suddenly realised that I had left my keys at home.
He didn't realise how late it was.

realise.definition: to achieve something that you were hoping for (formal)
realise.note: typical: realise an ambition, a dream, your potential, a goal NOT for: understanding a fact
examples: She never realised her dream of becoming a doctor.
The young player has not yet realised her full potential.

realise.definition: to be the thing that you feared would happen (of fears, usually passive)
realise.note: typical: fears were realised, worst fears realised NOT for: hopes and good events
examples: His worst fears were realised when the results came.
The company's fears were realised when sales fell.

realise.definition: to obtain or earn an amount of money, or to turn property into money by selling it (formal)
realise.note: typical: realise a profit, a gain, assets, a sum, from a sale NOT for: spending money
examples: The sale realised a profit of £10,000.
They had to realise some assets to pay the debt.

rebuild.definition: to build something again after it has been damaged or destroyed
rebuild.note: typical: rebuild a house, bridge, town, church, city after a war, fire NOT for: repairing a small fault
examples: The church was rebuilt after the fire.
The town was rebuilt after the earthquake.

rebuild.definition: to make something strong and successful again
rebuild.note: typical: rebuild your life, confidence, the economy, a business, a team NOT for: constructing a building
examples: It took years to rebuild the economy.
She is trying to rebuild her life after the accident.

recall.definition: to remember a particular fact, event or situation from the past
recall.note: typical: recall a name, an event, what happened, recall doing sth, as I recall NOT for: asking someone to return
examples: I can't recall his name.
She doesn't recall seeing anyone there.

recall.definition: to officially tell someone to come back to a place or group
recall.note: typical: recall an ambassador, a player, troops, a worker, from a post NOT for: remembering something
examples: The ambassador was recalled to London.
The coach recalled the injured player to the squad.

recall.definition: to ask people who bought a product to return it because of a fault
recall.note: typical: recall a car, product, model, batch, because of a fault NOT for: returning an item you do not like
examples: The company recalled thousands of faulty cars.
The toys were recalled because they were unsafe.

recall.definition: to bring information back onto a computer screen
recall.note: typical: recall a file, data, a document, a record, a menu NOT for: remembering a memory
examples: You can recall the last file with a single key.
The program recalls your previous settings.

recall.definition: to make you think of something because it is very similar
recall.note: typical: recall the past, an era, a scene, the style of NOT for: remembering a fact on purpose
examples: The furniture recalls the style of the 1960s.
His voice recalls that of his father.

recall.definition: to vote to remove someone from a political position (American English)
recall.note: typical: recall a governor, a mayor, an official, recall election NOT for: asking an ambassador to return
examples: Voters tried to recall the governor.
A campaign began to recall the mayor.

recognise.definition: to know who someone is or what something is because you have seen, heard or learned about them before
recognise.note: typical: recognise a face, a voice, a name, a symptom, a song NOT for: accepting a fact as true
examples: I didn't recognise you in your uniform.
The doctor recognised the symptoms at once.

recognise.definition: to officially accept that an organisation, government or document has legal or official authority
recognise.note: typical: recognise a government, a qualification, a union, a state, as NOT for: simply knowing someone's face
examples: Many countries recognised the new government.
The qualification is recognised across Europe.

recognise.definition: to accept or admit that something is true
recognise.note: typical: recognise that, a problem, the need for, the importance of NOT for: remembering a face
examples: We must recognise that change takes time.
He recognised how little he really knew.

recognise.definition: to realise that something or someone is important or very good (usually passive)
recognise.note: typical: be recognised as, widely, internationally, a recognised expert NOT for: knowing a person by sight
examples: She is recognised as a leading expert.
His work was widely recognised by his colleagues.

recognise.definition: to officially and publicly thank someone by giving them an honour
recognise.note: typical: be recognised for, bravery, service, achievements, with an award NOT for: accepting a fact
examples: He was recognised for saving many lives.
The firm recognised her years of service.

recommend.definition: to advise someone to do something, especially because you have special knowledge
recommend.note: typical: recommend that, recommend doing sth, doctors strongly recommend, the recommended dose NOT for: do not say 'recommend someone to do something'
examples: I recommend that you see a doctor.
Experts recommend drinking more water.

recommend.definition: to say that something or someone is good, or to suggest them for a particular purpose or job
recommend.note: typical: recommend a book, restaurant, hotel, lawyer, highly recommend sth to sb NOT for: do not say 'recommend someone something'
examples: Can you recommend a good hotel?
I highly recommend this film to everyone.

recover.definition: to get better after an illness, accident or shock
recover.note: typical: recover from an illness, an operation, a shock, fully, quickly NOT for: getting an object back
examples: She is recovering from a serious operation.
He took weeks to recover from the shock.

recover.definition: to return to a normal condition after a period of trouble or difficulty
recover.note: typical: the economy, market, industry, shares, sales recover NOT for: a person's health
examples: The tourist industry is slowly recovering.
Share prices recovered after the sharp fall.

recover.definition: to get back something that was taken from you, lost or almost destroyed
recover.note: typical: recover stolen goods, a body, a car, data, from the wreckage NOT for: getting better after illness
examples: The police recovered the stolen paintings.
Divers recovered two bodies from the wreck.

recover.definition: to get back an amount of money that you have spent or lost
recover.note: typical: recover money, costs, damages, a loss, a debt NOT for: getting an object back
examples: She went to court to recover damages.
The company hopes to recover its costs next year.

recover.definition: to get back an ability, a sense or control over your feelings or movements after a period without it
recover.note: typical: recover consciousness, your balance, your sight, your composure NOT for: getting stolen goods back
examples: He recovered consciousness an hour later.
She slipped but quickly recovered her balance.

reduce.definition: to make something smaller or less in size, amount or price
reduce.note: typical: reduce costs, crime, risk, prices, speed, by half, from X to Y NOT for: making something bigger
examples: The shop reduced all its coats by thirty per cent.
New rules should reduce the risk of accidents.

reduce.definition: to boil a liquid so that there is less of it and it becomes thicker (cooking)
reduce.note: typical: reduce a sauce, stock, wine, cream, by half NOT for: lowering a price
examples: Reduce the sauce until it coats the spoon.
Let the stock reduce for ten minutes.

reduce.definition: to become thinner by losing weight (especially American English)
reduce.note: typical: reducing diet, reduce to lose weight, a reducing plan NOT for: cutting costs
examples: She went on a diet to reduce before the wedding.
Many people try to reduce in January.

refer.definition: to mention or speak about someone or something
refer.note: typical: refer to a matter, a person, as, by name, indirectly NOT for: looking at a book for information
examples: She never referred to the argument again.
He likes to be referred to as 'Doctor'.

refer.definition: to look at a book, map, note or other source for information
refer.note: typical: refer to a dictionary, notes, a map, the manual, the guidelines NOT for: talking about a person
examples: The speaker spoke without referring to his notes.
Please refer to the manual if the machine stops.

refer.definition: to be about someone or something (of a statement, number or report)
refer.note: typical: refer to figures, a rule, a term, a word, the data NOT for: sending a person to someone
examples: These figures refer to sales in Europe only.
The word 'bank' can refer to a river edge.

refer.definition: to send someone or something to a person or organisation to be helped or dealt with
refer.note: typical: refer a patient, a case, a complaint, a problem to a specialist, a court NOT for: mentioning a person in conversation
examples: My doctor referred me to a heart specialist.
The complaint was referred to the manager.

refer.definition: to tell someone where to find information (formal)
refer.note: typical: readers are referred to, refer sb to a page, a chapter, a website NOT for: mentioning a topic
examples: Readers are referred to chapter five for details.
The note refers students to the library website.

reflect.definition: to show an image of a person or thing on a surface such as a mirror, glass or water (usually passive)
reflect.note: typical: be reflected in a mirror, window, water, the lake, glass NOT for: showing a feeling or situation
examples: Her face was reflected in the window.
The mountains were reflected in the still lake.

reflect.definition: to show or be a sign of a situation or feeling
reflect.note: typical: reflect concern, a change, the mood, opinion, be reflected in NOT for: thinking carefully
examples: The fall in sales reflects the weak economy.
Her paintings reflect her love of nature.

reflect.definition: to send back light, heat or sound from a surface
reflect.note: typical: reflect light, heat, sound, off a surface, white walls NOT for: showing a mood
examples: White roofs reflect the heat of the sun.
The sound reflected off the walls of the hall.

reflect.definition: to think carefully about something, or to say something you have been thinking about
reflect.note: typical: reflect on your life, a decision, the past, reflect that... NOT for: showing an image
examples: He sat quietly and reflected on the past year.
She reflected that she had never been so happy.

regard.definition: to think about someone or something in a particular way (not in the progressive)
regard.note: typical: regard sb/sth as, highly regarded, widely regarded as, regard with suspicion NOT for: looking at something physically
examples: Many people regard him as the best player ever.
The school is highly regarded in the region.

regard.definition: to look at someone or something in a particular way (formal)
regard.note: typical: regard sb coldly, calmly, thoughtfully, with curiosity NOT for: having an opinion of something
examples: She regarded him coldly across the table.
The old man regarded the stranger with curiosity.

register.definition: to put a name or fact on an official list or record
register.note: typical: register for a course, with a doctor, a birth, a car, a company NOT for: noticing something
examples: You must register with a doctor when you move here.
The baby's birth was registered yesterday.

register.definition: to officially state your opinion so that it is known (formal)
register.note: typical: register a protest, a complaint, an objection, your disapproval NOT for: signing up for a course
examples: The delegation registered a formal protest.
She registered her disapproval by leaving the room.

register.definition: to notice or realise something and remember it; or (of facts) to be noticed
register.note: typical: it didn't register, register a presence, a name, a detail NOT for: showing a number on a machine
examples: She told me her name, but it didn't register.
He did not register the change at first.

register.definition: to show an amount (of a machine or instrument)
register.note: typical: the thermometer, scale, earthquake registered NOT for: signing up for something
examples: The thermometer registered 38 degrees.
The earthquake registered 6.5 on the scale.

register.definition: to show or express a feeling (formal)
register.note: typical: her face, his eyes registered shock, surprise, anger, disbelief NOT for: noticing facts
examples: His face registered surprise.
Her expression registered deep disappointment.

register.definition: to send a parcel or letter by registered post (British English)
register.note: typical: register a parcel, letter, package, at the post office NOT for: signing up for a course
examples: I registered the parcel at the post office.
Did you register the letter?

reject.definition: to refuse to accept, believe in or agree with something
