reject.note: typical: reject an offer, a proposal, an idea, a claim, flatly, outright NOT for: choosing someone for a job
examples: She rejected his offer of help.
The committee rejected the proposal.

reject.definition: to not choose someone for a job, a course of study or similar place
reject.note: typical: reject an application, a candidate, an applicant, be rejected by NOT for: refusing an idea
examples: His application was rejected.
The university rejected her without an interview.

reject.definition: to throw away something that has just been made because its quality is not good enough
reject.note: typical: reject a batch, a product, faulty goods, items, defective NOT for: refusing a person
examples: Inspectors rejected the whole batch.
Any bottle with a crack is rejected.

reject.definition: to refuse to give someone love or attention
reject.note: typical: feel rejected, reject a child, a partner, a friend NOT for: refusing a business offer
examples: The child felt rejected by his parents.
She feared that her friends would reject her.

relate.definition: to be connected with something in some way
relate.note: typical: relate to, how the ideas relate, the charges relate to, closely related NOT for: telling a story
examples: The two ideas do not seem to relate.
These figures relate to last year's sales.

relate.definition: to show how two different things are connected
relate.note: typical: relate sth to sth, relate crime to poverty, relate cause to effect NOT for: telling a story
examples: The report tries to relate rising crime to unemployment.
Teachers should relate new ideas to what pupils already know.

relate.definition: to tell someone about events that have happened (formal)
relate.note: typical: relate a story, an event, an experience, a tale, relate sth to sb NOT for: being connected to a topic
examples: He related the whole story to the police.
She related how she had escaped.

relate.definition: to feel that you understand someone's problem or situation
relate.note: typical: relate to people, to children, to a character, I can relate to that NOT for: being connected by facts
examples: Many readers can relate to the main character.
He finds it hard to relate to his colleagues.

release.definition: to let someone go free after keeping them somewhere
release.note: typical: release a prisoner, hostage, animal, patient, from prison, hospital NOT for: making a film available
examples: The hostages were released yesterday.
The injured bird was released into the wild.

release.definition: to let news or official information be known and printed
release.note: typical: release figures, a statement, details, a report, a photo NOT for: letting someone go free
examples: The police have released the names of the victims.
The government released the new figures on Monday.

release.definition: to make a CD, film, video or game available for people to buy or see
release.note: typical: release an album, film, game, single, update, in March NOT for: publishing official news
examples: The band will release a new album in May.
The game will be released next spring.

release.definition: to stop holding something, or to let something fall
release.note: typical: release your grip, hold, a bomb, a rope, a button NOT for: freeing a person from prison
examples: He released his grip on the rope.
Planes released bombs over the city.

release.definition: to express or get rid of a feeling such as anger or worry
release.note: typical: release stress, tension, anger, emotion, frustration NOT for: letting a substance out
examples: Running helps me release stress.
She cried to release her emotions.

release.definition: to let a substance flow out
release.note: typical: release gas, oil, chemicals, heat, into the air, into the sea NOT for: letting a person go
examples: The factory released toxic gas into the air.
Oil was released into the sea.

release.definition: to allow someone not to do their duty or work, or to end their contract
release.note: typical: release sb from a contract, duties, a job; release staff NOT for: freeing a prisoner
examples: She asked to be released from her contract.
The firm released ten per cent of its staff.

release.definition: to move part of a machine so that it is no longer held or fastened in position
release.note: typical: release the brake, handbrake, catch, lever, the clutch NOT for: giving freedom to a person
examples: Release the handbrake before you drive off.
Press the lever to release the lock.

relieve.definition: to reduce someone's pain or unpleasant feelings
relieve.note: typical: relieve pain, tension, stress, anxiety, boredom, symptoms NOT for: replacing a worker
examples: The tablets relieved her headache.
A walk helped to relieve my stress.

relieve.definition: to make a problem less difficult or serious
relieve.note: typical: relieve poverty, pressure, congestion, unemployment, hardship NOT for: reducing a person's pain
examples: New roads should relieve traffic congestion.
The programme aims to relieve unemployment.

relieve.definition: to replace someone when they have finished their duty or need a rest
relieve.note: typical: relieve a guard, sentry, driver, nurse, at midnight NOT for: taking away a job as punishment
examples: The night guard will be relieved at six.
Another driver relieved him after four hours.

relieve.definition: to make something less dull and boring
relieve.note: typical: relieved by, relieve the boredom, monotony, a plain wall NOT for: reducing pain
examples: The plain wall was relieved by a bright picture.
Music helped relieve the boredom of the journey.

relieve.definition: to free a town that an enemy has surrounded (formal)
relieve.note: typical: relieve a town, city, fort, garrison, besieged NOT for: giving a rest to a worker
examples: Troops arrived to relieve the besieged town.
The army tried to relieve the fort.

rely.definition: to trust or depend on someone or something to do what you need or expect
rely.note: typical: rely on sb, rely on sth to do sth, rely on for NOT for: simply using something once
examples: You can rely on me to be on time.
Many people rely on the internet for news.

rely.definition: to depend on something in order to continue to live or exist
rely.note: typical: rely on income, aid, a river, rely heavily on, for water NOT for: trusting a friend
examples: The company relies heavily on a few big contracts.
The village relies on the river for its water.

remark.definition: to say something, especially about something you have just noticed
remark.note: typical: remark that, remark on, upon, 'It's cold,' he remarked, remark casually NOT for: noticing something silently
examples: 'It's very quiet here,' she remarked.
He remarked on the change in the weather.

repay.definition: to pay back money that you have borrowed
repay.note: typical: repay a loan, a debt, a mortgage, money, in full, over years NOT for: thanking someone with kind actions
examples: He repaid the loan within two years.
I'll repay you the money next week.

repay.definition: to do something for someone or give them something in return for their help
repay.note: typical: repay sb for sth, repay kindness, a favour, trust, generosity NOT for: paying back borrowed money
examples: How can I ever repay you for your help?
She repaid their kindness with a gift.

repay.definition: to be worth the time or effort that you spend on it
repay.note: typical: repay the effort, study, attention, time, repay careful reading NOT for: paying a loan
examples: The book repays careful reading.
The garden repays all the work you put into it.

replace.definition: to start doing something instead of another person, or to be used instead of another thing
replace.note: typical: replace sb on the team, replace the old system, be replaced by NOT for: putting something back where it was
examples: Email has largely replaced the letter.
She replaced her sister on the team.

replace.definition: to remove someone or something and put a new person or thing there
replace.note: typical: replace a tyre, battery, part, staff, replace sth with sth NOT for: putting something back in its old place
examples: I had to replace two tyres.
They replaced the old windows with new ones.

replace.definition: to get a new one of something that was broken, lost or stolen
replace.note: typical: replace a broken glass, a lost card, a stolen phone, vase NOT for: changing something that still works
examples: I will replace the vase I broke.
You can replace a lost card online.

replace.definition: to put something back where it was before
replace.note: typical: replace the lid, the book, the receiver, on the shelf NOT for: using something new instead of the old
examples: He replaced the book on the shelf.
Please replace the cap after use.

represent.definition: to officially speak or take action for another person or group
represent.note: typical: represent a company, a country, the workers, a client, at a meeting NOT for: standing for a symbol
examples: She represents the company at conferences.
The union represents most of the workers.

represent.definition: to speak officially for someone in a court of law
represent.note: typical: represent a client, represent yourself, in court, be represented by a lawyer NOT for: speaking for a company
examples: A famous lawyer will represent him in court.
She decided to represent herself at the trial.

represent.definition: to form or be something (linking verb)
represent.note: typical: represent a change, an advance, an increase, a threat, percent of NOT for: speaking for someone
examples: The new drug represents a major advance.
Exports represent half of our income.

represent.definition: to have been elected to a parliament or council by the people of a particular area
represent.note: typical: represent a district, constituency, state, area, in Congress NOT for: acting for a client
examples: She represents a district in the north.
He has represented the town in parliament for ten years.

represent.definition: to be a sign or mark that means something
represent.note: typical: represent a letter, number, amount; blue represents water on the map NOT for: being a symbol of an idea
examples: Blue areas on the map represent lakes.
Each letter represents a different sound.

represent.definition: to be a symbol of something
represent.note: typical: represent freedom, power, hope, a country, what it represents NOT for: being a map sign
examples: The dove represents peace.
He hated everything the school represented.

represent.definition: to take part in a sports event for your country, school or town
represent.note: typical: represent your country, club, school, at the Olympics NOT for: speaking for someone in court
examples: She is proud to represent her country at the Olympics.
He represented his school at football.

represent.definition: to be present at an event (usually passive: be represented)
represent.note: typical: be represented at a meeting, parade, conference, by delegates NOT for: representing a client
examples: All the local clubs were represented at the meeting.
Twenty countries were represented at the summit.

represent.definition: to describe someone or something in a particular way, especially in a way that is not true
represent.note: typical: represent sb/sth as sth, represent yourself as, in the media, falsely NOT for: standing for a letter
examples: The article represents him as a hero.
He represented himself as a doctor to get in.

request.definition: to ask for something in a polite or formal way
request.note: typical: request information, permission, a meeting, help, that..., be requested to NOT for: demanding something rudely
examples: You must request permission before you take photographs.
All members are requested to attend the meeting.

require.definition: to need something (more formal than need)
require.note: typical: require surgery, attention, care, skill, water, patience NOT for: wanting something you can do without
examples: The patient will require surgery.
These plants require plenty of water.

require.definition: if you are required to do or have something, a law or rule says you must
require.note: typical: be required to do sth, by law, require sb to, the rules require that NOT for: simply needing something
examples: All visitors are required to sign in.
The law requires drivers to wear seat belts.

reserve.definition: to arrange for a place such as a table, room or seat to be kept for you at a future time
reserve.note: typical: reserve a table, room, seat, ticket, in advance, for two NOT for: keeping something for later use at home
examples: I'd like to reserve a table for two.
You should reserve your seats in advance.

reserve.definition: to keep something so that it can be used by a particular person or for a particular purpose
reserve.note: typical: reserve sth for sb, parking, seats, reserved for NOT for: booking a hotel room
examples: A separate room is reserved for guests.
These parking spaces are reserved for staff.

reserve.definition: to keep part of something to use later in a process (especially in recipes)
reserve.note: typical: reserve a little, some sauce, the juice, liquid, for later NOT for: booking a table
examples: Reserve a little of the cheese for the top.
Reserve half of the liquid for the sauce.

reserve.definition: to use or show something only in one particular situation
reserve.note: typical: reserve your anger, a tone, praise, reserve sth for sb NOT for: booking a seat
examples: He reserves his best jokes for close friends.
She reserved her tone of voice for official visitors.

resist.definition: to stop yourself from having something you like very much or from doing something you want to do
resist.note: typical: can't resist, resist temptation, the urge to, resist chocolate NOT for: fighting against an attack
examples: I can never resist a piece of cake.
She resisted the urge to laugh.

resist.definition: to try to prevent a change from happening or to avoid being forced to do something
resist.note: typical: resist change, pressure, a proposal, calls to, strongly, fiercely NOT for: avoiding a treat
examples: The company resisted pressure to lower its prices.
Many staff resisted the changes.

resist.definition: to use force to stop something from happening
resist.note: typical: resist an attack, arrest, the enemy, violently, fiercely NOT for: avoiding temptation
examples: The protesters resisted arrest.
The soldiers resisted the attack for hours.

resolve.definition: to find a satisfactory way of dealing with a problem or difficulty
resolve.note: typical: resolve a dispute, conflict, problem, issue, crisis, by talks NOT for: making a personal decision
examples: The crisis was resolved by negotiation.
They met to resolve the dispute.

resolve.definition: to make a definite decision to do something
resolve.note: typical: resolve to do sth, resolve that..., firmly, never to NOT for: solving a problem
examples: After the argument she resolved never to speak to him again.
He resolved that he would stop smoking.

resolve.definition: to make a formal decision, especially by voting
resolve.note: typical: resolve to do sth, the Senate, committee, council resolved NOT for: a private decision
examples: The council resolved to build a new school.
The Senate resolved to accept the proposals.

resolve.definition: to separate something into its different parts (technical)
resolve.note: typical: resolve a sample, a mixture, a compound, DNA, into parts NOT for: solving a dispute
examples: The scientists resolved the sample into its parts.
The DNA was extracted and resolved.

resort.definition: to do something bad, extreme or difficult because you cannot think of any other way to deal with a problem
resort.note: typical: resort to violence, force, lies, begging, drastic measures NOT for: choosing a holiday place
examples: Some people resort to violence when they feel angry.
The farmers had to resort to selling their animals.

respond.definition: to do something as a reaction to something that has been said or done
respond.note: typical: respond to a request, a crisis, a threat, quickly, positively, by doing sth NOT for: getting better after treatment
examples: The government responded to the protests by changing the law.
Villagers responded with offers of food and shelter.

respond.definition: to say or write something as a reply
respond.note: typical: respond to an email, a letter, a question, an invitation, that... NOT for: reacting with an action
examples: She never responded to my message.
He responded that he was too busy to come.

respond.definition: to improve as a result of a particular kind of treatment
respond.note: typical: respond to treatment, medication, therapy, antibiotics, well, poorly NOT for: answering a question
examples: The patient responded well to the new drug.
Some infections do not respond to antibiotics.

restore.definition: to make something return to its former state or condition
restore.note: typical: restore order, peace, confidence, health, power, sight, relations NOT for: repairing an old building
examples: Police were called in to restore order after the riots.
The operation restored his hearing.

restore.definition: to bring back a positive feeling that people felt before
restore.note: typical: restore confidence, faith, trust, hope, public belief NOT for: repairing old objects
examples: The new leader tried to restore public trust in the bank.
Her kindness restored my faith in people.

restore.definition: to repair an old building, piece of furniture or painting so that it looks as it did originally
restore.note: typical: restore a church, a painting, a car, furniture, carefully, to its former glory NOT for: bringing back a feeling
examples: The old cinema has been beautifully restored.
He spends his weekends restoring vintage cars.

restore.definition: to give back something that was lost or taken from someone (formal)
restore.note: typical: restore sth to sb, land, property, rights, a territory NOT for: repairing a building
examples: The court restored the land to its rightful owners.
The treaty restored the islands to their former ruler.

restore.definition: to bring back a law, tax, right or practice
restore.note: typical: restore a law, the death penalty, a tax, a right, a custom NOT for: restoring a feeling
examples: Some politicians want to restore the old tax.
The campaign aims to restore workers' rights.

restrict.definition: to limit or control the size, amount or range of something
restrict.note: typical: restrict access, sales, the number of, growth, competition, to sth NOT for: limiting what a person can do or where they can go
examples: The new law restricts the sale of fireworks.
The museum restricts the number of visitors to fifty at a time.

restrict.definition: to limit someone's actions or movements
restrict.note: typical: restrict freedom, movement, a child, someone's life, severely NOT for: controlling an amount
examples: The narrow seats restricted my movement.
Poor health restricted her to the house.

result.definition: to happen or exist as the effect of something else
result.note: typical: result from an error, a mistake, a delay, the resulting loss, problems resulting from NOT for: causing something to happen
examples: Many injuries result from carelessness.
The delay resulted from a mistake in the schedule.

retire.definition: to stop working, usually because you have reached a certain age; or to be asked to stop working
retire.note: typical: retire at 65, from teaching, early, as a doctor, be forced to retire NOT for: going away to a quiet place
examples: My father retired from the post office last year.
She was retired early because of ill health.

retire.definition: to go away to a quiet place (formal)
retire.note: typical: retire to your room, to the library, to bed, for the evening NOT for: stopping work
examples: After dinner she retired to her study.
The guests retired to the garden.

retire.definition: to leave the courtroom to decide whether someone is guilty (of a jury)
retire.note: typical: the jury retired, retire to consider a verdict NOT for: a worker leaving a job
examples: The jury retired to consider its verdict.
The judge waited while the jury retired.

retire.note: typical: retire for the night, retire early, retire to bed NOT for: stopping a career
examples: He retired early and was soon asleep.
They retired for the night at ten o'clock.

reveal.definition: to make known something that was previously secret or unknown
reveal.note: typical: reveal a secret, the truth, details, the results, that..., the identity of NOT for: letting something be seen with the eyes
examples: The report revealed that the company had lied.
She refused to reveal her real name.

reveal.definition: to show something that was hidden or covered
reveal.note: typical: reveal a tattoo, a face, a painting, reveal itself, as the curtain opened NOT for: telling a secret
examples: When she lifted her sleeve it revealed a scar.
The clouds parted to reveal the mountain top.

review.definition: to examine and think about a situation or process carefully to see if changes are needed
review.note: typical: review a policy, a decision, the situation, the evidence, regularly, be reviewed NOT for: writing about a film or book
examples: The board will review the new rules next month.
The decision is being reviewed by the court.

review.definition: to write a short article that describes and judges a new book, film, play or similar work
review.note: typical: review a book, film, play, album, restaurant, for a newspaper NOT for: studying notes again
examples: She reviews films for a local newspaper.
The critic reviewed the new restaurant very favourably.

review.definition: to look again at something you have studied, such as notes (American English)
review.note: typical: review notes, the material, a chapter, for a test, before the exam NOT for: judging a film
examples: I need to review my notes before the test.
The students reviewed the chapter together.

review.definition: to describe and examine the main parts of a series of events or a period of time
review.note: typical: review the events, the year, the progress, the history of NOT for: examining a policy for changes
examples: The programme reviews the main events of the year.
In his speech he reviewed the history of the town.

review.definition: to officially inspect a group of soldiers, ships or similar at a military show
review.note: typical: review the troops, the fleet, the parade, the guard NOT for: writing a critique
examples: The queen reviewed the troops on parade.
The admiral reviewed the fleet from the deck.

revise.definition: to change something because of new information or ideas
revise.note: typical: revise a plan, an estimate, an opinion, a forecast, upwards, downwards NOT for: studying for an exam
examples: The company revised its sales forecast downwards.
After seeing the evidence he revised his opinion.

revise.definition: to study facts again in order to learn them before an examination (British English)
revise.note: typical: revise for an exam, a test, your notes, history, the night before NOT for: changing a plan
examples: I have to revise for my chemistry exam.
She spent the weekend revising her notes.

revise.definition: to change a piece of writing by adding information, improving it or correcting mistakes
revise.note: typical: revise a book, a text, a draft, an edition, a report, thoroughly NOT for: studying for a test
examples: The author revised the text for the second edition.
The manual needs to be revised.

reward.definition: to give something to someone because they have done something good or helpful or have worked for it
reward.note: typical: reward sb for sth, reward effort, loyalty, good behaviour, reward sb with sth NOT for: punishing someone
examples: The teacher rewarded the class with extra break time.
The company rewards staff for their loyalty.

reward.definition: to get something good as a result of hard work or effort (usually passive)
reward.note: typical: be rewarded with success, a prize, effort, patience was rewarded NOT for: giving a prize to someone
examples: Their hard work was rewarded with a place in the final.
Her patience was finally rewarded.

rise.definition: to increase in number, amount or value
rise.note: typical: rise by 5%, rise sharply, steadily, prices rise, rising costs NOT for: standing up or moving upwards through the air
examples: Prices have risen sharply this year.
The number of visitors rose by ten per cent.

rise.note: typical: smoke rises, water rises, the road rises, bubbles rise to the surface NOT for: becoming more expensive
examples: Smoke rose from the chimney.
The path rises steeply behind the village.

rise.note: typical: rise from your chair, rise to your feet, rise to speak NOT for: getting out of bed
examples: The judge rose and left the room.
Everyone rose to their feet when she entered.

rise.definition: to become important, powerful, successful or rich
rise.note: typical: rise to power, fame, prominence, rise through the ranks, rise to the top NOT for: prices going up
examples: He rose to the rank of general.
She rose through the ranks to become manager.

rise.definition: to be very tall or high above the surrounding area
rise.note: typical: rise above, rise from the sea, towers, cliffs, mountains rise NOT for: becoming successful
examples: Steep cliffs rise above the beach.
The tower rises over the old town.

rise.definition: to become louder or higher (of a sound or voice), or to be loud enough to be heard
rise.note: typical: voices rise, a sound rises from, rise above the noise NOT for: prices going up
examples: Her voice rose in anger.
The sound of music rose from the street.

rise.definition: to appear in the sky (of the sun or moon)
rise.note: typical: the sun, moon rises, in the east, at six NOT for: standing up
examples: The sun rises at six in June.
We watched the moon rise over the sea.

rise.definition: to be felt more and more strongly (of a feeling)
rise.note: typical: anger, hope, panic, excitement, tension rises NOT for: a price increasing
examples: Panic rose in her chest.
Their hopes rose when they heard the news.

rise.definition: to try to defeat the government or army that controls you (also rise up)
rise.note: typical: rise up, rise against, in revolt, in rebellion, the people rose NOT for: a price or a sound rising
examples: The people rose against the king.
The prisoners rose up and took control.

rise.definition: to become bigger because air is inside (of bread or cakes)
rise.note: typical: dough rises, bread, a cake, let it rise, for an hour NOT for: prices going up
examples: Leave the dough to rise for an hour.
The cake did not rise properly.

rise.definition: to get out of bed in the morning (literary)
rise.note: typical: rise early, at dawn, rise with the sun NOT for: standing up from a chair
examples: He rose at dawn and went fishing.
The family rises early on farm days.

rise.definition: to come alive again after dying
rise.note: typical: rise from the dead, rise from the grave, rise again NOT for: getting out of bed
examples: In the story, the hero rises from the dead.
Christians believe that Jesus rose from the dead.

rise.definition: to finish a formal meeting (of a court or parliament)
rise.note: typical: parliament, the court, the committee rises, until Monday NOT for: a crowd standing up
examples: Parliament rises for the summer next week.
The court will rise at five o'clock.

rise.note: typical: the wind rises, a storm, a gale, during the night NOT for: a sound getting louder
examples: The wind rose during the night.
As the wind rose, the boats returned to harbour.

rise.definition: to begin in a particular place (of a river)
rise.note: typical: the river rises in, the mountains, a spring, a lake NOT for: a river's water level going up
examples: The river rises in the mountains.
The Thames rises in the Cotswolds.

rot.definition: to decay by a gradual natural process, or to make something decay
rot.note: typical: rot away, teeth, wood, fruit, leave sth to rot NOT for: a plan failing
examples: Sugary drinks can rot your teeth.
The apples were left to rot on the ground.

ruin.definition: to spoil or destroy something completely
ruin.note: typical: ruin a holiday, a career, your life, your shoes, a surprise, completely NOT for: making a person poor
examples: The rain ruined our picnic.
One mistake could ruin his career.

ruin.definition: to make someone lose all their money
ruin.note: typical: ruin a business, a family, be financially ruined, ruined by a lawsuit NOT for: spoiling an event or an object
examples: The lawsuit nearly ruined the small company.
He was ruined by bad investments.

sample.definition: to taste food or drink to find out what it is like
sample.note: typical: sample the food, local dishes, wine, cheese, a chance to sample NOT for: asking people questions
examples: Visitors can sample local cheeses at the market.
We sampled several wines before we chose one.

sample.definition: to choose some people from a larger group in order to ask them questions or get information
sample.note: typical: sample customers, voters, adults, randomly, a sampled group NOT for: tasting food
examples: Researchers sampled two hundred teenagers.
About 500 households were sampled for the survey.

sample.definition: to try an activity or place in order to see what it is like
sample.note: typical: sample the delights, the nightlife, the atmosphere, country life NOT for: tasting something small
examples: Tourists come to sample the nightlife of the city.
He wanted to sample life on a farm.

sample.definition: to use a small part of a song or recording in a new piece of music
sample.note: typical: sample a song, a beat, a chorus, a record, be sampled by artists NOT for: tasting food
examples: The producer sampled an old jazz record.
Her song has been sampled by many rappers.

satisfy.definition: to make someone feel pleased by giving them what they want
satisfy.note: typical: satisfy a customer, a client, a parent, hard to satisfy, nothing satisfies NOT for: meeting a rule or standard
examples: Nothing I did seemed to satisfy my boss.
The new menu should satisfy every guest.

satisfy.definition: to provide what someone needs or wants
satisfy.note: typical: satisfy needs, demands, hunger, curiosity, appetite, a desire NOT for: convincing someone that something is true
examples: The course is designed to satisfy the needs of beginners.
A sandwich will not satisfy his hunger.

satisfy.definition: to make someone feel sure that something is right or true (formal)
satisfy.note: typical: satisfy sb of sth, satisfy yourself that, convince NOT for: giving someone what they want
examples: He tried to satisfy the police of his innocence.
She satisfied herself that the door was locked.

satisfy.definition: to be good enough for a particular purpose, rule or standard (formal)
satisfy.note: typical: satisfy requirements, conditions, criteria, standards NOT for: making a person happy
examples: Applicants must satisfy all the entry requirements.
The product does not satisfy safety standards.

scan.definition: to examine an area carefully but quickly, often looking for a particular person or thing
scan.note: typical: scan the horizon, a crowd, a room, the street, for sth, scan sth for sth NOT for: reading something quickly
examples: She scanned the crowd for her brother.
He scanned the horizon but saw no ships.

scan.definition: to read something quickly (also scan through)
scan.note: typical: scan a page, a list, the headlines, the newspaper, scan through NOT for: using a machine
examples: I scanned the list for my name.
He scanned the headlines over breakfast.

scan.definition: to use a machine that passes an electrical beam over something to form a picture of what is inside it
scan.note: typical: scan a patient, luggage, a brain, bags, scan for signs of NOT for: copying a document into a computer
examples: All bags are scanned at the airport.
Doctors scanned her brain for signs of damage.

scan.definition: to put a document or picture into a computer using a scanner
scan.note: typical: scan a document, a photo, a page, a form, scan sth into sth NOT for: examining a person's body
examples: I scanned the photos and emailed them to my aunt.
Please scan the form and send it back.

scan.definition: to have a regular pattern of beats (of poetry)
scan.note: typical: a line scans, a poem scans, a verse scans well, scan badly NOT for: reading something quickly
examples: The last line of the poem does not scan.
This verse scans perfectly.

scatter.definition: to throw or drop a lot of small things so that they spread over an area
scatter.note: typical: scatter seeds, petals, ashes, papers, toys, over the floor, across a field NOT for: people running away in different directions
examples: She scattered seeds across the flower bed.
The children scattered toys all over the floor.

scatter.definition: to move quickly away in different directions (of a group of people or animals); or to make a group do this
scatter.note: typical: the crowd scattered, birds scatter, scatter in all directions, scatter the protesters NOT for: throwing small things around
examples: The birds scattered when the dog ran into the field.
The police scattered the crowd.

schedule.definition: to plan that something will happen at a particular time (usually passive)
schedule.note: typical: be scheduled for, be scheduled to do sth, scheduled flights, scheduled departure NOT for: cancelling an event
examples: The meeting is scheduled for Monday morning.
The new film is scheduled to open in June.

secure.definition: to get or achieve something that will last, especially after a lot of effort
secure.note: typical: secure a deal, a contract, a place, a victory, funding, someone's release NOT for: fastening something so it cannot move
examples: The company secured a large contract.
Her late goal secured the team's place in the final.

secure.definition: to make something safe from attack, danger or loss
secure.note: typical: secure a building, a border, a network, secure the area, secure your data NOT for: winning a contract
examples: Soldiers secured the airport.
You should secure your home network with a password.

secure.definition: to fasten something firmly so that it cannot move or open
secure.note: typical: secure a door, a window, a load, a rope, a gate, with a lock NOT for: winning a deal
examples: He secured the boat with a strong rope.
Please secure all windows before you leave.

seek.definition: to try to achieve or get something (formal)
seek.note: typical: seek re-election, asylum, revenge, compensation, a solution, seek to do sth NOT for: looking for a lost object
examples: The company is seeking new ways to cut costs.
Thousands of people crossed the border seeking safety.

seek.definition: to ask someone for advice, help or assistance (formal)
seek.note: typical: seek advice, help, assistance, permission, medical advice, legal advice NOT for: trying to gain power
examples: If the pain continues, seek medical advice.
She sought help from a lawyer.

seek.definition: to look for someone or something (written)
seek.note: typical: seek employment, a partner, a job, seeking a flatmate, in adverts NOT for: asking for help
examples: Recent graduates are seeking employment.
The advert said the shop was seeking a manager.

select.definition: to choose someone or something by thinking carefully about which is best or most suitable
select.note: typical: select a candidate, a player, a winner, at random, select sb for sth, select sb to do sth NOT for: picking something without thinking
examples: The panel selected three candidates for interview.
She was selected for the national team.

separate.definition: to be between two places or things so that they are not touching
separate.note: typical: separate sth from sth, a wall, a river, a fence, a channel separates NOT for: dividing something into parts
examples: A narrow river separates the two villages.
A thin wall separates my room from my brother's.

separate.definition: to divide into different parts, or to make something do this
separate.note: typical: separate into groups, parts, sth from sth, separate the eggs, a sauce separates NOT for: a couple ending a relationship
examples: The teacher separated the class into four groups.
Separate the egg white from the yolk.

separate.definition: to stop living together (of a married couple or partners)
separate.note: typical: a couple separate, separated last year, legally separated NOT for: dividing objects into groups
examples: My parents separated when I was ten.
They separated a year ago but are not divorced.

separate.definition: to see that one thing or idea is different from another
separate.note: typical: separate fact from fiction, sth from sth, hard to separate NOT for: physically moving things apart
examples: It is hard to separate his work from his private life.
She cannot separate fact from rumour.

separate.definition: to move apart, or to make people or things move apart
separate.note: typical: separate fighting dogs, be separated from the group, in the crowd NOT for: ending a marriage
examples: A teacher stepped in to separate the two boys.
I got separated from my friends in the crowd.

separate.definition: to be the quality or fact that makes someone or something different from others
separate.note: typical: separate sth from sth, what separates, the gap that separates NOT for: being between two places
examples: Language separates humans from other animals.
Only skill separates the best players from the rest.

separate.definition: to be the amount by which two things differ, such as two teams in a competition
separate.note: typical: points separate the teams, a few seconds separate, only X separates NOT for: dividing into parts
examples: Only two points separate the top two teams.
Just a few seconds separated the runners.

set.definition: to put something down somewhere carefully
set.note: typical: set sth down, on the table, aside, set the tray on NOT for: preparing a table for a meal
examples: She set the tray down on the table.
He set the heavy box carefully on the floor.

set.definition: to put something firmly into a surface (usually passive)
set.note: typical: be set into the wall, floor, ground, ceiling, a jewel set in NOT for: placing something down loosely
examples: The posts must be set deep into the ground.
A small light was set into the ceiling.

set.definition: to place the action of a story, film or play in a particular time or place (usually passive)
set.note: typical: be set in Paris, in the future, in the 1920s, against a background NOT for: fixing a date for an event
examples: The film is set in Scotland in the 1700s.
The story is set against a background of war.

set.definition: to consider something in relation to other things
set.note: typical: set sth against sth, in context, beside, put side by side NOT for: starting something happening
examples: The cost must be set against the benefits.
The debate should be set in a wider context.

set.definition: to establish a way of doing something that others copy or accept as good
set.note: typical: set an example, a standard, a trend, the tone, a precedent, the pace NOT for: giving a student homework
examples: Parents should set a good example for their children.
The first speech set the tone for the whole meeting.

set.definition: to make something start happening or someone start doing something
set.note: typical: set sth in motion, set fire to, set sth on fire, set sb thinking NOT for: arranging a date or price
examples: Protesters set fire to two cars.
His words set me thinking about my future.

set.definition: to decide and state when something will happen, how much it will cost, or what should be done
set.note: typical: set a date, a price, a time, standards, limits, guidelines NOT for: putting something somewhere
examples: The council has set a date for the vote.
The shop sets its own prices.

set.definition: to start doing something in a determined way, or to tell someone to start doing something
set.note: typical: set to work, set about, set sb to work doing sth NOT for: starting a fire
examples: They set to work painting the fence.
The boys were set to work collecting wood.

set.definition: to move a switch or control on a machine so that it works at the time or in the way you want
set.note: typical: set the alarm, the timer, the oven, the heating, to record NOT for: becoming hard
examples: Did you set the alarm for six?
Set the oven to 180 degrees.

set.definition: to become hard and solid
set.note: typical: concrete, glue, jelly, cement, the mixture sets, to set NOT for: the sun going down
examples: How long does the glue take to set?
Leave the jelly in the fridge to set.

set.definition: to move down in the sky and disappear (of the sun or moon)
set.note: typical: the sun sets, at six, in the west, the setting sun NOT for: concrete hardening
examples: The sun sets early in winter.
We watched the sun set behind the hills.

set.definition: to say what you or someone else must try to achieve
set.note: typical: set a goal, a target, a task, a challenge, set yourself NOT for: breaking a record
examples: It is best to set realistic goals.
She set herself the task of learning Greek.

set.definition: to achieve the best result ever reached in a sport or competition
set.note: typical: set a record, a world record, a new time, a Olympic record NOT for: deciding a price
examples: She set a new world record in the 400 metres.
The team set a record for the most wins in a season.

set.definition: to arrange plates, knives, glasses and so on on a table so that it is ready for a meal
set.note: typical: set the table, for dinner, for six, lay the table (British) NOT for: putting an object down carefully
examples: Can you set the table for dinner?
He set the table for six people.

set.definition: to make a trap ready to catch an animal, or to plan a way to catch someone doing something wrong
set.note: typical: set a trap, for a mouse, for a thief, for a rival NOT for: putting something down
examples: He set a trap for the mice in the kitchen.
The police set a trap for the thieves.

set.definition: to settle into a particular expression (of a face or mouth)
set.note: typical: her face set, his mouth set, into a line, in a frown NOT for: concrete getting hard
examples: His face set into a stubborn frown.
Her mouth set in a hard line.

set.definition: to put a broken bone into the right position so that it can heal; or (of a bone) to join together again
set.note: typical: set a bone, a broken arm, a leg, set by a doctor, the bone sets NOT for: jelly or concrete hardening
examples: The doctor set his broken arm.
The bone should set in about six weeks.

set.definition: to give a student a piece of work to do (British English)
set.note: typical: set homework, an essay, a task, set sb sth, a test NOT for: writing exam questions
examples: The teacher set us a long essay.
Mr Hall always sets homework on Fridays.

set.definition: to write the questions for an examination (British English)
set.note: typical: set an exam, a paper, a test, set the questions NOT for: giving homework to a class
examples: The head of department sets the final exam.
Who set this paper?

set.definition: to arrange words and letters so that a book or newspaper is ready to be printed
set.note: typical: set type, set a page, a book, by hand, set in print NOT for: putting a table ready for a meal
examples: In those days, every page was set by hand.
The text was set in a clear modern type.

set.definition: to arrange wet hair so that it dries in a particular style
set.note: typical: set hair, her hair, have your hair set, with rollers NOT for: bones healing
examples: She had her hair set before the party.
He sets his mother's hair every week.

shape.definition: to influence something such as a belief or opinion and make it develop in a particular way
shape.note: typical: shape opinion, a belief, the future, someone's life, be shaped by NOT for: making a physical form from material
examples: Her childhood experiences shaped her view of the world.
The decision will shape the future of the town.

shape.definition: to make something have a particular shape, especially by pressing it
shape.note: typical: shape sth into sth, dough, clay, metal, shaped like NOT for: influencing opinions
examples: Shape the dough into small balls.
The potter shaped the clay into a bowl.

shelter.definition: to provide a place where someone or something is protected, especially from weather or danger
shelter.note: typical: shelter sb from the rain, wind, sun, shelter refugees, shelter sth NOT for: staying in a protected place yourself
examples: The wall shelters the garden from the wind.
The family sheltered refugees during the war.

shelter.definition: to stay in or under a place where you are protected from weather or danger
shelter.note: typical: shelter from the rain, the sun, a storm, under a tree, in a doorway NOT for: protecting someone else
examples: We sheltered from the rain under a tree.
Hikers sheltered in a cave during the storm.

shift.definition: to move from one place or position to another, or to make something move; (British informal) to move something by lifting or carrying it
shift.note: typical: shift your weight, position, a chair, a box, uncomfortably, in your seat NOT for: changing opinions
examples: He shifted in his seat and looked at his watch.
Can you help me shift this sofa?

shift.definition: to change a situation or discussion by giving attention to a different idea or subject
shift.note: typical: shift the focus, the emphasis, attention, the debate, onto, away from NOT for: moving a heavy object
examples: The minister tried to shift attention away from the crisis.
The focus has shifted to the cost of living.

shift.definition: to change (of opinions, beliefs or attitudes)
shift.note: typical: opinion shifts, attitudes shift, public mood, shift to the right NOT for: moving something physically
examples: Public opinion began to shift after the report.
Attitudes towards work have shifted a lot.

shift.definition: to change the way money is paid or spent
shift.note: typical: shift resources, funding, money, spending, shift sth towards NOT for: moving furniture
examples: The government wants to shift more money towards schools.
The company shifted resources to its online shop.

shift.definition: to remove dirt or marks from a surface or clothing (British English)
shift.note: typical: shift a stain, dirt, grease, a mark, will shift any stain NOT for: changing opinions
examples: This powder will shift most stains.
I can't shift this mark on the carpet.

shift.definition: to change gear when driving (especially American English)
shift.note: typical: shift gear, into second, down, up, shift into reverse NOT for: moving a heavy object
examples: She shifted into second gear.
He shifted down as the road became steep.

shift.definition: to sell a product, especially a lot of it (British informal)
shift.note: typical: shift stock, copies, units, a product, shift thousands NOT for: moving an object
examples: The shop shifted over a thousand copies last week.
They need to shift old stock before January.

signal.definition: to make a sound or an action in order to give information or tell someone to do something
signal.note: typical: signal to sb, signal for sth, signal that, the whistle signalled, with a wave NOT for: showing a direction in a vehicle
examples: The referee blew his whistle to signal the end of the game.
She signalled for the waiter to bring the bill.

signal.definition: to make something clear by what you say or do (used in news reports)
signal.note: typical: signal a willingness, readiness, intention, a change, signal that NOT for: waving to someone
examples: Both leaders signalled their willingness to talk.
The minister signalled that taxes would go up.

signal.definition: to be a sign that something is going to happen
signal.note: typical: signal the start, the end, a change, a new era, a warning NOT for: waving or giving a sound
examples: Longer days signal the end of winter.
The result signals a change in the party's fortunes.

signal.definition: to show the direction you intend to turn in a vehicle, using the lights
signal.note: typical: signal left, right, before turning, signal to turn, indicate NOT for: giving news or a sign of a future event
examples: You must signal before you turn.
He forgot to signal and a car almost hit him.

sink.definition: to go down below the surface of water, mud or similar
sink.note: typical: a boat sinks, a stone sinks, sink to the bottom, in the mud NOT for: damaging a ship deliberately
examples: The boat hit a rock and began to sink.
The coin sank to the bottom of the pool.

sink.definition: to damage a ship so badly that it sinks
sink.note: typical: sink a ship, a boat, a submarine, be sunk by a missile NOT for: a boat going under by itself
examples: The enemy sank three ships.
The yacht was sunk in a storm.

sink.definition: to move downwards to a lower level
sink.note: typical: the sun sinks, sink below, sink slowly, sink behind the hills NOT for: falling heavily into a seat
examples: The sun was sinking behind the hills.
Her head sank onto the pillow.

sink.definition: to fall down or sit down heavily, especially because you are tired or weak
sink.note: typical: sink into a chair, onto a sofa, to your knees, back, down, wearily NOT for: a sun or boat going down
examples: She sank into an armchair and closed her eyes.
He sank to his knees and prayed.

sink.definition: to gradually get into a worse condition
sink.note: typical: sink into poverty, depression, despair, debt, silence, sink deeper NOT for: sinking in water
examples: The company sank into debt.
After her loss, she sank into depression.

sink.definition: to go down in amount or value
sink.note: typical: sales sink, shares sink, sink to a low, sink below, drop NOT for: boats going under
examples: Share prices sank after the news.
The temperature sank to minus ten.

sink.definition: to become very quiet (of a voice)
sink.note: typical: her voice sank, to a whisper, to a murmur, into silence NOT for: a price falling
examples: Her voice sank to a whisper.
His voice sank as he told the secret.

sink.definition: to push your teeth or something sharp into flesh or food
sink.note: typical: sink your teeth into, a fork into, claws into, sink sth into sth NOT for: spending money
examples: The dog sank its teeth into the bone.
She sank her fork into the cake.

sink.definition: to dig a hole in the ground for something such as a well
sink.note: typical: sink a well, a shaft, a pole, a mine, into the ground NOT for: putting teeth into food
examples: They sank a well in the back garden.
Workers sank a new shaft at the mine.

sink.definition: to spend a lot of money on something
sink.note: typical: sink money into, savings into, sink sth in sth, a business NOT for: drinking
examples: They sank all their savings into the restaurant.
He sank thousands of pounds into the project.

sink.definition: to put a ball into a hole or basket in games such as golf or basketball
sink.note: typical: sink a putt, a ball, a basket, a shot, from ten feet NOT for: a ship going under
examples: She sank a long putt on the last hole.
He sank the ball from the free-throw line.

sink.definition: to drink alcohol, especially a lot of it (British informal)
sink.note: typical: sink a pint, a few drinks, a bottle, sink beers NOT for: going under water
examples: We sank a couple of pints after work.
He sank three beers in an hour.

slice.definition: to cut meat, bread, vegetables and similar food into thin flat pieces (also slice up)
slice.note: typical: slice bread, an onion, cheese, thinly slice, sliced ham NOT for: moving quickly through water or air
examples: Slice the tomatoes and put them on the bread.
He thinly sliced the cucumber.

slice.definition: to cut something easily with one movement of a sharp knife or edge
slice.note: typical: slice through, slice into, slice sth in two, a blade slices NOT for: cutting food into thin pieces on a board
examples: The knife sliced through the rope.
She sliced the orange in half.

slice.definition: to move quickly and easily through something such as water or air
slice.note: typical: slice through the water, the air, the waves, the clouds NOT for: cutting with a knife
examples: The boat sliced through the waves.
The bird sliced through the air.

slice.definition: to hit a ball so that it spins and goes to one side (in tennis or golf)
slice.note: typical: slice a shot, the ball, wide of the goal, a slice, in golf NOT for: cutting with a knife
examples: He sliced his shot wide of the goal.
The golfer sliced the ball into the trees.

sort.definition: to put things in a particular order or arrange them in groups according to size, type or similar
sort.note: typical: sort sth into groups, piles, by size, alphabetical order, sort letters NOT for: solving a problem
examples: She sorted the clothes into two piles.
The names are sorted into alphabetical order.

sort.definition: to deal with a situation so that all the problems are solved (British spoken)
sort.note: typical: sort a problem, it out, leave it to sb to sort, I'll sort it NOT for: arranging things in groups
examples: Leave it with me and I'll sort it.
Right, I'll leave this to the two of you to sort.

spill.definition: to let a liquid accidentally flow over the edge of a container, or (of a liquid) to flow out in this way
spill.note: typical: spill coffee, milk, water, a drink, over the table, down your shirt NOT for: people moving out of a place
examples: I spilled coffee all over my shirt.
The milk spilled on the floor.

spill.definition: to move or fall out of somewhere in large numbers
spill.note: typical: spill out of, spill onto the street, crowds, people, spill over NOT for: a liquid flowing from a cup
examples: Crowds spilled onto the street after the match.
Fans spilled out of the stadium.

split.definition: to disagree strongly, so that a group divides, or to make a group disagree and divide
split.note: typical: split a party, a church, be split over, on an issue, split from sth NOT for: dividing food between people
examples: The party split over the question of tax.
The issue has split the committee in two.

split.definition: to divide into different parts or groups, or to divide something into parts
split.note: typical: split into groups, sth into sections, split up, a class, a book NOT for: tearing along a line
examples: The class split into groups of four.
The book is split into three sections.

split.definition: to tear or break along a straight line
split.note: typical: split open, in two, in half, down the middle, a seam, a branch splits NOT for: sharing something out
examples: The seam of my trousers split.
The box split open and the apples fell out.

split.definition: to divide something and share it between two or more people
split.note: typical: split the bill, the cost, the profits, split sth between, split sth with sb NOT for: a couple separating
examples: We split the bill between the four of us.
He agreed to split the money with his brother.

split.definition: to cut part of someone's head or lip so that it bleeds
split.note: typical: split your lip, split your head open, in a fall, on a table NOT for: tearing cloth
examples: He fell and split his lip.
She split her head open on the edge of the table.

split.definition: to end a marriage or relationship (also split up)
split.note: typical: split up, split from your wife, the band split, couple split NOT for: dividing into groups
examples: The couple split up last year.
The band split after only two albums.

spoil.definition: to have a bad effect on something so that it is no longer attractive, enjoyable or useful
spoil.note: typical: spoil the fun, a holiday, a view, the taste, spoil everything NOT for: being too kind to a child
examples: Rain spoiled our picnic.
Litter has spoiled the park.

spoil.definition: to give a child everything it wants, often with the result that the child behaves badly
spoil.note: typical: spoil a child, spoil sb rotten, a spoilt child, an only child NOT for: ruining an event
examples: They spoil their youngest son.
Grandparents often spoil their grandchildren.

spoil.definition: to treat someone in a very kind or generous way
spoil.note: typical: spoil yourself, spoil sb on their birthday, a treat, with a gift NOT for: harming a child's behaviour
examples: I want to spoil you on your birthday.
Go on, spoil yourself and have dessert.

spoil.note: typical: food spoils, milk, fruit, meat spoils, in the heat, in the fridge NOT for: being too kind to someone
examples: Milk spoils quickly in hot weather.
Fish will spoil if it is not kept cold.

spoil.definition: to mark a ballot paper wrongly so that your vote does not count (British English)
spoil.note: typical: spoil a ballot paper, a vote, a spoilt ballot, in an election NOT for: decaying food
examples: He spoilt his ballot paper on purpose.
Several votes were spoilt by mistake.

spray.definition: to force liquid out of a container so that it comes out in a stream of very small drops and covers an area
spray.note: typical: spray paint, perfume, water, crops, sth with sth, spray sth onto NOT for: shooting bullets
examples: She sprayed herself with perfume.
Farmers spray the crops against insects.

spray.definition: to come out in a stream of small drops or bits (of a liquid or small pieces), or to make them do this
spray.note: typical: spray from, water sprays, champagne sprayed, spray out of NOT for: covering a surface on purpose
examples: Champagne sprayed from the bottle.
Water sprayed out of the broken pipe.

spray.definition: to shoot a lot of bullets towards a person or place very quickly
spray.note: typical: spray sb/sth with bullets, a crowd, a car, gunmen sprayed NOT for: using a spray can
examples: Gunmen sprayed the car with bullets.
Soldiers sprayed the building with gunfire.

spread.definition: to become larger or move so that more people or a larger area are affected
spread.note: typical: fire spreads, a disease, a stain, spread through, spread to, rapidly NOT for: putting butter on bread
examples: The fire quickly spread through the building.
The disease spread rapidly across the country.

spread.definition: to become known or used by more and more people; or to tell many people about something
spread.note: typical: news spreads, a rumour, spread the word, spread like wildfire NOT for: a disease affecting an area
examples: The news spread quickly around the town.
He loves to spread rumours about his colleagues.

spread.definition: to open something out, or arrange things so that they cover a flat surface (also spread out)
spread.note: typical: spread a map, a blanket, a cloth, spread sth on, across, over NOT for: putting a soft substance on bread
examples: He spread the map out on the table.
Papers were spread across the floor.

spread.definition: to cover or exist across a large area (also be spread out)
spread.note: typical: spread over, throughout, a region, spread across NOT for: becoming known by more people
examples: The company has shops spread throughout the country.
The forest spreads over the whole valley.

spread.definition: to put a soft substance over a surface, or to be soft enough to be put on a surface
spread.note: typical: spread butter, jam, paint, glue, spread sth on, with sth NOT for: arranging objects on a table
examples: She spread jam on her toast.
Warm the butter so that it spreads easily.

spread.definition: to move arms, fingers or legs far apart
spread.note: typical: spread your arms, fingers, legs, wings, hands, wide NOT for: covering a surface
examples: He spread his arms wide and smiled.
The bird spread its wings.

spread.definition: to do something over a period of time rather than all at once (also spread out)
spread.note: typical: spread payments, spread sth over, a longer period, throughout the summer NOT for: opening out a map
examples: Can I spread the payments over six months?
The concerts are spread throughout the summer.

spread.definition: to share or divide something among several people or things
spread.note: typical: spread the load, the cost, the burden, the risk, wealth, evenly NOT for: putting a soft substance on a surface
examples: The bills come out on different dates to spread the workload.
They want to spread the risk across several projects.

spread.definition: to slowly appear on someone's face (of an expression)
spread.note: typical: a smile spreads, over her face, across his face, slowly NOT for: a disease spreading
examples: A slow smile spread across her face.
A look of horror spread over his face.

stack.definition: to put things into a neat pile, or to form a neat pile (also stack up)
stack.note: typical: stack boxes, chairs, plates, books, stack sth on, stack up NOT for: filling a shelf
examples: He stacked the chairs against the wall.
The plates were stacked neatly in the cupboard.

stack.definition: to put neat piles of things on something, or to fill a place with piles of things
stack.note: typical: stack the shelves, be stacked with sth, boxes, supplies NOT for: making one pile of things
examples: She works at night stacking shelves.
The garage was stacked with boxes.

stamp.definition: to put your foot down onto the ground loudly and with a lot of force
stamp.note: typical: stamp your feet, your foot, stamp on, stamp in anger, with cold NOT for: walking noisily somewhere
examples: The audience stamped and shouted.
She stamped her foot in anger.

stamp.definition: to walk somewhere noisily by putting your feet down hard because you are angry
stamp.note: typical: stamp off, out of the room, up the stairs, around, angrily NOT for: pressing a mark on paper
examples: She stamped out of the room.
He stamped up the stairs and slammed his door.

stamp.definition: to put a pattern, sign or letters on something using a special tool
stamp.note: typical: stamp a passport, a form, a date, the word SECRET, stamp sth on sth NOT for: sticking a postage stamp
examples: The officer stamped my passport.
The date was stamped on the box.

stamp.definition: to have an important or lasting effect on someone or something
stamp.note: typical: stamped on your memory, stamp sth with, stamp your authority NOT for: marking a document
examples: The scene was stamped on my memory for years.
His years in the army stamped him with an air of authority.

stamp.definition: to stick a postage stamp onto a letter or parcel
stamp.note: typical: stamp a letter, a parcel, an envelope, stamped and addressed NOT for: marking a passport
examples: Don't forget to stamp the envelope.
The parcels were stamped and posted.

state.definition: to formally say or write a piece of information or your opinion
state.note: typical: state your name, an opinion, a fact, a policy, that..., clearly state NOT for: a document giving information
examples: Please state your name and address.
The witness stated that he had seen nobody.

state.definition: to contain information that is written clearly (of a document, newspaper, ticket or similar)
state.note: typical: the form states, a contract states, the label, the price is stated NOT for: speaking formally
examples: The contract states that payment is due in thirty days.
The price is stated on the back of the ticket.

stick.definition: to attach something to another thing with a substance, or to become attached to a surface
stick.note: typical: stick sth on, to, together, stick posters, a stamp, stick to NOT for: pushing a pointed object into something
examples: Someone had stuck posters all over the wall.
The stamp won't stick properly.

stick.definition: to push a pointed object into something, or to be pushed into something
stick.note: typical: stick sth into, a pin, a fork, a knife, stick through NOT for: attaching with glue
examples: She stuck a pin into the map.
He stuck his fork into a potato.

stick.definition: to put something somewhere quickly and without much care (informal)
stick.note: typical: stick it in the oven, the bag, the drawer, stick sth on NOT for: gluing something to a wall
examples: Just stick it in the microwave for a minute.
She stuck the letter in her pocket.

stick.definition: to put part of your body somewhere where it can be seen
stick.note: typical: stick your head out, your tongue out, your hand up, stick your head around the door NOT for: pushing a sharp object into something
examples: He stuck his head out of the window.
Don't stick your tongue out at people.

stick.definition: to become fixed in one position and difficult to move
stick.note: typical: a door sticks, a key, the wheels stuck, a drawer, stick fast NOT for: attaching with glue
examples: This door sticks in wet weather.
The car's wheels stuck fast in the mud.

stick.definition: to continue to be used by people (of a name that someone has invented)
stick.note: typical: the name stuck, a nickname, the label, it stuck NOT for: attaching with glue
examples: They called him Tiny as a joke and the name stuck.
The nickname stuck for the rest of his life.

stick.definition: to continue to accept a situation or person you do not like (British spoken)
stick.note: typical: can't stick sb, can't stick doing sth, his temper, the noise NOT for: attaching with glue
examples: I can't stick my sister's new boyfriend.
She can't stick working there any longer.

stock.definition: to keep a supply of a product in order to sell it (of a shop)
stock.note: typical: stock a product, a range, books, a wide range of, we stock NOT for: filling a place with supplies
examples: The shop stocks a wide range of kitchen equipment.
We don't stock that brand.

stock.definition: to fill something with a supply of something
stock.note: typical: stock sth with sth, a fridge, a shelf, a lake with fish, well stocked NOT for: selling products in a shop
examples: The fridge was stocked with drinks.
They stocked the lake with fish.

store.definition: to put things away and keep them until you need them
store.note: typical: store food, in a jar, in a cool place, store sth away, up NOT for: keeping data in a computer
examples: Store the beans in an airtight jar.
Squirrels store nuts for the winter.

store.definition: to keep facts or information in your brain or in a computer
store.note: typical: store data, information, files, in memory, on a disk, in the cloud NOT for: putting physical things away
examples: The files are stored on a server.
The brain stores a huge amount of information.

strain.definition: to injure a muscle or part of your body by using it too much
strain.note: typical: strain a muscle, your back, your eyes, your neck, your voice NOT for: separating food from liquid
examples: He strained a muscle in his leg during the match.
Don't read in the dark or you'll strain your eyes.

strain.definition: to try very hard to do something using all your strength or ability
strain.note: typical: strain to hear, to see, strain for air, strain your ears, your eyes NOT for: hurting a muscle
examples: She strained to hear what they were saying.
The swimmer strained for air.

strain.definition: to separate solid things from a liquid by pouring the mixture through something with small holes
strain.note: typical: strain pasta, the sauce, the soup, the water, through a sieve NOT for: injuring a muscle
examples: Strain the pasta and add the sauce.
She strained the tea into a cup.

strain.definition: to cause difficulties for something by making too much work or too many problems for it
strain.note: typical: strain relations, finances, resources, patience, the budget NOT for: pulling hard on a rope
examples: The costs will strain our budget.
The argument strained relations between the two countries.

strain.definition: to pull hard at something or push hard against something
strain.note: typical: strain at the lead, the rope, against the door, strain against NOT for: causing financial problems
examples: The dog strained at its lead.
The buttons strained against his shirt.

strengthen.definition: to become stronger, or to make something stronger
strengthen.note: typical: strengthen ties, bonds, relationships, resolve, friendship, steadily NOT for: a currency rising in value
examples: Their friendship has strengthened over the years.
The university wants to strengthen its links with local firms.

strengthen.definition: to make an organisation, army or team more powerful, especially by increasing the number or quality of the people in it
strengthen.note: typical: strengthen a team, an army, a squad, a force, with new players NOT for: making a wall stronger
examples: The team was strengthened by two new players.
The government has strengthened the police force.

strengthen.definition: to improve or make the financial situation of a country or company improve
strengthen.note: typical: strengthen the economy, the market, a company, the recovery NOT for: making friendships closer
examples: The new measures should strengthen the economy.
The economy has strengthened this year.

strengthen.definition: to increase in value, or to increase the value of money (of a currency)
strengthen.note: typical: the pound, the dollar, a currency strengthens, against the euro NOT for: making a team more powerful
examples: The pound has strengthened against the dollar.
The euro strengthened after the announcement.

strengthen.definition: to make something such as your body or a building stronger
strengthen.note: typical: strengthen a wall, a bridge, the muscles, your legs, the roof NOT for: improving a relationship
examples: Metal supports were added to strengthen the walls.
These exercises strengthen the back muscles.

strengthen.note: typical: strengthen a case, an argument, a claim, a theory, the evidence NOT for: building a wall
examples: New evidence has strengthened the case against him.
The results strengthen her argument.

strengthen.definition: to increase in force (of wind and similar)
strengthen.note: typical: the wind strengthens, a storm, a current, during the night NOT for: a currency rising
examples: The wind strengthened during the night.
The storm is expected to strengthen.

stress.definition: to emphasise a statement, fact or idea
stress.note: typical: stress the importance of, the need for, stress that, strongly NOT for: pronouncing a word louder
examples: The report stressed the need for more teachers.
She stressed that safety must come first.

stress.definition: to pronounce a word or part of a word so that it sounds louder or stronger
stress.note: typical: stress a syllable, a word, be stressed on, the second syllable NOT for: emphasising an idea
examples: The word 'machine' is stressed on the second syllable.
In English, we usually stress the first syllable of a noun like 'record'.

strike.definition: to hit or fall against the surface of something (written)
strike.note: typical: strike the ground, the wall, the roof, strike sb on the head, be struck by NOT for: deliberately hitting someone
examples: The ball struck him on the head.
Several cars were struck by falling branches.

strike.definition: to deliberately hit someone or something with your hand or a weapon (formal)
strike.note: typical: strike sb, strike a blow, strike sb across the face, with a stick NOT for: an object accidentally falling on someone
examples: He struck her hard across the face.
The victim had been struck with a heavy object.

strike.definition: if something strikes you, you think of it, notice it or realise that it is important or true
strike.note: typical: it struck me that, be struck by, a thought struck, what strikes you NOT for: hitting something physically
examples: It suddenly struck her that she had left the door open.
I was struck by how quiet the town was.

strike.definition: to seem to someone to have a particular quality
strike.note: typical: strike sb as odd, strange, funny, strike sb as being sth, it strikes me as NOT for: hitting something
examples: His jokes didn't strike me as very funny.
It struck me as odd that nobody was there.

strike.definition: to stop working as a protest (of workers)
strike.note: typical: workers, nurses, teachers strike, strike for higher pay, go on strike NOT for: attacking someone
examples: The nurses are striking for better pay.
Train drivers voted to strike next week.

strike.note: typical: strike again, strike at dawn, a killer, an army strikes, a target NOT for: workers stopping work
examples: The killer may strike again.
Rebel forces struck a military base in the north.

strike.definition: to damage or harm someone or something
strike.note: typical: strike at, strike at the heart of, strike a blow to, a law NOT for: hitting something with a hand
examples: The scandal struck a blow to the government's hopes.
This law strikes at the basic rights of workers.

strike.definition: to happen suddenly and begin to affect someone (of something bad)
strike.note: typical: disaster strikes, tragedy, a disease, an earthquake strikes, again NOT for: attacking someone on purpose
examples: Disaster struck when the engine failed.
A powerful earthquake struck the region on Monday.

strike.definition: to find a way of giving the right amount of importance to two things
strike.note: typical: strike a balance between, the right balance, a compromise NOT for: agreeing a business arrangement
examples: It is hard to strike a balance between work and family.
The new rules strike a fair balance between the two sides.

strike.definition: to agree on a deal or bargain
strike.note: typical: strike a deal, a bargain, an agreement, a compromise, with sb NOT for: finding a balance
examples: The two companies struck a deal after long talks.
They struck a bargain over the price.

strike.definition: to produce a flame by rubbing a match against a rough surface
strike.note: typical: strike a match, a light, a flame, on the box NOT for: hitting something with a weapon
examples: He struck a match and lit the candle.
She struck a match on the wall.

strike.definition: to find a supply of oil, gold or similar in the ground
strike.note: typical: strike oil, gold, water, a rich vein NOT for: making money suddenly in business
examples: The company struck oil off the coast.
Miners struck gold in the hills.

strike.definition: to hit and damage something (of lightning)
strike.note: typical: lightning strikes, a tree, a building, struck by lightning NOT for: a disaster beginning
examples: The old tree was struck by lightning.
Lightning struck the church tower.

strike.definition: to make a sound to show what time it is (of a clock)
strike.note: typical: the clock strikes, strike twelve, strike the hour, the church bell NOT for: workers stopping work
examples: The town clock struck midnight.
The church bell struck six.

strike.definition: to do something that gives you an advantage over an opponent
strike.note: typical: strike first, strike early, a goal, in the third minute NOT for: attacking in war
examples: Brazil struck first with a goal in the third minute.
The home side struck early in the second half.

struggle.definition: to try extremely hard to achieve something, even though it is very difficult
struggle.note: typical: struggle to do sth, struggle with, for, against, struggle to survive, to cope NOT for: physically fighting someone
examples: She is struggling to bring up three children alone.
Many families are struggling with high rents.

struggle.definition: to fight someone who is attacking or holding you, especially to escape; or (of two people) to fight for something
struggle.note: typical: struggle with a burglar, to escape, to free yourself, struggle for possession NOT for: trying to cope with a problem
examples: She struggled to free herself from his grip.
The two men struggled for the gun.

struggle.definition: to move somewhere with great difficulty
struggle.note: typical: struggle up a hill, out of, through the snow, to the door NOT for: fighting someone
examples: Walkers struggled up the steep hill.
He struggled through the deep snow.

struggle.definition: to be likely to fail, even though you are trying very hard
struggle.note: typical: a struggling business, artist, writer, struggle all season, a struggling team NOT for: moving with difficulty
examples: The team has been struggling all season.
He was a struggling artist living in a tiny room.

submit.definition: to give a plan, piece of writing or similar to someone in authority for them to consider or approve
submit.note: typical: submit an application, a report, a proposal, a claim, an essay, by Friday NOT for: agreeing to obey someone
examples: All applications must be submitted by Friday.
She submitted her essay a day late.

submit.definition: to agree to obey someone or something, or to go through a process, especially when you have no choice (formal)
submit.note: typical: submit to authority, a test, a search, an examination, to the will of NOT for: handing in a document
examples: The prisoners refused to submit to a search.
He submitted to the rules of the club.

submit.definition: to suggest or say something, especially in a court of law (formal, law)
submit.note: typical: submit that, I submit that, to the court, to the jury NOT for: handing in a form
examples: I submit that the jury has been misled.
The lawyer submitted that her client was innocent.

subscribe.definition: to pay money, usually once a year, to receive copies of a newspaper or magazine or to use a service
subscribe.note: typical: subscribe to a magazine, a newspaper, a channel, a service, a newsletter NOT for: agreeing with an idea
examples: You can subscribe to the magazine for thirty pounds a year.
She subscribes to several news websites.

subscribe.definition: to pay money regularly to be a member of an organisation or to help its work (British English)
subscribe.note: typical: subscribe to a charity, a club, a society, a group NOT for: receiving a magazine
examples: He subscribes to an environmental group.
Members subscribe to the club every year.

subscribe.definition: to apply to buy shares in a company (finance)
subscribe.note: typical: subscribe for shares, subscribe for up to, new shares, a share issue NOT for: receiving a magazine
examples: Each employee may subscribe for up to a hundred shares.
Investors subscribed for the new shares.

succeed.definition: to do what you tried or wanted to do
succeed.note: typical: succeed in doing sth, succeed in finding, completely, almost succeeded NOT for: taking someone's position
examples: She finally succeeded in finding a flat.
Very few people succeed in losing weight and keeping it off.

succeed.definition: to have the result or effect that was intended
succeed.note: typical: the plan, the treatment, the method, the attempt did not succeed NOT for: a person doing well in a career
examples: The new treatment did not succeed.
The plan succeeded beyond all our hopes.

succeed.definition: to do well in your job or career, especially because you have worked hard for a long time
succeed.note: typical: succeed as an actor, in business, in politics, in life NOT for: replacing someone in a role
examples: She hopes to succeed as a writer.
He succeeded in politics at a young age.

succeed.definition: to be the next person to take a position or job after someone else
succeed.note: typical: succeed sb as sth, to the throne, a leader, a manager, an heir NOT for: doing well at work
examples: Reeves will succeed Segal as director.
The prince will succeed his father to the throne.

succeed.definition: to come after or replace something else, especially another product
