succeed.note: typical: succeed a model, a product, a system, an earlier version NOT for: taking someone's job
examples: This model will succeed the popular older version.
The new law will succeed the one passed in 2001.

suffer.definition: to experience physical or mental pain
suffer.note: typical: suffer from a disease, pain, a bad back, suffer terribly, in silence NOT for: becoming worse in quality
examples: He suffers from a bad back.
The animal did not suffer and died quickly.

suffer.definition: to experience an unpleasant or difficult event or situation
suffer.note: typical: suffer a defeat, a loss, damage, an injury, a setback, the consequences NOT for: being in physical pain
examples: The team suffered a heavy defeat.
Many people suffered losses in the crash.

suffer.definition: to become worse in quality because a bad situation is affecting something or because nobody is taking care of it
suffer.note: typical: work, health, quality, safety, sales suffer, if costs are cut NOT for: feeling pain
examples: Safety may suffer if costs are cut.
My studies are suffering because I work so much.

suit.definition: to be acceptable, suitable or convenient for a particular person or situation
suit.note: typical: suit sb's needs, tastes, everyone, suit me fine, a time that suits NOT for: making someone look attractive
examples: Does Thursday suit you?
There are walks to suit all tastes.

suit.definition: to make someone look attractive (of clothes, colours or styles)
suit.note: typical: red suits you, a hairstyle, a coat, a colour, really suit NOT for: being convenient for someone
examples: That coat really suits you.
Short hair doesn't suit her.

suit.definition: to have the right qualities to do something (usually be suited to/for)
suit.note: typical: be suited to, for, well suited, ideally suited, best suited NOT for: looking attractive in clothes
examples: He is well suited to the job.
The land is ideally suited for farming.

sum.definition: to give the main information in a report, speech or similar in a short statement at the end (sum up)
sum.note: typical: sum up, to sum up, sum up an argument, sum up the discussion NOT for: describing something in a few words
examples: I will sum up at the end of the meeting.
In your last paragraph, sum up your main argument.

sum.definition: to explain the main facts of a case at the end of a trial (of a judge) (sum up)
sum.note: typical: the judge sums up, sum up the case, to the jury NOT for: ending a speech
examples: The judge will sum up tomorrow morning.
The judge summed up the case for the jury.

sum.definition: to describe something using only a few words (sum up)
sum.note: typical: sum sth up, in a word, in three words, can be summed up NOT for: explaining a legal case
examples: The problem can be summed up in three words.
He summed up the situation in one sentence.

sum.definition: to show the most typical qualities of someone or something (sum up)
sum.note: typical: sum sb up, sum up the spirit of, the attitude, the mood, perfectly NOT for: giving a short summary of a talk
examples: That one picture sums up the whole holiday.
His answer sums him up perfectly.

summarise.definition: to make a short statement giving only the main information and not the details of a plan, event, report or similar
summarise.note: typical: summarise a report, an article, the main points, the findings, briefly NOT for: describing something in great detail
examples: The authors summarise their views in the first chapter.
Can you summarise the story in two sentences?

supply.definition: to provide people with something that they need or want, especially regularly over a long period
supply.note: typical: supply sb with sth, supply sth to sb, power, water, food, information, supply goods NOT for: being full of something
examples: The farm supplies fresh eggs to local shops.
A local company supplied the school with computers.

supply.definition: to be provided with a lot or a little of something (usually passive, with an adverb)
supply.note: typical: be well supplied with, poorly supplied, generously supplied, be supplied with NOT for: providing goods to customers
examples: The kitchen was well supplied with food.
The camp was poorly supplied with water.

suppose.definition: to say that you think something is true, although you are not sure about it (spoken, as in I suppose)
suppose.note: typical: I suppose so, I suppose that, so I suppose, I suppose you're right NOT for: expecting someone to follow a rule
examples: I suppose you are right.
'Are you pleased?' 'Yes, I suppose so.'

suppose.definition: to be expected or required to do something, especially because of a rule or what someone in authority has said (be supposed to)
suppose.note: typical: be supposed to do sth, not supposed to, are we supposed to NOT for: being believed to be true
examples: We are supposed to check out by eleven o'clock.
You're not supposed to park here.

suppose.definition: to be expected or intended to happen, especially when it did not happen (be supposed to)
suppose.note: typical: was supposed to, were supposed to meet, to take place, to prevent NOT for: a rule that must be followed
examples: The meeting was supposed to take place on Tuesday, but it was postponed.
The new law is supposed to prevent crime.

suppose.definition: to be believed to be true by many people, although it may not be true (be supposed to)
suppose.note: typical: be supposed to be haunted, to be the best, to be very good NOT for: following instructions
examples: The castle is supposed to be haunted.
The film is supposed to be very good.

suppose.definition: to think that something is probably true, based on what you know
suppose.note: typical: suppose that, what makes you suppose, no reason to suppose, be supposed NOT for: saying you are not sure in speech
examples: There were many more deaths than was first supposed.
I have no reason to suppose he is lying.

suppose.definition: to expect that something will happen or be true and to base your plans on it (formal)
suppose.note: typical: the plan supposes, the model supposes, the theory supposes, a steady increase NOT for: guessing in conversation
examples: The company's plan supposes a steady rise in orders.
The theory supposes that prices will remain stable.

surround.definition: to be all around someone or something on every side (usually passive)
surround.note: typical: be surrounded by, trees, walls, water, a crowd, a garden surrounded by NOT for: being related to an event
examples: The house is surrounded by tall trees.
A crowd surrounded the car.

surround.definition: to have a lot of a particular type of people or things near you (be surrounded by)
surround.note: typical: be surrounded by friends, family, books, luxury, danger NOT for: standing around a building
examples: He is always surrounded by admirers.
She grew up surrounded by books.

surround.definition: to arrange yourselves in positions all the way around a place (of police or soldiers)
surround.note: typical: surround a building, a house, a town, police surrounded NOT for: being near many people
examples: Armed police surrounded the house.
Soldiers surrounded the village at dawn.

surround.definition: to be closely related to a situation or event
surround.note: typical: the events, issues, the mystery, secrecy, controversy surrounding NOT for: standing around a place
examples: The events surrounding his death are still a mystery.
Secrecy surrounds the project.

surround.definition: to choose to have certain people or things near you all the time (surround yourself with)
surround.note: typical: surround yourself with, friends, talented people, beautiful things NOT for: soldiers surrounding a town
examples: She surrounds herself with creative people.
He surrounded himself with beautiful objects.

suspect.definition: to think that something is probably true, especially something bad
suspect.note: typical: suspect that, strongly suspect, I suspect, suspect a problem NOT for: thinking a person is guilty
examples: I suspect that he is not telling the truth.
She suspected there was something wrong with the engine.

suspect.definition: to think that something bad has happened or is happening
suspect.note: typical: suspect murder, foul play, a fire, suspect nothing, suspect anything NOT for: thinking a person is guilty
examples: The doctors suspected pneumonia.
He never suspected anything.

suspect.definition: to think that someone is probably guilty of a crime
suspect.note: typical: suspect sb of (doing) sth, be suspected of, murder, theft, spying NOT for: doubting a reason
examples: Who do the police suspect?
He is suspected of stealing the money.

suspect.definition: to think that something is not honest or true
suspect.note: typical: suspect sb's motives, a story, a claim, an excuse, a reason NOT for: thinking a person committed a crime
examples: I began to suspect his motives.
She suspected his story was false.

suspend.definition: to officially stop something from continuing, especially for a short time
suspend.note: typical: suspend talks, sales, a service, a law, flights, until further notice NOT for: making someone leave a school or job
examples: Flights were suspended because of the fog.
Talks between the two countries have been suspended.

suspend.definition: to make someone leave their school or job for a short time, especially because they have broken the rules
suspend.note: typical: suspend sb from school, work, a team, a player, a police officer NOT for: stopping a service
examples: Dave was suspended from school for a week.
The player was suspended for three matches.

suspend.definition: to attach something to a high place so that it hangs down (formal)
suspend.note: typical: suspend sth from, the ceiling, a bridge, a lamp, by a rope NOT for: stopping an activity
examples: A large lamp was suspended from the ceiling.
The bridge is suspended from steel cables.

suspend.definition: to float in a liquid or in air without moving (technical, usually passive)
suspend.note: typical: be suspended in, a liquid, the air, water, particles, oil NOT for: hanging from a ceiling
examples: Tiny particles are suspended in the liquid.
Dust was suspended in the air.

swap.definition: to give something to someone and get something in return
swap.note: typical: swap sth for sth, swap sth with sb, swap seats, swap phone numbers, swap places NOT for: telling and getting information
examples: Do you want to swap umbrellas?
He swapped his old bike for a new camera.

swap.definition: to tell information to someone and be given information in return
swap.note: typical: swap ideas, stories, gossip, information, notes, tips NOT for: exchanging objects
examples: We met to swap ideas and information.
They sat in a corner and swapped gossip.

swap.definition: to do the thing that someone else has been doing and let them do the thing you have been doing (also swap over)
swap.note: typical: swap roles, jobs, swap over, swap with sb, after an hour NOT for: exchanging objects
examples: They decided to swap roles for the day.
You start on the windows and I'll do the walls, then we can swap over.

swap.definition: to stop using or get rid of one thing and put or get another in its place
swap.note: typical: swap sth for sth, swap buses, trains, cars, jeans for a skirt NOT for: telling information
examples: She swapped her long skirt for jeans.
We had to swap buses halfway through the journey.

swap.definition: to move one thing and put another thing in its place (also swap around)
swap.note: typical: swap sth around, sth with sth, the furniture, the pictures NOT for: stopping using something
examples: Why don't we swap the TV with the bookcase?
Someone had swapped all the books around.

swear.definition: to use rude and offensive language
swear.note: typical: swear at sb, in front of, swear loudly, swear and shout NOT for: making a promise
examples: Don't swear in front of the children.
He turned round and swore at me.

swear.definition: to promise that you will do something
swear.note: typical: swear to do sth, swear that, swear an oath, swear on your honour NOT for: saying a rude word
examples: He swore that he would get his revenge.
She swore never to return.

swear.definition: to say very strongly that what you are saying is true (informal)
swear.note: typical: I swear, swear that, swear blind, swear to God, can't swear to it NOT for: promising to do something
examples: I swear I never touched your purse.
I think it was ten o'clock, but I couldn't swear to it.

swear.definition: to make someone make a public official promise, especially in a court of law (also swear in)
swear.note: typical: swear an oath, witnesses swear to tell the truth, swear on the Bible NOT for: using bad language
examples: Witnesses have to swear to tell the truth.
The new president was sworn in on Monday.

sweep.definition: to clean dust or dirt from a floor or the ground using a brush with a long handle
sweep.note: typical: sweep the floor, the path, the leaves, sweep sth up, off, out NOT for: moving through a place with force
examples: She swept the kitchen floor.
Will you sweep the leaves off the patio?

sweep.definition: to move things from a surface with a brushing movement
sweep.note: typical: sweep sth into, off the table, sweep papers into a drawer NOT for: cleaning a floor with a broom
examples: He swept the crumbs off the table.
She swept the papers quickly into the drawer.

sweep.definition: to force someone or something to move in a particular direction
sweep.note: typical: be swept away, out to sea, along, by the current, by a crowd NOT for: cleaning a floor
examples: The windsurfer was swept out to sea.
She was swept along by the angry crowd.

sweep.definition: to move quickly together through a place (of a group of people or animals)
sweep.note: typical: sweep through, along, across, the crowd, the army swept through NOT for: winds or fire moving over an area
examples: The crowd swept through the gates of the stadium.
The army swept across the plain.

sweep.definition: to move quickly across a place with a lot of force (of winds, waves, fire and similar)
sweep.note: typical: storms, winds, fire, waves sweep across, through, the country NOT for: people moving as a group
examples: Violent storms swept the country.
Strong winds swept across the plains.

sweep.definition: to spread quickly through a place or group of people (of an idea, feeling or activity)
sweep.note: typical: sweep the country, through, across, a craze, a fashion, panic, fever NOT for: wind moving over land
examples: A new fashion swept the country.
Panic swept through the crowd.

tackle.definition: to try to deal with a difficult problem
tackle.note: typical: tackle a problem, an issue, crime, unemployment, a task, head on NOT for: trying to take a ball from a player
examples: The government must tackle the problem of unemployment.
It took twelve fire engines to tackle the blaze.

tackle.definition: in sport, to try to take the ball from an opponent, or to force a player to the ground to stop them running
tackle.note: typical: tackle a player, an opponent, from behind, tackle hard, in football, rugby NOT for: dealing with a problem
examples: He tackled the striker just outside the box.
The defender was sent off for tackling from behind.

tackle.definition: to talk to someone about a difficult problem in order to deal with it (British English)
tackle.note: typical: tackle sb about sth, tackle your boss, your son, your neighbour NOT for: sport
examples: When I tackled Susan about it, she admitted her mistake.
He decided to tackle his boss about the pay.

tackle.definition: to start fighting someone, especially a criminal
tackle.note: typical: tackle a burglar, an attacker, a thief, a gunman, single-handed NOT for: talking to a person about a problem
examples: I certainly couldn't tackle both of them on my own.
A passer-by tackled the thief and held him until the police arrived.

tend.definition: if something tends to happen, it often happens and is likely to happen again
tend.note: typical: tend to do sth, tend to be, tend to forget, tend to get, tend to think NOT for: looking after someone
examples: People tend to need less sleep as they get older.
My car tends to overheat in the summer.

tend.definition: to have one particular quality or feature more than others (tend towards)
tend.note: typical: tend towards, tend towards the left, a tendency, tend to extremes NOT for: something that often happens
examples: Charles tends towards obesity.
The design tends towards the minimal.

tend.definition: to move or develop in a particular direction (formal)
tend.note: typical: tend upwards, downwards, prices tend, rates tending up NOT for: usually doing something
examples: Interest rates are tending upwards.
Prices tend downwards in the summer.

term.definition: to use a particular word or expression to name or describe something (usually passive)
term.note: typical: be termed, sometimes termed, loosely termed, termed a failure, a success NOT for: ending something
examples: This condition is sometimes termed RSI.
The new rules are loosely termed 'reforms'.

threaten.definition: to say that you will cause someone harm or trouble if they do not do what you want
threaten.note: typical: threaten sb with sth, threaten to do sth, threaten that, threaten a strike NOT for: being likely to harm something
examples: He threatened to call the police.
The workers are threatening a strike if they do not get a pay increase.

threaten.definition: to be likely to harm or destroy something
threaten.note: typical: threaten the survival of, threaten to ruin, be threatened with destruction, an incident threatens NOT for: warning someone with words
examples: Poaching threatens the survival of the rhino.
Large areas of the jungle are threatened with destruction.

threaten.definition: if something bad threatens, it seems likely to happen
threaten.note: typical: a storm threatens, rain threatens, danger threatens, trouble threatened NOT for: saying you will harm someone
examples: Rain threatened all afternoon.
Trouble threatened when the two groups met.

trace.definition: to find someone or something that has disappeared by searching for them carefully
trace.note: typical: trace a missing person, a relative, a witness, the source of, a lost parcel NOT for: copying a drawing
examples: Police are trying to trace a woman seen near the accident.
She hired a detective to trace her missing brother.

trace.definition: to find the origins of when something began or where it came from
trace.note: typical: trace sth back to, trace your ancestry, a style, the origin of NOT for: finding a missing person
examples: They traced their family back to Scotland.
The style can be traced back to early medieval art.

trace.definition: to study or describe the history, development or progress of something
trace.note: typical: trace the history of, the development of, the rise of, the story of NOT for: copying a map
examples: The book traces the history of the English language.
The film traces her rise to fame.

trace.definition: to copy a drawing or map by putting transparent paper over it and drawing the lines you can see
trace.note: typical: trace a map, a picture, a shape, a drawing, on tracing paper NOT for: finding the origin of something
examples: She traced the map on thin paper.
The children traced the outline of a leaf.

trace.definition: to draw real or imaginary lines on the surface of something, usually with your finger
trace.note: typical: trace a pattern, a line, a shape, trace sth on, in the sand, the dust NOT for: copying a drawing on paper
examples: He traced a heart in the sand with his finger.
She traced the outline of the country on the globe.

trace.definition: to find out where a telephone call came from by using special electronic equipment
trace.note: typical: trace a call, the number, a signal, an email, be traced to NOT for: finding a missing person
examples: Police traced the call to a house in London.
The phone call was traced within half an hour.

track.definition: to search for a person or animal by following the marks, smell or other signs they leave behind
track.note: typical: track an animal, a criminal, a suspect, the trail, track sb to sth NOT for: recording how something develops
examples: The dogs tracked the wolf to its lair.
Police have been tracking the four men across the country.

track.definition: to record or study the behaviour or development of someone or something over time
track.note: typical: track progress, sales, spending, a parcel, the weather, by computer NOT for: following an animal
examples: The company tracks sales on a daily basis.
You can track your parcel online.

track.definition: to follow the movements of an aircraft or ship using radar
track.note: typical: track an aircraft, a ship, a satellite, a storm, by radar NOT for: following an animal's footprints
examples: Air controllers tracked the plane on radar.
The station tracks satellites all day.

track.definition: to move a film or television camera towards or away from a scene to follow the action
track.note: typical: track in, track out, a camera, tracking shot, a film crew NOT for: following an aircraft
examples: The camera tracks in on her face.
The cameraman tracked back as the actors walked away.

track.definition: to put schoolchildren into groups according to their ability (American English)
track.note: typical: track students, pupils, children, tracked classes, by ability NOT for: following an animal
examples: Some schools track students by ability.
The pupils are tracked into advanced and basic classes.

track.definition: to leave marks of mud or dirt behind you when you walk (American English)
track.note: typical: track mud, dirt, snow, sand, in, all over the floor NOT for: searching for someone
examples: Don't track mud all over the kitchen floor.
He tracked snow into the hall.

trade.definition: to buy and sell goods or services as your job or business
trade.note: typical: trade with, trade in, trade goods, trade for years, trade internationally NOT for: exchanging items with a friend
examples: The company trades in silk and tea.
India began trading with Europe in the 15th century.

trade.definition: to exist and operate as a business (British English)
trade.note: typical: trade under the name, cease trading, stop trading, trade profitably NOT for: buying and selling goods
examples: The firm trades under the name Lanski and Weber.
The company ceased trading last year.

trade.definition: to buy or sell something on the stock exchange (usually passive)
trade.note: typical: be traded, shares, stock, currencies, heavily traded, on the market NOT for: bartering with another person
examples: Over a million shares were traded today.
The stock is traded on the New York exchange.

trade.definition: to insult or hit each other during an argument or fight
trade.note: typical: trade insults, blows, punches, accusations, with each other NOT for: buying and selling goods
examples: The two politicians traded insults on live television.
The boxers traded punches in the first round.

trade.definition: to exchange something you have for something that someone else has (especially American English)
trade.note: typical: trade sth for sth, trade sth with sb, trade places, jobs, cards, stickers NOT for: running a business
examples: We traded necklaces.
I'd trade my camera for your bike.

transfer.definition: to move from one place, school, job or similar to another, or to make someone do this, especially within the same organisation
transfer.note: typical: transfer to, from, transfer sb to, a new branch, a new school, a different department NOT for: moving money between accounts
examples: He transferred from the Paris office to the London office.
They are transferring him to a special unit.

transfer.definition: to move from one place to another, or to move something from one place to another (formal)
transfer.note: typical: transfer sth to, from, transfer the meat to a plate, the data, the files, the exhibition transfers to NOT for: selling a player
examples: Transfer the meat to warm plates.
The exhibition transfers to York on 23rd January.

transfer.definition: to sell a sports player to another team
transfer.note: typical: transfer a player, be transferred for a fee, to Real Madrid, in the transfer window NOT for: moving an employee
examples: The striker was transferred for a fee of eight million pounds.
The club transferred its best player to a rival.

transfer.definition: to move money from one account or institution to another
transfer.note: typical: transfer money, funds, $500, transfer sth to your account, online NOT for: selling a sports player
examples: I'd like to transfer 500 pounds to my savings account.
Funds are transferred electronically.

transport.definition: to take goods, people or similar from one place to another in a vehicle
transport.note: typical: transport goods, oil, passengers, troops, by road, by rail, by air NOT for: imagining you are somewhere else
examples: Trucks are used to transport oil.
The statue was transported to London by sea.

transport.definition: to imagine that you are in another place or time because of something that you see or hear (be transported)
transport.note: typical: be transported back to, into, childhood, another world, by the music NOT for: carrying goods in a lorry
examples: One look and I was transported back to my childhood.
The music transported her to another world.

transport.definition: to feel very strong emotions of pleasure or happiness (literary; be transported with)
transport.note: typical: be transported with delight, joy, rapture, ecstasy NOT for: carrying goods by road
examples: She was transported with delight at the news.
He was transported with joy.

trap.definition: to prevent someone from escaping from somewhere, especially a dangerous place (usually passive)
trap.note: typical: be trapped, trapped underground, in the rubble, in a lift, in a burning car NOT for: feeling stuck in a bad situation
examples: Twenty miners were trapped underground.
Dozens of people were trapped in the rubble.

trap.definition: to be or feel unable to escape from a bad situation (be/feel trapped)
trap.note: typical: feel trapped, be trapped in a job, a marriage, a role, trapped by debt NOT for: being stuck in a physical place
examples: Julia felt trapped in her role as a wife and mother.
He felt trapped in a job he hated.

trap.definition: to catch an animal or bird using a trap
trap.note: typical: trap a rabbit, a fox, an animal, birds, fish, by hand NOT for: catching a criminal
examples: They trap rabbits for food.
He trapped a fox in the garden.

trap.definition: to catch someone by forcing them into a place from which they cannot escape
trap.note: typical: trap a criminal, a suspect, the enemy, trap sb in a corner NOT for: catching an animal
examples: The police trapped the thieves at a roadblock.
The army trapped the enemy in the valley.

trap.definition: to trick someone so that they do or say something they did not intend to
trap.note: typical: trap sb into doing sth, into saying, into signing, into a confession NOT for: catching an animal
examples: He was trapped into signing a confession.
The reporter tried to trap the minister into saying something foolish.

trap.definition: to get a part of your body crushed between two objects (British English)
trap.note: typical: trap your fingers, hand, finger, a trapped nerve, in the door NOT for: preventing someone from escaping
examples: Mind you don't trap your fingers in the door.
She had a trapped nerve in her neck.

undergo.definition: if you undergo a change or an unpleasant experience, it happens to you or is done to you
undergo.note: typical: undergo surgery, treatment, tests, training, change, massive changes NOT for: taking something voluntarily and enjoying it
examples: The country has undergone massive changes recently.
She has been undergoing tests since Monday.

unite.definition: to join together in order to achieve something, or to make people or groups do this
unite.note: typical: unite against, behind, unite to do sth, unite the country, a party united NOT for: being the same
examples: Party members united behind their leader.
In 1960 the regions united to form a new republic.

update.definition: to add the most recent information to something
update.note: typical: update a file, a list, a website, a record, an app, regularly NOT for: telling someone the latest news
examples: The files need updating.
We update our website every week.

update.definition: to make something more modern in the way it looks or operates
update.note: typical: update a system, procedures, a design, an image, a model NOT for: adding new information to a list
examples: The company plans to update its manufacturing procedures.
They updated the kitchen with new units.

update.definition: to tell someone the most recent information about a situation (spoken)
update.note: typical: update sb on sth, update me on, keep sb updated, update the team NOT for: modernising equipment
examples: Can you update me on what has happened?
The manager updated the team on the project.

urge.definition: to strongly suggest that someone does something
urge.note: typical: urge sb to do sth, urge caution, urge action, urge that, strongly urge NOT for: pushing someone physically
examples: She urged me to get in touch with a lawyer.
The charity urged quick action.

urge.definition: to make someone or something move in a particular direction by shouting, pushing or similar (formal)
urge.note: typical: urge sb forward, urge sb towards, urge a horse, urge sb into NOT for: giving strong advice
examples: He urged her forward with a hand under her elbow.
She urged him towards the door.

vary.definition: if several things of the same type vary, they are all different from each other
vary.note: typical: vary from sth to sth, vary in size, vary greatly, widely, vary according to NOT for: changing depending on a situation
examples: Test scores vary from school to school.
The plants vary in size and colour.

vary.definition: if something varies, it changes depending on the situation
vary.note: typical: vary according to, depending on, vary with the weather, it varies, vary slightly NOT for: being different from other things
examples: His mood varies according to the weather.
'What do you wear?' 'It varies.'

vary.definition: to change something to make it different
vary.note: typical: vary your diet, the routine, the menu, vary sth by NOT for: being different from other things
examples: You should vary your diet more.
The teacher varies the lessons to keep students interested.

view.definition: to think about something or someone in a particular way
view.note: typical: view sth as sth, with suspicion, caution, from a perspective, favourably NOT for: looking at something with your eyes
examples: The law should be viewed as a way of meeting social goals.
Local people viewed newcomers with suspicion.

view.definition: to look at something, especially because it is beautiful or you are interested in it (formal)
view.note: typical: view a painting, the gardens, the mountain, the exhibition, best viewed from NOT for: thinking about someone in a particular way
examples: The mountain is best viewed from the north side.
Thousands of tourists come to view the gardens every year.

view.definition: to go to see a house or property you are interested in buying or renting
view.note: typical: view a house, an apartment, a flat, a property, by appointment NOT for: watching a television programme
examples: We viewed three flats on Saturday.
The house can be viewed by appointment.

view.definition: to watch a television programme, film or similar (formal)
view.note: typical: view a film, a programme, a video, a clip, online, before its release NOT for: looking at a house
examples: Viewers can view the film online.
Critics viewed the film before its general release.

wander.definition: to walk slowly across or around an area, usually without a clear direction or purpose
wander.note: typical: wander around, through, the streets, the house, the mall, aimlessly, off NOT for: leaving where you should stay
examples: I'll wander around the mall for half an hour.
He was found wandering the streets of New York.

wander.definition: to walk away from where you are supposed to stay (also wander off)
wander.note: typical: wander off, away, a child, a dog, from the group, don't let sb wander NOT for: walking for pleasure
examples: Don't let the kids wander off.
The dog wandered away from the garden.

wander.definition: if your mind or thoughts wander, you stop paying attention to something, especially because you are bored or worried
wander.note: typical: your mind wanders, thoughts wander, attention wanders, during a lecture NOT for: eyes looking around
examples: Her mind wandered during the long speech.
My thoughts kept wandering to the holiday.

wander.definition: to start to talk about something not related to the main subject
wander.note: typical: wander from, off the point, the subject, the topic, wander off topic NOT for: walking around
examples: Pauline started to wander from the point.
The discussion wandered off the topic.

wander.definition: if your eyes or gaze wander, you look around slowly at different things
wander.note: typical: eyes wander, gaze wanders, wander over, round the room, across NOT for: your mind wandering
examples: His gaze wandered round the room.
Her eyes wandered over the crowd.

wander.definition: if a road or river wanders somewhere, it does not go straight but in curves
wander.note: typical: the river, the road, the path wanders, through, along, meander NOT for: a person walking aimlessly
examples: The river wanders through the valley.
A narrow path wanders up the hill.

weigh.definition: to have a particular weight (linking verb)
weigh.note: typical: weigh 50 kilos, how much, weigh a ton, a few grams, weigh little NOT for: considering something carefully
examples: The baby weighed three kilos at birth.
The box was so full of books that it weighed a ton.

weigh.definition: to use a machine to find out how much something or someone weighs
weigh.note: typical: weigh yourself, the flour, potatoes, on the scales, weigh a parcel NOT for: having a particular weight
examples: She weighed the flour on the scales.
Have you weighed yourself lately?

weigh.definition: to consider something carefully so that you can make a decision about it (also weigh up)
weigh.note: typical: weigh the evidence, the options, the risks, weigh sth against sth, weigh up NOT for: finding the weight of something
examples: The judge weighed the evidence carefully.
We have to weigh the benefits against the costs.

weigh.definition: to influence someone's opinion and the decision they make (formal)
weigh.note: typical: weigh against, in favour of, weigh heavily, weigh with the judge NOT for: considering a decision yourself
examples: Her evidence weighed strongly with the judge.
These facts will weigh in your favour.

whisper.definition: to speak or say something very quietly, using your breath rather than your voice
whisper.note: typical: whisper sth to sb, whisper in sb's ear, whisper about, softly NOT for: spreading a private rumour
examples: You don't have to whisper, no one can hear us.
'I've missed you,' he whispered in her ear.

whisper.definition: to say or suggest something privately or secretly
whisper.note: typical: whisper that, it is whispered that, rumours are whispered, in the corridors NOT for: speaking quietly to someone next to you
examples: Staff were whispering that the company was about to close.
It is whispered that she will resign.

wind.definition: to turn or twist something several times around something else
wind.note: typical: wind sth around, round sth, wind a scarf, wool, a bandage, thread NOT for: turning a clock key
examples: She wound the scarf around her neck.
He wound the rope around the post.

wind.definition: to turn part of a machine around several times in order to make it move or start working (also wind up)
wind.note: typical: wind a clock, a watch, a toy, wind up, a handle NOT for: winding wool around something
examples: Did you remember to wind the clock?
She wound the toy car up and let it go.

wind.definition: if a road, river or similar winds somewhere, it has many smooth bends
wind.note: typical: a road, river, path winds, wind through, along, wind its way, a winding road NOT for: turning a handle
examples: The road winds along the coast.
A narrow river winds through the valley.

wind.definition: to make a tape move in a machine (wind forward/back)
wind.note: typical: wind sth back, forward, a tape, a video, a film, a cassette NOT for: bending roads or rivers
examples: Can you wind the tape back a little?
He wound the video forward to the end.

wind.definition: to make someone have difficulty breathing, as a result of falling on something or being hit
wind.note: typical: be winded, winded by a punch, a fall, a blow, a kick NOT for: turning a handle
examples: The fall winded him and he lay still for a moment.
She was winded by a ball to the stomach.

withdraw.definition: to stop taking part in an activity or belonging to an organisation, or to make someone do this
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw from a competition, a race, a treaty, the union, withdraw sb from NOT for: taking money out of a bank
examples: A knee injury forced her to withdraw from the competition.
Parents can withdraw their children from religious lessons.

withdraw.definition: to stop giving support or money to someone or something, especially as a result of an official decision
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw support, funding, aid, labour, withdraw sth from NOT for: saying a remark was untrue
examples: The party has withdrawn its support for the leader.
The government decided to withdraw funding for the programme.

withdraw.definition: to say that you no longer will do what you said, such as a threat, offer or request
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw an offer, a threat, a request, a resignation, an application NOT for: taking back a statement
examples: After much persuasion he agreed to withdraw his resignation.
The company withdrew its offer.

withdraw.definition: to say that something you said earlier was completely untrue (formal)
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw a remark, a comment, an allegation, a claim, a statement NOT for: cancelling an offer
examples: He refused to withdraw his remarks.
The newspaper agreed to withdraw its allegations.

withdraw.definition: to stop offering a product or service for sale or use (usually passive)
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw sth from sale, the market, a drug, a product, a service NOT for: moving soldiers out of a place
examples: The drug has been withdrawn from the market.
The company withdrew the toy from sale.

withdraw.definition: to leave a place (of an army), or to make an army leave
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw troops, forces, an army, from a region, withdraw from NOT for: going to a quiet place
examples: The government decided to withdraw troops from the region.
The army withdrew from the city at night.

withdraw.definition: to leave a place, especially in order to be alone or go somewhere quiet
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw to, the garden, the study, a private room, for a talk NOT for: an army leaving a country
examples: We withdrew to the garden for a private talk.
The jury withdrew to consider its verdict.

withdraw.definition: to take money out of a bank account
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw cash, money, $500, from your account, from an ATM NOT for: removing a hand
examples: I'd like to withdraw 500 pounds from my account.
You can withdraw cash at any machine.

withdraw.definition: to move your hand, arm or finger from somewhere back to where it was before
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw your hand, arm, finger, from, quickly NOT for: taking cash out of a bank
examples: Claudia withdrew her hand from his.
He withdrew his arm from the water.

withdraw.definition: to take an object out from inside something (literary)
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw sth from sth, a document, a knife, a letter, a sword NOT for: moving a hand away
examples: She withdrew a document from her briefcase.
He withdrew a small key from his pocket.

withdraw.definition: to become quieter, less friendly and concerned only with your own thoughts
withdraw.note: typical: withdraw into yourself, from other people, from friends, feel withdrawn NOT for: leaving a place
examples: Ralph has withdrawn from the other children.
Many depressed people just withdraw into themselves.

witness.definition: to see something happen, especially a crime or accident
witness.note: typical: witness an accident, a crime, an attack, a murder, witness the event NOT for: signing a document
examples: Several residents witnessed the attack.
She witnessed the accident from her window.

witness.definition: to experience important events or changes
witness.note: typical: witness a change, an increase, the collapse of, a dramatic rise, witness history NOT for: seeing a crime
examples: Priests have witnessed an increase in religious intolerance.
Many of us witnessed huge changes in our lifetime.

witness.definition: to take place during a particular time or in a particular place (of a time or place)
witness.note: typical: the decade witnessed, recent years have witnessed, the city witnessed NOT for: a person seeing an event
examples: Recent years have witnessed the collapse of the steel industry.
The 1960s witnessed great social change.

witness.definition: to be present when an official document is signed, and sign it yourself to prove this
witness.note: typical: witness a signature, a will, a contract, a document, witness sb signing NOT for: seeing an accident
examples: Will you witness my signature?
Two people must witness the will.

witness.definition: to speak publicly about your Christian beliefs
witness.note: typical: witness to your faith, witness for Christ, testify, in public NOT for: seeing a crime
examples: He witnessed to his faith in front of the congregation.
The group travelled to witness for their church.

wreck.definition: to completely spoil something so that it cannot continue in a successful way
wreck.note: typical: wreck a career, a marriage, a plan, someone's life, a chance NOT for: damaging a vehicle or a building
examples: Injury threatened to wreck his sporting career.
It was drink that wrecked their marriage.

wreck.definition: to damage something such as a building or vehicle so badly that it cannot be repaired
wreck.note: typical: wreck a car, a house, a room, a boat, be wrecked in an accident NOT for: ruining a plan
examples: The car was completely wrecked in the accident.
The storm wrecked several houses.

wreck.definition: to badly damage a ship so that it sinks (usually passive)
wreck.note: typical: be wrecked, a ship wrecked off the coast, on the rocks, in a storm NOT for: ruining a plan
examples: The ship was wrecked off the coast of Africa.
Their boat was wrecked on the rocks.

adapt.definition: to gradually change your behaviour and attitudes in order to be successful in a new situation
adapt.note: typical: adapt to a new school, life, a situation, a climate, adapt yourself NOT for: changing an object for a new use
examples: The children are finding it hard to adapt to the new school.
Animals must adapt to a changing climate.

adapt.definition: to change something to make it suitable for a different purpose
adapt.note: typical: adapt sth to, for, adapt a car, a room, materials, a recipe NOT for: changing yourself to a new place
examples: The car has been adapted to take unleaded fuel.
These teaching materials can be adapted for older children.

adapt.definition: to change a book or play so that it can be made into a film, television programme or similar (usually passive)
adapt.note: typical: be adapted for film, television, the stage, a novel adapted NOT for: changing yourself to a place
examples: The novel was adapted for television.
Many children buy books after they have been adapted for the screen.

address.definition: to write the name and address of the person you are sending something to on an envelope or package
address.note: typical: address an envelope, a package, a letter, address sth to sb, self-addressed NOT for: speaking to someone
examples: The letter was addressed to me.
Please send a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

address.definition: to start trying to solve a problem (formal)
address.note: typical: address a problem, an issue, a question, concerns, needs, address yourself to NOT for: making a speech
examples: The government must address the problem of housing.
Our products address the needs of real users.

address.note: typical: address sb, address the man, turn to address, address a remark to NOT for: writing on an envelope
examples: She turned to address the man on her left.
He addressed the child in a gentle voice.

address.definition: to say or write remarks, complaints or similar directly to a particular person (formal)
address.note: typical: address a remark to, a complaint to, address your comments to NOT for: giving a speech to a crowd
examples: You will have to address your comments to the manager.
He addressed his question to the chairman.

address.definition: to make a formal speech to a large group of people
address.note: typical: address a meeting, a conference, an audience, the nation, the crowd NOT for: speaking to one person
examples: The president addressed the nation on television.
He addressed an audience of ten thousand supporters.

address.definition: to use a particular title or name when speaking or writing to someone
address.note: typical: address sb as sth, as Sir, as Doctor, by their first name, formally NOT for: making a speech
examples: The president should be addressed as 'Mr President'.
The students address their teacher as 'Miss'.

adjust.definition: to gradually become familiar with a new situation
adjust.note: typical: adjust to a new life, to doing sth, to the dark, adjust quickly NOT for: changing a machine slightly
examples: It took a few seconds for her eyes to adjust to the darkness.
My parents had trouble adjusting to living in a flat.

adjust.definition: to change or move something slightly to improve it or make it more suitable for a particular purpose
adjust.note: typical: adjust the brakes, the temperature, the volume, the seasoning, the settings NOT for: moving clothes into place
examples: Check and adjust the brakes regularly.
Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning.

adjust.definition: to move something you are wearing slightly so that it is neater or more comfortable
adjust.note: typical: adjust your glasses, tie, hat, collar, clothing, your seat belt NOT for: changing a machine's setting
examples: He paused to adjust his glasses.
She adjusted her tie before the interview.

allocate.definition: to use something, such as money or time, for a particular purpose
allocate.note: typical: allocate funds, money, time, resources, space, allocate sth to sth NOT for: giving jobs to specific people
examples: The council allocated money for a new playground.
We should allocate more time to this task.

allocate.definition: to give something to a particular person or group as their share
allocate.note: typical: allocate sth to sb, seats, rooms, tasks, places, be allocated NOT for: using money for a purpose
examples: Each student was allocated a locker.
The tickets were allocated to the first applicants.

analyse.definition: to examine or think about something carefully in order to understand it
analyse.note: typical: analyse data, results, a situation, a problem, why, the evidence NOT for: testing a substance in a lab
examples: She still needs to analyse the data.
You need to analyse why you feel so upset.

analyse.definition: to examine a substance to see what it is made of
analyse.note: typical: analyse a sample, blood, soil, water, a substance, in a lab NOT for: thinking about a problem
examples: The cell samples were analysed in a laboratory.
Scientists analysed the soil for chemicals.

analyse.definition: to examine someone's mental or emotional problems by using psychoanalysis
analyse.note: typical: analyse a patient, a client, be analysed, by a psychiatrist NOT for: testing a substance
examples: The therapist analysed his dreams.
She was analysed by a leading psychiatrist.

appoint.definition: to choose someone for a position or a job
appoint.note: typical: appoint sb as sth, appoint sb to sth, appoint sb to do sth, a new manager, a committee NOT for: arranging a time or a place
examples: She was appointed as head teacher.
A committee was appointed to consider the plans.

appoint.definition: to arrange or decide a time or place for something to happen (formal)
appoint.note: typical: appoint a time, a day, a place, the appointed time, at the appointed hour NOT for: choosing someone for a job
examples: The committee appointed a day in June for the celebrations.
Everyone arrived at the appointed time.

assess.definition: to make a judgment about a person or situation after thinking carefully about it
assess.note: typical: assess the impact, the risk, the damage, the situation, a student, a candidate NOT for: calculating the value of something
examples: The report assesses the impact of advertising on children.
Teachers assess pupils' progress every term.

assess.definition: to calculate the value or cost of something
assess.note: typical: assess the value, the cost, the damage, be assessed at, a property NOT for: judging a person
examples: The value of the business was assessed at 1.25 million pounds.
An expert will assess the damage to the roof.

assign.definition: to give someone a particular job or make them responsible for a particular person or thing
assign.note: typical: assign sb a task, to a project, assign sb to do sth, be assigned to NOT for: giving a time or a code to something
examples: I've been assigned the task of looking after new students.
He was assigned to investigate the accident.

assign.definition: to give a particular time, value, place or similar to something
assign.note: typical: assign a time, a code, a value, a number, a seat, assign sth to sth NOT for: giving someone a job
examples: How much time have you assigned for the meeting?
A code was assigned to each batch of work.

assign.definition: to give money, equipment or similar to someone to use
assign.note: typical: assign sth to sb, a room, a bodyguard, a car, a desk NOT for: giving a task to someone
examples: A personal bodyguard had been assigned to her.
They assigned me a small room.

assure.definition: to tell someone that something will definitely happen or is definitely true so that they are less worried
assure.note: typical: assure sb that, assure sb of sth, I can assure you, be assured NOT for: checking something yourself
examples: Her doctor assured us that she would be fine.
I can assure you that the document is genuine.

assure.definition: to make something certain to happen or to be achieved
assure.note: typical: assure success, victory, promotion, assure sb of sth, a place NOT for: telling someone not to worry
examples: Excellent reviews have assured the film's success.
A win on Saturday will assure them of promotion.

assure.definition: to check that something is correct or true (formal; assure yourself)
assure.note: typical: assure yourself that, assure yourself of, check, make certain NOT for: promising someone
examples: He waited a moment to assure himself that he was not being followed.
She took steps to assure herself of his honesty.

authorise.definition: to give official permission for something, or to give someone the official right to do something
authorise.note: typical: authorise sb to do sth, a payment, an action, an investigation, authorised by NOT for: writing a book
examples: The manager authorised the payment.
Napoleon III authorised Haussmann to rebuild Paris.

bet.definition: to risk money on the result of a race, game, competition or other future event
bet.note: typical: bet on a horse, a game, bet sb that, bet money, bet against, bet heavily NOT for: saying you are fairly sure of something
examples: She bet all her money on a horse that came last.
He bet me ten pounds that I wouldn't do it.

bet.definition: to say that you are fairly sure that something is true or will happen (spoken, as in I bet)
bet.note: typical: I bet, I bet you, I'll bet, bet you can't, bet he forgot NOT for: risking money on a race
examples: I bet she won't come.
'I was so angry.' 'I bet you were.'

betray.definition: to be disloyal to someone who trusts you, so that they are harmed or upset
betray.note: typical: betray a friend, a trust, betray sb to sb, betray a confidence, feel betrayed NOT for: showing a feeling by accident
examples: He felt that she had betrayed him.
I would never betray a confidence.

betray.definition: to be disloyal to your country, company or similar, for example by giving secret information to its enemies
betray.note: typical: betray your country, a cause, a company, the party, for money NOT for: hurting a friend
examples: People who betray their country for money are called traitors.
He betrayed the company's secrets to a rival.

betray.definition: to show feelings that you are trying to hide
betray.note: typical: betray nervousness, fear, emotion, betray nothing, voice betrayed NOT for: being disloyal to a friend
examples: His voice betrayed his nervousness.
His face betrayed nothing.

betray.definition: to show that something is true or exists, especially when it is not easily noticed
betray.note: typical: betray sb's presence, the fact that, a sound betrayed, give away NOT for: showing hidden emotions
examples: The slightest sound might betray his presence.
The crumpled sheets betrayed the fact that someone had slept there.

betray.definition: to stop supporting your old beliefs and principles, especially in order to get power or avoid trouble
betray.note: typical: betray your beliefs, principles, ideals, values, betray your own NOT for: telling a secret
examples: The party was accused of betraying its principles.
He betrayed his ideals for a place in government.

blame.definition: to say or think that someone or something is responsible for something bad
blame.note: typical: blame sb for sth, blame sth on sb, blame yourself, widely blamed, unfairly blamed NOT for: describing who is at fault with 'to blame'
examples: Don't blame me; it's not my fault.
The report blames poor safety standards for the accident.

blame.definition: to be responsible for something bad (be to blame)
blame.note: typical: be to blame for, partly to blame, largely to blame, who is to blame NOT for: saying someone caused a problem
examples: Officials believe that more than one person may be to blame for the fire.
Television is partly to blame.

boost.definition: to increase or improve something and make it more successful
boost.note: typical: boost sales, confidence, morale, the economy, tourism, profits NOT for: lifting a person
examples: The new resort has boosted tourism.
The win boosted the team's confidence.

boost.definition: to help someone reach a higher place by lifting or pushing them (also boost up)
boost.note: typical: boost sb up, boost sb over a wall, onto a horse, onto a ledge NOT for: improving sales
examples: He boosted her up onto the wall.
She boosted the child up so that he could see.

boost.definition: to make a spacecraft go up into space or in a particular direction (of a rocket or motor)
boost.note: typical: a rocket boosts, a motor boosts, boost a spacecraft, boost a satellite NOT for: improving morale
examples: The rocket boosted the satellite into orbit.
A powerful motor boosts the craft out of the atmosphere.

boost.note: typical: boost a car, a bike, a phone, a wallet, boost from a shop NOT for: increasing something
examples: He got arrested for boosting cars.
Someone boosted my bike last night.

broaden.definition: to increase something such as your knowledge, experience or range of activities
broaden.note: typical: broaden your knowledge, horizons, experience, mind, range, outlook NOT for: making something physically wider
examples: The course helps school-leavers broaden their knowledge of work.
Travel broadens the mind.

broaden.definition: to affect or include more people or things, or to make something do this
broaden.note: typical: broaden the appeal, the discussion, the scope, broaden to include NOT for: making a road wider
examples: The party must broaden its appeal to younger voters.
I want to broaden the discussion to other aspects of the problem.

broaden.definition: to make something wider, or to become wider
broaden.note: typical: broaden a road, a pavement, a smile, a river, a path, broaden out NOT for: increasing your knowledge
examples: Mark's smile broadened.
The council decided to broaden the pavement.

campaign.definition: to lead or take part in a series of actions intended to achieve a particular social or political result
campaign.note: typical: campaign for, campaign against, campaign for change, a group campaigning, tirelessly NOT for: standing in an election
examples: A group is campaigning against the destruction of the rainforest.
She has campaigned for equal pay for years.

cancel.definition: to decide that something that was officially planned will not happen
cancel.note: typical: cancel a flight, a meeting, a concert, an appointment, a match, be cancelled NOT for: ending a contract or a subscription
examples: Our flight was cancelled.
I'm afraid I'll have to cancel our meeting tomorrow.

cancel.definition: to end an agreement or arrangement that you have with someone
cancel.note: typical: cancel a reservation, a contract, a subscription, an order, a debt NOT for: calling off an event
examples: I phoned the hotel to cancel my reservation.
The bank agreed to cancel all the company's debts.

cancel.definition: to say officially that a document can no longer be used or no longer has any legal effect
cancel.note: typical: cancel a cheque, a card, a ticket, a passport, a visa NOT for: calling off an event
examples: I phoned the bank to cancel the cheque.
The airline cancelled his ticket.

chase.definition: to quickly follow someone or something in order to catch them
chase.note: typical: chase a thief, a car, a ball, chase after, chase sb along, down NOT for: forcing someone to leave
examples: The dogs saw him running and chased him.
Police chased the suspect along the street.

chase.definition: to make someone or something leave, especially by following them a short distance and threatening them
chase.note: typical: chase sb away, off, out of, chase the dog out of the garden NOT for: following someone to catch them
examples: Anne went to chase the dog out of the garden.
The farmer chased the boys off his land.

chase.definition: to use a lot of time and effort trying to get something such as work or money
chase.note: typical: chase a job, a story, a payment, money, chase after sth, chase a deal NOT for: following a person in a race
examples: Reporters were chasing after a story.
Major companies are chasing top graduates.

chase.definition: to rush or hurry somewhere (British English)
chase.note: typical: chase around, up, down, chase about getting things organised NOT for: running after a criminal
examples: I spent the morning chasing around getting everything organised.
She chased up and down the stairs all day.

chase.definition: to try hard to make someone notice you and pay attention to you because you want a romantic relationship with them
chase.note: typical: chase a girl, a boy, a man, a woman, be chased, chase after NOT for: chasing a thief
examples: 'Sometimes a girl wants to be chased,' Amelia said.
He spent years chasing after her.

chase.definition: to decorate metal with a special tool (technical)
chase.note: typical: chase silver, gold, metal, chased silver, a chased pattern NOT for: following someone
examples: The craftsman chased the silver cup by hand.
The box was made of chased silver.

cheer.definition: to shout as a way of showing happiness, praise, approval or support
cheer.note: typical: cheer wildly, loudly, cheer sb, cheer and clap, the crowd cheered NOT for: making someone feel more hopeful
examples: Everybody cheered when the firemen arrived.
The spectators cheered the winner wildly.

cheer.definition: to make someone feel more hopeful when they are worried
cheer.note: typical: cheer sb, cheer the nation, news that cheered them all, cheering news NOT for: shouting in support
examples: By late afternoon there came news that cheered them all.
The warm weather cheered everyone.

coincide.definition: to happen at the same time as something else, especially by chance
coincide.note: typical: coincide with, planned to coincide, dates coincide, holidays coincide NOT for: ideas or opinions being the same
examples: His entry to the party coincided with his marriage.
The show is timed to coincide with the launch of a new book.

coincide.definition: if two people's ideas or opinions coincide, they are the same
coincide.note: typical: opinions coincide, interests coincide, views coincide, coincide with NOT for: events happening at the same time
examples: The interests of the two countries may not coincide.
Her views coincided perfectly with mine.

coincide.definition: to meet or be in the same place
coincide.note: typical: coincide in part, a route coincides, the border coincides with, the road coincides NOT for: events happening together
examples: The journey coincides in part with the old Roman road.
The boundary coincides with the river.

collaborate.definition: to work together with a person or group in order to achieve something, especially in science or art
collaborate.note: typical: collaborate with, on, to do sth, in doing sth, closely, scientists collaborate NOT for: helping an enemy in war
examples: The two nations are collaborating on several satellite projects.
Researchers are collaborating to develop a vaccine.

collaborate.definition: to help a country that your country is fighting a war with, especially one that has taken control of your country
collaborate.note: typical: collaborate with the enemy, the invaders, the occupiers, accused of collaborating NOT for: working with a partner on a project
examples: Vigilantes began searching for anyone who had collaborated with the enemy.
She was accused of collaborating with the occupying army.

collide.definition: to hit something or someone that is moving in a different direction from you
collide.note: typical: collide with, collide head-on, a car and a van collided, in mid-air NOT for: having a disagreement
examples: A car and a van collided on the motorway.
The two players collided with each other going for the ball.

collide.definition: if ideas, interests or groups collide, they come into serious conflict with each other
collide.note: typical: interests collide, worlds collide, cultures collide, collide with NOT for: vehicles hitting each other
examples: The interests of the two companies were bound to collide.
Different cultures collide in this city.

compensate.definition: to replace or balance the effect of something bad
compensate.note: typical: compensate for sth, make up for, compensate for a lack of, lose in one way and gain in another NOT for: paying someone money
examples: Because my left eye is weak, my right eye has to work harder to compensate.
Her intelligence more than compensates for her lack of experience.

compensate.definition: to pay someone money because they have suffered injury, loss or damage
compensate.note: typical: compensate sb for sth, victims, workers, customers, compensate for loss NOT for: balancing something bad
examples: The firm will compensate workers for their loss of earnings.
The government promised to compensate the victims of the flood.

compile.definition: to make a book, list, record or similar using different pieces of information, music or other material
compile.note: typical: compile a list, a report, a dictionary, an album, compile sth from sth NOT for: turning code into a program
examples: The report was compiled from a survey of 5,000 households.
She compiled a list of useful websites.

compile.definition: to put a set of instructions into a computer in a form that it can understand and use (technical)
compile.note: typical: compile a program, code, source code, software, compile and run NOT for: collecting information for a report
examples: You need to compile the code before you can run it.
The software compiles in a few seconds.

comply.definition: to do what you have to do or are asked to do (formal)
comply.note: typical: comply with the law, the rules, regulations, a request, an order, fail to comply NOT for: choosing to do something freely
examples: Failure to comply with the regulations will result in prosecution.
The newspaper agreed to comply.

compose.definition: to be formed from a number of substances, parts or people (be composed of)
compose.note: typical: be composed of, the committee, water, a team composed of NOT for: writing music
examples: Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen.
The committee is composed of ten members.

compose.definition: to combine together to form something (formal)
compose.note: typical: compose a sector, a team, a whole, make up, the firms that compose NOT for: writing a poem
examples: More than seventeen million firms compose the business sector.
The ten smaller states compose the union.

compose.definition: to write a piece of music

compose.definition: to try hard to become calm after feeling angry, upset or excited (compose yourself, your face, your thoughts)

compose.definition: to arrange the parts of a painting, photograph or scene in a way that achieves a particular result
compose.note: typical: compose a photo, a picture, a shot, a scene, a painting, carefully NOT for: writing a letter

conclude.definition: to decide that something is true after considering all the information you have

conclude.definition: to complete something you have been doing, especially for a long time (formal)

conclude.definition: to end something such as a meeting, book, event or speech by doing or saying one final thing

conclude.definition: to finish arranging an agreement, treaty or contract successfully

conduct.definition: to carry out a particular activity or process, especially in order to get information or prove facts

conduct.definition: to stand in front of a group of musicians or singers and direct their playing or singing

conduct.definition: to behave in a particular way (formal; conduct yourself)

conduct.definition: to allow electricity or heat to travel along or through something

conduct.definition: to take or lead someone somewhere (formal)
conduct.note: typical: conduct sb to sth, a conducted tour, conduct guests, be conducted to NOT for: allowing heat to pass through

configure.definition: to arrange something, especially computer equipment, so that it works with other equipment (technical)

confront.definition: if a problem or difficulty confronts you, it appears and needs to be dealt with
confront.note: typical: be confronted with, problems confront, a choice, a dilemma, the challenge confronting NOT for: facing an enemy

console.definition: to make someone feel better when they are feeling sad or disappointed
console.note: typical: console sb, console yourself with, console a child, a widow, try to console NOT for: giving advice

construct.definition: to build something such as a house, bridge or road
construct.note: typical: construct a bridge, a road, a building, a model, construct sth from, of NOT for: forming an argument

construct.definition: to form something such as a sentence, argument or system by joining words, ideas or parts together

construct.note: typical: construct a square, a triangle, a circle, with a ruler, with a compass NOT for: building something

consult.definition: to ask for information or advice from someone because it is their job to know something
consult.note: typical: consult a doctor, a lawyer, an expert, consult with sb, consult sb about sth NOT for: looking something up in a book

consult.definition: to discuss something with someone so that you can make a decision together
consult.note: typical: consult with, consult sb before, consult the staff, the public, without consulting NOT for: asking a professional for advice

consult.definition: to look for information in a book, map, list or similar
consult.note: typical: consult a dictionary, a map, a timetable, the manual, a guide NOT for: asking a person for advice

contribute.definition: to give money, help, ideas or similar to something that a lot of other people are also involved in
contribute.note: typical: contribute to, towards, contribute money, time, ideas, contribute sth to sth NOT for: helping to cause something

contribute.definition: to help to make something happen
contribute.note: typical: contribute to, a factor, contribute significantly, to the problem, to the decline NOT for: giving money to a fund

contribute.definition: to write articles, stories, poems or similar for a newspaper or magazine
contribute.note: typical: contribute to a magazine, a newspaper, a book, an article, contribute regularly NOT for: giving money

convert.definition: to change something into a different form, or into something that can be used for a different purpose; or (of something) to change into a different form

convert.definition: to score extra points after a try or touchdown in rugby or American football

convey.definition: to communicate or express something, with or without using words
convey.note: typical: convey a message, an idea, a sense of, an impression, convey sth to sb NOT for: carrying goods from one place to another

convey.definition: to take or carry something from one place to another (formal)

convey.definition: to legally change the possession of property from one person to another (law)

coordinate.definition: to organise an activity so that the people involved in it work well together and achieve a good result

coordinate.note: typical: coordinate with, colours coordinate, curtains and cushions, coordinate your outfit NOT for: organising people

cure.note: typical: cure unemployment, poverty, a problem, an ill, the economy NOT for: healing a sick person

He could hardly drag himself up the stairs.

drag.definition: to persuade or force someone to go somewhere with you when they do not want to
drag.note: typical: drag sb to a party, a concert, a shop, informal NOT for: pulling someone physically
examples: My sister dragged me to a dance class.
I had to drag my brother to the dentist.

drag.definition: to move words, pictures or files on a computer screen by pulling them with the mouse
drag.note: typical: drag and drop, drag a file, an icon, a window NOT for: pulling a physical object
examples: You can drag the photo into the folder.
Drag the box to make the window bigger.

drag.definition: if time or an event drags, it seems to go very slowly because nothing interesting is happening
drag.note: typical: the day drags, a meeting drags, time drags NOT for: pulling things; no object
examples: The lesson seemed to drag on forever.
Monday mornings always drag.

drag.definition: if something is dragging along the ground, part of it is touching the ground as you move
drag.note: typical: dragging in the mud, along the floor, behind you NOT for: pulling something on purpose
examples: Your scarf is dragging on the floor.
The broken wing was dragging along the ground.

elaborate.definition: to give more details or new information about something
elaborate.note: typical: elaborate on, refuse to elaborate, elaborate further NOT for: making something complicated
examples: She refused to elaborate on her reasons for leaving.
Could you elaborate a little on that point?

eliminate.definition: to completely get rid of something that is unnecessary or unwanted
eliminate.note: typical: eliminate a risk, a need, errors, waste, a problem, eliminate sth from sth NOT for: knocking a team out of a contest
examples: New software has eliminated most of the errors.
Doctors hope to eliminate the disease within ten years.

eliminate.definition: to defeat a team or person in a competition so that they no longer take part in it
eliminate.note: typical: be eliminated in the first round, be eliminated from the competition, usually passive NOT for: removing unwanted things
examples: Our team was eliminated in the semi-final.
Two contestants are eliminated every week.

eliminate.definition: to kill someone in order to prevent them from causing trouble
eliminate.note: typical: eliminate a rival, an enemy, a witness NOT for: everyday removal of problems
examples: The dictator eliminated everyone who opposed him.
Gangs fought to eliminate their rivals.

embrace.definition: to put your arms around someone and hold them in a friendly or loving way
embrace.note: typical: embrace warmly, embrace each other, they embraced NOT for: accepting ideas
examples: She ran to the door and embraced her mother.
The two old friends embraced at the station.

embrace.definition: to eagerly accept an idea, belief, change or opportunity
embrace.note: typical: embrace change, an idea, a new technology, a religion, a challenge, formal NOT for: physical hugging
examples: The company has embraced new technology.
Many young people quickly embraced the new style of music.

embrace.definition: to include something as part of a larger group or subject
embrace.note: typical: embrace a wide range of, formal; written style NOT for: hugging or welcoming ideas
examples: The course embraces history, art and politics.
Her interests embrace everything from chemistry to jazz.

emerge.definition: to appear or come out from somewhere
emerge.note: typical: emerge from behind, from a building, from the water, from the shadows NOT for: facts becoming known
examples: The sun emerged from behind the clouds.
A small boy emerged from the crowd.

emerge.definition: if facts emerge, they become known after being hidden or secret
emerge.note: typical: the truth emerged, it later emerged that, details emerged NOT for: coming out of a place
examples: Eventually the truth emerged.
It later emerged that the manager had known about the problem.

emerge.definition: to come out of a difficult experience
emerge.note: typical: emerge from a crisis, a war, a divorce, a recession, emerge stronger NOT for: appearing from a place
examples: She emerged from the illness a stronger person.
The country is slowly emerging from recession.

emerge.definition: to begin to be known or noticed
emerge.note: typical: emerge as, a new leader emerges, a pattern emerges, a trend emerges NOT for: physically coming out
examples: A clear pattern emerged from the results.
He emerged as the leading candidate for the job.

emphasise.definition: to say something in a strong way to show that it is important
emphasise.note: typical: emphasise the importance of, the need for, emphasise that NOT for: making a word louder
examples: The report emphasises the importance of regular exercise.
The teacher emphasised that everyone must arrive on time.

emphasise.definition: to say a word or phrase louder or higher than others to give it more importance
emphasise.note: typical: emphasise a word, a syllable, a phrase NOT for: stressing a general point
examples: He emphasised the last word of the sentence.
In this word, you emphasise the second syllable.

emphasise.note: typical: emphasise the shape of, a colour, a feature, a feeling NOT for: speaking about importance
examples: The dark frame emphasises the colours in the painting.
The cut of the dress emphasised her height.

enable.definition: to make it possible for someone to do something, or for something to happen
enable.note: typical: enable sb to do sth, enable sth to happen, technology enables NOT for: forcing someone to act
examples: The loan enabled her to buy a small flat.
New software enables users to share files easily.

endanger.definition: to put someone or something in danger of being hurt, damaged or destroyed
endanger.note: typical: endanger lives, health, safety, an endangered species NOT for: actually causing harm
examples: Drivers who speed endanger the lives of others.
Pollution is endangering the fish in the river.

endure.definition: to be in a difficult or painful situation for a long time without complaining
endure.note: typical: endure pain, hardship, suffering, endure doing sth NOT for: things that remain in existence
examples: The soldiers endured months of cold and hunger.
I can't endure waiting any longer.

endure.definition: to remain alive or continue to exist for a long time
endure.note: typical: friendship endures, memories endure, a tradition endures, enduring NOT for: suffering something unpleasant; no object
examples: Their friendship has endured for fifty years.
Her stories have endured for generations.

enforce.definition: to make people obey a rule or law
enforce.note: typical: enforce a law, a rule, a ban, a contract, strictly enforced NOT for: forcing personal opinions on someone
examples: The police enforce the speed limit on this road.
The school strictly enforces its rules about phones.

enforce.definition: to make something happen or force someone to do something
enforce.note: typical: enforce sth on sb, enforce discipline, enforce silence NOT for: obeying laws
examples: The teacher enforced silence in the classroom.
They tried to enforce their ideas on the whole team.

engage.definition: to be doing something or become involved in an activity
engage.note: typical: engage in, engage in talks, in a conversation, in crime, be engaged in NOT for: being engaged to marry
examples: The two countries have engaged in talks for several months.
Students should engage in regular exercise.

engage.definition: to attract someone's attention and keep them interested
engage.note: typical: engage sb's interest, attention, engage sb in conversation NOT for: employing someone
examples: The toy did not engage the child's interest for long.
A good teacher knows how to engage a class.

engage.definition: to get involved with other people or ideas and try to understand them
engage.note: typical: engage with sb, engage with ideas, a community, a problem NOT for: being busy with an activity
examples: Politicians must engage with young voters.
Do you have the energy to engage with your children after work?

engage.definition: to employ someone to do a particular job, especially a professional
engage.note: typical: engage a lawyer, a tutor, a consultant, formal NOT for: attracting attention
examples: Her father engaged a tutor to help her with maths.
The firm engaged an expert to examine the building.

enhance.definition: to improve something or make it better, stronger or more valuable
enhance.note: typical: enhance a reputation, performance, quality, appearance, experience NOT for: making something bigger in size only
examples: Good lighting will enhance any room.
The publicity has enhanced his reputation.

eradicate.definition: to completely get rid of something such as a disease or a social problem
eradicate.note: typical: eradicate a disease, poverty, crime, corruption, eradicate sth from sth NOT for: partly reducing a problem
examples: The disease was finally eradicated from the country.
The government wants to eradicate poverty.

escalate.definition: if fighting, violence or a bad situation escalates, or if someone escalates it, it becomes much worse
escalate.note: typical: a conflict, a dispute, violence, a crisis escalates, escalate into NOT for: prices or amounts simply rising
