examples: The argument quickly escalated into a fight.
Neither side wants to escalate the conflict.

escalate.definition: to become higher or increase, or to make something do this
escalate.note: typical: costs escalate, prices escalate, escalating costs NOT for: a conflict becoming worse
examples: Building costs have escalated sharply.
Escalating prices forced many families to move away.

evaluate.definition: to judge how good, useful or successful something is
evaluate.note: typical: evaluate a plan, the effectiveness of, the performance of, evaluate options NOT for: calculating a number only
examples: We need to evaluate the success of the campaign.
Teachers evaluate each student's progress every term.

evolve.definition: if an animal or plant evolves, it changes gradually over a very long period of time
evolve.note: typical: species evolve, evolve from, evolve into, evolve a feature NOT for: ideas or businesses changing
examples: Birds evolved from small dinosaurs.
Many animals have evolved ways to hide from predators.

evolve.definition: to develop and change gradually over a long period of time
evolve.note: typical: an idea, a system, a style evolves, evolve into, evolve from NOT for: biological change in species
examples: The small shop evolved into a large company.
Our teaching methods have evolved over the years.

exceed.definition: to be more than a particular number or amount
exceed.note: typical: exceed the limit, expectations, a total, a budget, exceed $/£/% NOT for: breaking a rule or law
examples: Working hours must not exceed forty a week.
The final cost greatly exceeded our expectations.

exceed.definition: to go beyond what rules or laws say you are allowed to do
exceed.note: typical: exceed the speed limit, your authority, your powers NOT for: being more than an amount
examples: The driver was fined for exceeding the speed limit.
The officer exceeded his authority by ordering the search.

exhibit.definition: to show something in a public place so that people can go to see it
exhibit.note: typical: exhibit paintings, work, photographs, exhibit at a gallery NOT for: showing a feeling or quality
examples: Her paintings have been exhibited in several countries.
The museum will exhibit the ancient coins next month.

exhibit.definition: to clearly show a particular quality, emotion or ability
exhibit.note: typical: exhibit signs, symptoms, behaviour, courage, formal NOT for: putting objects on public display
examples: The patient was exhibiting signs of stress.
The children exhibited great curiosity about the machine.

exploit.definition: to treat someone unfairly by making them work or do things for you while giving them very little in return
exploit.note: typical: exploit workers, children, employees, exploit sb's generosity NOT for: using resources fully
examples: Some employers exploit migrant workers by paying them very little.
He felt that his friends were exploiting his kindness.

exploit.definition: to try to get as much as you can out of a situation, sometimes unfairly
exploit.note: typical: exploit a situation, a weakness, a mistake, an opportunity NOT for: developing natural resources
examples: The company exploited the confusion to raise its prices.
Opponents exploited every weakness in his argument.

exploit.definition: to use something fully and effectively
exploit.note: typical: exploit potential, talent, an advantage, a market, technology NOT for: treating people unfairly
examples: The team failed to exploit its chances in the first half.
The firm hopes to exploit the potential of the new technology.

exploit.definition: to develop and use minerals, forests, oil and similar resources for business or industry
exploit.note: typical: exploit resources, oil, coal, forests, reserves NOT for: using an opportunity
examples: The country plans to exploit its large reserves of natural gas.
Companies began to exploit the forests of the region.

expose.definition: to show something that is usually covered or hidden
expose.note: typical: expose a scar, a wire, a root, skin, expose sth to sth NOT for: revealing a secret
examples: He lifted his shirt to expose a long scar.
The storm exposed the roots of the old tree.

expose.definition: to put someone in a situation where they are not protected from something dangerous or unpleasant
expose.note: typical: be exposed to danger, radiation, risk, expose yourself to criticism NOT for: revealing the truth
examples: Workers were exposed to high levels of dust.
Speaking out could expose you to criticism.

expose.definition: to show the truth about someone or something, especially when it is bad
expose.note: typical: expose a scandal, a lie, a fraud, expose sb as sth NOT for: uncovering a physical object
examples: The newspaper exposed the minister as a liar.
The report exposes serious weaknesses in the system.

expose.definition: to give someone the chance to experience or learn about something new
expose.note: typical: expose sb to ideas, art, other cultures, a language NOT for: putting someone in danger
examples: Travel exposes young people to different ways of life.
She was exposed to classical music from an early age.

extract.definition: to remove an object from somewhere, especially with difficulty
extract.note: typical: extract a tooth, a bullet, an object from sth, formal NOT for: getting information
examples: The dentist had to extract two of his teeth.
He extracted a small key from his pocket.

extract.definition: to carefully remove a substance from something that contains it, using a machine or a chemical process
extract.note: typical: extract oil, juice, minerals, metal, a substance from sth NOT for: taking text from a book
examples: Oil is extracted from the seeds.
The process extracts pure copper from the rock.

extract.definition: to get something such as information, money or help from someone who does not want to give it
extract.note: typical: extract information, a promise, a confession, extract sth from sb NOT for: removing physical objects
examples: The police failed to extract a confession from him.
She extracted a promise from her brother not to tell.

extract.definition: to take information or a short piece of writing from a book or document
extract.note: typical: extract data, a quotation, a passage, figures NOT for: getting something from someone unwilling
examples: We need to extract the relevant data from the report.
She extracted three short quotations from the novel.

extract.definition: to get an advantage or good thing from a situation
extract.note: typical: extract the maximum benefit, value, advantage from sth NOT for: removing objects or substances
examples: The company tries to extract the most value from every customer.
Politicians hope to extract some advantage from the crisis.

facilitate.definition: to make it easier for a process or activity to happen
facilitate.note: typical: facilitate learning, trade, communication, a discussion, formal NOT for: making something happen by force
examples: Computers can facilitate language learning.
The new road should facilitate trade between the two towns.

finance.definition: to provide money, especially a lot of money, to pay for something
finance.note: typical: finance a project, a purchase, a war, be financed by NOT for: managing money in general
examples: The concerts are financed by the city council.
She financed her studies by working at night.

forecast.definition: to say what is likely to happen in the future, based on the information you have now
forecast.note: typical: forecast rain, growth, sales, forecast that NOT for: telling a story about the past
examples: Rain is forecast for the weekend.
Experts forecast that prices will rise next year.

foster.definition: to help a skill, feeling or idea develop over a period of time
foster.note: typical: foster a sense of, cooperation, talent, understanding, growth NOT for: looking after someone else's child
examples: The club aims to foster a spirit of teamwork.
Good teachers foster curiosity in their students.

foster.definition: to take someone else's child into your family for a period of time without becoming their legal parent
foster.note: typical: foster a child, foster children, fostering NOT for: encouraging an idea
examples: They fostered several children over the years.
The couple decided to foster a young boy.

gain.definition: to obtain or achieve something you want or need
gain.note: typical: gain control, power, a degree, independence, victory, gain sth NOT for: becoming heavier or higher in number
examples: She gained a degree in biology.
The party gained control of the council.

gain.definition: to gradually get more and more of a quality or feeling, especially a useful one
gain.note: typical: gain experience, confidence, popularity, a reputation, gain in sth NOT for: obtaining a prize or goal
examples: The young players gradually gained confidence.
The sport has gained in popularity in recent years.

gain.definition: to get an advantage from a situation, opportunity or event
gain.note: typical: gain from, stand to gain, a lot to be gained, gain an advantage NOT for: increasing in amount
examples: Who stands to gain from the new law?
There is nothing to be gained by arguing.

gain.definition: to increase in weight, speed, height or value
gain.note: typical: gain weight, speed, height, gain in value, shares gain NOT for: obtaining a skill or advantage
examples: He has gained a lot of weight recently.
The shares gained five per cent on Monday.

gain.definition: to manage to enter a place, building or organisation
gain.note: typical: gain access, gain entry, gain admission to sth NOT for: obtaining skills
examples: The thieves gained entry through a back window.
Students must pass an exam to gain admission to the school.

gain.definition: to learn or find out about something, especially to understand it better
gain.note: typical: gain an understanding, an insight, an impression of sth NOT for: obtaining things you want
examples: The visit helped me gain a better understanding of the problem.
She gained an impression of the town from a few short walks.

gain.definition: if a clock or watch gains, it shows a time that is ahead of the correct time
gain.note: typical: a clock gains, a watch gains (time) NOT for: increasing in amount or weight
examples: My watch gains about two minutes a week.
The old clock gains time in warm weather.

gain.definition: to reach a place, especially after effort or difficulty
gain.note: typical: gain the shore, the summit, the bank, literary style NOT for: entering a building or organisation
examples: The swimmer finally gained the river bank.
After a long climb they gained the summit.

generate.definition: to produce or cause something, such as ideas, jobs, profit or interest
generate.note: typical: generate ideas, income, profits, jobs, interest, support NOT for: producing electricity or heat
examples: The new factory will generate hundreds of jobs.
The film generated a lot of interest.

generate.definition: to produce heat, electricity or another form of energy
generate.note: typical: generate electricity, power, heat NOT for: producing ideas or profit
examples: Wind turbines generate electricity for the village.
The engine generates a great deal of heat.

grant.definition: to give someone something or allow them to have something they have asked for
grant.note: typical: grant a request, permission, a licence, a wish, grant sb sth, formal NOT for: admitting something is true
examples: The council granted him permission to build a garage.
The judge granted their request for more time.

grant.definition: to admit that something is true although it does not support your main argument
grant.note: typical: I grant you (that), grant that NOT for: giving permission
examples: He is clever, I grant you, but he is also very lazy.
I'll grant that the plan is cheap, but it is also risky.

halt.definition: to prevent someone or something from continuing, used especially in news reports
halt.note: typical: halt a decline, production, work, a plan, a project NOT for: stopping to rest or stand still
examples: Safety concerns led the firm to halt work on the bridge.
Officials failed to halt the spread of the disease.

halt.note: typical: the parade/car/train halted, halt at/by NOT for: stopping something else
examples: The train halted outside the station.
The soldiers halted at the edge of the forest.

harm.definition: to have a bad effect on something
harm.note: typical: harm the environment, the economy, someone's chances, a reputation NOT for: physically hurting a person
examples: Chemicals from the factory harm the environment.
Cutting the budget could harm the school's results.

harm.definition: to physically hurt a person or animal
harm.note: typical: harm a child, an animal, a person, never harm NOT for: damaging things or systems
examples: The kidnappers did not harm the boy.
The dog would never harm anyone.

harm.definition: to make people have a worse opinion of a person or group
harm.note: typical: harm sb's image, reputation, career NOT for: physical injury
examples: The scandal harmed the senator's reputation.
Such comments will harm the party's image.

humiliate.definition: to make someone feel ashamed or stupid, especially when other people are present
humiliate.note: typical: humiliate sb in front of others, feel humiliated, publicly humiliate NOT for: simply disappointing someone
examples: Her boss humiliated her in front of the whole team.
He felt humiliated when his mistake was read out loud.

illustrate.definition: to make the meaning of something clearer by giving examples
illustrate.note: typical: illustrate a point, an idea, illustrate with examples, diagrams NOT for: drawing pictures for a book
examples: Let me give an example to illustrate the point.
The teacher illustrated her talk with diagrams.

illustrate.definition: to be an example that shows that something is true or that a fact exists
illustrate.note: typical: illustrate that, illustrate how, illustrate the problem NOT for: drawing pictures
examples: This case illustrates how easily mistakes can happen.
The results illustrate a basic weakness in the system.

illustrate.definition: to put pictures in a book, article or other text
illustrate.note: typical: illustrate a book, a story, an article, be illustrated with NOT for: explaining with examples
examples: She illustrated the children's book herself.
The guide is illustrated with colour photographs.

implement.definition: to take action or make changes that have officially been decided should happen
implement.note: typical: implement a policy, a plan, a decision, a change, a system NOT for: simply thinking about a plan
examples: The government will implement the new tax rules next year.
The school has implemented several of the committee's suggestions.

imply.definition: to suggest that something is true without saying so directly
imply.note: typical: imply that, imply criticism, an implied threat NOT for: proving something exists
examples: I did not mean to imply that you were lying.
His silence seemed to imply agreement.

imply.definition: if a fact or event implies something, it shows that it is likely to be true
imply.note: typical: imply that, the results imply, the evidence implies NOT for: a speaker suggesting something
examples: The high level of dust implies that the room has not been used.
The figures imply that sales are falling.

imply.definition: if one thing implies another, it proves that the second thing exists or must be present
imply.note: typical: democracy implies, success does not imply NOT for: a person hinting at something
examples: Democracy implies respect for individual freedom.
High profits do not necessarily imply efficiency.

impose.definition: if someone in authority imposes a rule, punishment or tax, they force people to accept it
impose.note: typical: impose a fine, a ban, a tax, sanctions, impose sth on sb NOT for: asking for a favour
examples: The court imposed a heavy fine on the company.
The government imposed a ban on the sale of ivory.

impose.definition: to force someone to have the same ideas, beliefs or ways of doing things as you
impose.note: typical: impose your views, beliefs, values, will on sb NOT for: laws or punishments
examples: Parents should not impose their own beliefs on their children.
He tried to impose his will on the whole group.

impose.definition: to expect or ask someone to do something for you when this is not convenient for them
impose.note: typical: impose on/upon sb, don't want to impose, formal NOT for: forcing rules or ideas on people
examples: I don't want to impose on you, but could I stay one night?
She felt that her neighbours were imposing on her kindness.

impose.definition: to have a bad effect on something or someone and cause problems for them
impose.note: typical: impose a burden, strain, hardship, pressure on sb/sth NOT for: official rules or taxes
examples: Military spending imposes a huge strain on the economy.
The long delays imposed hardship on local families.

incorporate.definition: to include something as part of a group, system, plan or whole
incorporate.note: typical: incorporate sth into/in sth, incorporate features, ideas, changes NOT for: setting up a legal company
examples: The architects incorporated many green features into the design.
Several of our ideas were incorporated in the new law.

initiate.definition: to make something important begin, such as a plan, process or discussion
initiate.note: typical: initiate a process, a debate, talks, legal action, a project NOT for: simply starting a car or an everyday task
examples: The council has initiated a review of the city's parking rules.
She initiated the talks by sending a short letter to both sides.

initiate.definition: to introduce someone to a new subject, skill or experience
initiate.note: typical: initiate sb into sth, initiate sb into a hobby, a craft, a skill NOT for: starting a process or plan
examples: My uncle initiated me into the art of bread baking.
The students were initiated into the basics of coding in their first week.

initiate.definition: to accept someone as a member of a group or society, usually through a special ceremony
initiate.note: typical: initiate sb into sth, initiate new members into a club, a society NOT for: ordinary hiring or joining a team
examples: New members are initiated into the society at a candlelit ceremony.
Young men in the village were initiated into the community at sixteen.

inspect.definition: to look at something very carefully to find out about its condition or to find faults
inspect.note: typical: inspect the damage, a car, a document, inspect sth for sth NOT for: a quick glance
examples: The mechanic inspected the engine for oil leaks.
He inspected the contract line by line before signing.

inspect.definition: to make an official visit to a place to check that everything is correct and rules are followed
inspect.note: typical: inspect a school, a factory, a restaurant, troops NOT for: private or casual visits
examples: Health officers inspect the restaurant kitchen every six months.
The general walked along the line to inspect the soldiers.

integrate.definition: to combine two or more things so that they work together well as one system
integrate.note: typical: integrate sth into/with sth, integrate software, ideas, services NOT for: simply putting things in a pile
examples: The app integrates easily with most calendar programs.
The school integrated art and science into a single project.

integrate.definition: to become a full, accepted part of a group or community, or to help someone do this
integrate.note: typical: integrate into a community, a team, a school, integrate newcomers NOT for: combining objects or systems
examples: It took the family a year to integrate into their new neighbourhood.
The programme helps refugees integrate into the local community.

integrate.definition: to end the practice of keeping people of different races apart, especially in schools (mainly American English)
integrate.note: typical: integrate schools, buses, neighbourhoods (AmE) NOT for: general mixing of ideas or software
examples: Many southern schools were integrated in the 1960s.
The city council voted to integrate its public swimming pools.

interpret.definition: to translate spoken words from one language into another
interpret.note: typical: interpret for sb, interpret at a meeting, a conference NOT for: translating written text
examples: She interpreted for the delegation during the meeting.
He works at the courts, interpreting for people who do not speak English.

interpret.definition: to decide that something has a particular meaning
interpret.note: typical: interpret sth as sth, interpret a silence, a gesture, a result NOT for: translating languages
examples: Many people interpreted his silence as agreement.
The data can be interpreted in more than one way.

interpret.definition: to explain the meaning of something
interpret.note: typical: interpret a dream, a law, a poem, a result NOT for: spoken translation
examples: Scientists are still trying to interpret the signals from the probe.
The judge must interpret the law as it is written.

interpret.definition: to perform a piece of music or a role in a way that shows your own ideas about it
interpret.note: typical: interpret a role, a song, a piece of music NOT for: ordinary explanation
examples: The pianist interprets Chopin with great tenderness.
The actor interpreted the part of the king as weak and afraid.

intervene.definition: to become involved in a situation in order to change what is happening
intervene.note: typical: intervene in a dispute, a fight, a conflict, intervene to stop sth NOT for: joining a game or activity for fun
examples: A teacher intervened to stop the argument.
The government may intervene to protect local farmers.

intervene.definition: to interrupt someone who is speaking
intervene.note: typical: intervene in a discussion, 'X,' he intervened NOT for: stopping a physical fight
examples: "That is not true," Maria intervened.
He intervened with a question just as the speaker finished.

intervene.definition: to happen in a way that delays or interrupts something else
intervene.note: typical: war, illness or a problem intervenes NOT for: people choosing to get involved
examples: She planned to travel, but illness intervened.
The match would have finished earlier, but heavy rain intervened.

intervene.definition: to come between two events, when talking about a period of time
intervene.note: typical: the intervening years, months that intervened NOT for: people acting
examples: I saw him again after the two years that intervened.
Little changed in the weeks that intervened between the two visits.

invest.definition: to put money into shares, property or other things in the hope of making a profit
invest.note: typical: invest in shares, property, gold, invest money in sth NOT for: spending money on daily goods
examples: She invested her savings in a small apartment.
Many people invest in gold when prices are unstable.

invest.definition: to spend a large amount of money on something to improve it or help it succeed
invest.note: typical: invest in education, equipment, roads, invest millions in sth NOT for: buying shares for profit
examples: The company invested millions in a new factory.
The city plans to invest in cycle lanes and public parks.

invest.definition: to use a lot of time, effort or emotion in something so that it will succeed
invest.note: typical: invest time, energy, effort in sth NOT for: money-making deals
examples: He invested years of effort in learning the violin.
The team invested a lot of energy in the project.

isolate.definition: to keep a person, group or place apart from others
isolate.note: typical: isolate a patient, a village, a country, isolate sb from sb NOT for: ordinary solitude by choice
examples: Floods isolated the village for three days.
Sick animals should be isolated from the rest of the herd.

isolate.definition: to think about an idea or problem separately from other things connected with it
isolate.note: typical: isolate a problem, a cause, a factor, isolate sth from sth NOT for: physically separating people
examples: It is hard to isolate one cause of the company's failure.
The engineers isolated the problem to a single faulty part.

isolate.definition: to separate a substance, disease or similar thing from others so that it can be studied
isolate.note: typical: isolate a virus, a gene, a chemical NOT for: keeping people apart
examples: Researchers isolated the virus from a water sample.
The scientist isolated a rare chemical from the plant.

license.definition: to give official permission for someone to do or sell something, or for an activity to take place
license.note: typical: be licensed to do sth, license a drug, a business, a driver NOT for: the noun licence
examples: The shop is licensed to sell medicine.
The new drug was licensed for use last spring.

manipulate.definition: to control or influence someone cleverly, often unfairly, so that they do what you want
manipulate.note: typical: manipulate people, voters, a child, manipulate sb into (doing) sth NOT for: skilful handling of objects
examples: He manipulated his friends into lending him money.
Advertisers can manipulate how people feel about a product.

manipulate.definition: to work with information, figures or systems skilfully to get the result you want
manipulate.note: typical: manipulate data, figures, images, the market NOT for: moving a heavy object by hand
examples: The program lets you manipulate photos in many ways.
The company was accused of manipulating its sales figures.

manipulate.definition: to move and press bones or muscles with the hands to ease pain (medical use)
manipulate.note: typical: manipulate a joint, the spine, a muscle NOT for: influencing people
examples: The therapist manipulated his stiff shoulder.
A doctor manipulated the baby's hip gently during the check.

manipulate.definition: to handle or move something with skill
manipulate.note: typical: manipulate a tool, a puppet, controls, an instrument NOT for: deceiving people
examples: The surgeon manipulated the tiny instrument with great care.
She manipulated the puppet so it seemed to walk.

melt.definition: to change from solid to liquid because of heat, or to make something do this
melt.note: typical: ice, snow, butter, chocolate melts, melt sth NOT for: water changing to steam
examples: The snow began to melt in the afternoon sun.
Melt the chocolate in a bowl over hot water.

melt.note: typical: melt away, fears, doubts, a crowd melts NOT for: solid things becoming liquid
examples: His doubts slowly melted away.
The crowd melted into the dark side streets.

melt.definition: to become less angry and begin to feel kinder or more sympathetic
melt.note: typical: melt at a look, a smile, sb's heart melts NOT for: heating food
examples: Her anger melted when she saw his sad face.
My heart melted when the puppy looked up at me.

minimise.definition: to reduce something bad or unwanted to the lowest possible level
minimise.note: typical: minimise risk, costs, damage, disruption, waste NOT for: making something bigger
examples: The company works hard to minimise delays for passengers.
Wear a helmet to minimise the risk of injury.

minimise.definition: to make something seem less serious or important than it really is
minimise.note: typical: minimise a problem, a threat, the importance of sth NOT for: reducing physical size
examples: The minister tried to minimise the scale of the crisis.
Don't minimise how hard this has been for her.

minimise.definition: to make a window or program on a computer screen very small so that it stays open but out of the way
minimise.note: typical: minimise a window, a program, an app NOT for: closing a program
examples: I minimised the video and went back to my email.
Click the button in the corner to minimise the window.

mislead.definition: to make someone believe something that is not true by giving false or incomplete information
mislead.note: typical: mislead the public, customers, investors, mislead sb about/into sth NOT for: giving the wrong directions by accident
examples: The advert misled customers about the price.
Don't be misled by his friendly manner.

mistake.note: typical: mistake sb's meaning, intentions, words NOT for: making an error in doing something
examples: I mistook his joke for an insult.
She mistook my silence for anger.

mock.definition: to laugh at someone or something in an unkind way, or to copy them to make them look foolish
mock.note: typical: mock sb, mock sb's accent, mock a decision NOT for: gentle friendly teasing
examples: The older boys mocked him for his accent.
Critics mocked the plan as a waste of money.

modify.definition: to make small changes to something in order to improve it or make it more suitable
modify.note: typical: modify a design, a plan, a program, a rule, modify sth to do sth NOT for: completely replacing something
examples: The team modified the recipe to make it less sweet.
The rules were modified after the first season.

modify.definition: to limit or change the meaning of a word or phrase in grammar, as an adjective or adverb does
modify.note: typical: an adjective modifies a noun, an adverb modifies a verb NOT for: changing a design or plan
examples: In 'red car', the adjective 'red' modifies the noun 'car'.
The adverb 'quickly' modifies the verb in 'She quickly left'.

mould.definition: to shape a soft substance by pressing it or by putting it into a container
mould.note: typical: mould clay, dough, plastic, mould sth into sth NOT for: fungus growing on food
examples: She moulded the clay into a small bowl.
The workers moulded hot plastic into chairs.

mould.definition: to influence how someone's character or ideas develop
mould.note: typical: mould sb into sth, mould character, opinion, young people NOT for: shaping a physical material
examples: Good teachers can mould young minds.
The coach moulded the players into a strong team.

mould.definition: to fit closely to the shape of something, or to make something do this
mould.note: typical: mould to sth, mould itself to the body NOT for: forming a substance in a container
examples: The soft shoe moulds itself to your foot.
Her wet dress moulded to her body in the wind.

nominate.definition: to officially suggest someone or something for a position, duty or prize
nominate.note: typical: nominate sb for/as sth, nominate a candidate, a film, nominate sb to do sth NOT for: giving someone a job directly
examples: She was nominated for the best actress award.
The party nominated him as its candidate for mayor.

nominate.definition: to choose someone for a particular job or role
nominate.note: typical: nominate sb as sth, nominate a successor, a deputy NOT for: suggesting someone for a prize
examples: The director nominated her as his successor.
The president nominated a new head of the bank.

notify.definition: to officially or formally tell someone about something
notify.note: typical: notify sb of sth, notify the police, authorities, customers, notify sb that NOT for: telling a friend casually
examples: You will be notified of the result by email.
Please notify the school if your child is ill.

obey.definition: to do what someone in authority tells you to do, or what a law or rule says you must do
obey.note: typical: obey orders, the law, the rules, a command, a parent NOT for: following advice or a fashion
examples: Soldiers must obey the orders of their officers.
The dog sat down and obeyed at once.

originate.definition: to come from a particular place or situation, or to begin in a particular way
originate.note: typical: originate in/from/with/as sth, a custom, a tradition, a rumour originates NOT for: inventing something yourself
examples: The tradition originated in a small village in Germany.
The rumour originated with a false news story.

originate.definition: to have the idea for something and start it
originate.note: typical: originate a technique, an idea, a style NOT for: coming from a place
examples: The technique was originated by an Italian artist.
She originated the idea of a school garden.

overcome.definition: to successfully deal with a feeling or problem that stops you from achieving something
overcome.note: typical: overcome a problem, difficulty, fear, shyness, obstacle, addiction NOT for: winning a match or battle
examples: She worked hard to overcome her fear of flying.
The team overcame many difficulties before opening the shop.

overcome.definition: to make someone extremely ill or unconscious because they breathe smoke or gas (usually passive)
overcome.note: typical: be overcome by smoke, fumes, gas, heat NOT for: strong emotions
examples: Two workers were overcome by fumes in the tunnel.
He was overcome by smoke and had to be carried out.

overcome.definition: to affect someone so strongly with an emotion that they cannot behave normally
overcome.note: typical: be overcome with/by grief, emotion, joy, guilt, relief NOT for: solving a problem
examples: She was overcome with grief at the funeral.
He was so overcome by relief that he could not speak.

overcome.definition: to fight against someone or something and win
overcome.note: typical: overcome an opponent, an enemy, a rival, a team NOT for: dealing with a personal problem
examples: The home side overcame their rivals in the final minute.
The small army overcame the invaders after a long struggle.

overlook.definition: to fail to notice something, or not see how important it is
overlook.note: typical: overlook a detail, a mistake, a fact, an error, easy to overlook NOT for: forgiving bad behaviour
examples: It is easy to overlook a small error in a long report.
Nobody should overlook how much work the volunteers do.

overlook.definition: to forgive someone's mistake or bad behaviour and take no action
overlook.note: typical: overlook a fault, a mistake, rudeness, sb's behaviour NOT for: failing to notice something
examples: I am willing to overlook your mistake this time.
She overlooked his bad manners because he was so kind.

overlook.definition: to have a view of a place, usually from above
overlook.note: typical: a house, room, hotel, balcony overlooks the sea, a garden, a valley NOT for: ignoring a person
examples: Our hotel room overlooks the harbour.
The old castle overlooks a quiet valley.

oversee.definition: to be in charge of a job or group of workers and make sure the work is done properly
oversee.note: typical: oversee a project, a team, an operation, production NOT for: noticing something by accident
examples: A senior engineer will oversee the construction of the bridge.
She oversees a team of twelve nurses.

overwhelm.definition: to affect someone so strongly with an emotion that they cannot think clearly
overwhelm.note: typical: be overwhelmed by/with joy, grief, guilt, homesickness NOT for: work that is too much to deal with
examples: She was overwhelmed by sadness at the news.
The children were overwhelmed with excitement on the last day.

overwhelm.definition: to be too much or too difficult for someone to deal with
overwhelm.note: typical: be overwhelmed by/with work, requests, problems, overwhelm sb with sth NOT for: strong feelings of joy or grief
examples: The office was overwhelmed by the number of applications.
Don't overwhelm new students with too much information.

perceive.definition: to understand or think of something or someone in a particular way
perceive.note: typical: perceive sth/sb as sth, perceive sb to be sth, a perceived threat, risk NOT for: seeing with the eyes
examples: Many customers perceive the brand as old-fashioned.
What is perceived as rude in one country may be polite in another.

perceive.definition: to notice, see or recognize something (formal)
perceive.note: typical: perceive a change, a difference, a sound, perceive that NOT for: giving an opinion about someone
examples: She perceived a slight change in his mood.
He perceived that there was no way out of the problem.

persist.definition: to continue to do something even though it is difficult or other people do not agree
persist.note: typical: persist in/with sth, persist in doing sth, persist despite NOT for: bad conditions that continue
examples: He persisted in his efforts despite many failures.
She persisted with her studies even when money was short.

persist.definition: to continue to exist or happen, especially when something is bad
persist.note: typical: pain, problems, doubts, symptoms, rumours persist NOT for: people carrying on with a task
examples: If the pain persists, see a doctor.
Doubts about the plan persisted for months.

portray.definition: to show or describe someone or something in a particular way
portray.note: typical: portray sb/sth as sth, portray sb as a hero, a victim, a villain NOT for: acting a part
examples: The newspaper portrayed the mayor as a hard-working leader.
Religion is often portrayed in a negative way in the film.

portray.definition: to describe or represent someone or something in a painting, picture or piece of writing
portray.note: typical: a painting, a novel, a film portrays sth NOT for: acting a character
examples: The painting portrays a battle at sea.
The novel portrays the struggles of a poor farming family.

portray.definition: to act the part of a character in a play, film or television programme
portray.note: typical: portray a character, a king, a doctor NOT for: describing real people in writing
examples: She portrays a young doctor in the new series.
The actor portrayed the president with great skill.

praise.definition: to say that you admire and approve of someone or something, especially in public
praise.note: typical: praise sb for sth, praise a performance, a decision, a team NOT for: flattering someone insincerely
examples: The teacher praised the class for their hard work.
Critics praised the film as a masterpiece.

praise.definition: to express respect and thanks to God
praise.note: typical: praise God, praise the Lord, praise sb in song NOT for: ordinary praise of people
examples: The choir gathered to praise God in song.
They knelt to praise the Lord for the harvest.

prioritise.definition: to put things in order of importance so that you deal with the most important first
prioritise.note: typical: prioritise tasks, goals, needs, projects NOT for: making a plan for a trip
examples: You need to prioritise your tasks before the deadline.
The hospital prioritises patients with the most serious injuries.

prioritise.definition: to treat something as more important than other things and deal with it first
prioritise.note: typical: prioritise safety, education, health, a problem NOT for: sorting a list in order
examples: The government says it will prioritise public transport.
Many parents prioritise their children's education over holidays.

process.definition: to treat food, materials or goods in order to make them ready for use or sale
process.note: typical: process food, milk, oil, raw materials, processed cheese NOT for: dealing with documents
examples: The factory processes tomatoes into sauce.
Raw cotton is processed before it is made into cloth.

process.definition: to deal with an official document or request in the usual way
process.note: typical: process an application, a claim, a payment, an order NOT for: treating food or materials
examples: The office will process your application within two weeks.
Banks can process payments in a few seconds.

process.definition: to deal with information using a computer
process.note: typical: process data, information, images NOT for: official forms done by hand
examples: The software processes thousands of records every minute.
New computers can process large files much faster.

process.definition: to develop a photograph from film so that the picture can be seen
process.note: typical: process film, photographs, prints (technical) NOT for: editing images on a computer
examples: He processed the film in a darkroom.
The shop will process your photographs in one hour.

prohibit.definition: to say officially that something is not allowed by law or by a rule
prohibit.note: typical: prohibit smoking, the sale of sth, be prohibited from doing sth NOT for: a person simply not wanting something
examples: Smoking is strictly prohibited in the building.
The law prohibits children from working at night.

prohibit.definition: to make something impossible or to stop it from happening (formal)
prohibit.note: typical: costs, rules, distance prohibit sth NOT for: official bans by law
examples: The high cost prohibits many people from buying a home.
Heavy snow prohibited any further progress up the mountain.

project.definition: to calculate what something will be in the future using the information you have now
project.note: typical: project growth, sales, costs, be projected to rise NOT for: showing a film on a screen
examples: The company projects sales of ten million next year.
Costs are projected to rise by five percent.

project.definition: to stick out beyond an edge or surface
project.note: typical: project from/out of/through sth, a ledge, a balcony projects NOT for: throwing something forward
examples: A small balcony projects from the second floor.
Her front teeth projected slightly.

project.definition: to make a picture of a film or photograph appear on a screen or flat surface
project.note: typical: project sth onto sth, project a slide, an image NOT for: showing a feeling
examples: The teacher projected the map onto the wall.
The film was projected onto a huge white screen.

project.definition: to try to make other people have a particular idea about you
project.note: typical: project an image, confidence, project yourself as sth NOT for: calculating figures
examples: She worked hard to project a confident image.
The candidate projected himself as a man of the people.

project.definition: to be planned to happen in the future
project.note: typical: the projected opening, closure, cost, date NOT for: sticking out
examples: The projected opening of the new library is next spring.
The projected cost of the bridge has doubled.

project.definition: to speak clearly and loudly so that everyone in a big room can hear you
project.note: typical: project your voice, project to the back of the hall NOT for: showing images
examples: Actors learn to project their voices to the back of the theatre.
He projected his voice so the whole hall could hear.

project.definition: to make something move upwards or forwards with great force
project.note: typical: a plant projects seeds, project sth over a distance NOT for: showing a film
examples: The plant projects its seeds over a wide area.
The machine projects balls across the court at high speed.

project.definition: to help someone quickly reach success or a much better position
project.note: typical: project sb into/onto sth, project sb to fame NOT for: forecasting numbers
examples: His first hit song projected him into the spotlight.
The role projected the young actress to fame.

project.definition: to imagine that someone else feels the same emotions as you do
project.note: typical: project sth onto sb, project your fears, insecurity NOT for: showing a picture
examples: You are projecting your own fears onto your children.
He projects his anger onto other people.

prompt.definition: to make someone decide to do something
prompt.note: typical: prompt sb to do sth, what prompted you to NOT for: reminding an actor of lines
examples: What prompted you to change your job?
The news prompted her to call her mother.

prompt.definition: to make people say or do something as a reaction
prompt.note: typical: prompt a reaction, a protest, an outcry, a debate, a question NOT for: making someone decide in advance
examples: The accident prompted an inquiry.
His speech prompted a lively debate.

prompt.definition: to help a speaker who has paused by suggesting how to continue
prompt.note: typical: prompt sb, 'X?' she prompted NOT for: reminding an actor on stage
examples: "And then?" she prompted gently.
He paused, so I prompted him with the name.

prompt.definition: to ask a computer user to do something, especially by showing a message
prompt.note: typical: prompt sb for sth, prompt the user for a password NOT for: helping a speaker
examples: The screen will prompt you for a password.
The program prompts users to save their work.

prompt.definition: to remind an actor of the next words in a speech
prompt.note: typical: prompt an actor, the prompter prompts NOT for: asking a computer user to act
examples: A stage assistant prompted the actor when he forgot his line.
She stood at the side of the stage to prompt the cast.

provoke.definition: to cause a reaction or feeling, especially a sudden one
provoke.note: typical: provoke a protest, an outcry, criticism, a debate, a reaction NOT for: making a person angry on purpose
examples: The proposal provoked widespread criticism.
The novel provoked fierce debate among readers.

provoke.definition: to make someone angry, especially deliberately
provoke.note: typical: provoke sb, provoke an animal, provoke sb into doing sth NOT for: causing a debate or protest
examples: The dog would not have attacked if it had not been provoked.
He tried to provoke her into an argument.

reassure.definition: to make someone feel calmer and less worried or frightened
reassure.note: typical: reassure sb (that), reassure customers, parents, patients NOT for: promising something in a contract
examples: The doctor reassured the nervous patient.
He reassured her that everything would be fine.

recruit.definition: to find new people to work for a company or join an organization
recruit.note: typical: recruit staff, workers, volunteers, recruit sb to do sth NOT for: joining the army
examples: The company is recruiting new engineers.
The charity recruited fifty volunteers for the event.

recruit.definition: to get people to join the army, navy or another armed force
recruit.note: typical: recruit soldiers, young men NOT for: hiring office staff
examples: The army recruited thousands of young men that year.
Most of the village men were recruited within a week.

reform.definition: to improve a system, law or organization by making many changes to it
reform.note: typical: reform the law, the tax system, education, the police NOT for: a person changing their habits
examples: The government plans to reform the tax system.
They want to reform the way schools are funded.

reform.definition: to change your behaviour and become a better person, or to make someone do this
reform.note: typical: reform a criminal, a reformed character, a reformed smoker NOT for: changing a system
examples: After prison he reformed and found a steady job.
The programme aims to reform young offenders.

reform.definition: to start to exist again, or to come together again as a group
reform.note: typical: a band, a company, a group reforms NOT for: improving a law or system
examples: The band reformed after ten years apart.
The soldiers reformed their lines after the attack.

regulate.definition: to control an activity or process, especially by rules
regulate.note: typical: regulate trade, the use of sth, the industry, the market NOT for: adjusting a machine or the body
examples: Strict laws regulate the use of chemicals in food.
The government regulates the banking industry.

regulate.definition: to make a machine or the body work at a particular speed or temperature
regulate.note: typical: regulate temperature, body heat, a flow, the speed NOT for: controlling an industry by law
examples: A thermostat regulates the temperature of the room.
Sweating helps the body regulate its heat.

reinforce.definition: to give support to an opinion, idea or feeling and make it stronger
reinforce.note: typical: reinforce a belief, an idea, a stereotype, a message NOT for: strengthening a wall or a building
examples: The film reinforces the idea that success means money.
Repeating the lesson helps reinforce what pupils have learned.

reinforce.definition: to make part of a building, structure or piece of clothing stronger
reinforce.note: typical: reinforce a wall, a bridge, a floor, with steel NOT for: supporting an opinion
examples: Workers reinforced the old bridge with steel beams.
The jacket is reinforced at the elbows.

reinforce.definition: to make a group of people, especially an army, stronger by adding more people or equipment
reinforce.note: typical: reinforce troops, a team, a force NOT for: strengthening a building
examples: The general reinforced the army with fresh troops.
The club reinforced its squad with two new players.

rescue.definition: to save someone or something from a situation of danger or harm
rescue.note: typical: rescue sb/sth from sth, rescue a child, a climber, an animal NOT for: simply helping with a task
examples: Firefighters rescued two people from the burning house.
Volunteers rescued the dog from the river.

retrieve.definition: to go and get something back from a place, especially something lost, dropped or left behind
retrieve.note: typical: retrieve a bag, a ball, a body, retrieve sth from sth NOT for: getting something for the first time
examples: He climbed down the bank to retrieve his phone from the mud.
Divers retrieved the box from the bottom of the lake.

retrieve.definition: to find and get back information that is stored in a computer or database
retrieve.note: typical: retrieve data, a file, a record, information from a database NOT for: physically fetching an object
examples: The system can retrieve any customer record in a few seconds.
I could not retrieve the deleted file from the backup.

retrieve.definition: to make a bad situation acceptable again after a serious mistake or problem (British English)
retrieve.note: typical: retrieve the situation NOT for: collecting a lost object
examples: A late goal helped the team retrieve the situation after a poor first half.
The manager tried to retrieve the situation by apologising to the client in person.

rob.definition: to take money or property from a person or place illegally, often by using force or threats
rob.note: typical: rob a bank, a shop, a tourist, rob sb of sth NOT for: the stolen thing as the object (say steal money, not rob money)
examples: Two men robbed the post office at gunpoint.
They robbed him of his wallet and his watch.

rub.definition: to press your hand or a cloth against a surface and move it backwards and forwards
rub.note: typical: rub your eyes, your hands, your back, rub sth with sth NOT for: touching something lightly just once
examples: He rubbed his tired eyes and looked at the clock.
She rubbed the window with a cloth until it shone.

rub.definition: to press one thing against another and move it around
rub.note: typical: rub sth against/on sth, rub two things together NOT for: wiping a surface clean
examples: The boy rubbed two sticks together to make a spark.
The cat rubbed its head against my hand.

rub.definition: if shoes, clothes or machine parts rub, they keep moving against a surface and cause pain or damage
rub.note: typical: shoes, a strap, a collar, a part rub NOT for: a person deliberately rubbing something
examples: These new boots rub at the back of my heel.
The belt is rubbing against the metal casing and wearing it away.

rub.definition: to spread a substance over or into a surface by pressing and moving it with your fingers or a cloth
rub.note: typical: rub cream, oil, polish on/into sth NOT for: pouring or spraying a liquid
examples: Rub a little oil into the wood before you paint it.
He rubbed lotion onto his sunburnt shoulders.

rush.definition: to move very quickly, usually because you need to get somewhere soon
rush.note: typical: rush past, out, into a room, down the stairs NOT for: moving at a slow or normal pace
examples: The children rushed out of the classroom when the bell rang.
Shoppers rushed past me towards the exit.

rush.definition: to hurry to do something straight away without delay
rush.note: typical: rush to help, to finish, to answer, to pack NOT for: doing something slowly or later
examples: Neighbours rushed to help when the fire started.
She rushed to reply before the deadline passed.

rush.definition: to do or decide something too quickly, without taking enough care
rush.note: typical: rush a decision, rush into marriage, rush things, rush through sth NOT for: acting quickly for a good reason
examples: Don't rush your decision; take a few days to think about it.
I was rushing through the essay and made several mistakes.

rush.definition: to take or send someone or something somewhere very fast, usually because of an emergency
rush.note: typical: rush sb to hospital, rush supplies to sth NOT for: ordinary, planned delivery
examples: The injured cyclist was rushed to hospital by ambulance.
The charity rushed blankets and food to the flooded town.

rush.definition: to try to make someone act or decide more quickly than they want to
rush.note: typical: rush sb, rush sb into (doing) sth NOT for: hurrying yourself
examples: Take your time; I don't want to rush you.
The salesman tried to rush us into signing the contract.

rush.definition: if water or another liquid rushes somewhere, it moves there very quickly
rush.note: typical: water, a river, a stream, floodwater rushes through/down sth NOT for: a slow, calm flow
examples: Floodwater rushed through the narrow streets.
A stream rushed down the hillside after the storm.

rush.definition: to attack a person or place suddenly, as a group
rush.note: typical: rush the guard, the gate, the stage NOT for: a slow, planned attack by one person
examples: Protesters rushed the gates and forced them open.
Fans rushed the stage as the band began to play.

rush.definition: in American English, of a student club, to hold events to decide who can join; or of a student, to go through the process of trying to be accepted into such a club
rush.note: typical: rush a fraternity, a sorority, rush week NOT for: joining an ordinary club or team in British English
examples: Many first-year students rush a fraternity in the autumn.
The sorority rushed forty new students this semester.

rush.definition: in some ball games, to carry the ball forward by running with it
rush.note: typical: rush the ball, rush for 100 yards NOT for: passing or kicking the ball
examples: The running back rushed for more than a hundred yards.
He rushed the ball up the middle for a first down.

scratch.definition: to rub your skin with your nails because it itches or feels uncomfortable
scratch.note: typical: scratch your head, your arm, an itch, scratch at sth NOT for: hurting someone on purpose
examples: He scratched his arm where the mosquito had bitten him.
Try not to scratch, or the rash will get worse.

scratch.definition: to cut someone's skin slightly with your nails or something sharp
scratch.note: typical: scratch sb's face, scratch yourself on sth NOT for: a deep or serious wound
examples: The cat scratched her hand when she picked it up.
I scratched my leg on the rose bush.

scratch.definition: to make a small cut or mark on a surface by pulling something sharp across it
scratch.note: typical: scratch a car, a table, scratch your name on sth NOT for: breaking or smashing something
examples: Someone has scratched my car with a key.
He scratched his initials on the desk.

scratch.definition: if an animal scratches, it rubs its feet or claws against something, often making a noise
scratch.note: typical: a dog, a cat, a hen scratches at sth NOT for: people scratching an itch
examples: The dog scratched at the door to be let out.
Hens scratched in the dirt looking for seeds.

scratch.definition: to remove something from a surface by rubbing it with something sharp
scratch.note: typical: scratch off paint, scratch away dirt, scratch sth off sth NOT for: wiping with a soft cloth
examples: She scratched the old paint off the window frame with a knife.
He scratched the frost away from the windscreen with a plastic card.

scratch.definition: to remove a word or name from a piece of writing by drawing a line through it
scratch.note: typical: scratch a name from a list, scratch out a word NOT for: erasing pencil with a rubber
examples: I scratched Tom's name off the guest list.
She scratched the wrong answer and wrote another one.

scratch.definition: if something sharp scratches, it makes a rough noise as it moves across a surface
scratch.note: typical: a pen, chalk, a branch, a nail scratches on/against sth NOT for: a smooth, quiet movement
examples: His pen scratched across the page as he wrote quickly.
A branch scratched against the window all night.

scratch.definition: to decide not to do something, such as an idea or a plan (informal)
scratch.note: typical: scratch a plan, an idea, a trip, a project NOT for: cutting skin or marking a surface
examples: We had to scratch the picnic because of the rain.
The company scratched the idea after the tests failed.

scratch.definition: to withdraw from a race or competition, or to remove someone from it (informal)
scratch.note: typical: scratch a horse, scratch from a race NOT for: losing a race
examples: The champion scratched from the race with a leg injury.
The owner scratched his horse an hour before the start.

scream.definition: to make a loud, high sound with your voice because you are hurt, frightened or excited
scream.note: typical: scream in terror, in pain, with laughter, a baby screams NOT for: speaking quietly
examples: The passengers screamed as the plane dropped suddenly.
The baby was screaming with hunger.

scream.definition: to shout words in a very loud, high voice, often because you are angry or frightened
scream.note: typical: scream for help, scream at sb, scream abuse, scream out sth NOT for: calling in a normal voice
examples: She screamed at the driver to stop the car.
'Run!' he screamed, pointing at the flames.

scream.definition: if something screams, it makes a very loud, high noise
scream.note: typical: a siren, an engine, brakes, a jet screams NOT for: soft or low sounds
examples: Police sirens screamed through the empty streets.
The engine screamed as the car accelerated.

settle.definition: to end an argument or solve a disagreement
settle.note: typical: settle a dispute, a lawsuit, an argument, settle out of court NOT for: paying a bill
examples: The two companies settled the dispute without going to court.
A quick look at the map settled the argument about which way to go.

settle.definition: to decide something finally, so that you can make firm arrangements
settle.note: typical: it's settled, nothing is settled yet, that settles it NOT for: a decision that may still change
examples: Nothing is settled yet, so please don't tell anyone.
It's settled, then: we leave at eight on Friday.

settle.definition: to go to a place where nobody has lived permanently before and start living there
settle.note: typical: settle a territory, an island, be settled by pioneers NOT for: visiting a place for a short time
examples: The valley was settled by farmers in the 1800s.
Pioneers settled the plains of the Midwest.

settle.definition: to go to live in a new place and stay there for a long time
settle.note: typical: settle in a city, in a village, abroad NOT for: a short holiday
examples: After years of travelling, she settled in Lisbon.
Many families settled in the suburbs after the war.

settle.definition: to put yourself or someone else into a comfortable position
settle.note: typical: settle yourself in an armchair, settle sb into a chair NOT for: moving house
examples: He settled himself into the armchair with a book.
The nurse settled the patient against the pillows.

settle.definition: to become quiet and calm, or to make someone or something quiet and calm
settle.note: typical: settle a baby, settle your nerves, the class settles NOT for: ending an argument
examples: The children settled quickly once the teacher began the story.
A warm drink helped settle her nerves before the interview.

settle.definition: if dust, snow, a bird or an insect settles, it comes down and rests on a surface
settle.note: typical: dust, snow, a bird, a fly settles on sth NOT for: a person sitting down
examples: A thin layer of dust had settled on the furniture.
A butterfly settled on her sleeve.

settle.definition: if a building or the ground settles, it sinks slowly to a lower level
settle.note: typical: the ground, the soil, the foundations, a house settles NOT for: a sudden collapse
examples: The old house has settled a few centimetres over the years.
Cracks appeared as the soil settled under the new road.

settle.definition: to pay money that you owe
settle.note: typical: settle a bill, an account, a debt, a claim NOT for: lending money to someone
examples: Please settle your account before the end of the month.
He settled the restaurant bill with his credit card.

settle.definition: if an expression settles on someone's face, it stays there (written)
settle.note: typical: a frown, a smile, a look of calm settles on sb's face NOT for: a quick, passing expression
examples: A look of calm settled on his face as the music began.
An anxious frown settled on her forehead as she read the letter.

settle.definition: if your stomach settles, or something settles it, it stops feeling uncomfortable or sick
settle.note: typical: settle your stomach, an upset stomach settles NOT for: calming a person's feelings in general
examples: Ginger tea helps to settle my stomach.
His stomach settled after he had eaten some dry toast.

simulate.definition: to produce something that is not real but looks, sounds or feels like the real thing
simulate.note: typical: simulate conditions, an environment, a flight, an explosion NOT for: making something genuinely real
examples: The machine simulates the low gravity found on the Moon.
Pilots use computers to simulate emergency landings.

simulate.definition: to pretend to have a feeling (formal)
simulate.note: typical: simulate grief, interest, surprise, enthusiasm NOT for: really feeling an emotion
examples: He simulated surprise when they gave him the present.
She tried to simulate interest during the long speech.

slide.definition: to move smoothly over a surface while staying in contact with it, or to make something move in this way
slide.note: typical: slide across ice, slide a door open, slide sth along/across sth NOT for: lifting or jumping
examples: The children slid across the frozen pond.
She slid the drawer shut with her foot.

slide.definition: to move somewhere quietly and smoothly, or to move something in this way
slide.note: typical: slide into a seat, slide out of a room, slide sth into a pocket NOT for: moving noisily or fast
examples: He slid into the back row just as the film began.
She slid the letter into her bag without a word.

slide.definition: if prices, amounts or rates slide, they become lower
slide.note: typical: shares, prices, the dollar, sales slide NOT for: a rise in numbers
examples: Share prices slid for the third day in a row.
Sales slid by ten per cent last quarter.

slide.definition: to gradually become worse, or to begin to have a problem
slide.note: typical: slide into recession, into debt, into chaos, standards slide NOT for: a sudden change
examples: The country slid into economic crisis.
His grades began to slide after he stopped studying.

slip.definition: to slide by accident and fall or lose your balance a little
slip.note: typical: slip on ice, on a wet floor, on the stairs NOT for: moving on purpose
examples: She slipped on the wet steps and hurt her ankle.
He slipped on the ice but managed to stay on his feet.

slip.definition: to go somewhere quietly without other people noticing
slip.note: typical: slip out, slip away, slip into a room, slip past sb NOT for: leaving loudly or openly
examples: He slipped out of the meeting without anyone noticing.
The thief slipped through the back door.

slip.definition: to put something somewhere quietly or smoothly
slip.note: typical: slip sth into a pocket, a bag, under a door NOT for: dropping something carelessly
examples: She slipped the key into her pocket.
He slipped a note under the door.

slip.definition: to give someone something secretly or without attracting attention
slip.note: typical: slip sb money, slip sth to sb NOT for: handing something over openly
examples: The waiter slipped her a folded note.
My uncle slipped me twenty pounds when Mum wasn't looking.

slip.definition: to move smoothly off or away from a place or from someone's hold, often by accident
slip.note: typical: slip off, down, from sb's grasp, a ring slips off a finger NOT for: falling heavily
examples: The towel slipped from his shoulders.
The glass slipped out of my hand and broke.

slip.definition: if a knife or tool slips, it moves by accident so that it cuts or hits the wrong thing
slip.note: typical: a knife, a blade, a screwdriver slips NOT for: a person losing their balance
examples: The knife slipped and cut his thumb.
Her screwdriver slipped and scratched the paint.

slip.definition: to become worse or lower than before
slip.note: typical: standards, popularity, profits, results slip NOT for: physically sliding
examples: Standards at the school have slipped in recent years.
The company's profits slipped in the last quarter.

slip.definition: to gradually move into a particular, usually bad, condition
slip.note: typical: slip into debt, into a coma, behind schedule NOT for: a sudden change
examples: The patient slipped into a coma during the night.
The project slipped behind schedule because of delays.

slip.definition: to put on or take off a piece of clothing quickly and easily
slip.note: typical: slip on a coat, slip off your shoes, slip out of a dress NOT for: getting dressed slowly and carefully
examples: She slipped on her shoes and ran to the door.
He slipped out of his wet jacket and hung it up.

slip.definition: if time slips away or past, it passes quickly
slip.note: typical: time, the hours, the days slip away, past, by NOT for: time that feels slow
examples: The summer slipped by before we knew it.
Time is slipping away, so we must decide now.

slip.definition: to get free from something that was holding you
slip.note: typical: slip a lead, a collar, a rope NOT for: escaping by force
examples: The horse slipped its halter and ran into the field.
The dog slipped its lead and ran across the road.

specify.definition: to state something clearly and in exact detail
specify.note: typical: specify a date, a size, the rules, specify who/what/how NOT for: mentioning something vaguely
examples: The contract specifies the date by which payment must be made.
Please specify which colour you would like.

sponsor.definition: to give money to a sports event, theatre or organisation, especially in exchange for the right to advertise
sponsor.note: typical: sponsor a race, a team, a festival, a concert NOT for: giving a private gift to a friend
examples: A local bank sponsors the town's football team.
The tournament is sponsored by a sportswear company.

sponsor.definition: to support someone by paying for their studies, training or living costs
sponsor.note: typical: sponsor a student, a child, an athlete NOT for: paying for advertising
examples: A charity sponsors the education of children in poor villages.
His employer sponsored him through a master's degree.

sponsor.definition: to officially support a proposal for a new law
sponsor.note: typical: sponsor a bill, a law, a resolution NOT for: only voting for a law
examples: Two senators sponsored the new environmental bill.
She sponsored a motion to ban plastic bags in the city.

sponsor.definition: to agree to help someone or to be responsible for what they do, for example when they apply for a visa
sponsor.note: typical: sponsor a refugee, an immigrant, a visa application NOT for: giving money to a sports team
examples: A local church agreed to sponsor the refugee family.
My cousin's employer sponsored her work visa.

sponsor.definition: to agree to give someone money for charity if they walk, run or swim a certain distance
sponsor.note: typical: sponsor a runner, a friend, a walker NOT for: sponsoring a company or event
examples: I sponsored my sister to run ten kilometres for the hospital.
Everyone in the office sponsored him for the charity swim.

stabilise.definition: to become firm, steady or unchanging, or to make something firm and steady
stabilise.note: typical: stabilise the economy, prices, a patient's condition, a situation NOT for: causing sudden change
examples: Doctors managed to stabilise the patient's condition.
Prices have stabilised after months of rises.

standardise.definition: to make all the things of one type the same as each other
standardise.note: typical: standardise procedures, forms, tests, spelling, sizes NOT for: making things different
examples: The company wants to standardise its forms across all offices.
Efforts to standardise road signs in the region took years.

stare.definition: to look at someone or something for a long time without moving your eyes away
stare.note: typical: stare at sb/sth, stare into space, stare in disbelief NOT for: taking a quick look
examples: The little boy stared at the huge dog.
She stared out of the window for an hour.

stimulate.definition: to encourage an activity, process or development to begin or to grow further
stimulate.note: typical: stimulate growth, demand, the economy, trade NOT for: reducing or stopping something
examples: Lower interest rates may stimulate economic growth.
The festival aims to stimulate tourism in the region.

stimulate.definition: to encourage someone by making them excited and interested in something
stimulate.note: typical: stimulate interest, curiosity, imagination, stimulate sb to do sth NOT for: boring or tiring someone
examples: The museum visit stimulated her interest in history.
Good teachers stimulate students to ask questions.

stimulate.definition: to make a plant or part of the body become more active or stronger
stimulate.note: typical: stimulate growth, the nerves, the muscles, the appetite NOT for: calming something down
examples: Sunlight stimulates the growth of the plant.
The massage stimulates blood flow in the legs.

streamline.definition: to make a business, process or organisation work in a simpler and more effective way
streamline.note: typical: streamline production, a process, procedures, a company NOT for: making a system more complicated
examples: The company streamlined its ordering system to save time.
We need to streamline the application process.

streamline.definition: to give something a smooth shape so that it moves easily through air or water
streamline.note: typical: streamline a car, a train, an aircraft, a boat NOT for: making a shape rougher
examples: Designers streamlined the train's nose to reduce drag.
The bicycle frame was streamlined to cut wind resistance.

stretch.definition: to make something longer, wider or looser by pulling it, or (of a material) to become longer or looser when pulled
stretch.note: typical: stretch a sweater, elastic, a rubber band, shoes NOT for: breaking something by force
examples: He stretched the elastic band until it was very thin.
Cotton socks stretch when you wash them in hot water.

stretch.definition: to straighten your arms, legs or body to their full length
stretch.note: typical: stretch your legs, your arms, stretch before exercise NOT for: reaching for an object
examples: He yawned and stretched his arms above his head.
Runners should stretch before a race.

stretch.definition: to reach a long way, especially in order to get something
stretch.note: typical: stretch across, over, up for sth NOT for: moving a short distance
examples: She stretched across the table for the salt.
He stretched up to reach the top shelf.

stretch.definition: to pull something so that it is tight
stretch.note: typical: stretch a rope, a net, canvas, a cloth over sth NOT for: loosening something
examples: They stretched a rope between two trees.
The artist stretched the canvas tightly over a wooden frame.

stretch.definition: to continue over a period of time or in a series, or to make something do this
stretch.note: typical: stretch over years, into the night, stretch a lead NOT for: something that lasts only a moment
examples: The meeting stretched into the evening.
The team stretched their lead to ten points.

stretch.definition: to spread out or cover a large area
stretch.note: typical: a beach, a road, a forest, a queue stretches to/along/around sth NOT for: a small area
examples: The desert stretches for hundreds of miles.
A long queue stretched around the block.

stretch.definition: to allow something that is not normally allowed by a rule or limit (British English)
stretch.note: typical: stretch the rules, stretch a point NOT for: secretly breaking the law
examples: Just this once, I'll stretch the rules and let you in early.
The teacher stretched the deadline by two days.

stretch.definition: to make money, food or other supplies last longer by using less of it at a time
stretch.note: typical: stretch a budget, your savings, a meal, a salary NOT for: spending something quickly
examples: She stretched the stew to feed six people.
We had to stretch our savings until June.

stretch.definition: to make someone use all of their skill, ability or intelligence
stretch.note: typical: stretch students, a team, a child, stretch sb's abilities NOT for: giving someone easy work
examples: The new project really stretched the whole team.
Gifted pupils need work that stretches them.

subject.definition: to force a country or group of people to be ruled by you and control them very strictly (formal)
subject.note: typical: subject a nation, a people, a region NOT for: the school subject or the subject of a sentence
examples: For centuries the empire subjected the surrounding kingdoms.
The general planned to subject the northern provinces.

supplement.definition: to add something, especially to what you earn or eat, in order to bring it up to an acceptable level
supplement.note: typical: supplement your income, your salary, your diet, supplement sth with sth NOT for: replacing something completely
examples: She supplements her salary by teaching evening classes.
Many athletes supplement their diet with vitamins.

suppress.definition: to stop people from opposing the government or from protesting, usually by using force
suppress.note: typical: suppress a revolt, a rebellion, a protest, opposition NOT for: calming a single person
examples: Soldiers were sent in to suppress the uprising.
The regime suppressed all opposition parties.

suppress.definition: to prevent important information or opinions from becoming known to the public
suppress.note: typical: suppress evidence, a report, the truth, news NOT for: simply forgetting something
examples: The company tried to suppress the results of the safety study.
Officials were accused of suppressing the facts.

suppress.definition: to stop yourself from showing a feeling or reaction
suppress.note: typical: suppress a smile, a laugh, anger, a yawn, your feelings NOT for: expressing an emotion openly
examples: She could barely suppress a laugh during the speech.
He suppressed his anger and kept quiet.

suppress.definition: to prevent something from growing, developing or working effectively
suppress.note: typical: suppress growth, the immune system, the appetite, a cough NOT for: encouraging something to grow
examples: Some drugs suppress the body's immune system.
Dense trees suppress the growth of grass underneath.

surrender.definition: to say officially that you want to stop fighting because you know you cannot win
surrender.note: typical: an army, rebels, soldiers, a city surrender NOT for: winning a battle
examples: The rebels surrendered after three days of fighting.
The enemy was given an hour to surrender.

surrender.definition: to go to the police or the authorities and say that you will stop trying to escape
surrender.note: typical: surrender to the police, surrender yourself to sb NOT for: being caught against your will
examples: The wanted man surrendered himself to the police this morning.
After a week on the run, she surrendered to the authorities.

surrender.definition: to give up something or someone, especially because you are forced to
surrender.note: typical: surrender weapons, power, your passport, your independence NOT for: giving a gift freely
examples: The rebels agreed to surrender their weapons.
He was forced to surrender his seat on the board.

surrender.definition: to allow yourself to be controlled or influenced by something
surrender.note: typical: surrender to temptation, to sleep, to despair NOT for: resisting something
examples: She surrendered to the temptation and ate the whole cake.
He finally surrendered to exhaustion and fell asleep.

surrender.definition: to give something such as a ticket, licence or passport to an official (formal)
surrender.note: typical: surrender a licence, a passport, a ticket, surrender sth to sb NOT for: handing over a weapon in war
examples: Drivers who lose their licence must surrender it to the court.
He surrendered his passport at the border.

sustain.definition: to make something continue to exist or happen for a period of time
sustain.note: typical: sustain growth, interest, a relationship, an effort NOT for: starting something new
examples: It is hard to sustain economic growth during a recession.
The teacher found it difficult to sustain the children's attention.

sustain.definition: to suffer damage, injury or loss (formal)
sustain.note: typical: sustain injuries, damage, losses NOT for: causing damage to others
examples: Two passengers sustained serious injuries in the crash.
The roof sustained heavy damage in the storm.

sustain.definition: if food or drink sustains a person, animal or plant, it keeps them alive and able to continue (formal)
sustain.note: typical: sustain a population, a family, sb through the winter NOT for: a meal eaten for pleasure
examples: A little bread and water was all that sustained the prisoners.
The crops can barely sustain the village.

sustain.definition: to make someone feel strong and hopeful (formal)
sustain.note: typical: sustain sb through hard times, hope, faith NOT for: making someone feel tired
examples: Her faith sustained her through the long illness.
The hope of seeing his family again sustained him.

sustain.definition: to hold up the weight of something (formal)
sustain.note: typical: sustain a weight, a load NOT for: lifting something with your hands
examples: The old bridge cannot sustain heavy lorries.
The shelf was too weak to sustain the weight of the books.

sustain.definition: to support an idea or argument, or to show that it is right (formal)
sustain.note: typical: sustain an argument, a claim, a theory, a charge NOT for: attacking an argument
examples: The evidence does not sustain his claim.
That theory is hard to sustain in the light of new data.

symbolise.definition: to represent a quality, idea or feeling
symbolise.note: typical: symbolise freedom, peace, hope, power NOT for: simply being a sign of a physical thing
examples: The dove symbolises peace in many cultures.
The new bridge symbolises the friendship between the two cities.

target.definition: to make something have an effect on a particular limited group or area
target.note: typical: target customers, young people, a market, target sth at sb NOT for: aiming at everyone
examples: The advert was designed to target teenagers.
The scheme targets families on low incomes.
