target.definition: to aim something at a target
target.note: typical: target missiles, a weapon, a laser at sth NOT for: choosing a person to criticise
examples: The missiles were targeted at military bases.
The system targets the laser at the centre of the screen.

target.definition: to choose a particular person or place to attack or criticise
target.note: typical: be targeted by thieves, terrorists, critics NOT for: choosing a customer group
examples: Small shops were targeted by thieves last month.
The journalist was targeted by online trolls.

tarnish.definition: if an event or fact tarnishes someone's reputation or image, it makes it worse
tarnish.note: typical: tarnish a reputation, an image, a record, a name NOT for: damaging a metal object
examples: The scandal tarnished the company's reputation.
One mistake should not tarnish a lifetime of good work.

tarnish.definition: if a metal tarnishes, or if something tarnishes it, it becomes dull and loses its shine
tarnish.note: typical: silver, copper, brass tarnishes NOT for: damaging someone's reputation
examples: Silver tarnishes quickly in damp air.
The salty air had tarnished the brass handles.

tear.definition: to damage paper, cloth or a similar material by pulling it hard or by catching it on something sharp, or (of such a material) to split
tear.note: typical: tear a page, a shirt, a hole in sth, tear sth open NOT for: breaking something hard like glass
examples: She tore her jacket on a nail.
This old paper tears very easily.

tear.definition: to run or drive very fast, especially in a careless or dangerous way
tear.note: typical: tear down the road, tear off, tear into a room NOT for: moving slowly
examples: The children tore down the hill on their bikes.
He tore out of the house without his coat.

tear.definition: to pull something violently away from a person or place
tear.note: typical: tear sth from sb's hand, tear sth off sth NOT for: gently taking something
examples: He tore the letter from my hand.
The wind almost tore the roof off the shed.

tear.definition: if you are torn, you cannot decide what to do because you have different feelings or wishes
tear.note: typical: be torn between two things, torn between A and B NOT for: a simple choice
examples: She was torn between staying at home and taking the job abroad.
He felt torn between loyalty to his friend and his duty.

tear.definition: if a country or group is torn, it is divided by serious disagreement or fighting
tear.note: typical: be torn by war, a war-torn country, torn by conflict NOT for: a person who cannot decide
examples: The country was torn by civil war.
The party was torn by arguments over its leader.

tear.definition: to damage a muscle or ligament
tear.note: typical: tear a muscle, a ligament, a tendon NOT for: ripping cloth or paper
examples: The footballer tore a muscle in his thigh.
She tore a ligament in her knee while skiing.

tear.definition: to move violently and no longer be attached to something
tear.note: typical: tear loose, tear free NOT for: pulling something off on purpose
examples: One corner of the tent tore loose in the gale.
The boat tore loose from its mooring.

terminate.definition: if something terminates, or if you terminate it, it ends (formal)
terminate.note: typical: terminate a contract, an agreement, a pregnancy, employment NOT for: a pause or short break
examples: The company decided to terminate the contract.
The agreement terminates at the end of the year.

terminate.definition: if a train, bus or ship terminates at a place, its journey ends there
terminate.note: typical: a train, a bus, a service terminates at/in sth NOT for: a stop in the middle of a route
examples: This train terminates at Central Station.
The ferry terminates at the island's main harbour.

thrive.definition: to become very successful, or to grow strong and healthy (formal)
thrive.note: typical: a business, plants, children, a community thrives NOT for: surviving with difficulty
examples: Palm trees thrive in warm, wet climates.
The small shop thrived even during the recession.

transform.definition: to change the appearance, form or character of something or someone completely, especially in a way that improves it
transform.note: typical: transform a city, a life, a room, transform sth into sth NOT for: a small or slight change
examples: The new park has transformed the neighbourhood.
The film transformed her from a shy girl into a star.

transmit.definition: to send out electronic signals, messages or programmes using radio, television or similar equipment
transmit.note: typical: transmit a signal, data, a programme, live NOT for: sending a letter by post
examples: The match will be transmitted live around the world.
The device transmits data to a central computer.

transmit.definition: to pass something from one person, place or thing to another (formal)
transmit.note: typical: transmit a disease, knowledge, a message, transmit sth to sb NOT for: electronic broadcasting
examples: Mosquitoes can transmit the virus to humans.
Customs are transmitted from one generation to the next.

transmit.definition: if an object or substance transmits sound or light, it lets the sound or light pass through or along it
transmit.note: typical: glass, a cable, a wall transmits light, sound NOT for: blocking light or sound
examples: Glass transmits light but blocks most heat.
Water transmits sound better than air does.

trigger.definition: to make something happen very quickly, especially a series of events or a strong reaction
trigger.note: typical: trigger a reaction, an attack, a memory, a crisis, trigger sth off NOT for: preventing something
examples: The shooting triggered a wave of protests.
The smell of the sea triggered a happy memory.

trigger.definition: to make a device such as an alarm or a bomb start to work
trigger.note: typical: trigger an alarm, a sensor, a bomb NOT for: switching something off
examples: A cat walking past triggered the burglar alarm.
The explosion was triggered by remote control.

trip.definition: to hit something with your foot by accident so that you fall or almost fall
trip.note: typical: trip on a step, trip over a cable, trip over your feet NOT for: slipping on a wet surface
examples: He tripped over a loose stone and fell.
She tripped on the bottom stair and dropped her bag.

trip.definition: to make someone fall by putting your foot in front of them as they move
trip.note: typical: trip an opponent, a player, trip sb up NOT for: falling by accident
examples: The defender was sent off for tripping the striker.
A boy stuck out his foot and tripped her.

trip.definition: to switch on a piece of electrical equipment by accident
trip.note: typical: trip an alarm, a switch, a circuit breaker NOT for: deliberately turning something on
examples: The intruder tripped the alarm as he climbed in.
Too many machines tripped the switch.

trip.definition: to walk, run or dance with quick, light steps (literary)
trip.note: typical: trip down the path, trip along, trip across a room NOT for: stumbling
examples: A little girl came tripping down the lane.
The dancers tripped lightly across the stage.

trip.definition: to experience strange mental effects after taking a drug (informal)
trip.note: typical: be tripping, trip out NOT for: going on a journey
examples: He said he had been tripping all night.
The doctor warned that the drug could make people trip.

trust.definition: to believe that someone is honest and will not do anything bad or wrong
trust.note: typical: trust sb, trust sb completely, trust sb to do sth NOT for: only liking someone
examples: I would trust her with my life.
You can't trust a man who lies so easily.

trust.definition: to be sure that something is correct or right, or to believe in and rely on something
trust.note: typical: trust sb's judgement, trust the statistics, trust your instincts NOT for: doubting something
examples: Can we trust these figures?
You should trust your instincts in a situation like that.

trust.definition: to be sure that something will work properly or do what you expect
trust.note: typical: trust sth to do sth, not trust your legs, your voice NOT for: a person you do not know well
examples: You can't trust the trains to run on time.
He did not trust his legs to carry him up the hill.

trust.definition: to hope that something is true (spoken, formal)
trust.note: typical: I trust (that) NOT for: believing a person is honest
examples: I trust you had a pleasant journey.
I trust that you will arrive on time.

undermine.definition: to gradually make someone or something less strong, confident or effective
undermine.note: typical: undermine confidence, authority, a position, health, a system NOT for: a sudden, complete destruction
examples: Constant criticism began to undermine her confidence.
The scandal undermined the minister's authority.

undertake.definition: to accept that you are responsible for a piece of work and start to do it (formal)
undertake.note: typical: undertake a task, a project, research, a study NOT for: refusing a job
examples: The team undertook a detailed study of the river.
She undertook the task of organising the whole event.

undertake.definition: to promise or agree to do something (formal)
undertake.note: typical: undertake to do sth NOT for: only thinking about doing something
examples: The builder undertook to finish the work by June.
They undertook to pay the money back within a year.

utilise.definition: to use something for a particular purpose (formal)
utilise.note: typical: utilise resources, space, technology, skills NOT for: wasting something
examples: The school utilises every classroom in the building.
We must utilise our limited resources carefully.

validate.definition: to prove that something is true or correct, or to make a document or agreement officially acceptable (formal)
validate.note: typical: validate a claim, a result, a theory, a ticket, a contract NOT for: rejecting a claim
examples: Further research is needed to validate the results.
The court validated the will.

validate.definition: to make someone feel that their ideas and feelings are respected and taken seriously
validate.note: typical: validate sb's feelings, concerns, experiences NOT for: criticising someone
examples: A good friend will validate your feelings instead of ignoring them.
Many patients feel validated when someone listens.

validate.definition: in American English, to put a special mark on a parking ticket to show that the parking fee will be paid by a business
validate.note: typical: validate a parking ticket, validate parking NOT for: checking a document is correct
examples: The shop will validate your parking ticket if you spend $20.
Ask the cashier to validate your ticket before you leave.

wrap.definition: to cover something by putting paper, cloth or another material around it
wrap.note: typical: wrap a present, a gift, a parcel, wrap sth in sth NOT for: unwrapping something
examples: She wrapped the present in blue paper.
He wrapped a scarf around his neck.

wrap.definition: to put your arms, legs or fingers around something and hold it
wrap.note: typical: wrap your arms around sb/sth NOT for: covering something with paper
examples: He wrapped his arms around his daughter.
The baby wrapped her fingers around his thumb.

yield.definition: to produce a result, answer or piece of information
yield.note: typical: yield results, information, answers, evidence NOT for: giving up
examples: The research has yielded some surprising results.
The search yielded no new evidence.

yield.definition: to produce crops, profits or another amount of something
yield.note: typical: yield a profit, a return, a crop, barrels of oil NOT for: using something up
examples: The investment should yield a good return.
The new wells could yield millions of barrels of oil.

yield.definition: to allow yourself to be forced or persuaded to do something, or to stop having something
yield.note: typical: yield to pressure, demands, temptation NOT for: moving a physical object
examples: The government refused to yield to the demands of the protesters.
In the end she yielded to temptation and bought the dress.

yield.definition: in American English, to let other traffic go first on a larger road
yield.note: typical: yield to traffic, to pedestrians, a yield sign NOT for: stopping for no reason
examples: Drivers must yield to traffic on the main road.
He yielded to the ambulance coming up behind him.

yield.definition: to move, bend or break because of physical force or pressure
yield.note: typical: the ground, a surface, a door yields NOT for: staying firm
examples: The old door finally yielded under his shoulder.
The surface should yield slightly when you press it.

adhere.definition: to stick firmly to a surface or to something else (formal)
adhere.note: typical: adhere to a surface, tape adhering to skin, mud adhering to boots NOT for: following rules (that is the phrasal use 'adhere to')
examples: The sticky label would not adhere to the wet bottle.
Small particles of dust adhere to the screen.

alleviate.definition: to make something painful, difficult or unpleasant less serious
alleviate.note: typical: alleviate pain, poverty, suffering, pressure, the problem NOT for: curing or completely removing something
examples: The nurse gave him a drink to alleviate his sore throat.
New bus routes should alleviate traffic problems in the city centre.

articulate.definition: to express ideas or feelings clearly in words
articulate.note: typical: articulate a view, a concern, a vision, your feelings NOT for: simply saying something aloud without explaining ideas
examples: She struggled to articulate why she felt so uneasy about the plan.
The report articulates the aims of the project very clearly.

articulate.definition: to pronounce words or sounds clearly and carefully
articulate.note: typical: articulate words, a sentence, each syllable NOT for: speaking loudly
examples: The teacher asked the children to articulate each word slowly.
After the injury to his jaw, he could hardly articulate his consonants.

articulate.definition: to be joined to another part in a way that allows movement (technical; of bones)
articulate.note: typical: a bone articulates with another bone, a joint NOT for: machines being attached in general
examples: The upper arm bone articulates with the shoulder blade.
The skull articulates with the top of the spine.

articulate.definition: to be connected or related to another system or idea so that the two work together (formal)
articulate.note: typical: articulate with a course, a system, a framework NOT for: expressing an opinion
examples: The new training course is designed to articulate with the national exams.
Each stage of the programme articulates with the next.

ascertain.definition: to find out something, especially by checking facts carefully (formal)
ascertain.note: typical: ascertain the facts, the cause, whether/what/how NOT for: guessing or assuming
examples: Investigators are trying to ascertain the cause of the fire.
We need to ascertain whether the figures are correct before we publish them.

attain.definition: to succeed in getting or achieving something, usually after effort or a long time (formal)
attain.note: typical: attain a goal, a position, success, independence NOT for: getting something easily or by luck
examples: She worked for years to attain the rank of captain.
The country attained independence in 1960.

attain.definition: to reach a particular level, age, size or condition (formal)
attain.note: typical: attain a height, speed, weight, level NOT for: reaching a place
examples: The temperature attained a record high last July.
The young tree had attained a height of three metres.

attribute.definition: to believe or say that something is caused by a particular thing
attribute.note: typical: attribute a rise/fall/success to sth NOT for: giving or awarding something to someone
examples: Doctors attribute the fall in deaths to better treatment.
He attributed his poor exam result to a lack of sleep.

attribute.definition: to believe that a work, statement or idea was created or said by a particular person
attribute.note: typical: attribute a painting, a quotation, a saying to sb NOT for: proving who really made something
examples: This quotation is often attributed to Mark Twain.
Experts attribute the portrait to a little-known Dutch painter.

attribute.definition: to believe that someone or something has a particular quality or feature
attribute.note: typical: attribute intelligence, magical powers, motives to sb NOT for: describing a quality you have actually observed
examples: Ancient people attributed magical powers to the stone.
Don't attribute bad intentions to him without any proof.

avert.definition: to prevent something unpleasant or dangerous from happening
avert.note: typical: avert a crisis, disaster, war, danger NOT for: stopping something that has already happened
examples: Quick action by the pilot averted a disaster.
The two sides met in an effort to avert a strike.

avert.definition: to turn your eyes or face away so that you do not see something
avert.note: typical: avert your eyes, gaze, face NOT for: turning your whole body away
examples: She averted her eyes from the terrible scene.
He averted his gaze when the teacher looked at him.

bolster.definition: to make someone feel more confident or positive
bolster.note: typical: bolster confidence, morale, spirits, hopes NOT for: making someone physically stronger
examples: The good news bolstered the team's confidence.
A kind letter from her friends bolstered her spirits.

bolster.definition: to make something stronger or better
bolster.note: typical: bolster the economy, a case, support, security NOT for: building a new thing from nothing
examples: The government plans to bolster the economy with new spending.
She added more evidence to bolster her argument.

commence.definition: to begin or start something, or to begin (formal)
commence.note: typical: work/talks/the meeting commences, commence proceedings, commence doing sth NOT for: everyday spoken English, where start is normal
examples: The ceremony will commence at noon.
The company commenced building work in March.

concede.definition: to admit that something is true or correct, although you do not want to
concede.note: typical: concede that, concede a point, concede (that) it is true NOT for: happily agreeing
examples: Even his critics conceded that he had done a good job.
She finally conceded that she had made a mistake.

concede.definition: to admit that you have lost or are not going to win
concede.note: typical: concede defeat, the election, the match, the race NOT for: giving up a job
examples: The candidate conceded defeat on election night.
After three hours of play, he conceded the game.

concede.definition: to allow the other side to score a goal or point in a game
concede.note: typical: concede a goal, a point, a penalty NOT for: scoring yourself
examples: The goalkeeper conceded two goals in the first half.
The team has conceded very few points this season.

concede.definition: to give something such as a right or power to someone, often unwillingly
concede.note: typical: concede power, rights, territory to sb NOT for: giving a gift happily
examples: The government conceded more powers to the regions.
The owners conceded a pay rise to the workers.

conceive.definition: to imagine or think about something in a particular way (formal)
conceive.note: typical: conceive of sth, can't conceive that/why/how NOT for: physically making something
examples: I cannot conceive of life without music.
He could not conceive that the plan might fail.

conceive.definition: to think of a new idea or plan and develop it in your mind
conceive.note: typical: conceive an idea, a plan, a design, a project NOT for: building or carrying out a plan
examples: The architect conceived the building as a series of open spaces.
The project was originally conceived in the 1990s.

conceive.note: typical: conceive a child, difficulty conceiving, unable to conceive NOT for: giving birth
examples: The couple had been trying to conceive for two years.
She conceived soon after the wedding.

condemn.definition: to say very strongly that you think something or someone is morally wrong
condemn.note: typical: condemn violence, an attack, a decision, condemn sb for sth NOT for: mild disagreement
examples: World leaders condemned the attack.
Many people condemned him for lying to the public.

condemn.definition: to give someone a severe punishment after deciding they are guilty
condemn.note: typical: condemn sb to death/prison NOT for: ordinary criticism or small fines
examples: The court condemned the man to life in prison.
The killer was condemned to death.

condemn.definition: to force someone to live in an unpleasant way or to do something unpleasant
condemn.note: typical: condemn sb to a life of poverty/misery NOT for: choosing something freely
examples: A lack of education condemned many of them to poverty.
His illness condemned him to spend years in bed.

condemn.definition: to officially state that a building or object is not safe enough to be used
condemn.note: typical: a condemned building, condemn a house as unsafe NOT for: destroying something right away
examples: The old bridge was condemned after the inspection.
The council condemned the building as a danger to the public.

confer.definition: to discuss something with other people before making a decision
confer.note: typical: confer with colleagues, lawyers, advisers NOT for: talking about unimportant things
examples: The doctors conferred briefly before telling the family.
She conferred with her lawyer before signing.

confer.definition: to officially give someone a title, degree or honour (formal)
confer.note: typical: confer a degree, title, honour, status on sb NOT for: giving an ordinary gift
examples: The university conferred an honorary degree on the writer.
The king conferred a title on the general.

conform.definition: to behave in the way that most other people in your group or society do
conform.note: typical: conform to expectations, pressure to conform NOT for: being forced by law only
examples: Teenagers often feel pressure to conform.
She refused to conform to what people expected of her.

conform.definition: to obey a rule, law or standard
conform.note: typical: conform to/with rules, regulations, standards NOT for: breaking rules
examples: All new buildings must conform with safety regulations.
The toys conform to European safety standards.

conform.definition: to be similar to what people expect or think is usual
conform.note: typical: conform to a pattern, stereotype, model, ideal NOT for: being exactly the same
examples: The results conformed to the usual pattern.
He does not conform to the stereotype of a scientist.

consolidate.definition: to make your position, power or success stronger so that it lasts longer
consolidate.note: typical: consolidate a position, a lead, power, a victory NOT for: starting something new
examples: The team consolidated its lead with a second goal.
The company has consolidated its position as market leader.

consolidate.definition: to combine several things into one so that they work better or are easier to manage
consolidate.note: typical: consolidate debts, information, businesses, accounts NOT for: simply collecting things without joining them
examples: He took out a loan to consolidate his debts.
The firm plans to consolidate its offices in one building.

contemplate.definition: to think about something that you might do in the future
contemplate.note: typical: contemplate doing sth, a move, a change, resignation NOT for: deciding quickly
examples: He contemplated changing his job.
They never contemplated moving abroad.

contemplate.definition: to accept or consider the possibility that something is true or might happen
contemplate.note: typical: too awful/terrible to contemplate NOT for: believing something is certain
examples: The idea of losing the farm was too painful to contemplate.
She could not contemplate the thought of failure.

contemplate.definition: to think about something seriously and for a long time
contemplate.note: typical: contemplate the future, a problem, what/whether NOT for: a quick thought
examples: He sat by the lake and contemplated his future.
She contemplated whether to accept the offer.

contend.definition: to compete against someone in order to win or gain something
contend.note: typical: contend for power, a title, a prize NOT for: cooperating
examples: Three teams are contending for the championship.
Several parties contended for control of the city.

contend.definition: to argue or state that something is true
contend.note: typical: contend that ... NOT for: proving something is true
examples: Some scientists contend that the climate is changing faster than expected.
The lawyer contended that her client was not at the scene.

correspond.definition: to match or fit with something, so that parts or information relate to each other
correspond.note: typical: correspond to/with sth, figures/numbers/details correspond NOT for: being exactly identical
examples: The numbers on the list correspond to points on the map.
Her story does not correspond with the evidence.

correspond.definition: to be very similar to or the same as something else
correspond.note: typical: correspond closely/roughly/exactly to sth NOT for: being completely different
examples: His job roughly corresponds to that of a manager in our company.
The English word does not correspond exactly to the French one.

correspond.definition: to write letters to someone and receive letters from them
correspond.note: typical: correspond with sb, correspond regularly NOT for: talking on the phone
examples: The two friends corresponded for many years.
She corresponded with a pen friend in Japan.

cultivate.definition: to prepare land and grow crops or plants on it
cultivate.note: typical: cultivate land, soil, a field, crops NOT for: only picking wild plants
examples: Farmers have cultivated this valley for centuries.
The soil was too poor to cultivate.

cultivate.definition: to plant and take care of a particular crop (formal)
cultivate.note: typical: cultivate rice, tea, grapes NOT for: everyday speech, where grow is normal
examples: They cultivate coffee on the mountain slopes.
The region cultivates a wide variety of fruit.

cultivate.definition: to work hard to develop a skill, attitude or quality
cultivate.note: typical: cultivate an image, a habit, a skill, a taste NOT for: quality that develops naturally without effort
examples: She tried to cultivate a calm and patient attitude.
The company has cultivated a friendly image.

cultivate.definition: to make an effort to develop a friendship with someone, especially someone useful
cultivate.note: typical: cultivate a friendship, a contact, a relationship NOT for: ordinary friendship without any aim
examples: He cultivated the friendship of several important politicians.
She cultivated the director because she wanted a better job.

curb.definition: to control or limit something in order to stop it causing harm
curb.note: typical: curb spending, violence, inflation, the spread of sth NOT for: stopping something completely
examples: The city introduced new rules to curb traffic.
Doctors are trying to curb the spread of the disease.

decipher.definition: to work out the meaning of something that is difficult to read or understand
decipher.note: typical: decipher handwriting, a message, a sign, an inscription NOT for: reading something that is easy to read
examples: She tried to decipher the doctor's handwriting.
Scientists finally deciphered the ancient inscription.

decipher.definition: to turn a message written in code into ordinary language
decipher.note: typical: decipher a code, a secret message NOT for: writing a message in code
examples: The spies could not decipher the coded letter.
He used a key to decipher the secret message.

deduce.definition: to reach a conclusion by using the facts and knowledge you have (formal)
deduce.note: typical: deduce that, deduce sth from sth NOT for: guessing without evidence
examples: From the footprints, the detective deduced that the thief was tall.
What can we deduce from these results?

defy.definition: to refuse to obey a rule, law or person in authority
defy.note: typical: defy the law, an order, authority, the government NOT for: simply forgetting a rule
examples: The protesters openly defied the ban.
The boy defied his parents and went out.

defy.definition: to be almost impossible to describe, explain or believe
defy.note: typical: defy description, explanation, belief, analysis NOT for: things that are merely difficult
examples: The beauty of the view defies description.
His behaviour defies explanation.

defy.definition: to happen in a way that goes against what you would normally expect
defy.note: typical: defy logic, the odds, gravity, expectations NOT for: breaking a rule
examples: The small team defied the odds and won the cup.
The old man's good health defies his age.

delve.definition: to try to find more information about something by searching deeply
delve.note: typical: delve into the past, a subject, records, history NOT for: a quick look
examples: The book delves into the causes of the war.
She delved deeper into the company's history.

delve.definition: to search for something by putting your hand deep into a bag or container
delve.note: typical: delve into a bag, pocket, drawer NOT for: looking with your eyes only
examples: He delved into his bag for his keys.
She delved into her pocket and found a coin.

depict.definition: to describe someone or something in writing or speech, or to show them in a painting, picture or film (formal)
depict.note: typical: depict life, a scene, a person, depict sb as sth NOT for: copying or reproducing exactly
examples: The painting depicts a village market in the 1800s.
The novel depicts her as a strong and clever woman.

deploy.definition: to organise or move soldiers, equipment or weapons so that they are in position and ready to be used
deploy.note: typical: deploy troops, forces, weapons, missiles, police NOT for: ordinary travelling
examples: The army deployed extra troops along the border.
Police were deployed around the stadium.

deploy.definition: to use something for a particular purpose, especially to get a result (formal)
deploy.note: typical: deploy resources, skills, arguments, technology NOT for: everyday use of simple objects
examples: The company deployed all its resources to meet the deadline.
The lawyer deployed several clever arguments.

deprive.definition: to prevent someone from having something they need or should have
deprive.note: typical: deprive sb of sth, deprived of sleep, food, rights, freedom NOT for: taking something for a short time
examples: The prisoners were deprived of food and sleep.
Poverty deprived the children of a good education.

derive.definition: to get something, especially a benefit or pleasant feeling, from something
derive.note: typical: derive pleasure, benefit, satisfaction, comfort from sth NOT for: buying or taking an object
examples: She derived great pleasure from her garden.
Many workers derive comfort from a daily routine.

derive.definition: to come from or develop from something else
derive.note: typical: derive from, be derived from, a word derives from Latin NOT for: causing something
examples: The word 'kindergarten' derives from German.
Many of his ideas derive from old traditions.

derive.definition: to obtain a chemical substance from another substance (technical)
derive.note: typical: be derived from sth, a compound, a drug, an oil NOT for: everyday cooking or making food
examples: The medicine is derived from tree bark.
This acid is derived from fruit.

designate.definition: to choose someone or something for a particular job or purpose
designate.note: typical: be designated sth, designate sth as/for sth, designate sb to do sth NOT for: choosing something casually
examples: The area was designated a national park.
She was designated to lead the new team.

designate.definition: to show or mean something by using a particular sign or name
designate.note: typical: designated by a symbol, colour, letter NOT for: describing something in detail
examples: Rivers are designated by blue lines on the map.
The letters 'WC' designate the toilets.

deter.definition: to stop someone from doing something by making them think it will be difficult or have bad results
deter.note: typical: deter sb from (doing) sth, deter crime, thieves, investors NOT for: forbidding by law
examples: High prices deter many people from travelling.
The alarm was installed to deter burglars.

dictate.definition: to say words aloud for someone else to write down
dictate.note: typical: dictate a letter, a message, notes to sb NOT for: copying written text
examples: The manager dictated a letter to his assistant.
She dictated her answers to the interviewer.

dictate.definition: to tell someone exactly what they must do or how they must behave
dictate.note: typical: dictate terms, dictate to sb, dictate how/what NOT for: giving friendly advice
examples: I won't let anyone dictate how I live.
The winners dictated the terms of the peace treaty.

dictate.definition: to control or strongly influence something
dictate.note: typical: dictate what/how, circumstances dictate, the weather dictates NOT for: a person giving orders
examples: The weather will dictate our plans for the day.
Cost often dictates which option we choose.

differentiate.definition: to see or show the difference between things or people
differentiate.note: typical: differentiate between sth and sth, differentiate A from B NOT for: making things the same
examples: Young children cannot always differentiate between fantasy and reality.
It is hard to differentiate one twin from the other.

differentiate.definition: to be the feature that makes one thing clearly different from another
differentiate.note: typical: what differentiates A from B, differentiate a product from others NOT for: comparing without finding a difference
examples: Its bright colour differentiates this bird from similar species.
What differentiates your product from the others?

differentiate.definition: to treat people or things differently, often in an unfair way
differentiate.note: typical: differentiate between men and women, groups NOT for: treating everyone equally
examples: The law should not differentiate between rich and poor.
Some employers differentiate between men and women in pay.

discard.definition: to get rid of something you no longer want
discard.note: typical: discard old clothes, rubbish, an idea, a plan NOT for: giving something to a friend
examples: He discarded his old shoes and bought a new pair.
Please discard the packaging after use.

discard.definition: to put down a card you do not want in a card game
discard.note: typical: discard a card, a queen, a two NOT for: picking up a card
examples: She discarded a king and picked up a new card.
He had to discard two cards from his hand.

discern.definition: to notice or understand something by thinking about it carefully (formal)
discern.note: typical: discern what/why/how, discern a pattern, a difference, a motive NOT for: seeing something obvious
examples: It was hard to discern why he was so angry.
Experts can discern a pattern in the data.

discern.definition: to be able to see something by looking carefully (formal)
discern.note: typical: discern a shape, a figure, a light in the distance NOT for: seeing clearly and easily
examples: We could just discern a boat in the fog.
He discerned a faint light in the distance.

discredit.definition: to make people stop respecting or trusting someone or something
discredit.note: typical: discredit a witness, a government, a person, evidence NOT for: criticising politely
examples: The newspaper tried to discredit the minister.
Her lawyers tried to discredit the witness.

discredit.definition: to make people stop believing in an idea or theory
discredit.note: typical: a discredited theory, idea, method NOT for: proving an idea is true
examples: The old theory has since been discredited.
Later research discredited these methods.

dispatch.definition: to send someone or something somewhere for a particular purpose (formal)
dispatch.note: typical: dispatch goods, a letter, a team, a reporter NOT for: ordinary posting of a message by a person at home
examples: The shop dispatches orders within two days.
A team of doctors was dispatched to the village.

dispatch.definition: to deal with someone or finish a task quickly and effectively
dispatch.note: typical: dispatch an opponent, a task, a job NOT for: doing something slowly
examples: She dispatched her opponent in two sets.
He dispatched the paperwork in an hour.

dispel.definition: to make something go away, especially a belief, idea or feeling
dispel.note: typical: dispel a myth, doubt, fear, rumour, fog, the darkness NOT for: removing physical objects
examples: The announcement dispelled all our fears.
The sun came out and dispelled the mist.

dispose.definition: to arrange things or put them in particular places (formal)
dispose.note: typical: be disposed around/along/in a room, garden, hall NOT for: throwing things away (that is the phrasal use 'dispose of')
examples: The statues were disposed along the garden path.
Chairs were disposed in a circle around the room.

divert.definition: to change the use of something such as money, time or resources
divert.note: typical: divert funds, money, resources into/from sth NOT for: wasting something
examples: The company diverted money from advertising into research.
Officials diverted funds to the flood areas.

divert.definition: to change the direction in which something travels
divert.note: typical: divert traffic, a river, a flight, a road NOT for: stopping something completely
examples: Traffic was diverted because of the accident.
The flight was diverted to another airport.

divert.definition: to arrange for your telephone calls to go to another number
divert.note: typical: divert your phone, calls NOT for: ending a call
examples: I will divert my calls to my mobile while I am away.
Remember to divert the office phone before you leave.

divert.definition: to take someone's attention away from something on purpose
divert.note: typical: divert attention away from sth NOT for: entertaining someone
examples: The magician diverted the audience's attention.
The politician tried to divert attention from the scandal.

drift.definition: to move slowly on water or in the air
drift.note: typical: drift out to sea, smoke/clouds/a boat drifts NOT for: moving fast or with an engine
examples: The boat drifted slowly down the river.
Smoke drifted across the field.

drift.definition: to move or do something without any plan or purpose
drift.note: typical: drift around, drift into a job, drift away NOT for: moving with a clear goal
examples: He drifted around Europe for a year.
She just drifted into teaching.

drift.definition: to gradually change from one condition or situation into another without noticing
drift.note: typical: drift into sleep, drift in and out of consciousness NOT for: sudden change
examples: He drifted off to sleep in front of the TV.
The patient drifted in and out of consciousness.

drift.definition: to change slowly, when talking about values or prices
drift.note: typical: prices, the dollar, shares drift lower/higher NOT for: sudden big changes
examples: Share prices drifted lower during the afternoon.
The dollar drifted down against the euro.

drift.definition: to be blown into large piles by the wind, when talking about snow or sand
drift.note: typical: snow, sand drifts NOT for: rain or water
examples: The snow drifted against the garden wall.
Sand drifted across the road in the strong wind.

dwell.definition: to live in a particular place (literary or very formal)
dwell.note: typical: dwell in a forest/village/cave, dwell among people NOT for: ordinary modern talk about where you live (use live)
examples: Hermits once dwelt in the caves above the valley.
The villagers dwell in small stone houses by the river.

embark.definition: to get onto a ship or plane, or to put people or goods onto one
embark.note: typical: embark at a port, embark passengers/cargo NOT for: getting on a bus or train; starting a new activity (that is embark on)
examples: The passengers embarked at Southampton early in the morning.
The airline began to embark its first group of travellers.

emulate.definition: to copy someone's actions or achievements because you admire them
emulate.note: typical: emulate a hero/success/example NOT for: copying in order to mock or cheat
examples: Many young players try to emulate their favourite footballers.
She hoped to emulate her mother's success in business.

endorse.definition: to publicly say that you support or approve of someone or something
endorse.note: typical: endorse a plan/candidate/proposal NOT for: private or half-hearted agreement
examples: The union voted to endorse the new agreement.
Several newspapers endorsed her campaign for mayor.

endorse.definition: to say publicly, usually in an advertisement, that you like and use a product
endorse.note: typical: endorse a brand/product/trainer NOT for: ordinary shop recommendations from friends
examples: The footballer was paid millions to endorse a sports drink.
Few actors will endorse a product they have never used.

endorse.definition: to sign the back of a cheque so that it can be paid to someone
endorse.note: typical: endorse a cheque NOT for: signing a normal letter or contract
examples: You must endorse the cheque before the bank will accept it.
He endorsed the cheque and handed it to the cashier.

endorse.definition: to record an official penalty on a driving licence (British English, usually passive)
endorse.note: typical: licence endorsed for speeding NOT for: fines paid in cash or other kinds of punishment
examples: His licence was endorsed after he was caught speeding twice.
A driver can lose the right to drive if the licence is endorsed too often.

enrich.definition: to make something better in quality, especially by adding something to it
enrich.note: typical: enrich the soil/your life/a diet NOT for: simply making something bigger
examples: Compost will enrich the soil in the garden.
Travelling can enrich your understanding of other cultures.

enrich.definition: to make a person or a country richer
enrich.note: typical: enrich a family/nation/owner NOT for: improving someone's character
examples: The oil trade enriched the whole region.
Dishonest managers enriched themselves at the company's expense.

enrich.definition: to increase the amount of a particular substance in a material so that it works better (technical)
enrich.note: typical: enrich uranium/fuel NOT for: everyday cooking or farming
examples: The plant is used to enrich uranium for power stations.
Engineers can enrich the fuel to make it last longer.

entail.definition: to involve something as a necessary part or result
entail.note: typical: entail risk/expense/hard work, entail doing sth NOT for: things that are only possible or optional
examples: The new job will entail a lot of travel.
Running a restaurant entails working very long hours.

entitle.definition: to give someone the official right to have or do something
entitle.note: typical: be entitled to sth, entitle sb to do sth NOT for: giving a book or film a name
examples: Every employee is entitled to four weeks of paid holiday.
This ticket entitles you to free entry all week.

entitle.definition: to give a book, film or play a particular title (usually passive)
entitle.note: typical: a book/film entitled X NOT for: giving someone a right
examples: She wrote a short novel entitled The Last Train.
He gave a talk entitled 'Cities of the Future'.

envisage.definition: to think that something is likely to happen in the future
envisage.note: typical: envisage a problem/change, envisage doing sth NOT for: imagining something unreal or fantasy
examples: We never envisaged that the project would take so long.
I don't envisage moving house in the next few years.

erode.definition: if wind, water or weather erodes rock or soil, or if rock or soil erodes, its surface is slowly worn away
erode.note: typical: erode cliffs/soil/a coastline NOT for: sudden destruction
examples: The sea has slowly eroded the cliffs along this coast.
Heavy rain can erode the soil on steep hillsides.

erode.definition: to slowly reduce or weaken something such as power, confidence or trust
erode.note: typical: erode confidence/support/rights NOT for: quick or dramatic loss
examples: Constant criticism began to erode her confidence.
Rising prices have eroded the value of people's savings.

evade.definition: to avoid answering a question or talking about something, especially to hide the truth
evade.note: typical: evade a question/the issue NOT for: simply not hearing a question
examples: The minister kept trying to evade the reporter's question.
He evaded the issue by changing the subject.

evade.definition: to avoid doing or dealing with something that you should do
evade.note: typical: evade responsibility/a duty NOT for: legitimate delay
examples: You cannot evade your responsibilities as a parent.
Some people try to evade military service.

evade.definition: to avoid paying money that you should pay, such as tax
evade.note: typical: evade tax/duty NOT for: legal ways of paying less (use avoid)
examples: The company was fined for evading tax for several years.
He was caught trying to evade customs duty at the airport.

evade.definition: to escape from someone who is trying to catch you
evade.note: typical: evade the police/capture/a pursuer NOT for: avoiding a minor nuisance
examples: The thief managed to evade the police for three weeks.
The fox evaded the dogs by running into the river.

evoke.definition: to make someone feel an emotion or remember something
evoke.note: typical: evoke memories/sympathy/a response NOT for: physically producing an object
examples: The smell of fresh bread evoked memories of her grandmother's kitchen.
The photograph evoked a strong sense of sadness.

exacerbate.definition: to make a bad situation, problem or feeling worse
exacerbate.note: typical: exacerbate a problem/tension/pain NOT for: making something good better
examples: Lack of sleep can exacerbate stress.
The new tax only exacerbated the country's economic problems.

exasperate.definition: to make someone very annoyed, especially by something that keeps happening
exasperate.note: typical: exasperate a teacher/parent/colleague NOT for: mild irritation or sudden anger
examples: His constant lateness exasperated his manager.
It exasperates me when people ignore the rules.

excel.definition: to do something very well, or much better than most people
excel.note: typical: excel at/in sth NOT for: doing something only adequately
examples: She has always excelled at mathematics.
The team excels in defence and rarely lets in a goal.

execute.definition: to kill someone as an official punishment
execute.note: typical: execute a prisoner/traitor NOT for: murder or killing in battle
examples: The prisoner was executed for treason.
Many countries no longer execute criminals.

execute.definition: to carry out a plan, order, or piece of work
execute.note: typical: execute a plan/order/strategy NOT for: only planning something
examples: The team executed the plan perfectly.
The soldiers failed to execute the general's orders.

execute.definition: to make a computer run a program or command
execute.note: typical: execute a program/command/script NOT for: writing code
examples: The computer will execute the command as soon as you press enter.
The script failed to execute because of a missing file.

exempt.definition: to officially free someone from a duty, rule or payment that applies to others
exempt.note: typical: exempt sb from tax/service/a rule NOT for: refusing someone or banning something
examples: The law exempts small businesses from the new fee.
Students with medical problems can be exempted from sports lessons.

exert.definition: to use power, influence or effort to make something happen
exert.note: typical: exert pressure/influence/authority NOT for: using ordinary physical objects
examples: Environmental groups are exerting pressure on the government.
The moon exerts a strong pull on the sea.

exert.definition: to make yourself work very hard, using a lot of energy
exert.note: typical: exert yourself, especially physically or mentally NOT for: relaxing or light effort
examples: The doctor told him not to exert himself for a few weeks.
She exerted herself to finish the report on time.

fabricate.definition: to invent a story, report or piece of information in order to deceive people
fabricate.note: typical: fabricate evidence/a story/an excuse NOT for: honest mistakes
examples: The reporter was fired for fabricating quotes.
Officers were accused of fabricating evidence against him.

fabricate.definition: to make or produce goods or equipment, especially in a factory (technical)
fabricate.note: typical: fabricate parts/metal/components NOT for: cooking or crafting by hand
examples: The company fabricates steel parts for bridges.
Engineers fabricated a new part to fit the old machine.

falter.definition: to become weaker and less able to continue effectively
falter.note: typical: the economy/campaign falters NOT for: ending suddenly
examples: The country's economy began to falter last year.
Their campaign faltered when the funding ran out.

falter.definition: to speak in a weak, uncertain voice that keeps stopping
falter.note: typical: voice falters, 'No,' she faltered NOT for: speaking loudly or clearly
examples: His voice faltered as he read the sad news.
'I don't know,' she faltered.

falter.definition: to become less sure or determined about what you want to do
falter.note: typical: falter in your resolve/belief NOT for: quitting at once
examples: She never faltered in her determination to win.
His courage faltered when he saw the size of the mountain.

falter.definition: to stop moving or move unsteadily because you suddenly feel weak or afraid
falter.note: typical: falter on a path/step NOT for: running or walking steadily
examples: The old man faltered on the steps and grabbed the rail.
She faltered at the door, afraid to go in.

fathom.definition: to understand something after thinking about it carefully
fathom.note: typical: fathom (out) why/how/what, usually in negatives NOT for: measuring depth of water as a noun/unit
examples: I can't fathom why he left without saying goodbye.
Scientists still cannot fathom how the birds find their way.

feign.definition: to pretend to have a particular feeling or to be ill, asleep, etc.
feign.note: typical: feign illness/interest/surprise/sleep NOT for: pretending to be a different person
examples: She feigned a headache to avoid going to the meeting.
He feigned sleep so that his parents would leave the room.

flourish.definition: to develop well and be successful
flourish.note: typical: business/trade/the arts flourish NOT for: a short burst of success
examples: Small businesses flourished in the new shopping district.
The arts flourished under the king's rule.

flourish.definition: to grow well and be healthy
flourish.note: typical: plants/crops flourish in good soil NOT for: people recovering from illness
examples: Tomatoes flourish in warm, sunny gardens.
Most plants will flourish in rich soil.

flourish.definition: to wave something in your hand so that people notice it
flourish.note: typical: flourish a ticket/letter/sword NOT for: waving to greet someone
examples: He flourished the winning ticket in front of the crowd.
She flourished a letter and demanded to see the manager.

foresee.definition: to know or expect that something will happen before it happens
foresee.note: typical: foresee a problem/change/difficulty, can't/couldn't foresee NOT for: wishing or planning for something
examples: Nobody could have foreseen the sudden change in the weather.
Few experts foresaw how quickly prices would rise.

forge.definition: to develop something new, especially a strong relationship or agreement
forge.note: typical: forge a relationship/alliance/link/career NOT for: breaking or ending ties
examples: The two countries forged a close alliance after the war.
She forged strong friendships during her first year at university.

forge.definition: to make an illegal copy of something in order to deceive people
forge.note: typical: forge a signature/banknote/document/passport NOT for: honest copies or imitations
examples: He was arrested for forging his boss's signature.
The gang forged passports and sold them abroad.

forge.definition: to shape metal by heating it and hitting it
forge.note: typical: forge iron/steel/a sword NOT for: casting metal in a mould or just melting it
examples: The blacksmith forged a new gate from iron bars.
Swords like these were forged by hand.

forgo.definition: to do without something pleasant or enjoyable
forgo.note: typical: forgo a holiday/dessert/a pay rise NOT for: forgetting to do something (use forget)
examples: I decided to forgo dessert and have only coffee.
She had to forgo her holiday to save money.

formulate.definition: to develop a plan, idea, theory or set of rules and work out the details
formulate.note: typical: formulate a plan/policy/theory/strategy NOT for: a quick or casual idea
examples: The government formulated a new policy on housing.
Einstein formulated the theory of relativity.

formulate.definition: to think carefully about what to say and then say it clearly
formulate.note: typical: formulate a reply/question/response NOT for: speaking without thinking
examples: She took a moment to formulate her answer.
I'm still trying to formulate my thoughts on the issue.

glance.definition: to look quickly at someone or something
glance.note: typical: glance at/up/around, glance at your watch NOT for: looking for a long time or carefully
examples: He glanced at his watch and stood up.
She glanced over her shoulder to see who was there.

glance.definition: to read something quickly without paying close attention
glance.note: typical: glance at/through a report/page/newspaper NOT for: reading carefully
examples: Could you glance through this letter before I send it?
He glanced at the headlines on the way to work.

glean.definition: to find out information slowly and with some difficulty, often from several sources
glean.note: typical: glean information/facts/details from sth NOT for: getting information quickly or directly
examples: We gleaned most of the details from newspaper reports.
The police gleaned useful facts from the witnesses.

glean.definition: to collect grain left in a field after the main harvest
glean.note: typical: glean grain/corn/fields NOT for: harvesting a whole crop
examples: Poor families were allowed to glean the fields after the harvest.
They spent the autumn gleaning wheat that the farmers had missed.

harbor.definition: to keep a bad thought, fear or hope in your mind for a long time
harbor.note: typical: harbor a grudge/doubts/resentment NOT for: passing thoughts
examples: She still harbored a grudge against her old boss.
He had long harbored the hope of becoming a pilot.

harbor.definition: to contain something harmful or hidden
harbor.note: typical: harbor germs/bacteria/a danger NOT for: holding useful things
examples: Dirty sponges can harbor harmful bacteria.
The old building harbored many hidden dangers.

harbor.definition: to hide and protect someone, especially a criminal
harbor.note: typical: harbor a criminal/fugitive/refugee NOT for: giving ordinary help to a friend
examples: The family was punished for harboring a fugitive.
Some villagers harbored the escaped prisoners for weeks.

harness.definition: to control and use the natural power of something to produce energy or achieve something
harness.note: typical: harness wind/solar power/energy/talent NOT for: simply owning a resource
examples: The company hopes to harness the power of the sun.
Engineers found a way to harness the river's energy.

harness.definition: to fasten an animal to something using a harness, or to fasten two animals together
harness.note: typical: harness a horse/ox to a cart NOT for: tying up an animal without equipment
examples: The farmer harnessed the oxen to the plough.
They harnessed two horses together to pull the wagon.

harness.definition: to put a harness on a horse or other animal
harness.note: typical: harness a horse/pony/dog NOT for: saddling or feeding an animal
examples: She harnessed the pony before the ride.
He harnessed the sled dogs early in the morning.

hinder.definition: to make it difficult for something to develop or succeed
hinder.note: typical: hinder progress/development/a recovery NOT for: making something completely impossible (use prevent)
examples: Bad weather hindered the rescue effort.
Lack of money has hindered the research.

hinge.definition: to depend completely on something (used with 'on' or 'upon')
hinge.note: typical: hinge on/upon a decision/result/outcome NOT for: depending slightly or in part
examples: The whole plan hinges on getting funding.
His future hinges on the result of the exam.

ignite.definition: to start burning, or to make something start burning
ignite.note: typical: ignite fuel/gas/a fire/petrol NOT for: slow, gentle warming
examples: The petrol tank suddenly ignited.
A spark ignited the dry grass.

ignite.definition: to start a dangerous situation, strong feeling or argument
ignite.note: typical: ignite a war/debate/anger/passion NOT for: calming a situation
examples: The speech ignited a fierce debate about taxes.
The arrest ignited riots across the city.

illuminate.definition: to make light shine on something or to fill a place with light
illuminate.note: typical: illuminate a room/street/building/face NOT for: heating something
examples: A single lamp illuminated the room.
Fireworks illuminated the night sky.

illuminate.definition: to make something much clearer and easier to understand (formal)
illuminate.note: typical: illuminate an issue/problem/subject NOT for: making something more complicated
examples: The report illuminated the causes of the crisis.
Her lecture illuminated many difficult ideas.

immerse.definition: to put someone or something deep into a liquid so that they are completely covered
immerse.note: typical: immerse sth in water/liquid NOT for: lightly wetting something
examples: Immerse the vegetables in cold water for ten minutes.
The nurse told him to immerse his hand in cool water.

immerse.definition: to become completely involved in an activity (immerse yourself)
immerse.note: typical: immerse yourself in work/study/a book NOT for: only doing something briefly
examples: She immersed herself in her studies for the whole summer.
He immersed himself in the local culture.

impair.definition: to damage something or make it worse than it should be
impair.note: typical: impair vision/hearing/judgement/performance NOT for: destroying something completely
examples: Alcohol can impair your judgement.
The injury impaired his ability to walk.

impart.definition: to give a particular quality to something (formal)
impart.note: typical: impart flavour/a quality/a feeling to sth NOT for: giving physical objects
examples: A little lemon will impart a fresh taste to the sauce.
The old furniture imparted a sense of calm to the room.

impart.definition: to pass information, knowledge or wisdom to someone (formal)
impart.note: typical: impart knowledge/news/wisdom/information NOT for: simply telling a casual story
examples: The teacher loves to impart her knowledge to young students.
He had important news to impart.

impede.definition: to make it difficult for someone or something to move forward or make progress
impede.note: typical: impede progress/traffic/movement/an investigation NOT for: stopping something completely
examples: Fallen trees impeded the rescue teams.
Heavy snow impeded traffic on the main roads.

indulge.definition: to allow yourself to do or have something you enjoy, especially something that may be bad for you
indulge.note: typical: indulge in sth, indulge yourself NOT for: doing something you dislike
examples: He rarely indulged in sweets when he was dieting.
You can indulge yourself on holiday.

indulge.definition: to let someone have or do whatever they want, even if it is not good for them
indulge.note: typical: indulge a child/whim/desire NOT for: strict or sensible treatment
examples: The grandparents indulged the children with sweets and toys.
She indulged his every whim.

indulge.definition: to take part in an activity, especially an illegal or disapproved one
indulge.note: typical: indulge in crime/gossip/illegal activities NOT for: ordinary hobbies
examples: The gang indulged in petty crime.
Some students indulge in cheating during exams.

infer.definition: to form an opinion that something is probably true because of the information you have
infer.note: typical: infer sth from sth, infer that NOT for: guessing without evidence or stating a fact
examples: We can infer from the results that the plan failed.
Nothing can be inferred from one small example.

infiltrate.definition: to secretly join an organisation or enter a place in order to find out information or cause harm
infiltrate.note: typical: infiltrate a group/network/enemy territory NOT for: joining openly
examples: The journalist infiltrated the gang to write about its activities.
Rebel soldiers infiltrated the city at night.

infiltrate.definition: to secretly put people into an organisation or place in order to spy or cause harm
infiltrate.note: typical: infiltrate agents/spies into sth NOT for: hiring staff openly
examples: The police infiltrated an officer into the criminal group.
The enemy tried to infiltrate spies into the government.

infiltrate.definition: to gradually become part of something, used especially to show disapproval
infiltrate.note: typical: infiltrate schools/the media/politics NOT for: joining something by choice with approval
examples: Advertising has infiltrated almost every part of daily life.
Extreme ideas had slowly infiltrated the party.

infuse.definition: to fill someone or something with a particular feeling or quality (formal)
infuse.note: typical: be infused with hope/humour/energy NOT for: pouring a liquid into something
examples: Her paintings are infused with warmth and light.
The new coach infused the team with fresh energy.

infuse.definition: to leave tea or herbs in very hot water so that their flavour passes into it, or for this to happen
infuse.note: typical: infuse tea/herbs, let it infuse NOT for: boiling food hard or cooking it in oil
examples: Infuse the mint leaves in hot water for five minutes.
Let the tea infuse for a few minutes before you drink it.

inhabit.definition: to live in a particular place (used of animals or people)
inhabit.note: typical: inhabit an island/forest/region, be inhabited by sth NOT for: staying somewhere only for a short time
examples: Wild goats inhabit the steep mountains.
Only a few hundred people inhabit the island.

inhibit.definition: to prevent something from growing or developing well
inhibit.note: typical: inhibit growth/development/learning NOT for: stopping something completely
examples: Cold weather can inhibit the growth of plants.
A lack of money may inhibit the company's development.

inhibit.definition: to make someone feel too embarrassed or nervous to do or say what they want
inhibit.note: typical: inhibit sb from doing sth NOT for: physically stopping someone
examples: The camera in the room inhibited the children from speaking freely.
Fear of failure can inhibit people from trying new things.

instigate.definition: to make a process or action start, especially one connected with law or politics
instigate.note: typical: instigate reforms/an inquiry/legal action NOT for: simply taking part in something
examples: The new manager instigated a series of reforms.
The police instigated an inquiry into the accident.

instigate.definition: to persuade someone to do something bad or violent
instigate.note: typical: instigate violence/a riot/a revolt NOT for: encouraging good behaviour
examples: Leaders were accused of instigating the riots.
He instigated a quarrel between the two families.

instill.definition: to teach someone to think, behave or feel in a particular way over a period of time
instill.note: typical: instill confidence/discipline/values in/into sb NOT for: teaching facts or skills quickly
examples: Good teachers instill a love of reading in their pupils.
Parents try to instill good manners in their children.

intercept.definition: to stop someone or something that is going from one place to another before they get there
intercept.note: typical: intercept a message/ball/missile/call NOT for: stopping something for a long time or catching something after delivery
examples: Police intercepted the drugs at the border.
The defender intercepted the pass and ran forward.

interfere.definition: to get involved in a situation where you are not wanted or needed
interfere.note: typical: interfere in sth, interfere in other people's affairs NOT for: helping when someone asks you to
examples: I try not to interfere in my children's arguments.
Foreign governments should not interfere in the country's politics.

intimidate.definition: to frighten or threaten someone so that they do what you want
intimidate.note: typical: intimidate witnesses/voters/opponents NOT for: making someone slightly nervous
examples: The gang tried to intimidate the witnesses into silence.
He used threats to intimidate his neighbours.

intimidate.definition: to make someone feel worried and not confident
intimidate.note: typical: be intimidated by a person/place/task NOT for: threatening people on purpose
examples: The huge crowd intimidated the young singer.
The thought of speaking in public intimidates me.

intrigue.definition: to make someone very interested because something seems strange or mysterious
intrigue.note: typical: intrigue sb, be intrigued by sth NOT for: making someone bored or annoyed
examples: The old map intrigued the children.
Her strange behaviour intrigued everyone at the party.

inundate.definition: to receive so much of something that you cannot deal with it easily (usually passive)
inundate.note: typical: be inundated with requests/calls/letters/complaints NOT for: a small or easy amount of work
examples: After the advert, the shop was inundated with orders.
The office was inundated with calls after the broadcast.

inundate.definition: to cover an area with a large amount of water (formal)
inundate.note: typical: inundate fields/a valley/a town NOT for: a light shower or small spill
examples: The river burst its banks and inundated the village.
Heavy rain inundated the low-lying fields.

invoke.definition: to use a law or rule as the reason for doing something (formal)
invoke.note: typical: invoke a law/rule/right/clause NOT for: obeying a rule without mentioning it
examples: The company invoked a clause in the contract to cancel the deal.
The country threatened to invoke economic sanctions.

invoke.definition: to make a particular idea, image or feeling appear in people's minds
invoke.note: typical: invoke images/memories/the spirit of sth NOT for: describing something in detail
examples: The painting invokes images of the mountains in winter.
In his speech he invoked the memory of the founders.

invoke.definition: to call on a god, spirit or higher power for help (formal)
invoke.note: typical: invoke a god/spirit/the gods NOT for: asking an ordinary person for help
examples: The priest invoked the blessing of the gods.
They invoked the spirits of their ancestors during the ceremony.

jeopardise.definition: to risk losing or spoiling something important
jeopardise.note: typical: jeopardise a plan/job/peace process/health NOT for: simply damaging something unimportant
examples: Rude behaviour could jeopardise your chances of getting the job.
The strike may jeopardise the whole project.

kindle.definition: to make a fire start to burn, or to start burning
kindle.note: typical: kindle a fire/flames/the logs NOT for: starting a car engine
examples: He kindled a small fire with dry sticks.
The logs kindled quickly in the dry air.

kindle.definition: to make someone feel interested, excited or hopeful
kindle.note: typical: kindle interest/hope/a love of sth in sb NOT for: causing anger or fear
examples: Her teacher kindled a love of music in her.
The speech kindled new hope among the workers.

lament.definition: to express feelings of great sadness about something (written)
lament.note: typical: lament a death/loss/the passing of sth NOT for: mild disappointment
examples: The nation lamented the death of its leader.
Fans lamented the loss of the old stadium.

lament.definition: to express annoyance or disappointment about something you think is unfair or unsatisfactory
lament.note: typical: lament that, lament the lack/decline of sth NOT for: quietly accepting a situation
examples: He lamented that nobody had listened to his advice.
She lamented the lack of public interest in the project.

languish.definition: to be forced to stay in an unpleasant place or situation for a long time
languish.note: typical: languish in prison/jail/a camp NOT for: choosing to rest somewhere
examples: He languished in prison for ten years.
Hundreds of refugees languished in the camp.

languish.definition: to fail to improve, develop or succeed
languish.note: typical: languish at the bottom of a table, markets/shares languish NOT for: growing quickly or flourishing
examples: The housing market continued to languish.
The team languished at the bottom of the league.

leap.definition: to jump high into the air or a long way, or to jump over something
leap.note: typical: leap over/onto/from sth NOT for: small steps or slow movement
examples: The cat leapt onto the table.
She leapt over the fence and ran across the field.

leap.definition: to move very quickly and with a lot of energy
leap.note: typical: leap up/out of bed/to your feet NOT for: moving slowly or lazily
examples: He leapt out of bed when the alarm rang.
She leapt to her feet and started to shout.

leap.definition: to increase quickly by a large amount
leap.note: typical: prices/profits/numbers leap (to sth) NOT for: slow or small increases
examples: Profits leapt to a record level last year.
The price of oil leapt by ten per cent.

leap.definition: if your heart leaps, to feel a sudden surge of surprise, joy or excitement (literary)
leap.note: typical: your heart leaps NOT for: a physical heart problem
examples: Her heart leapt when she saw him at the station.
My heart leapt at the sound of her voice.

legislate.definition: to make a law about something
legislate.note: typical: legislate on/for/against sth NOT for: enforcing or obeying a law
examples: Parliament voted to legislate against smoking in public places.
The government promised to legislate on equal pay.

legislate.definition: to think about how something may affect your plans and prepare for it (legislate for sth)
legislate.note: typical: legislate for bad weather/problems/the unexpected NOT for: making laws
examples: You cannot legislate for every possible problem.
We tried to legislate for bad weather on the day.

liberate.definition: to free someone from feelings or conditions that make their life difficult or unhappy
liberate.note: typical: liberate sb from poverty/fear/housework NOT for: freeing animals from a cage
examples: Education can liberate people from poverty.
The new machine liberated her from hours of housework.

liberate.definition: to free prisoners, a city or a country from someone's control
liberate.note: typical: liberate a city/country/prisoners NOT for: simply opening a door or a box
examples: Allied armies liberated the city in 1944.
Soldiers liberated hundreds of prisoners from the camp.

lure.definition: to persuade someone to do something, especially something wrong or dangerous, by making it seem attractive
lure.note: typical: lure sb into/away/with sth NOT for: giving an honest invitation
examples: The advertisement lured many people into buying the product.
Computer games lure children away from their homework.

lure.definition: to attract customers, workers or money from another company or place
lure.note: typical: lure sb back/away from sth NOT for: forcing someone to move
examples: The bank offered high salaries to lure talented staff away.
The shop used low prices to lure customers back.

magnify.definition: to make something look bigger or sound louder, usually with special equipment
magnify.note: typical: magnify sth (with/by sth), a lens or screen magnifying an image NOT for: describing something that simply grows in number
examples: The microscope magnifies the cells two hundred times.
A small speaker magnifies the sound of his voice.

magnify.definition: to make something seem more important than it really is
magnify.note: typical: magnify a problem/risk/danger NOT for: accurately describing a serious situation
examples: The newspaper magnified a minor disagreement into a national scandal.
Fear can magnify even small problems.

magnify.definition: to make a bad situation much worse or more serious
magnify.note: typical: magnify the effects/damage (often passive) NOT for: improving a situation
examples: Poor planning magnified the effects of the storm.
The delay was magnified by a series of technical failures.

manifest.definition: to show a feeling, attitude or quality clearly
manifest.note: typical: manifest sth in/as/through sth (formal, often passive) NOT for: everyday casual talk about showing off
examples: The students manifested great interest in the project.
Her kindness is manifested in everything she does.

manifest.definition: to appear or become easy to see (said of a problem or sign)
manifest.note: typical: manifest itself NOT for: a person appearing at a place
examples: The disease first manifested itself as a mild cough.
His nervousness manifested itself in constant fidgeting.

marginalise.definition: to treat a person or group as unimportant and give them little power or attention
marginalise.note: typical: marginalise a group/minority/community (often passive) NOT for: reducing the size of a margin or border
examples: Many rural communities feel marginalised by the government.
The new policy risks marginalising older workers.

mediate.definition: to try to settle an argument between two people or groups by talking to both sides
mediate.note: typical: mediate between sb and sb, mediate in a dispute NOT for: taking one side in a quarrel
examples: A neutral judge mediated between the two companies.
The president offered to mediate the peace talks.

mediate.definition: to change the effect or influence of something, especially to make it less strong or harmful
mediate.note: typical: mediate the effect/influence of sth (formal or technical, often passive) NOT for: settling a conflict between people
examples: A healthy diet may mediate the effects of stress.
Education can mediate the influence of family background.

mesmerise.definition: to hold someone's attention so completely that they cannot look away or think of anything else
mesmerise.note: typical: be mesmerised by sb/sth (usually passive) NOT for: sending someone to sleep or boring them
examples: The audience was mesmerised by the dancer's performance.
The children sat mesmerised by the flickering fire.

migrate.definition: to travel regularly from one part of the world to another, as birds and animals do
migrate.note: typical: animals/birds/fish migrate (from/to a place) NOT for: a single trip made by one person on holiday
examples: Many birds migrate south before winter.
Whales migrate thousands of kilometres each year.

migrate.definition: to go and live in another area or country, usually to find work
migrate.note: typical: people migrate (from/to a place) NOT for: moving to a different house in the same town
examples: Thousands of young people migrate to the cities every year.
His grandparents migrated from Poland in the 1950s.

migrate.definition: to start using a different computer system, or to move data or software from one system to another
migrate.note: typical: migrate (sth) from/to a system NOT for: moving physical objects between rooms
examples: The company is migrating its email to a new server.
We migrated all our files to the cloud last month.

mimic.definition: to copy the way someone speaks or behaves, often to make people laugh
mimic.note: typical: mimic a voice/accent/gesture NOT for: copying a document or file
examples: He can mimic any teacher's voice perfectly.
The little girl mimicked her brother's walk.

mimic.definition: to behave or work in exactly the same way as something else
mimic.note: typical: mimic the action/behaviour/function of sth NOT for: politely following good advice
examples: The drug mimics the action of natural hormones.
The software mimics the way the human brain learns.

mimic.definition: to look or sound very like something else, as an animal or plant may
mimic.note: typical: an animal/plant/insect mimics sth NOT for: people dressing in similar clothes
examples: Some harmless insects mimic the colours of wasps.
The bird can mimic the sound of a telephone.

mitigate.definition: to make something less harmful, serious or unpleasant
mitigate.note: typical: mitigate the effects/risk/damage of sth (formal) NOT for: getting rid of a problem completely
examples: New walls were built to mitigate the effects of flooding.
The company took steps to mitigate the risk of data loss.

mobilise.definition: to encourage people to support something in an active way
mobilise.note: typical: mobilise support/opinion/voters NOT for: moving people physically to another place
examples: The charity mobilised thousands of volunteers.
She worked to mobilise public opinion against the road.

mobilise.definition: to start using the people or things you have in order to achieve something
mobilise.note: typical: mobilise resources/funds/forces NOT for: saving resources for later
examples: The government mobilised all its resources to deal with the crisis.
They failed to mobilise enough money for the project.

mobilise.definition: to prepare an army or country to fight a war
mobilise.note: typical: a country mobilises (its forces/army) NOT for: sending soldiers home
examples: The country mobilised its army after the invasion.
Troops were mobilised along the border.

mobilise.definition: to help part of the body to move more easily, as a therapist does
mobilise.note: typical: mobilise a joint/shoulder/patient (medical) NOT for: making a person sit still
examples: The physiotherapist mobilised the patient's stiff shoulder.
Gentle exercises help to mobilise the joints.

muster.definition: to gather enough courage, support or energy to do something, usually with difficulty
muster.note: typical: muster (up) courage/support/energy NOT for: gathering small physical objects
examples: He finally mustered the courage to speak to her.
The minister is trying to muster support for the plan.

muster.definition: to come together in a group, or to bring people together, especially soldiers
muster.note: typical: muster troops/an army/volunteers NOT for: a single person arriving alone
examples: The soldiers mustered in the square at dawn.
The king mustered an army to defend the city.
