neglect.definition: to fail to look after someone or something properly
neglect.note: typical: neglect a child/garden/building (often passive) NOT for: deliberately destroying something
examples: He neglected his garden for years.
The old house has been badly neglected.

neglect.definition: to pay too little attention to something
neglect.note: typical: neglect your duty/responsibilities/studies NOT for: paying careful attention
examples: Historians have neglected this period of history.
She was accused of neglecting her duties.

neglect.definition: to fail to do something, usually because you forgot or did not think it important
neglect.note: typical: neglect to do sth (formal) NOT for: refusing loudly to do something
examples: He neglected to mention that he was leaving.
They neglected to lock the door.

nurture.definition: to help a plan, idea, skill or feeling to develop
nurture.note: typical: nurture talent/an idea/a relationship (formal, often passive) NOT for: stopping something from growing
examples: The school nurtures young musical talent.
She nurtured a hope that she would return home.

nurture.definition: to feed and care for a child or plant while it is growing
nurture.note: typical: nurture a child/plant/seedling NOT for: looking after a sick adult in hospital
examples: The seedlings were nurtured in a warm greenhouse.
He was nurtured by loving grandparents.

obscure.definition: to make something difficult to know or understand
obscure.note: typical: obscure the truth/fact/issue NOT for: explaining something clearly
examples: Too much detail can obscure the main point.
Recent profits have obscured the company's deeper problems.

obscure.definition: to prevent something from being seen or heard clearly
obscure.note: typical: obscure a view/sun/sign (often passive) NOT for: making something brighter
examples: Thick fog obscured the road ahead.
The moon was obscured by clouds.

obstruct.definition: to block a road, passage or view so that nothing can pass or be seen
obstruct.note: typical: obstruct a road/path/view/entrance NOT for: clearing a path
examples: A broken-down lorry obstructed the road.
The tall hedge obstructs our view of the sea.

obstruct.definition: to prevent or delay something by making it difficult
obstruct.note: typical: obstruct progress/justice/the police NOT for: helping an official process
examples: Protesters tried to obstruct the building work.
He was charged with obstructing the police.

orchestrate.definition: to organise an event or plan carefully, often secretly
orchestrate.note: typical: orchestrate a campaign/attack/protest (often passive) NOT for: performing a task by yourself without planning
examples: The campaign was carefully orchestrated by his advisers.
Rebels orchestrated the attack from abroad.

orchestrate.definition: to arrange a piece of music so that an orchestra can play it
orchestrate.note: typical: orchestrate a piece/melody/score NOT for: conducting an orchestra on stage
examples: He orchestrated the piano piece for strings and brass.
The film score was orchestrated by a famous composer.

oust.definition: to force someone out of a position of power, usually to take their place
oust.note: typical: oust sb from sth (power/office/leadership) NOT for: politely asking someone to resign
examples: The generals ousted the president in a coup.
She was ousted from her job as chairwoman.

outperform.definition: to do better or be more successful than someone or something else
outperform.note: typical: outperform rivals/the market/competitors NOT for: doing worse than expected
examples: Our team outperformed all its rivals.
Small companies often outperform larger ones.

outweigh.definition: to be more important or valuable than something else
outweigh.note: typical: advantages/benefits outweigh disadvantages/risks NOT for: measuring the actual weight of an object
examples: The benefits of the plan outweigh the costs.
For her, the risks far outweighed the possible gains.

overhaul.definition: to repair or replace the necessary parts of a machine or system that is not working properly
overhaul.note: typical: overhaul an engine/machine/system NOT for: making a small quick repair
examples: A mechanic is overhauling the engine.
The railway signals were completely overhauled.

overhaul.definition: to change a system or method in order to improve it
overhaul.note: typical: overhaul a system/policy/process NOT for: making a tiny adjustment
examples: The government plans to overhaul the tax system.
The school overhauled its entire curriculum.

overshadow.definition: to make someone or something seem less important or impressive
overshadow.note: typical: overshadow sb's achievements/success (often passive) NOT for: giving praise to someone
examples: Her fame overshadowed her husband's achievements.
The team's earlier success was overshadowed by this defeat.

overshadow.definition: to make a time or event less enjoyable by causing sadness or worry
overshadow.note: typical: overshadow an event/occasion/period NOT for: adding to the happiness of an occasion
examples: The threat of war overshadowed the holidays.
His illness overshadowed the wedding.

overshadow.definition: to be much taller than a place and very close to it, so that it is in shadow
overshadow.note: typical: a tall building/mountain overshadows a place (often passive) NOT for: a small object casting a shadow
examples: The village is overshadowed by high mountains.
A huge tower overshadows the little garden.

overturn.definition: to turn upside down or fall over on its side
overturn.note: typical: overturn a chair/boat/car, a vehicle overturns NOT for: turning something gently around
examples: The waiter overturned a tray of glasses.
The lorry overturned on the icy road.

overturn.definition: to change a decision or result so that it becomes the opposite of what it was
overturn.note: typical: overturn a decision/verdict/ruling/conviction NOT for: confirming a decision
examples: The court overturned his conviction.
The committee overturned the earlier ban.

overturn.definition: to remove a government from power suddenly, especially by using violence
overturn.note: typical: overturn a government/regime NOT for: a normal change after an election
examples: The army overturned the government in a night.
Rebels hoped to overturn the regime.

penetrate.definition: to enter something and pass or spread through it, especially with difficulty
penetrate.note: typical: penetrate armour/walls/the skin/the forest; light/sound penetrates NOT for: walking through an open door
examples: Bullets can penetrate thin metal.
Sunlight barely penetrated the thick forest.

penetrate.definition: to start selling things in a new area or country, or to gain influence there
penetrate.note: typical: penetrate a market/country NOT for: simply visiting a country as a tourist
examples: The company has penetrated the Asian market.
Foreign brands slowly penetrated the local economy.

penetrate.definition: to succeed in being accepted into a group or organisation, sometimes to find out its secrets
penetrate.note: typical: penetrate a group/organisation/network NOT for: joining openly with no secret aim
examples: Spies penetrated the government's security service.
Police penetrated the criminal gang.

penetrate.definition: to succeed in understanding something, or (of an idea) to be understood with difficulty (formal)
penetrate.note: typical: penetrate a mystery/secret; an idea/message penetrates NOT for: understanding something that is easy
examples: Scientists are trying to penetrate the mysteries of the brain.
My warning did not seem to penetrate his mind.

penetrate.definition: to see into or through something when this is difficult
penetrate.note: typical: penetrate the darkness/gloom/fog NOT for: looking at something that is clearly visible
examples: Her eyes could not penetrate the darkness.
No torch could penetrate the thick fog.

perpetuate.definition: to make a situation or attitude, especially a bad one, continue for a long time
perpetuate.note: typical: perpetuate a myth/stereotype/inequality/cycle NOT for: ending a problem
examples: Such films perpetuate stereotypes about old people.
The system perpetuates inequality.

pinpoint.definition: to discover or explain exactly what the facts or the cause of a problem are
pinpoint.note: typical: pinpoint the cause/problem/reason NOT for: guessing roughly
examples: Engineers tried to pinpoint the cause of the fault.
It is hard to pinpoint exactly why sales fell.

pinpoint.definition: to find or show the exact position of something
pinpoint.note: typical: pinpoint a location/position/target NOT for: giving a rough direction
examples: Rescuers pinpointed the position of the missing boat.
The map pinpoints every village in the valley.

plague.definition: to cause pain, suffering or trouble to someone for a long time
plague.note: typical: be plagued by/with sth (often passive) NOT for: one short problem
examples: He was plagued by back pain for years.
Financial problems plagued the company.

plague.definition: to annoy someone by asking for something many times or asking many questions
plague.note: typical: plague sb with sth NOT for: a single polite question
examples: The children plagued her with questions.
Reporters plagued the actor for an interview.

plummet.definition: to suddenly and quickly decrease in value or amount
plummet.note: typical: prices/profits/sales/temperatures plummet NOT for: a slow or small fall
examples: Share prices plummeted after the news.
Temperatures plummeted overnight.

plummet.definition: to fall suddenly and quickly from a high place
plummet.note: typical: plummet to the ground/towards the earth NOT for: controlled flight
examples: The plane plummeted into the sea.
A rock plummeted down the cliff.

ponder.definition: to spend time thinking carefully about a problem, a difficult question or something that has happened (formal)
ponder.note: typical: ponder a question/problem; ponder on/over/about sth; ponder whether/how/what NOT for: a quick decision
examples: She pondered the offer for several days.
He pondered whether to accept the job.

postpone.definition: to change the date or time of a planned event to a later one
postpone.note: typical: postpone a meeting/match/trip/decision NOT for: cancelling something for good
examples: The match was postponed until Sunday.
They postponed the wedding because of illness.

precede.definition: to happen or exist before something else, or to come before it in a series (formal)
precede.note: typical: precede an event; be preceded by sth NOT for: coming after something
examples: A short speech preceded the dinner.
The earthquake was preceded by small tremors.

precede.definition: to go somewhere before someone else
precede.note: typical: precede sb into/down/along sth NOT for: following behind someone
examples: The guide preceded us along the path.
A security guard preceded the president into the hall.

prescribe.definition: to say what medicine or treatment a sick person should have
prescribe.note: typical: prescribe sb sth, prescribe sth for sth NOT for: buying medicine yourself
examples: The doctor prescribed antibiotics for his infection.
She was prescribed a strong painkiller.

prescribe.definition: to state officially what should be done in a particular situation (formal)
prescribe.note: typical: prescribe a punishment/rule/procedure; the law prescribes sth NOT for: suggesting an unofficial idea
examples: The law prescribes a heavy fine for this offence.
The rules prescribe how the form must be completed.

abscond.definition: to escape from a place where you are not allowed to leave, such as a prison or home
abscond.note: typical: abscond from prison/a home NOT for: leaving openly with permission
examples: The boy absconded from the children's home.
A prisoner absconded during the transfer.

abscond.definition: to leave secretly while taking something that does not belong to you
abscond.note: typical: abscond with the money/funds NOT for: leaving on holiday
examples: The clerk absconded with the company's funds.
He absconded with his partner's savings.

annihilate.definition: to destroy something or someone completely
annihilate.note: typical: annihilate a city/army/enemy NOT for: small damage
examples: The bomb could annihilate an entire city.
The army was annihilated in one battle.

annihilate.definition: to defeat someone easily and completely in a game or competition
annihilate.note: typical: annihilate an opponent/rival NOT for: a narrow win
examples: The champion annihilated his opponent in the first round.
Our team annihilated their rivals 8-0.

arbitrate.definition: to officially judge how an argument between two opposing sides should be settled
arbitrate.note: typical: arbitrate between/in sth NOT for: taking sides
examples: A committee arbitrated between the union and the company.
The court will arbitrate in the dispute.

beckon.definition: to make a signal with your hand to show someone you want them to come or follow
beckon.note: typical: beckon (to) sb, beckon sb over/forward NOT for: waving goodbye
examples: She beckoned the waiter over.
He beckoned to us to follow him.

beckon.definition: to appear so attractive that you want to have it (of a place or opportunity)
beckon.note: typical: a career/city/opportunity beckons NOT for: something unattractive
examples: The bright lights of the city beckoned.
A new career in television beckoned.

beckon.definition: to be likely to happen to someone in the future
beckon.note: typical: something beckons for sb NOT for: past events
examples: Success beckons for the young player.
A long break beckons for the team.

berate.definition: to speak angrily to someone because they have done something wrong (formal)
berate.note: typical: berate sb for sth NOT for: gentle advice
examples: The manager berated them for being late.
She berated herself for the mistake.

besiege.definition: to surround a city or castle with military force until the people inside give it up
besiege.note: typical: besiege a city/castle/fortress NOT for: fighting in open land
examples: Rebels besieged the palace for weeks.
The army besieged the town.

besiege.definition: to surround someone with people, worries or thoughts (often passive)
besiege.note: typical: be besieged by reporters/doubts NOT for: a friendly visit
examples: The singer was besieged by fans.
He was besieged by doubts.

besiege.definition: to receive a very large number of letters, requests or calls
besiege.note: typical: be besieged with requests/calls/letters NOT for: a few messages
examples: The office was besieged with calls.
The charity was besieged with offers of help.

bewilder.definition: to confuse someone completely, so that they do not understand (often passive)
bewilder.note: typical: bewilder sb, be bewildered by sth NOT for: explaining clearly
examples: The complicated rules bewildered the visitors.
I was bewildered by his sudden anger.

brandish.definition: to wave something around in a threatening or showy way, especially a weapon
brandish.note: typical: brandish a knife/gun/sword NOT for: carrying something quietly
examples: A man brandished a knife.
She brandished her ticket at the guard.

commandeer.definition: to take someone else's property for your own use, especially in a war or emergency
commandeer.note: typical: commandeer a car/building/vehicle NOT for: buying or renting something
examples: The army commandeered several trucks.
Soldiers commandeered the hotel.

compartmentalise.definition: to divide something into separate areas or groups
compartmentalise.note: typical: compartmentalise your life/work/knowledge NOT for: mixing things together
examples: He tries to compartmentalise his work and family life.
The school compartmentalises subjects.

cower.definition: to bend low or move back because you are frightened
cower.note: typical: cower in a corner/behind sth/against a wall NOT for: standing proudly
examples: The dog cowered under the table during the storm.
The children cowered behind their mother.

dissipate.definition: to gradually become weaker or less before disappearing completely, or to make something do this (formal)
dissipate.note: typical: anger/fear/smoke/heat dissipates NOT for: a sudden explosion
examples: His anger slowly dissipated.
The morning mist dissipated in the sun.

dissipate.definition: to waste something valuable such as time, money or energy
dissipate.note: typical: dissipate a fortune/energy/resources NOT for: saving or investing carefully
examples: He dissipated his inheritance within a few years.
Don't dissipate your energy on small tasks.

divulge.definition: to reveal information that should be secret (formal)
divulge.note: typical: divulge a secret/name/details NOT for: telling something that is already public
examples: The bank refused to divulge its client's name.
I cannot divulge what he told me.

ebb.definition: if the tide ebbs, it flows away from the shore
ebb.note: typical: the tide ebbs NOT for: a rising tide
examples: The tide began to ebb at noon.
Boats were left on the sand as the sea ebbed.

ebb.definition: to gradually become weaker or less (usually ebb away)
ebb.note: typical: enthusiasm/strength/life ebbs (away) NOT for: a sudden change
examples: Her strength slowly ebbed away.
Support for the plan began to ebb.

elope.definition: to leave home secretly in order to get married
elope.note: typical: elope with sb NOT for: planning a big public wedding
examples: The couple eloped because their parents disapproved.
She eloped with her childhood friend.

embolden.note: typical: be emboldened by sth/to do sth NOT for: making someone afraid
examples: Emboldened by her smile, he spoke to her.
Early success emboldened the team to take more risks.

enunciate.definition: to pronounce words clearly and carefully
enunciate.note: typical: enunciate each word/syllable NOT for: mumbling
examples: The teacher asked us to enunciate every word.
She enunciated slowly so that everyone could understand.

enunciate.definition: to express an idea clearly and exactly (formal)
enunciate.note: typical: enunciate a principle/theory/policy NOT for: hinting vaguely
examples: The president enunciated a new policy.
He enunciated the basic principles of the theory.

garble.definition: to mix up or confuse a message or piece of information so that it is hard to understand
garble.note: typical: garble a message/statement/story (often passive) NOT for: delivering a message clearly
examples: The bad connection garbled his message.
The report garbled the facts of the story.

goad.definition: to make someone do something by annoying or encouraging them until they do it
goad.note: typical: goad sb into (doing) sth, goad sb on NOT for: gently asking for help
examples: His friends goaded him into accepting the dare.
The crowd goaded the player on with insults.

goad.definition: to push animals ahead of you with a sharp stick
goad.note: typical: goad cattle/oxen NOT for: feeding animals
examples: The farmer goaded the oxen along the road.
He goaded the cattle into the pen.

hearten.definition: to make someone feel happier and more hopeful (usually passive)
hearten.note: typical: be heartened by sth NOT for: making someone sad
examples: We were heartened by the good news.
She was heartened by their support.

immobilise.definition: to prevent someone or something from moving
immobilise.note: typical: immobilise a limb/patient/vehicle NOT for: helping someone to move
examples: The doctor immobilised his broken leg.
The injured man was immobilised on a stretcher.

immobilise.note: typical: immobilise a car/engine/system NOT for: repairing a machine
examples: The alarm immobilises the engine.
A software fault immobilised the whole network.

interlock.definition: if two or more things interlock, they fit firmly together
interlock.note: typical: pieces/parts/gears interlock NOT for: things that stay apart
examples: The pieces of the puzzle interlock.
The two gears interlock perfectly.

invigorate.definition: to make someone feel healthier, stronger and full of energy
invigorate.note: typical: an invigorating walk/swim; be invigorated NOT for: tiring someone out
examples: A cold shower always invigorates me.
He felt invigorated after the swim.

invigorate.definition: to make the people in a group or organisation excited again so that they want to succeed (usually passive)
invigorate.note: typical: invigorate a team/economy/church/movement NOT for: making people lose interest
examples: The new manager invigorated the whole department.
The economy was invigorated by new investment.

mystify.definition: to be so strange or confusing that someone cannot understand or explain it
mystify.note: typical: be mystified by sth NOT for: explaining clearly
examples: Her sudden disappearance mystified her friends.
The strange noises mystified the scientists.

can.definition: to be able to do something, or to know how to do it
can.note: typical: can + base verb; can/can't NOT for: things that are impossible
examples: She can speak three languages.
Even a small computer can store a lot of information.

can.definition: used to ask someone to do something or give you something (spoken)
can.note: typical: Can you/I ...? NOT for: very formal requests
examples: Can you pass me the salt, please?
Can I have a glass of water?

can.definition: to be allowed to do something, or to have the right or power to do it
can.note: typical: can/can't + verb NOT for: things that are not allowed
examples: You can park here after six o'clock.
Any citizen can vote in this election.

can.definition: used to say that something is possible
can.note: typical: can be + past participle NOT for: things that are certain
examples: A solution can be found.
The boxes can be stored flat.

can.definition: used with verbs of perception and thinking, to say that someone sees, hears or understands something
can.note: typical: can see/hear/smell/feel/understand/remember NOT for: continuous forms like is seeing
examples: I can hear music from next door.
He can't remember where he parked.

can.definition: used in negatives to say that you do not believe something is true
can.note: typical: can't be/can't have been NOT for: positive guesses
examples: This can't be the right road.
She can't be older than twenty.

can.definition: used in questions and negatives to say someone should not do something
can.note: typical: can't expect/can't go on NOT for: things that are allowed
examples: You can't expect people to work for nothing.
We can't go on living like this.

can.definition: used when you are surprised or angry (spoken)
can.note: typical: You can't be serious!; How can you ...? NOT for: calm statements
examples: You can't be serious!
How can you be so careless?

can.definition: used to say what sometimes happens or how someone sometimes behaves
can.note: typical: can be + adjective NOT for: things that never change
examples: It can be very cold here at night.
Peter can be really annoying.

can.definition: used to tell someone in an angry way to do something (spoken)
can.note: typical: you can + verb (angry command) NOT for: polite requests
examples: You can stop shouting right now.
If you don't like it, you can leave.

could.definition: used as the past tense of can to say what someone was able to do or allowed to do in the past
could.note: typical: could + base verb NOT for: single past actions that actually happened (use was able to)
examples: By the age of five, she could read.
We couldn't get tickets because they were sold out.

could.definition: used to say that something is possible or might happen, or (with have) was possible but did not happen
could.note: typical: could + verb / could have + past participle NOT for: things that are certain
examples: It could be weeks before we get a reply.
You could have been killed.

could.definition: used to emphasise strong feelings by saying what you feel like doing (spoken)
could.note: typical: I could scream/kill/cry NOT for: real plans to act
examples: I was so angry I could scream.
I was so relieved I could have kissed them all.

could.definition: used to make a polite request (spoken)
could.note: typical: Could you/I ...? NOT for: orders
examples: Could you help me with these boxes?
Could I borrow your pen?

could.note: typical: You could + verb NOT for: firm orders
examples: You could ask your doctor for advice.
We could meet next week.

could.definition: used to show you are annoyed about someone's behaviour (spoken)
could.note: typical: You could have told me; How could you ...? NOT for: friendly suggestions
examples: You could have told me you were late!
How could you be so careless?

may.definition: used to say there is a possibility that something will happen or is true, but it is not certain
may.note: typical: may + base verb / may have + past participle NOT for: things that are certain
examples: I may be late, so don't wait for me.
They may have called while you were out.

may.definition: used to say that something can be done in a particular way
may.note: typical: may be + past participle (formal) NOT for: things that are impossible
examples: The problem may be solved in several ways.
The data may be used for research.

may.definition: used to say that someone is allowed to do something, or to ask politely for permission
may.note: typical: may I/we ...? (formal) NOT for: casual talk with friends
examples: You may go now.
May I come in?

may.definition: used to say, ask or suggest something politely (spoken, formal)
may.note: typical: if I may say so; may I ask/suggest NOT for: rude or blunt comments
examples: May I suggest that you think again?
Who, may I ask, is she?

may.definition: used to say that although one thing is true, something very different is also true
may.note: typical: may + adj, but ...; strange as it may seem NOT for: things that are not contrasted
examples: I may be slow, but I make few mistakes.
Strange as it may seem, I enjoyed the work.

may.definition: used to express a wish or hope (formal)
may.note: typical: may sb/sth + verb NOT for: plain facts about the future
examples: May they rest in peace.
Long may it continue!

may.definition: used after 'so that' or 'in order that' to show purpose (formal)
may.note: typical: so that sb may + verb NOT for: everyday spoken English
examples: He saved money so that his children may study abroad.
She worked hard in order that her family may live well.

might.definition: used to say there is a possibility that something will happen or is true, or that it was possible but did not happen
might.note: typical: might + base verb / might have + past participle NOT for: things that are certain
examples: I might be a few minutes late.
We might have been killed.

might.definition: used to suggest politely what someone should do
might.note: typical: you might + verb NOT for: strict orders
examples: You might try the Internet.
It might be a good idea to move the plants.

might.definition: used to ask politely for permission, or to report that someone asked for permission
might.note: typical: might I ...?; asked if he might ... NOT for: casual requests among friends
examples: Might I borrow your pen?
He asked if he might come in.

might.definition: used when you are annoyed because someone has not done something they should do
might.note: typical: you might at least + verb NOT for: friendly suggestions
examples: You might at least say thank you.
They might have cleaned up before they left.

must.definition: to have to do something because it is necessary or important, or because of a law or order
must.note: typical: must + base verb NOT for: past obligations (use had to)
examples: All passengers must wear seat belts.
Accidents must be reported at once.

must.definition: used in negatives to say that something should not happen, because of a rule or the situation
must.note: typical: mustn't/must not + verb NOT for: things that are merely unnecessary (use don't have to)
examples: You mustn't talk to your mother like that.
This book must not be removed from the library.

must.definition: used to say you think something is very likely true or very likely happened
must.note: typical: must be / must have + past participle NOT for: things that are only slightly possible
examples: Sam must be nearly ninety now.
You must have been really upset.

must.definition: used to suggest someone should do something, especially because you think they will enjoy it (spoken, especially British)
must.note: typical: You must come/see/try ... NOT for: strict orders
examples: You must come and stay with us.
We must do this again.

must.definition: used to say that you intend or want to do something (spoken, especially British)
must.note: typical: I must + verb NOT for: plans for other people
examples: I must call her tonight.
I must go now.

must.definition: used to emphasise what you are saying (spoken)
must.note: typical: I must admit/say/confess NOT for: obligations
examples: I must say, it gave me quite a shock.
I must admit I was nervous.

must.definition: used to tell someone their behaviour upsets or annoys you (spoken)
must.note: typical: (Why) must you ...? NOT for: polite requests
examples: Must you spoil everything?
Why must you always be so rude?

ought to.definition: used to say that someone should do something because it is the best or most sensible thing to do
ought to.note: typical: ought to + base verb; ought to have + past participle NOT for: things that are certain or already done
examples: You really ought to quit smoking.
You ought to have been studying, not playing games.

ought to.definition: used to make a suggestion about something you think is a good idea, especially in a social situation
ought to.note: typical: We/You ought to ... NOT for: strict orders
examples: We ought to get together soon.
You ought to meet him; he is really nice.

ought to.definition: used to say that someone should do something or something should happen because it is morally right or fair
ought to.note: typical: ought (not) to + verb NOT for: things that are merely convenient
examples: You ought to be ashamed of yourself.
The courts ought to treat everyone in exactly the same way.

ought to.definition: used to say that you think something will probably happen or is probably true
ought to.note: typical: ought to be/win/arrive NOT for: things you are sure about
examples: He left two hours ago, so he ought to be there by now.
They ought to win; they have trained hard.

shall.definition: used to make a suggestion or ask what the other person wants (spoken)
shall.note: typical: Shall I/we ...? NOT for: statements
examples: Shall I open the window?
What shall we have for dinner?

shall.definition: used to say what you will do in the future (formal, especially British)
shall.note: typical: I/we shall + base verb NOT for: other people's future actions in everyday talk
examples: We shall be away next week.
I shall have finished by Friday.

shall.definition: used in official documents to state an order, law or promise (formal)
shall.note: typical: shall + base verb in contracts and rules NOT for: casual speech
examples: All payments shall be made in cash.
The tenant shall pay the rent monthly.

should.definition: used to say what is the right or sensible thing to do, or what would have been right but was not done
should.note: typical: should + base verb / should have + past participle NOT for: things that are impossible or already certain
examples: You should apologise to her.
They should have called the police.

should.definition: used to give or ask for advice
should.note: typical: I should ... if I were you; What should I do? NOT for: orders with no choice
examples: What should I do about this letter?
You should see a doctor about that cough.

should.definition: used to say that you expect something to happen or be true, or that it was expected but did not happen
should.note: typical: should be/should have + past participle NOT for: things you are sure about
examples: It should be sunny tomorrow.
It was an easy test and he should have passed.

should.definition: used to say what is the correct amount or the correct way of doing something
should.note: typical: should + verb in rules and descriptions NOT for: personal opinions about what is nice
examples: Every sentence should start with a capital letter.
There should be twelve tickets, not ten.

should.definition: used in official orders and instructions (formal)
should.note: typical: Passengers/Applicants should + verb NOT for: friendly chat
examples: Passengers should proceed to Gate 12.
Visitors should report to reception.

should.definition: used in a clause beginning with 'that' after certain adjectives and verbs (especially British)
should.note: typical: It is essential/strange that ... should ... NOT for: everyday plain statements
examples: It is strange that you should say that.
They demanded that there should be an inquiry.

should.definition: used to talk about something that may possibly happen or be true
should.note: typical: in case ... should; Should you need ..., ... NOT for: things that are certain
examples: He took a map in case anything should go wrong.
Should you need any help, please phone me.

should.definition: used after I or we to say what you would do if something happened (formal, especially British)
should.note: typical: I/we should + verb NOT for: strong advice to other people
examples: If anyone treated me like that, I should complain.
I should be surprised if many people voted for him.

should.definition: used to ask politely for something, offer to do something or say that you want something (formal, especially British)
should.note: typical: I should like/be grateful NOT for: casual requests among friends
examples: I should be grateful if you could send me the details.
I should like a long cool drink.

will.definition: used to say what is going to happen in the future
will.note: typical: will + base verb; will have + past participle NOT for: things that happened in the past
examples: I will call you tomorrow.
The shop will be closed on Monday.

will.definition: used to say that someone is willing or ready to do something, or (won't) that they refuse
will.note: typical: will/won't + verb NOT for: strong force or necessity
examples: Dr Weir will see you now.
The baby won't eat anything.

will.definition: used to ask someone to do something (spoken)
will.note: typical: Will you ...?; ..., will you? NOT for: formal offers
examples: Will you phone me later?
Shut the door, will you?

will.definition: used to say what always happens in a particular situation or is generally true
will.note: typical: will + verb (general truth) NOT for: single future events
examples: Oil will float on water.
Accidents will happen.

will.definition: used like 'can' to show what is possible
will.note: typical: will + verb (capacity) NOT for: unlikely situations
examples: This car will hold five people comfortably.
The hall will seat three hundred.

will.definition: used to say that you think something is true
will.note: typical: will be (assumption) NOT for: things you doubt
examples: That will be Tim coming home now.
As you will have noticed, there are some gaps.

will.definition: used to give an order or state a rule (spoken)
will.note: typical: You will + verb; Will you ...! NOT for: polite requests
examples: Will you be quiet!
Every employee will carry an identity card at all times.

will.definition: used to offer something to someone or invite them to do something (spoken)
will.note: typical: Will you have ...?; Won't you ...? NOT for: requests for help
examples: Will you have some more tea?
Won't you sit down?

will.definition: to try to make something happen by thinking about it very hard
will.note: typical: will sb to do sth NOT for: real physical effort
examples: She willed herself not to cry.
He willed the car to start.

will.definition: to officially give something you own to someone after you die
will.note: typical: will sth to sb NOT for: giving a gift while alive
examples: He willed his house to his daughter.
She willed her paintings to the museum.

would.definition: used to say what someone intended to do or what was expected to happen (as seen from the past)
would.note: typical: said/knew (that) ... would NOT for: things said about the present
examples: They said they would meet us at the station.
She knew it would be a hard day.

would.definition: used for the result of a possible, imagined or unreal situation, including things that did not happen
would.note: typical: would + verb / would have + past participle NOT for: real facts about the present
examples: What would you do if you won a million pounds?
I would have phoned you, but there wasn't time.

would.definition: used to say that something happened often or regularly in the past
would.note: typical: would often/always + verb NOT for: one single past event
examples: On summer evenings they would sit in the garden.
He would often take a nap after lunch.

would.definition: used to ask someone politely to do something (spoken)
would.note: typical: Would you ...? Would you mind ...? NOT for: orders
examples: Would you shut the window, please?
Would you mind waiting outside?

would.definition: used to offer something or invite someone politely (spoken)
would.note: typical: Would you like ...? NOT for: impolite offers
examples: Would you like a coffee?
Would you be interested in coming with us?

would.definition: used to say that someone wants something or wants to do something (spoken)
would.note: typical: would like/love/prefer/hate; would rather NOT for: plain facts about what someone actually does
examples: I'd love a coffee.
My parents would like to meet you.

would.definition: used after 'so that' to show that someone was trying to make something happen or to stop it
would.note: typical: so that ... would/wouldn't NOT for: present-tense purposes
examples: We packed the books in boxes so that they wouldn't get damaged.
She left early so that she would not miss the train.

would.definition: used in the negative to say that someone refused to do something, or that something would not work
would.note: typical: wouldn't + verb NOT for: a future refusal
examples: He wouldn't give us any money.
The door wouldn't open, however hard she pushed.

would.definition: used when giving or asking for advice (spoken)
would.note: typical: I would ... if I were you NOT for: strict orders
examples: I'd try to get there early if you can.
What would you do if you were in my position?

would.definition: used to give your opinion when you are not very sure (spoken)
would.note: typical: I would think/imagine/say NOT for: things you are certain about
examples: I would think he'd be happier in a different school.
I would imagine it cost a lot.

would.definition: used to say that an action is typical or expected, usually to show disapproval (spoken)
would.note: typical: You would ...! She would say that NOT for: pleasant surprises
examples: You would go and spoil it, wouldn't you!
She insists she was innocent, but she would say that.
